News.title: Rosie O’Donnell apologizes to Wynonna Judd over Trump assumption
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Rosie O’Donnell has apologized to longtime friend Wynonna Judd after wrongly assuming she supports Donald Trump.

The former TV host, 64, said on a podcast in August that Judd, 62, is the only Trump supporter that she keeps in touch with amid her public feud with the president. However, the country legend pushed back on O’Donnell’s remarks in a recent interview with People, in which she said the comment was a “complete assumption.”

O’Donnell publicly apologized in an Instagram post Wednesday, writing: “I was wrong to assume Wy was a Trump supporter just because she performed at marlargo - but as she told me she has sung for seven presidents on both sides of the aisle. My apologies here publicly (as I first made them privately) #friendship.”

She then encouraged her followers to go see the “I Saw the Light” singer in concert, saying, “she’s touring her new album now - go see her SING like no one else on earth.”

Judd performed at Trump’s Florida Mar-a-Lago club in 2023, but the president was not in attendance at the time.

Rosie O'Donnell mistakenly pegged Wynonna Judd as a Trump supporter ( Getty Images )

O’Donnell is one of Trump’s most vocal critics and has even credited him as part of the reason why she left the U.S. to move to Ireland.

On The Tangle podcast in August, O’Donnell said: “Now, I am friends with Wynonna Judd, who I love very much, and I’ve known her for many, many years. And she is a supporter of Trump. And somehow, we never bring it up. I give her a grace in a way.

“She’s had so much in her life... And I really love her, and I care about her, and, for some reason, I’m able to put that aside when we interact.”

Judd told People: “I’ve never spoken to [O’Donnell] about politics in my life. She doesn’t know anything about my stuff. I’m an independent.”

She went on to tell the magazine, “I don’t know where it came [from]. It’s complete assumption,” she said. “I heard it and I went, ‘What the…?’ I don’t ever remember talking to her about this, so she’s just assuming.’ I just don’t want drama. So if there’s going to be drama [about it], I’m like, ‘Oh for crap’s sake, there’s so much going on right now in the world. Can we just love each other?’”

News.title: Six-year-old curses at cops after shooting teacher in the chest at elementary school
News.content:
A six-year-old repeatedly cursed at police officers after shooting his teacher in the chest at a Virginia elementary school, newly unsealed bodycam footage revealed.

Teacher Abby Zwerner was shot in the chest by the child at Richneck Elementary School in Newport News, Virginia, in January 2023. She survived and later won a $10m suit after jurors found warnings about the child having a gun were ignored.

In the footage, reading specialist Amy Kovac is seen retraining the boy who curses at officers, offers to fight them and admits to stealing the gun from his mother.

News.title: Scientists discover unique ‘phoenix’ planet that was born from a dying star
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Astronomers believe they have found a planet unlike any previously seen – and it is made up of the pieces of a dying sun.

They believe that it is the first time that we have ever seen a “second-generation” planet of this kind: a world made up of pieces of the dead star that it now orbits.

"Second-generation planets are worlds that form out of the material a star casts off as it dies,” said Jamie Williams, a PhD student at the University of Warwick, who led the research.

“They're incredibly rare, and finding one around a white dwarf was completely unexpected. It's a bit like finding a planet that has risen from the ashes of the very star it once orbited."

Astronomers have spotted possible “reborn” worlds of this kind around the intense stars known as pulsars before. But it is the first time that one has been seen around a white dwarf – and, since those dead stars are much more common in the universe, it suggests there might be more of those reborn worlds around than we have previously thought.

White dwarfs are the collapsed cores that are left behind when a star runs out of fuel. They pull in material from panels that are nearby, and leave behind a chemical signature that astronomers can use to understand the planets that are in orbit around them.

Artists impression of the second-generation planet orbiting HS 0209+0832, the first such planet to be found orbiting a white dwarf ( Snehalata Sahu/University of Warwick )

In the new research, scientists looked at a white dwarf named HS 0209+0832. As they did, they found an unusual chemical signature, including vast amounts of a material called niobium that is created as a star dies, but has not been found in a white dwarf before.

Astronomers believe that the signal is happening because the white dwarf is feeding off a newly formed giant planet that is nearby. And that giant planet was itself made out of pieces left behind as the star died and became a white dwarf, they said.

That finding gained further credence after researchers used data from Nasa’s TESS telescope. That showed a faint signal coming from the planet that repeats every 4.4 days, which would bee explained by a Jupiter-sized planet that was orbiting closely around the white dwarf.

Given it is so close to the star, material from the planet’s outer atmosphere is likely boiling away because of the radiation from its dead sun, the researchers suggest. As that escaped material hits the white dwarf’s surface, it produces the unusual chemical signature.

If it is confirmed, the planet would not only be the first ever planet of this kind ever seen. It would also allow for a new way to find more of them, by looking for the same chemical signature in the light of other dead stars.

It might also represent another opportunity in the search for habitable worlds and the alien life that might live on them. A better understanding of how planets of this kind form will help us understand whether planets around white dwarfs are habitable – and planets around white dwarfs are relatively easy to spot.

The work is reported in a new paper, ‘1 Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf’, published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

In the same issue, a separate study looked at other kinds of dwarf stars. Researchers found a binary system in which a brown dwarf and red dwarf orbit around each other – and observations and modelling suggests that material is flowing from the brown dwarf onto the red dwarf, a process that has also never been seen before.

That work is reported in a separate paper, ‘Stable mass transfer from a substellar object onto an M dwarf’, published in the same journal.

News.title: US military planes worth up to $3.3 billion now lost or damaged in Iran war, Congress report says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The U.S. military has seen 81 fixed-wing or rotary-wing aircraft worth as much as $3.3 billion damaged or destroyed in President Donald Trump’s war with Iran so far, according to a Congressional Research Service report.

Trump launched his Operation Epic Fury airstrikes against Tehran, in partnership with Israel, on February 28, since when it has seen airplanes, helicopters and drones hit in retaliatory strikes.

The total cited includes a costly F-35A fighter jet and a four-engine E-3 Sentry among the casualties, while MQ-9 Reaper drones, used for surveillance and search-and-rescue operations, account for more than half of the losses.

Based on figures from the Congressional Budget Office, the report places the total cost of the destruction at between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, depending on whether or not the Department of Defense ultimately moves to replace the lost assets.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump’s war in Iran has seen 81 U.S. aircraft damaged or destroyed, including one F-35A fighter jet (file photo) ( AFP/Getty )

Some of the aircraft included in the count have been repaired and returned to service, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets that sustained only light damage when Iran struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan last month.

The total cost of the Iran conflict is more difficult to calculate but, one month into the war, analysts predicted that the U.S. was burning through $500 million a day on it. The DOD inspector general more recently estimated the price tag as $33.4 billion from its first day until June 30.

CNN now cites sources who put the overall cost even higher at $45 billion, that figure excluding the cost of infrastructure damage to U.S. military bases in the Gulf targeted by Iran in its retaliatory strikes.

In addition to the damage done to its own assets and those of its regional allies, the war has also taken the lives of 19 American soldiers and seen hundreds more injured.

open image in gallery A E-3 Sentry like the one pictured is also among the aerial casualties of the war (file photo) ( AFP/Getty )

Meanwhile, the blockading of the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway through which 20 percent of global oil shipments pass, has driven up gas prices for consumers, intensifying the affordability crisis at home.

In his latest comments on the conflict, Trump has said his Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff is making progress in negotiations with Tehran but suggested that reaching a deal is not his preferred outcome.

“I think the deal isn’t really something that I want to do, but they’re willing to offer us anything to stop,” the president told his supporters Wednesday at a pre-midterms rally in San Antonio, Texas.

Trump and his national security team have discussed the possibility of restarting large-scale US military operations in Iran in the coming weeks, according to NBC News, including potential strikes ahead of next month’s elections.

News.title: Schoolgirl walked into classroom and told teacher ‘Sir, I’ve been stabbed’ after attack, court hears
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A teenage girl described running and telling a teacher “Sir, I’ve been stabbed” after she was knifed in the back at her school, a court heard.

A boy, who was aged 15 at the time, is on trial at King’s Lynn Crown Court accused of her attempted murder at Thorpe St Andrew School near Norwich on 11 March.

The girl, then aged 15, told police in a video-recorded interview played to jurors on Thursday that she had seen a masked person dressed “head to toe in black, no school uniform on whatsoever”.

She said she turned away and it “felt like he touched me on the shoulder, then it felt like he punched me”.

She said she “didn’t know I was stabbed at this point” but she “started running”.

She said the boy, who is now aged 16 and cannot be identified for legal reasons, did not say anything to her and she did not recognise him.

The girl described struggling to open a door, adding she was “struggling because everything was going numb and feeling weak”.

open image in gallery A boy, who was aged 15 at the time, is on trial at King’s Lynn Crown Court accused of her attempted murder at Thorpe St Andrew School near Norwich on 11 March ( PA Wire )

The girl said she went into a classroom and “I went ‘Sir, I’ve been stabbed’”.

She said the school lockdown bell went off and school staff gave first aid.

She said that once she had opened the door “I felt sharp pain shooting through my back, I went like that and it was blood all over my hands”.

She said in the interview that was carried out days after the incident: “I don’t think it’s hit me properly yet.

“It’s just a bit of a shock.”

Asked if she had had any issues with anyone at school, she replied: “No.”

She said that when she first saw the person dressed in black, “he had his hands in his pockets and he was just standing there”.

She said he was wearing a black mask and had his hood “over his forehead”.

She said she had looked at him and didn’t “think much of it” but when she turned away she was attacked.

open image in gallery Police attended Thorpe St Andrew School after a teenage girl was stabbed ( PA Wire )

“It felt like he punched me,” she said.

“I thought he was about to keep throwing punches.”

Stephen Rose KC, defending, asked the girl, who came to court to give evidence, whether she had had any issues with the boy and she said she had not.

She wiped tears from her eyes and asked for a break during her evidence.

Christopher Paxton KC, opening the prosecution case, said the boy had written notes including about his “hatred for women” and had an interest in serial killers.

He said that one note, pinned up in the boy’s bedroom, said: “My barren world… Hello to all readers out there in the UK and perhaps even the world.

open image in gallery Stephen Rose KC, defending, asked the girl, who came to court to give evidence, whether she had had any issues with the boy and she said she had not ( PA )

“If you’re reading this, I am either dead or in custody.

“I imagine the police will be the first to read this and seize it as evidence, so I will make something very clear.

“I made this decision to do so on my own.

“Nobody told me to. Just me.

“Nobody knew I wanted to do this. Not a single soul.”

In another note, Mr Paxton said the boy wrote: “My whole life I’ve felt an attraction to violence.

“I don’t know the reason. My brain clicks at the thought of chaos. Of blood. Of murder.”

The note continued: “I’ve seen killers being admired. I want admiration.”

Mr Paxton told jurors: “We the prosecution say his intention is made plain not just by those moments of the stabbing but made plain by his notes and his obsession with killing and being fuelled by hatred.”

The boy denies attempted murder and the trial continues.

News.title: What you should know before taking melatonin to help you sleep
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Whether you’re struggling with jet lag, are a shift worker who sleeps during the day, or someone with more severe insomnia, you might have wondered if melatonin can help you get a better sleep.

Melatonin is a hormone made in the brain to regulate your daily sleep-wake cycle. It tells your internal body clock to get sleepy when it’s dark.

Melatonin supplements are a synthetic version of this hormone that people can take to help them sleep.

But they won’t work for all sleep conditions. So what can you take it for?

First, how does melatonin work?

Melatonin works by slowing or stopping neuron firing in the area of the brain called the hypothalamus. This is the brain’s master biological clock.

Your eyes detect when darkness falls, triggering the brain to produce melatonin.

open image in gallery Melatonin gummies for children can look and taste like sweets ( Getty/iStock )

Because you need lower light levels, or darkness, to trigger melatonin release, sleep can be a problem for people living at very high or low latitudes. In summer the sun may not set, or it is only dark for a few hours per day, and that affects melatonin production. And in winter the sun may never come up, or you get only a few hours of sunlight.

For those in the rest of the world, if you suffer from low levels of melatonin – which can happen as you age – it can make it harder to sleep.

When can melatonin help you sleep better?

There are several diseases and conditions that affect sleep, but only two have evidence that they are treatable with melatonin supplements.

Melatonin has been shown to be effective in reducing and preventing jet lag. It’s of most benefit if you fly across more than five time zones. This includes from Europe back to Australia and flying to the Americas from Australia. To be most effective, the melatonin should be taken as close to when you want to go to sleep as possible.

There appears to be some benefit to taking melatonin for those who have difficulty sleeping during the day due to shift work. It has been shown to improve the duration of your sleep after a night shift, but it doesn’t appear to improve other aspects of quality sleep, such as alertness, sleepiness, or fatigue at work.

open image in gallery Insomnia is when you regularly struggle to fall asleep, stay asleep, or when you often wake too early ( Getty/iStock )

General, or chronic, insomnia is when you regularly struggle to fall asleep, stay asleep, or when you often wake too early. Unfortunately, if you suffer from chronic insomnia, the evidence indicates melatonin supplements are unlikely to work.

The pain and discomfort of chronic kidney disease and cancer, and its treatment, can make it more difficult to sleep. But the science is unclear whether melatonin can help with sleep due to those conditions. So for either, it is best for you to speak with your doctor before trying a supplement.

People with dementia can have difficulty sleeping due to the disease’s ability to damage the brain’s internal clock. However, the science indicates that melatonin is not effective for this condition.

How to access the medicine

Melatonin is available in different doses and formulations in Australia.

While homeopathic products are available in Australia, they either do not contain melatonin or have a dose so low that they are ineffective. Any benefit will be from a placebo effect.

Pharmacists can supply controlled-release tablets that contain 2mg or less of melatonin for the short-term treatment of sleep problems for people aged 55 or over. These are available over the counter as a pharmacist-only medicine.

About the authors Nial Wheate is a Professor of Pharmaceutical Chemistry, Macquarie University. Wai-Jo Jocelin Chan is a Pharmacist and Lecturer, UNSW ; University of Sydney. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Controlled-release melatonin formulations release melatonin slowly and steadily in the body throughout the eight-hour sleep period. This is more suited for managing age-related sleep issues caused by reduced natural melatonin production as we get older.

Immediate-release products that contain 5mg or less of melatonin are also available. The short-lived peak of melatonin that comes from this formulation is more suitable for managing jet lag. Pharmacists can supply these to adults 18 years and older for jet lag.

All other formulations above these dosages are prescription-only. They are used for the short-term management of other types of sleep problems, including those that occur alongside neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism.

What are the side effects?

Melatonin is generally well-tolerated. The side effects are generally minor and short-lived and include daytime sleepiness, headaches, nausea and dizziness.

Avoid taking melatonin before driving, as it may affect your attention and reaction time.

A study has found that daily 1,000 to 6,600mg doses of melatonin may cause a loss of sleep and weight loss in people with depression and Huntington’s disease.

There is little research, and inconsistent results, about the side effects of longer-term melatonin use (greater than six months).

What else can help with sleep?

Other than taking melatonin, there are a few techniques that can be used to help with sleep. The first is to keep a regular bed and wake-up time, including on weekends. This can help to regulate your body clock.

If you’re unable to fall asleep after 20 minutes, get up and do something relaxing, then return to bed when you feel sleepy.

Avoid exposure to bright light from computers, televisions and phone screens one to two hours before bed, as this can prevent your body from releasing natural melatonin.

It’s also important to create a good sleeping environment. Make sure your bedroom temperature is cool, and the room is comfortable, quiet and dark enough.

News.title: Police raids on Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s royal properties were unlawful
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and Thames Valley Police have agreed in court that search warrants that allowed officers to raid two of his royal properties earlier this year were unlawful.

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor, who was not in attendance at the hearing, launched a legal claim in the High Court against the force over the lawfulness of search warrants granted to them by a judge at the Old Bailey earlier this year.

The warrants allowed officers to raid his residence on the Sandringham Estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, in February.

open image in gallery Mr Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested in February ( AFP/Getty )

Mr Justice Hilliard said a “significant error” was made in the application for the search warrants.

The court heard that a condition for the granting of a warrant under section eight of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE) is that the judge is “satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the material sought does not include items subject to legal privilege or which constitute what is called Special Procedure material.”

Special Procedure material includes material which a person gained or created in the course of any trade, business, profession, or any paid or unpaid office and which is expected to be confidential.

Mr Justice Hilliard said that Thames Valley Police had conceded that the judge “could not properly have been satisfied” that there were grounds for believing the material to be searched was not subject to legal privilege or Special Procedure material.

He said the presence of such material was “expressly envisaged” in the application for the warrants and that it was “inherent in the nature of the alleged offences” under investigation, that the material was likely to be subject to such privilege.

But the judge also said that “the fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring an investigation to an end, or mean that the whole of the investigation was unlawful”.

He added the staff in the documents will not be publicly named.

Thames Valley Police has since made an application to keep possession of the seized material on the grounds it could be seized again under a different provision. This is disputed by Mr Mountbatten-Windsor, but the court heard a decision on this application is not expected until next year.

Thames Valley Police said its investigation into “alleged misconduct in public office by a man in his sixties from Norfolk remains ongoing”.

The High Court had quashed the search warrants in July, which a police spokesperson explained “relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgement on our ongoing investigation”.

“We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout,” they added.

“We accept the position that the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.

“Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation.”

open image in gallery The gates of Royal Lodge, the former home of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor ( PA Wire )

The former Duke was arrested on his 66th birthday on suspicion of misconduct in public office following allegations he shared sensitive information with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein during his time as the UK’s trade envoy.

He was interviewed under caution before being released. Mr Mountbatten-Windsor has always strenuously denied any wrongdoing.

Misconduct in public office (MIPO) is a criminal offence that concerns serious wilful abuse, or neglect, of the power or responsibilities pertaining to the public office held.

Thames Valley Police previously said officers are continuing to assess a wide range of aspects covered under the offence as part of their investigation. The offence can include possible financial criminality, sex offences, fraud, corruption, and perverting the course of justice.

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor has rarely been seen in public after he was forced to leave Royal Lodge in February and move to the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk.

The King stripped his brother of both his right to be a prince and his dukedom over his association with Epstein in October last year.

News.title: Energy theft rising as cost of electricity soars
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A growing number of bill payers have been stealing energy as rising fuel costs hit finances, new figures have revealed.

Electricity thefts confirmed by energy suppliers have risen from 17,422 incidents in 2021-2022 to 21,354 in 2025-2026, data obtained by Stay Energy Safe shows.

This 22 per cent increase comes as energy costs remain persistently high following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, when Ofgem’s price cap reached a record £4,279. The government’s energy price guarantee policy, in place from 2022 to 2023, capped this at £2,500.

From an average of around £1,331 in 2021 before this crisis, Ofgem’s price cap has reached an average of £1,664 this year.

The most concentrated increase in energy theft has come from commercial electricity customers, marking a stark 276 per cent increase, from 996 cases in 2021-2022 to 3,747 in 2025-2026.

London was the top hotspot for incidents, with more than 2,000 reported in the last financial year. These were most concentrated in north London, at 643 confirmed thefts.

Next in the list was Birmingham at 1,008 thefts, followed by Liverpool (975), Glasgow (855), Manchester (742) and Leeds (732).

In the UK, stealing electricity carries a maximum sentence of five years in jail and an unlimited fine.

Stay Energy Safe, which is run by charity Crimestoppers, also warned stealing energy can carry serious dangers to health.

A spokesperson said: “Latest figures from the industry confirm that more than 100,000 confirmed energy theft offences in five years is a stark warning that this is far from a victimless crime.

A growing number of bill payers have started stealing energy as rising fuel costs hit finances, new figures have revealed ( Getty/iStock )

“Tampered meters can cause fires, explosions and electrocution, while energy theft can be part of serious organised crime.

“It also pushes up costs for other households and businesses, meaning we all ultimately pay the price.

“The sustained rise in offences shows why it’s so important that people understand the dangers, know what to look out for and feel confident reporting their concerns.

“Whether it’s a bypassed meter, unusual wiring or suspicious activity around a meter box or mains service cables, we urge anyone with concerns to report it anonymously. You could be preventing a fire, protecting a neighbour or even saving a life.”

The findings come amid concerns that higher energy rates could be reached again as conflict in the Middle East continues to push up costs worldwide. Respected forecaster Cornwall Insight has predicted a price cap of £1,999 for January, which would bring bills to their highest level since August 2023.

News.title: From Yale to the Congo: The mathematician who became one of Africa’s most intrepid reporters
News.content:
Sundaram has a lot of experience with the Rwandan methods of control. After spending 17 months in DRC, he moved to Kigali and he is eloquent about the convoluted effects of dictatorship. “Living in Rwanda taught me so much about how dictatorships function internally and how counter-intuitive they can be. A friend of mine who was working in public health told me ‘When we ask people in India to wash their hands we get a 30 per cent success rate from a campaign, but when we need people in Rwanda to wash their hands, we just need to slip a line in one of Kagame’s speeches and we get a 90 per cent success rate. That’s fantastic isn’t it?’

“And I said, ‘well is it? It’s great for short term health outcomes but what does that say about society? Isn’t democracy about people choosing freely? What if the government tells them to do something bad – like what happened in the genocide when people were told to kill all the Tutsis?’

“Kagame and his army stopped the genocide, and he has restored peace, but he governs using the same system that was used to perpetrate the genocide.”

In Bad News: Last Journalists in a Dictatorship, the book Sundaram went on to write about his time in Rwanda teaching journalists, he describes a more extreme version of this phenomenon, recalling how Kagame once commented that thatched roofs on huts were primitive. “And the local authorities took that as a sign that he didn’t like thatched roofs, and that they should get rid of them. And without replacements being built, people climbed up and dismantled their own thatched roofs. And I saw these villages with houses which just had mud walls without roofs, and the families were sitting outside with their children and their goats, the thatch strewn on the ground. In the rain, quite often. The children would get sick, and it was like a war zone.

“At the end of my time in Congo, I was at a UN base and they were digging latrines, when they found some human bones. They stopped digging and alerted the press, and I happened to be in Goma nearby.” He subsequently found out that it was one of a series of mass graves containing the bodies of Congolese killed by forces controlled by Kagame. “And so when I arrived I had a sense of what Rwanda had done in Congo, but I didn’t fully appreciate the extent to which it was totalitarian. I’d heard that the country was a shining example of progress – aid programs were successful, and poverty reduction programs. The streets were clean, public services functioned. I was living in a nice house with a big garden provided by the journalism programme I was working in.”

Many European governments, including Britain, are enamoured with Rwanda, because, says Sundaram, “dictatorships can be very efficient”. But it is a “mirage of a country”, he says.

The teaching programme he was running was briefed not to challenge the government on any level, and an embassy official told him that if any of the journalists mentioned repression they would be expelled.

“Layer by layer, as I began to talk to the journalists I was training, the true story unravelled. The first instance was when one of them left the programme, and I heard him on the radio one day praising the president, but with a degree of flattery that was completely exaggerated, and I didn’t understand why. The rest of the class were reluctant to talk about it but eventually I learned that another student had been beaten to a coma on the day he criticised the president.

“I started to realise that my class contained some of the most courageous journalists in the country.” As a foreigner, if he transgressed, Sundaram could have his visa cancelled or get kicked out, or even locked up for a couple of days, but for the Rwandan journalists, everything was at stake. They could be killed or their families threatened.

“But still they persisted, and they took me around the country and showed me all the things the government didn’t want anyone to see – things they couldn’t report on because it was too dangerous, so they wanted to show me because they wanted somebody to speak up. It’s really a book about them – they’ve been my greatest teachers in journalism.”

News.title: I tried Amazon’s new iPad rival – and there’s one standout feature
News.content:
Amazon says that this tablet has three times the computing power and nine times the graphics power of any previous Amazon tablet, so this is a significant boost in performance to previous models.

That will make light tasks, such as crunching through emails, browser-based activity like online shopping and document work. With a keyboard factored in, it could work as a laptop alternative for some. The same could be said of the iPad Air, although with recent price increases from Apple and the matte screen, for my money, this is a better proposition.

The premium makeover that comes with the Alexa Tablet Pro includes a slim aluminium design, with flattened edges, so it looks like an iPad or Samsung tablet, only 6.5mm thick. The Pro version only comes in the Graphite colour seen here. All models in the new line-up feel more grown-up and less like kid’s tablets than the Fire range. Plus the switch to proper Android over Fire OS is welcome and will result in better app compatibility (although I noticed that these tablets were running Android 16, which is now an old version).

It has a battery that’s good for 16 hours of video playback and supports 27W charging. There are cameras front and rear although like any tablet, these won’t be as good as your phone, while there’s support for Dolby Atmos from the speakers, so your movies will sound decent.

The AI capabilities are a step up

As the name suggests, Amazon is keen to promote the AI element here. It has customised the interface slightly with access to Alexa+ meaning you can utilise Amazon’s AI at any time to ask about what’s on the screen, to control smart home devices or search for content. If you are a keen Alexa user, then that will be a plus, but for me it’s not the headline news.

News.title: Kenyan authorities scramble to find passengers on Ebola flight
News.content:
Authorities are racing to track down passengers who boarded a flight from Uganda to Kenya on Saturday alongside a man infected with Ebola.

The man travelled by bus from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the epicentre of an Ebola outbreak that has killed 4,000 people, to Kampala, Uganda. He then boarded a flight to Nairobi on Saturday, October 3, which was operated by the African airline Jambojet.

The patient went to a hospital in Nairobi and died just 48 hours later, meaning the journey took place in the final days of infection, the stage at which patients who die of the disease are most contagious. By October 6 authorities had tracked down 28 contacts, including family members of the deceased, but said they urgently needed to track down 23 passengers and crew who had travelled on the same flight.

The man is Kenya’s first ever case of the disease. Ebola does not typically spread through the air like Covid-19 or measles, requiring close contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person to spread. However, an aeroplane cabin significantly intensifies these risks because passengers share cramped spaces for prolonged periods and touch the same surfaces, such as a cabin toilet.

“We are working closely with the Ministry of Health, Port Health Services and other relevant authorities to support the ongoing public health response, including the identification and management of the other guests and crew who may have been in contact with the individual,” a spokesperson for Jambojet said on Tuesday.

After landing in Kenya, airport staff screened the patient, standard protocol for people travelling from at-risk countries during the current Ebola outbreak, but allowed him to continue his journey into Nairobi.

Kenya’s health ministry director-general, Patrick Amoth, said the patient may have passed through airport screening because medication had masked his symptoms.

News.title: Africa embraces ‘Go to Work on an Egg’ to boost maternal health and nutrition
News.content:
The sun is barely up when villagers start queuing for eggs at the metal gate of Shamim Haried’s home.

By noon, all that day’s supply is usually sold out, but people keep coming and asking if there are any left.

Demand is so high that arguments can break out in the queue, says the mother-of-two who lives outside Malawi’s capital, Lilongwe.

Her eggs are cheaper and fresher than those sold in the market.

“The people almost fight for eggs: it’s hard to watch,” she explains.

“Eggs are the cheapest healthy protein that they can get and it’s better for them to buy here than anywhere else.”

Her flock of 1,400 chickens lay around 1,000 eggs each day, but she reckons she could sell three times that.

News.title: What is pneumonic plague? Symptoms and how it spreads
News.content:
The death of a researcher at a plague laboratory in Siberia has prompted the World Health Organization to press Moscow for answers.

Russian officials have yet to share details of what caused the worker’s illness, and this information vacuum has fuelled speculation.

But what is the disease, and how much of a threat does it pose?

What is pneumonic plague?

Plague is a rare and serious infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals such as rodents and their fleas. Pneumonic plague is the most virulent of plague’s three forms, and is a severe infection of the lungs.

The other types are bubonic plague – the Black Death that laid waste to much of Europe during the Middle Ages – which attacks the lymph nodes, and septicaemic plague, which attacks the blood. Either can develop into the pneumonic form if the infection spreads.

Pneumonic plague is rarer than the bubonic form, but more dangerous.

Each year, the world records an estimated 1,000 to 3,000 plague cases of all types, though the number fluctuates.

Most cases are bubonic, and spread by the bite of an infected flea, and most occur in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of Congo. But infections are also found in countries including Russia, India, China and the United States.

News.title: Weight loss jabs are safe for obese teenagers, WHO announces
News.content:
Obese teenagers can safely be given weight-loss drugs and undergo bariatric surgery, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.

The recommendations form part of the first set of global guidelines released by the WHO for the treatment of obese children and adolescents.

Previously, the WHO only recommended weight-loss drugs like Mounjaro and Wegovy and bariatric surgery, which alters the stomach and reduces appetite, for the treatment of obese adults – defined as someone with a body mass index of 30 or above.

However, the new guidelines say children over the age of 10 can safely be given the drugs, as well as undergo weight-loss surgery, if all other options, like managed exercise and diet programmes, have been exhausted. Children under that age should not be given drugs or surgery.

Obese children in the UK are currently not eligible for weight-loss drugs or surgery on the NHS, although specialised clinics may offer them to children over 12 under very strict conditions.

The WHO recommends first and foremost that obese children and teenagers undertake a structured diet programme and physical activity, which for children over five should include an average of at least 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous activity across the week.

According to Unicef an estimated 188 million children and adolescents are obese, and last year, the number of overweight children exceeded the number of underweight children for the first time in history.

While obesity rates are beginning to plateau in many rich countries, childhood obesity is rising rapidly in the developing world, including in sub-Saharan Africa, which is home to nearly a quarter of the world’s overweight children.

The drivers of obesity are complex, but experts believe a switch from traditional, fibre-rich diets to cheap, high-fat, high-sugar food has played a significant role in growing global obesity rates.

Obesity at any age carries significant health risks – but the consequences are thought to be more acute if obesity begins in childhood, accelerating the development of severe and life-threatening conditions, including type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular dysfunction, and liver disease.

The WHO guidelines also emphasise the importance of addressing mental health issues that are often associated with obesity and contribute to unhealthy eating patterns – including anxiety and depression, low self-esteem, and bullying.

“Our priority must be to ensure that every child and adolescent can access quality care and supportive environments from an early age, helping them achieve and maintain a healthy weight and laying the foundation for lifelong health and well-being,” Dr Luz María De Regil, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, WHO.

Sports.title: Will Man City be allowed to play in the Champions League next season?
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER City have endured one of the most turbulent international breaks of any club in recent memory.

The club were found guilty of serious financial breaches by the Premier League, a ruling that was upheld by an independent commission that has led City to announce that they will be appealing the verdict.

An excerpt from City’s club statement, in which they deny any wrongdoing, reads: “The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.



“The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.”



But what does mean for their European hopes next season? Could they still play in the UEFA Champions League in 2026-27?

Read on below for all you need to know about the scenarios for their potential exclusion from European competition.

Will Man City be allowed to play in the Champions League next season?

The Citizens are currently appealing the Premier League’s ruling which, at present, has no bearing itself on City’s possible qualification for Europe next season.

In order to take part in a UEFA club competition – be it the Champions League, Europa League or Conference League – every team requires a UEFA licence.

While these licences are issued by the Football Association (FA) that in turn delegates that responsibility to the Premier League.

None of the team’s charges relating to a breach of the Premier League’s financial rules would currently see them disqualified from Europe.



However, should City face sanctions such as a large points deduction that would not allow them to qualify via the Premier League – they could still do so by winning either the Carabao Cup or the FA Cup.

They face Brighton in the fourth round of the former competition on 28 October, while they will join the latter once it reaches the Third Round Proper.

Will UEFA stop Man City from playing in Europe?

UEFA could also still open a disciplinary matter against City should European football’s governing body wish to pursue a route to remove them from one of its competitions.

In 2020, Man City had a two-year Champions League ban overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

After a lengthy investigation, City were found guilty by UEFA’s Club Financial Control Body (CFCB) of falsely inflating their sponsorship revenues when submitting accounts as part of the FFP compliance process.



But City scored a major victory at the time by winning their appeal and will be hoping for a similar outcome in the near future following the Premier League ruling.

That appeal process is ongoing and it remains to be seen how it will affect their European prospects for next season.

Sports.title: Harry Kane targeted in ambitious MLS transfer after England captain admitted to NFL dream upon retirement
Sports.content:
Next

HARRY KANE has been targeted to help turn MLS into one of the world’s leading leagues.

England skipper Kane admitted he could end his playing days States-side, even keeping alive his dream of transforming into an NFL kicker.



And MLS commissioner Dan Garber admitted Kane following the likes of David Beckham and Lionel Messi to become a marquee player for the competition would continue its growth in status.

Garber said: “I’d love for Harry Kane to do that.



“For me, it is the fulfilment of the dream that we had to build a proper soccer league that would drive a soccer nation.

“That sounds colloquial but actually we have that written down. We wanted to create something that would have the Harry Kanes of the world say ‘I’d kind of like to play in MLS’. And I think Messi proved that.”

Garber, stepping down from his role after 27 years at the end of December, feels the arrivals of Beckham at LA Galaxy in 2007 and the Messi at Beckham-owned Inter Miami 16 years later were signposts for MLS’ direction of travel.

Speaking at Leaders Week London 2026 at Stamford Bridge, he added: “David was foundational – and Lio’s been transformational.

“From the day David arrived in LA and did three hours of media interviews in the hot sun I knew we had something special in him.

“He believed in the league so much. His contract allowed him to buy an option on a team.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

“That option turned into Miami, that Miami team turned into the new stadium, which is one of the great small stadiums in the entire world.

“And it gave us an opportunity to have a platform for the greatest player in the history of the game.

“It’s just remarkable to me how focused, committed, loyal, competitive, Lionel Messi is.

“David started by getting people to ask ‘who are these Yanks and what are they doing?’ so that there isn’t a person in the world that doesn’t know about Major League Soccer.



“Then Messi has taken us to where we are, with a vision to become one of the top leagues in the world.

“Visions aren’t something you do tomorrow. Visions are things that take a generation.

“But I believe that we’ll be among the most competitive leagues in the world.”

Sports.title: San Siro’s greatest moments, from champagne football to Bob Marley’s historic gig, as demolishment plans are revealed
Sports.content:
Next

THANKS for the memories, San Siro.

Demolishment plans have been confirmed for the iconic football stadium, as its residents AC and Inter Milan get ready for life in a new arena.



Construction on a new smaller stadium is set to begin next year and is expected to cost an incredible £1.84billion (€2.15bn) and house 71,500 fans.

It is expected to be completed by 2032, in time for the Euros the Italians will be hosting with Turkey that year.



Adjacent to it, the old site will be torn down, leaving behind plenty of incredible moments to remember.

SunSport rounds up the San Siro’s most iconic moments, starting with a football revolutionary.

Champagne football

In a four-year spell between 1987-1991, pioneering Italian coach Arrigo Sacchi changed the game in Italy.

Fans were used to defensive football, playing on the counter, individual man-marking and low-scoring matches.

But Sacchi ripped up that blueprint to build an AC Milan team that zonally pressed in a compact 4-4-2 system.

Their high-line and offside trap was marshalled by legendary defender Franco Baresi, which compressed space in midfield and suffocated its opponents.



Fluid movement in attack was provided by the club’s Dutch trio, Marco Van Basten, Ruud Gullit and Frank Rijkaard.

The football was incredible. The results even more spectacular.



They won the Scudetto in 1988, in Sacchi’s first season at the club, conceding just 14 goals.

Then, in 1989 and 1990 they won back-to-back to European Cups, first defeating Steaua București 4-0 and a year later edging out Benfica 1-0.

A highlight from the 1988-89 European Cup run came in the second leg of the semi-final against Real Madrid.

Milan ripped the Spaniards to pieces, winning 5-0, in front of 73,000 fans. The fact there were five different scorers showed how much a team they were.

Three is the magic number

Seeing their rivals score such incredible success with a trio of foreign superstars from one country, Inter thought they could mirror that strategy.



In 1988, Inter signed German stars Lothar Matthäus and Andreas Brehme from Bayern Munich.

A year later, they added Jürgen Klinsmann from VfB Stuttgart.

With Matthäus and Brehme in tow, they wrestled the title off AC Milan in 1989.



The rivalry between both sets of players spilled into disputes at international level.

The then West Germany and the Netherlands endured fiercely competitive matches at Euro 1988 and the 1990 World Cup.

Rijkaard and Rudi Voller were sent off at Italia ’90 – with the Dutch star famously spitting at the German forward as they left the pitch.

Bob Marley

It’s not just brilliant football that the San Siro has housed.

Over the years, music’s finest, such as the Rolling Stones, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, David Bowie and U2 have all appeared in concert on stage on the pitch.



However, the most iconic show belongs to Bob Marley.

In 1980, he played at the stadium to an estimated 120,000 fans, all coming in peace in what was a cultural watershed moment.

Incredibly, it was the largest audience Marley ever played to, before he died in 1981.

It was the largest attendance ever recorded for a music show in Italy, until 2017, when Italian singer Vasco Rossi played an open-air concert in Modena Park.



World Cup giant-killing

Football-related, but absolutely nothing to do with AC or Inter, the San Siro saw, perhaps, the World Cup giant-killing of all time.

A well-fancied Argentina team swanned into Italia ’90 as world champions from their exploits in 1986.

Their first match was against an unknown Cameroon side, who were expected to wilt against Diego Maradona and Co, at the San Siro.



Far from it. Argentina fell to a shock 1-0 defeat, thanks to François Omam-Biyik’s unforgettable header.

It was an iconic moment, although it didn’t harm the Argies too much.

They reached the final, only to be beaten by West Germany in the final.

The taming of Barcelona

Real Madrid aren’t the only team to have been tamed at the San Siro.



One of the greatest European nights the stadium has ever seen saw Jose Mourinho’s Inter overcome Pep Guardiola’s 2010 Barcelona team.

This was a Barcelona team that had Lionel Messi, Xavi, Sergio Busquets and Zlatan Ibrahimovic.

But Inter had Wesley Sneijder, Samuel Eto’o and legendary captain Javier Zanetti.

Despite conceding first to a Pedro goal, the Italians rallied to win 3-1 and set themselves up perfectly for the second leg.



Sneijder, Maicon and Diego Milito were the scorers that night.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The win allowed Jose to park the bus in the second leg, and they did just that, with ten men with over an hour of the game left, to record a 3-2 aggregate win and cue hysteria from the Special One on the sidelines.

That year, Inter won a historic treble. But, it wouldn’t have been possible if that magical night at the San Siro in the first leg never happened.

Sports.title: Arsenal files: Arteta picks LA Rams’ coach’s brains on title defence and Raheem Sterling’s son making own way in academy
Sports.content:
Next

MIKEL ARTETA and LA Rams coach Sean McVay have been “sharing notes” on how not to flop after a title-winning season.

Arteta and McVay have a strong relationship and are regularly in contact, given both Arsenal and the Rams fall under the Kroenke Sports and Entertainment umbrella.



The pair have spoken in length in the past and Mikel is now leaning on McVay to navigate his first season after winning the Premier League.

The Rams had their worst season under McVay the year after he led them to the Super Bowl, losing 12 games and winning just five.



Arteta will be hoping to avoid a similar disaster after leading Arsenal to their first league title in 22 years last season and has been speaking to McVay to get some tips on how to do just that.

KSE executive Kevin Demoff said: “We’re fortunate that Mikel and Sean have such a good relationship.

“I think it’s probably two of the strongest relationships in our whole ecosystem. They can share notes from what it’s like to go through a title.

“Our worst year with the Rams was the year after we won the Super Bowl and Sean kind of hit rock bottom. He and Mikel have talked about that.

“How do you get through that year when you finally break through and win in that relief? And you can see it, both with Sean and Mikel, what it meant to them to finally break through after years of coming close.

“Then how do you translate that into the next year when you have got to go push your club and you got to get back there and not let that one title define you or say that that was ultimately success?”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Arteta came under fire during the summer when he made a number of difficult decisions around transfers.

The Arsenal chief was criticised by sections of the fanbase for selling Gabriel Martinelli to Al Hilal after his contribution to the Gunners’ journey since Arteta’s arrival.

Demoff reckons that squad turnover is one of the most important areas to navigate for McVay and Arteta after winning a major honour.

He added: “You can’t keep all your players after you win a title. How do you pick and choose the right ones?



“How do you respond to the fan narrative that these are the guys who won you a title?

“But you need to move on from them to grow for the future, even if it’s not immediate.

“Sports is the best blend of short term and long term.

“When you look at it that way, the short term after you win a title feels so different than the short term any other time because there’s an acute goal of ‘you gotta get back’.

“I think being able to share notes about, ‘hey, maybe it’s not as acute as you think,’ helps you actually in the long term go chase that title again.”



NWAN TO FORGET

ETHAN NWANERI needed to be comforted by Conor Coady at full-time of England Under-21’s goalless draw against Slovakia last week.

The Borussia Dortmund loanee started the game, but cut a frustrated figure when he was substituted by Young Lions boss Lee Carsley in the 71st minute.

Following the full-time whistle, Nwaneri needed an arm around the shoulder from Coady, who is currently working as an assistant coach for Carsley’s U21s.

The 19-year-old impressed during his time on the pitch, completing 98 per cent of his passes and firing three shots goalwards.

Nwaneri was starved of minutes during his loan spell at Marseille in the second half of last season and is yet to play a full 90 minutes for Dortmund this term.



UNUSUAL HAV-IT

KAI HAVERTZ has revealed the unusual superstition that means he wears long sleeve shirts no matter the temperature.

Havertz, 27, always opts for the winter jersey even when temperatures are soaring and won’t be changing his ways any time soon.

He said: “It’s a superstition. I think it’s the thing I just feel most comfortable with on the pitch, I don’t know why, but I can’t look down and see my body and see my arm without a shirt.



“It just developed like this, and people were laughing at me when I turned up in the World Cup or in the training camp in Singapore, 45°C with a long sleeve in training or in the game.

“But that’s how I like it, and my head just always tells me to wear long sleeves, so I can’t wear short sleeves anymore.”

NO MESSING

ARSENAL Under-16s are set to participate in the Messi Cup later this month.

The Young Guns will take part in the competition that was set up by Lionel Messi and his production company 525 Rosario.

Arsenal will join Chelsea, Barcelona, Atletico Madrid, Inter Miami, Benfica, Palmeiras, Inter, Ajax and a host of other clubs across the globe in the Miami tournament.



There is no confirmation of which Arsenal youngsters will play in the tournament yet, but it could be an opportunity for the likes of Jaden Maghoma and Luis Munoz to shine again.

Last year’s edition of the tournament was won by River Plate U16s, while Manchester City and Chelsea both reached the semi-finals.

STERLING EFFORT

RAHEEM STERLING’S son Thiago is already picking up awards in the Arsenal academy.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Thiago, nine, joined the Gunners’ youth ranks when his dad was on the books at the Emirates in 2024 and has been impressive ever since.

The youngster earned the Under-10s Corey Price Cup Player of the Tournament earlier this month and is looking to follow in his dad’s footsteps by making it pro one day.

Sports.title: Russell Martin confronted by Leicester fan after latest woeful defeat and tells him ‘you’ve been s*** ever since’
Sports.content:
Next

LEICESTER boss Russell Martin got into a tense exchange with a fan following their latest woeful defeat – and told him the Foxes have been “s***” for two years.

Martin, 40, has endured a tough start to life as Foxes boss.



His side have just two wins from seven games in League One – and suffered a 4-0 defeat at home to Oxford last month.

However, during the international break they have played two matches in the Jersey Mike’s Trophy.



The first was a 6-1 win over Fulham Under-21s.

But on Tuesday, Leicester went down 2-1 at Stevenage.



And after the nightmare result, a disgruntled Leicester fan who had travelled more than 200 miles waited to confront Martin as he left Broadhall Way.

The ex-Southampton and Rangers boss posed for a few selfies before taking his time to get into a frank but respectful conversation.

The fan’s video of their back-and-forth has been seen more than 2.7million times on social media – and it ended with Martin’s X-rated yet honest putdown of the state of Leicester City.

The fan – who goes by @FilbertSt1884 on X – started: “Russell, I’ve come from Exeter to watch this, I go everywhere to watch this club.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Fixtures Results Table Notts 12:30 LEO Oxford U Plymouth 12:30 LEO Wimbledon Bradford 15:00 LEO L Orient Cambridge U 15:00 LEO Blackpool Doncaster 15:00 LEO Burton Huddersfield 15:00 LEO Sheff Wed Leicester 15:00 LEO Peterborough Reading 1 – 1 LEO Bradford L Orient 0 – 2 LEO Plymouth Burton 1 – 3 LEO Huddersfield Wycombe 2 – 2 LEO Reading Stockport 1 – 0 LEO Peterborough Plymouth 0 – 1 LEO Burton

“I want you to succeed, but don’t play the football the owners want you to play, play the football that we want you to play. We’re not giving you personal abuse…”

Martin laughed back: “Well, you are but…”

The fan replied: “But we gave (Enzo) Maresca it.”

Martin then turned to stats: “We’ve had 135 shots in five games. That’s attacking football.”

The fan disagreed but Martin insisted: “But it is, 135 shots in five games is attacking.”



The fan then moaned: “It’s too predictable. It takes too long to get to those chances.”

Martin stuck by his methods and continued: “I disagree. We’re going to disagree on this.”

The supporter then suggested Martin will join a long list of managers who have left Leicester in recent years and leave the club “going round in circles”.

But Martin is adament he will stick by his methods, even if it costs him his job.

The former Scotland defender added: “That’s fine, I live and die by the sword.



“You got promoted with Enzo [Maresca] by the way, you’ve been s*** since then.”

The fan replied that even a lot of Leicester fans were unhappy with Maresca’s style of play but Martin concluded: “You got promoted with 96 points. What do you want?

“Because you had Gary Rowett, you had Marti Cifuentes, Ruud van Nistelrooy.

“We’ve had more shots in five games than you’ve had in 10/15 last season, I don’t know what you want.

“We’ll win and when we win, we’ll be fine and you’ll enjoy it. I appreciate the support.”



The minute-long chat went viral on social media – with many users chipping in with their view and agreeing with Martin, who handled the situation well.

One said: “Martin dealt with that very well imo.”

Another wrote: “I don’t rate him as a manager at all but nothing wrong with being honest, Leicester have been s*** for years that’s why they’re in the third division.”

But a third added: “Don’t have an issue with this. Gave the fan time, didn’t raise his voice or become abusive to him.”

And a final user commented: “Fair play to him, stood his ground. The sneaky recording him was out of order.

“Martin made some valid points and handled it coolly. I have no interest in that club or manager but I hope he succeeds.”

Sports.title: International footballer arrested in match fixing probe after suspected bribery and illegal gambling referred to police
Sports.content:
Add us as a preferred source

STAR SHOCK International footballer arrested in match fixing probe after suspected bribery and illegal gambling referred to police







Next

AN international footballer has been arrested on suspicion of assisting a betting syndicate.

Winger Soukphachan Lueanthala played for Laos at the 2026 Asean Championship over the summer.



Following the tournament, an investigation was launched into alleged bribery, illegal gambling and match fixing.

According to The Guardian, Lueanthala has been accused of assisting a Vietnamese betting syndicate during the summer’s tournament.



The 24-year-old is alleged to have “given instructions” to his team-mates at the Asean Championships.

He is also accused of being the “link” between involved parties.

The Asean Championship is contested between nations from South East Asia.

Laos finished bottom of Group B; losing 5-0 to Thailand, 4-0 to Malaysia, 4-1 to the Philippines and 7-2 to Myanmar.

The Laos Football Federation subsequently launched an investigation in August before handing their findings over to cops.

Lueanthala plays for Salavan United in his homeland.



He has earned 20 caps for Laos, and featured in three of their four matches at the summer’s tournament – but was an unused substitute in the heavy defeat to Myanmar.

Lueanthala played in all of Laos’ matches at the 2024 Asean Championship.

Laos performed far more competitively on that occasion, earning two draws.

They lost 4-1 to Vietnam before a 3-3 draw with Indonesia and 1-1 clash with the Philippines, before finishing their campaign with a 3-2 defeat to Myanmar.

Sports.content:
Man City icon David Silva comes out of retirement aged 40 after accepting surprise offer

Former Spain and Manchester City star David Silva has announced on Wednesday he is coming out of retirement to play in the Hong Kong Premier League

View 2 Images David Silva is back in football (Image: (Joe Prior/Visionhaus via Getty Images))

David Silva has clarified that his move to Hong Kong side Supreme Sha Tin is to play one match and not a full season. The Manchester City great hung up his boots back in 2023 after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament injury.

‌



‌



But it was confirmed on Wednesday that he was planning to come out of retirement to play for the Hong Kong Premier League side. Explaining his decision, the former Spain international said: “I am very happy to join Supreme Sha Tin for this experience.

‌



“I am really looking forward to going to Hong Kong to enjoy the culture, the people and the food in Sha Tin and the football in Hong Kong. I can’t wait to go, so I look forward to seeing you all soon.”

‌



But Silva moved on Thursday to confirm that his return is just to play one match. Speaking to El Partidazo de COPE in his homeland, he said: "I am surprised because in the end it is only to play one match.

“The news made it look like I had signed for a season and it has kept me busy all afternoon. It is a league match, but it is still just one match.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta still bears scar of Champions League heartbreak - 'I have poison in my veins'
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta still bears scar of Champions League heartbreak - 'I have poison in my veins'

Mikel Arteta is excited about the future with Arsenal after signing a lucrative new contract, but the Spaniard is also driven by what happened against Paris Saint-Germain in May

View 2 Images Arsenal were left devastated in last season's Champions League final (Image: 2026 Marc Atkins)

Mikel Arteta has revealed that the pain of losing the Champions League final against Paris Saint-Germain is acting as "poison in my veins" as he looks to avenge Arsenal's defeat.

‌



‌



Arteta ended Arsenal's 22-year wait for the Premier League title in May, but their breakthrough season after three successive second-place finishes was tinged with sadness. The Gunners were beaten on penalties by PSG after a tense 1-1 draw in Budapest just 11 days after they lifted the Premier League trophy.

‌



Arteta took over as Arsenal manager in December 2019 and has overseen an upturn in the club's fortunes. His work was recognised this week when the owners handed him a new contract until 2030 which makes him the Premier League's highest-paid manager, on nearly £20million per year.

‌



Arsenal are focused on trying to defend their Premier League crown this season, but Arteta is clearly motivated to challenge PSG in the Champions League as well following the French giants' back-to-back titles. Asked by The Athletic whether the defeat on May 30 was akin to what Arsene Wenger called a "scar on my heart", Arteta was unequivocal.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



“I still have the scar, like Arsene says. I still have that poison in my veins," he said. "It has to stay there because that’s when you learn and that probably is going to be a massive driver for me and everybody.”

Arteta has signed up for another four years at the helm in north London and is clearly relishing every aspect of the challenge of keeping Arsenal at the top of the game.

“Globally, with our supporters? Great," he said. "How are we going to build the next three squads? Great. How the rules of the game are going to change us, and how we’re going to stay ahead of that to take advantage? Great.

‌



View 2 Images Mikel Arteta recently signed a new contract at Arsenal (Image: Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

"But this is going to happen if every single day we look after what we built. We make it a little bit better, like software that is upgrading and upgrading. When can it stop is infinite.”

His words echo those he said after signing his new contract. “It’s a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal,” Arteta said.

Article continues below

“This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue. We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together."

After a three-week international break to reflect on the 3-0 defeat by Brighton, Arsenal are back in action on Saturday against Leeds. They are then in Champions League action against Lille at the Emirates Stadium, with fixtures coming thick and fast across all competitions.

Sports.title: Man City discover stance on playing in EFL as chiefs 'make punishment feelings clear'
Sports.content:
Man City discover stance on playing in EFL as chiefs 'make punishment feelings clear'

Manchester City have launched an appeal after being found guilty of 114 charges brought against them by the Premier League

View 2 Images Man City could be forced to play in the EFL (Image: AP)

Manchester City have been told they should drop to the bottom of the English football pyramid and work their way back up following last week's verdict on their financial charges. An independent commission found City guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.

‌



‌



The club were found to have used 'sham' contracts to disguise more than £830million in funding between 2009 and 2018. However, City continue to strongly deny any wrongdoing and have launched an appeal against the verdict.

‌



The club have adopted a siege mentality in the aftermath of the ruling, reassuring players and staff that they have 'irrefutable evidence' which they believe will clear their name. An independent three-person panel will now oversee City's appeal, with a decision expected before the end of the year.

‌



A key part of the club’s defence is expected to centre on the claim that the 'sham' deals were legitimate and funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than City's owners at the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG). The commission has the power to relegate City, impose unlimited fines, hand out points deductions or issue a transfer ban.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

It also remains to be seen whether the club could be stripped of the titles they won during the nine-year period in question. There has been plenty of debate over what punishment City should receive, with several senior figures from the Premier League and English Football League (EFL) speaking to the i Paper about what they believe should happen.

‌



"They should go all the way to the bottom of the pyramid," one EFL source told The i Paper.

One EFL club executive added: "I don’t know all the details, but if they are guilty of all this, at the end of the day, depending on how passionately you believe in it, the integrity of the game is at stake.

"Why should we be forced to play alongside City as their punishment? Does it make it okay for League One clubs to cheat, if they are playing against Manchester City for points? You have to earn your place in any league in English football. Why should City be placed anywhere?"

‌



Leicester City's presence in League One this season has already demonstrated the potential impact of having a major club in the division, with one senior EFL executive pointing to the increased interest surrounding their fixtures.

View 2 Images Enzo Maresca could end up managing City in the Championship - or lower (Image: Adam Davy/PA Wire)

"We are seeing what having a giant of a club like Leicester City in League One this season does for interest," a senior EFL executive told the newspaper. "We sold out straight away for that. Imagine the demand for City tickets.

‌



"We have never made losses like this before. We cannot keep going like this, so anything that helps that is a bonus. The chance to go up against a giant like City would get more eyes on the league, attract investors, and get us gate receipts we wouldn’t normally get."

According to Section W, Rule 54 of the Premier League's handbook, City could face a punishment ranging from a reprimand to expulsion from the competition.

A source close to the youth recruitment process in Manchester also highlighted the potential knock-on effect of any severe punishment for City. "Local clubs thrive off getting players who drop out of City’s academy, who have had a fantastic footballing upbringing there.

Article continues below

"If they went down the divisions, so many clubs would lose that." There is still a long way to go before the outcome of City's appeal becomes clear, with the independent panel now set to consider the club's case.
