Sports.title: Man City charges: Club facing second sanction as Pep Guardiola's return confirmed
Sports.content:
Man City charges: Club facing second sanction as Pep Guardiola's return confirmed

Manchester City face a tense wait as they appeal after being found guilty of 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules

View 3 Images Pep Guardiola is doubling down in his support for Manchester City (Image: Carl Recine, Getty Images)

With the international break now over eyes turn back to the Premier League for Manchester City. The full squad return to training on Thursday as they gear up for the clash against Liverpool at Anfield, but the talk pre-match is bound to be dominated by the charges handing over City.

‌



‌



It was confirmed during the break that the club have been found guilty of 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules. An independent panel rules that City used 'sham' sponsorship deals to inflate their revenue between 2009 and 2018, something that City strongly deny.

‌



The club have submitted an appeal against the ruling, with a new three-person panel set to hear evidence. City claim to have 'irrefutable evidence' that proves their innocence in the case.

‌



Why Pep Guardiola is returning to Man City for the first time since guilty verdict READ MORE :

FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

Should City's appeal prove unsuccessful and the guilty verdict remains, the club faces a range of potential sanctions, including fines, points deductions, transfer bans, or relegation from the Premier League.

It appears there is still much to unfold before the matter reaches its conclusion. Here's a look at the latest developments:.

‌



Pep Guardiola's return

Former City manager Pep Guardiola will make his maiden return to the Etihad Stadium since his departure, for Wednesday night's Champions League fixture against Paris Saint-Germain. The Spaniard demonstrated his backing for City on social media the day following the confirmation of the guilty verdicts.

He wrote: "I want every single fan to know I am here; more than ever. I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano, CEO], the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters. Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."

In a further show of solidarity, Guardiola will be present at the match against PSG.

‌



View 3 Images Pep Guardiola will be back to show his support (Image: Martin Rickett/PA Wire)

Double jeopardy

City face the prospect of a second sanction should the guilty verdict survive an appeal, with Sky Sports reporting that UEFA are monitoring the situation closely. The governing body will reportedly weigh up whether to intervene once a definitive outcome has been reached.

City were handed a two-year ban from European football back in 2020 after being found guilty of breaching UEFA's financial fair play regulations. The club, however, successfully overturned the ban on appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS ).

‌



The report indicates that the Premier League had access to documents and evidence that were unavailable to UEFA when they were building their own case against City in 2020.

Dressing room reassurances

City's players have been given assurances by the club that 'sporting justice' will prevail, according to the representative of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. The full squad are due to return to training for the first time since the verdict on Thursday, as they gear up for Sunday's Premier League showdown against Liverpool.

Speaking to Radio Napoli Centrale, Enzo Raiola said: "Will the Manchester City chaos change anything? No, nothing will change for us or for Gigio.

‌



"News comes out periodically. The club has spoken with Gigio and everyone is calm.

"Now there are important games against Liverpool and PSG, then sporting justice will take its course. But Gigio has had reassurances from Manchester City."

View 3 Images Gianluigi Donnarumma's agent has spoken about the Man City charges. (Image: Carl Recine, Getty Images)

‌



HMRC investigation

City were reportedly placed under scrutiny by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) in 2018 over potential tax evasion. The Financial Times reports that a civil investigation was launched into the club's tax affairs following the leak of emails by Der Spiegel in the same year.

The report indicates that the investigation was never formally concluded, having been carried out under the Code of Practice 8 framework, which does not encompass suspicions of deliberate fraud.

City sought guidance from external lawyers over the matter. HMRC ultimately took no action following the probe.

‌



Former captain speaks out

Former City skipper Kyle Walker has stated that the memories of his achievements at the club cannot be erased, despite the prospect of titles being stripped. The full-back was an integral figure between 2017 and 2025, claiming the Champions League and 13 domestic honours across his eight years at the club.

Speaking to talkSPORT, he said: "Obviously it doesn't look great. I know it's in an appeal stage so, for me to start commenting on the legal action and everything like that, probably it's not going to do myself justice or anyone involved in it.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



"But, at a personal level, I can say the lads, we spent many and many a great year celebrating many trophies and everything like that and that's something that, whatever happens, they can't take away from us because we've experienced them nights.

"So, whatever will be, will be, and it's just down to the appeal now and what goes from there."

He added: It's something that we probably don't want to talk about because we want to be looked upon as winning them trophies, winning them the right way.

Article continues below

"It's very difficult because we've worked very hard for them, and not just us, I look at the fans as well.

"I look at the fans that have travelled up and down the country, travelled abroad to Istanbul when we won the treble and stuff like that, and they deserve that night as well."

Sports.title: Ex-Man City star Manuel Akanji worried about losing titles despite Kyle Walker's confident blast
Sports.content:
Ex-Man City star Manuel Akanji worried about losing titles despite Kyle Walker's confident blast

Former Manchester City players Manuel Akanji and Kyle Walker have given their reactions after the club were found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules over nine years

View 2 Images Manuel Akanji and Kyle Walker have discussed Manchester City's guilty verdict (Image: Richard Sellers/Getty Images)

Manuel Akanji has admitted he is concerned that his achievements at Manchester City could be taken away from him in the wake of the club being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.

‌



‌



An independent commission ruled that City were guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League. They were found to have used "sham" contracts to disguise funding worth over £830million between 2009 and 2018.

‌



City are still steadfastly protesting their innocence and have launched an appeal. The club have adopted a siege mentality, reassuring their players and staff that they have 'irrefutable evidence' that will clear their name.

‌



As revealed by Mirror Football last week, former manager Pep Guardiola will attend City's Champions League game against Paris Saint-Germain on Tuesday as a show of support. But comments from Akanji, who played for the club between 2022 and 2025, helping them to win two Premier League titles, the Champions League and the FA Cup, has hinted at the mood among City alumni.

Man City charges LIVE: Champions League concern raised as Pep Guardiola return confirmed READ MORE :

Premier League urged to 'resolve' Man City case amicably by Sheikh Mansour dealmaker READ MORE :

"I’m still in touch with a few players, but I don’t know any more than you do. We were told to stay calm, that they had everything under control and nothing major had happened," the Swiss international, who now plays for Inter Milan, said in an interview with Nau.

"I trust the people in charge at Man City that that’s the case. I hope I don’t lose my titles. That would be a bit of a shame. But I’m only seeing it all in the news, too. Who knows what else they might dig up."

‌



The commission has the power to relegate City, impose unlimited fines, points deductions or transfer bans, but is very unlikely to retrospectively strip the club of its titles during the nine-year period. Akanji joined City in 2022, four years after the period the Premier League's allegations relate to.

View 2 Images Kyle Walker and Manuel Akanji were part of a very successful period for Manchester City (Image: Visionhaus/Getty Images)

City chief executive Ferran Soriano addressed club employees in a video after the verdict, claiming the verdict was based on "a single false accusation" which supports "the Premier League's conspiracy theory" against them.

‌



His message promised to "take care of our extended City family" and that appears to have resonated with Walker. The veteran defender played for City from 2017 to 2025 - a period which included six Premier League titles, the Champions League, two FA Cups, the Club World Cup and four Carabao Cups.

Walker told talkSPORT: “Obviously it doesn’t look great. I know it’s in an appeal stage so, for me to start commenting on the legal action and everything like that, probably it’s not going to do myself justice or anyone involved in it.

“But, at a personal level, I can say the lads, we spent many and many a great year celebrating many trophies and everything like that and that’s something that, whatever happens, they can’t take away from us because we’ve experienced them nights.

Article continues below

“So, whatever will be, will be, and it’s just down to the appeal now and what goes from there.”

Sports.title: Gary Neville was robbed – Pundit Ballon d'Or has turned into glorified popularity contest
Sports.content:
Gary Neville was robbed – Pundit Ballon d'Or has turned into glorified popularity contest

Gary Neville is the best football pundit in the country and if you disagree you have a very skewed view of what punditry is

View 3 Images Gary Neville deserved to win the inaugural Pundit Ballon d'Or (Image: Getty Images)

So, the votes have been tallied in Mirror Football's inaugural 'Pundit Ballon d'Or', and we officially have our grand finale. It's Roy Keane versus Ian Wright.

‌



‌



The terrifying, perpetually unimpressed Manchester United legend against the joyously optimistic Arsenal icon. It's a blockbuster match-up. There's just one massive, glaring problem: you've all voted for the wrong people.

‌



The whole competition was ruined in the semi-finals, when you lot eliminated the one man who actually deserved to win it: Gary Alexander Neville.

‌



The fact that G-Nev was dumped out in the final four was an absolute travesty and it's time we had a serious conversation about what makes a great pundit - and why the electorate lost their collective minds.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



To understand why Neville was robbed, we have to ask a fundamental question: what actually makes a good football pundit? For my money, it boils down to two distinct pillars: analysis and entertainment. Crucially, they have to arrive in that exact order.

Primarily, a pundit's job is to educate. It's to take a messy, chaotic 45 minutes of football, freeze it, dissect it, and point out the tiny, vital details the rest of us missed while we were screaming at the referee. We need experts to teach us something new, explain the broader context, and sprinkle snippets of insightful gold dust throughout the broadcast. We do not need a highly-paid ex-pro just to state the bleeding obvious... like so many of them do.

Entertainment, of course, is essential. It's TV, after all. We want to laugh, cheer, and enjoy ourselves. But pure entertainment without real tactical insight is as pointless a game as playing count the hairs on Alan Shearer's head.

‌



If we just wanted loud, boisterous vibes, we'd stick a microphone in front of Big John down the pub, or replace half-time analysis with 15 minutes of studio bantz set to a constant soundtrack of Micah Richards' booming cackle. We don't need comedians masquerading as analysts - we need experts who can actually spot and explain the mechanics of the game.

Which brings us to our two finalists. Look, I get why Keane and Wright made the showpiece. The latter bounds into the studio with the infectious, tail-wagging energy of a golden retriever. And the former can be absolutely box office - the deadpan, grumpy grandad at Christmas who might flip the Monopoly board if you look at him funny. They make fantastic TV.

View 3 Images Roy Keane and Ian Wright are popular - but popularity does not necessarily make a great pundit (Image: Getty)

‌



But are they top-tier pundits? Not really. They are both inherently average at the actual job of analysis.

When either of them starts talking during a half-time break, you don't actually have to listen. You already know what's coming. We don't need them to tell us how brilliantly Manchester City have attacked when they are 4-0 up, or how shaky Destiny Udogie looks when Tottenham are imploding. It's entertaining, sure, but very rarely chin-scratching or thought-provoking.

Which brings us back to the rightful champion. Gary Neville - alongside Jamie Carragher, whose elimination in the round of 16 remains a crime in itself - is one of the very few who genuinely strikes the perfect balance.

‌



Is he biased? Absolutely. Can he be a little insufferable? Without a doubt. But whether you like him or lump him, Neville actually does the job. He spots the subtle tactical tweaks we completely miss from the sofa and translates complex match dynamics into plain English.

View 3 Images Gary Neville offers expert insight in an entertaining way like few others - if any - do (Image: James Gill - Danehouse, Getty Images)

When a Roy Keane says: "That's a dreadful shot," a Gary Neville explains: "You can see he leans back a fraction because he expects the centre-back to clatter into him - that's why he skews it." It's night and day. Chalk and cheese. The Champions League and the Johnstone's Paint Trophy.

‌



Neville doesn't drone on about the obvious - he tells you things you didn't know, but definitely should. And crucially, he does it all while being wildly entertaining. He's sharp, cohesive, and unafraid to say controversial things. His gloriously spiky, love-hate squabbling with Carragher is modern TV gold. He can be furious, effusive, or funny - but he is always, always worth listening to. If a pundit isn't worth listening to, they aren't a good pundit.

By crowning a 'Keano' or a 'Wrighty', the Pundit Ballon d'Or will officially become a glorified popularity contest. If the prompt was "Who is your favourite bloke to watch the footy with?", then fine - both finalists have a case.

But if we're talking about the best pundit? The one who actually masters the art of football analysis? Keane and Wright shouldn't be anywhere near the final, let alone the trophy. You voted with your hearts, not your heads. Gary Neville is the true, uncrowned king of the gogglebox, and deep down, you all know it.

Sports.title: Man City charges: Agent speaks out, punishment agreement, UEFA consider action
Sports.content:
Manchester City are still waiting to discover their punishment for being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules, though they have appealed the decision

Hello and welcome to Mirror Football's live blog on Wednesday, October 7, where we will bring you the latest after an independent commission found Manchester City guilty of breaking Premier League rules in a strongly-worded report released last week.

City were found to have inflated revenue by more than £830million over a nine-season period between 2009-10 and 2017-18. However, the Etihad club have since appealed against the decision and continue to deny any wrongdoing.

However, it is being reported that Premier League clubs believe City should be expelled from the top flight next season if their appeal against the financial charges fails. That’s according to Sky Sports, who are reporting that clubs in the top-flight believe a points deduction would not be sufficient if it resulted in City spending just one season outside the Premier League.

UEFA are also believed to be monitoring developments and will wait until the end of the Premier League's disciplinary process before deciding whether to take any potential action against City.

The Financial Times is reporting that HMRC probed City in 2018 over whether it used complex arrangements to underpay tax. The report claims a civil investigation into the club’s tax affairs followed the publication of leaked internal emails by Der Spiegel in 2018. The Financial Times says Man City and HMRC declined to comment.

And former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher believes City should face a multi-year punishment for their financial misdemeanours. There is still much discussion about potential outcomes, so stay right here for all of the latest...

Sports.title: Alcaraz: Tennis schedule 'pushing players too much'
Sports.content:
Carlos Alcaraz believes tennis' relentless schedule is "going in the wrong direction" and feels players are being "pushed" to feature in too many tournaments.

The world No 3, who will play his Shanghai Masters opener on Saturday, was speaking two days after successfully defending the Japan Open for his third title of an injury-hit year which saw him miss four and a half months between April and August with a wrist issue.

World No 1 Jannik Sinner announced this week that he has ended his season early due to a knee problem.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports commentator Liam Broady says it is a blow to the game that Sinner's 2026 has ended prematurely

Alcaraz said: "One of the reasons we had to see the players who are getting injured, they [ATP officials] are pushing us too much out of the line sometimes to play a lot of tournaments, to play a lot of matches.

"It's getting in the wrong direction.

"I just wish Jannik the best for these months, just to be in good shape for the next season.

"Hopefully see him soon, but they have to see a little bit what's going on on the tour along with the players."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Alcaraz's victory over Jiri Lehecka in the final of the Japan Open

Djokovic: Sinner has to think long term

Sinner has not played since beating Alexander Zverev in the Wimbledon final in July.

Novak Djokovic, who claimed his 102nd career title at the China Open on Tuesday, said of the Italian calling time on his 2026 campaign: "He's been the best player in the world, been a dominant force for the last couple of years along with Carlos [Alcaraz].

"For sure tennis misses him but at the same time he has to think long term.

"That's smart because as someone that always tried to have the big picture ‌in my mind, I really support that kind of thinking and mindset.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sinner took to social media to let fans know his season is over as he looks to recover from a knee issue

"It's important that you give yourself more years to your career, so you have more chances to accomplish all of your ⁠objectives.

"If you're away from the tour for so long and then make a comeback, you have to deal with more things than you normally have to deal with. You're evaluating with your team constantly.

"When you get the green light to be able to compete, then it's mental. You're on the court and you're thinking: 'Am I really completely healed and free to make this run?'

"For him if it's a knee, it's affecting everything, affecting every single movement."

Sports.title: Rabada misses out on South Africa side for first Test vs Australia
Sports.content:
South Africa fast bowler Kagiso Rabada misses out on ‌the first Test of the three-match series against Australia in Durban as he continues to recover from a hamstring injury suffered in June.

Naming their side for the series opener, which starts on Friday - live on Sky Sports Cricket from 7.30am (play starts 8.30am) - South Africa have instead opted for two spinners, Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj, while Anrich Nortje is a surprise selection.

Rabada trained with the team at Kingsmead on Thursday, and it's hopeful he'll still have a part to play in the second and third Tests, the first of which in Gqeberha starts on October 18.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player In 2018, footage emerged of Australia opener Cameron Bancroft using a foreign object to alter the condition of the ball against South Africa, which was later revealed to be sandpaper

"It ‌wasn't an easy decision," South Africa captain Temba Bavuma said on Thursday. "I think we did go the conservative route, to give him a couple ​of extra days to get closer to where he can be at 100 per cent fitness.

"Obviously for us, as ⁠soon as he gets the green ⁠light from the medical team, we expect him to be in the starting lineup."

As for the recall of 32-year-old pacer Nortje, more than three years since he last played first-class cricket, Bavuma said: "It's hard to ignore his X factor.

Image: Anrich Nortje last played Test cricket for South Africa in March 2023

"There aren't many guys around who are bowling 150 (kph) plus. And I think as a batter that's not something that I ⁠would look forward to."

Bavuma added on the selection of both Harmer and Maharaj: "Those ​spin twins, if I can call them that, have added another ​dimension to our bowling attack.

"As much as we've always been about ⁠fast bowling, when conditions have allowed for spinners to come into the game they've been able to play an effective role.

"If the conditions play that way, the whole team ⁠is confident in that they can put the ​opposition under pressure. I think there's a healthy competition between them ​so that always helps."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Former South Africa captain Shaun Pollock joined Nasser and Athers to discuss South Africa's upcoming series against Australia and described his experience working on the infamous 'Sandpapergate' Test Match in 2018.

Australia toy with controversial selection of Maddinson

Australia, still yet to name their team for the first Test, are toying with their own bold selection and the potential recall of batter Nic Maddinson.

Maddinson played three Test matches for Australia in late 2016, averaging 6.75, with his career since stalled by injury, mental health issues, and then a testicular cancer diagnosis that sidelined him for most of last year.

As a result, the 34-year-old hasn't played a first-class match since March 2025, but it was he who got the nod last week as a late addition to the touring squad due to injuries to Cameron Green and Josh Inglis.

Former Australian opener Matthew Hayden was critical of the call up, saying on the All Over Bar The Cricket podcast: "We are promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we've seen in a generation of cricket.

"And if we continue to lay that out and expect a bloke averaging 35 is going to average 55 in Test match cricket, then [selectors] George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide, you are dreaming.

"I will just put it that simply. You are frigging dreaming. You are piling up this dog s*** explanation and, in my opinion, disrespecting first-class cricket.

"You should be picking guys averaging 45 or more, and you can't, because they don't want to play. They don't want to play this version of the game.

"Mitch Marsh is a good example. He is making millions of dollars playing cricket all over the world for franchises. This is the fundamental problem we have."

Watch the first Test between South Africa and Australia live on Sky Sports Cricket from Friday (7.30am on air, 8.30am first ball). Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract.

Sports.title: Guardiola set to attend Man City's first home game since guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola is expected to attend next week's Champions League match against Paris Saint-Germain, marking his first appearance at the Etihad Stadium since departing last summer.

His visit coincides with a turbulent period for the club, which were found guilty of multiple Premier League financial rule breaches following a long-running investigation - a decision City have appealed. The club deny all the charges against them.

Guardiola, who steered the club to six Premier League titles and a Champions League during a decorated decade in charge, publicly backed City's board and supporters after the ruling, stating he remains entirely behind the team.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Neville gives his thoughts on a potential punishment for Manchester City after they were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission. City deny all charges and have lodged an appeal

He is expected to be in attendance on October 14 when Enzo Maresca's side takes on Paris Saint-Germain, shortly after City resume their domestic campaign away at Liverpool, live on Sky Sports.

Lineker urges Manchester City to 'own it' and accept punishment

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Lineker gives his thoughts on Manchester City after an independent commission found them guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18. Man City deny all charges and have lodged an appeal

Gary Lineker called on Manchester City to "own" and "accept whatever punishment" they are given for the "good of the game".

City have been accused of breaking financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18. An independent commission concluded that more than £830m of owner funding was used to inflate revenues and enable the club to comply with Premier League and UEFA regulations through a series of "sham" arrangements. The club have protested their innocence and appealed.

"Obviously, it looks really bad for Manchester City, and bad for the game, too," former England captain Lineker said.

Liverpool

Manchester City Sunday 11th October 4:00pm Kick off 4:30pm

"When they talk about the 'Premier League conspiracy theories', you just think to yourself, 'well, this is actually the last thing in the world that the Premier League would want'.

"So, I'd love to see Man City now just own it and just say, 'okay, we got it wrong but for the good of the game, we'll accept it and we'll accept whatever punishment comes our way and we'll carry on'.

"That would be a blessing and save their face a little bit at the moment, although it doesn't look likely."

Pressed as to whether City should be stripped of the three league titles they won during that period, 65-year-old Lineker, who was speaking at a Leaders Week conference at Stamford Bridge, said: "I wouldn't be surprised if it goes down that route. But who suffers from that? The players and the fans."

Meanwhile, Kyle Walker, who spent eight years at Manchester City - winning the Champions League as well as 12 major domestic honours - before his departure in 2025, said the players will always have the memories of their achievements "whatever happens".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ahead of Sunday's showdown, we look back at some of the most memorable Premier League moments between Liverpool and Manchester City

Speaking on talkSPORT, Burnley right-back Walker said: "Obviously it doesn't look great. I know it's in an appeal stage so, for me to start commenting on the legal action and everything like that, probably it's not going to do myself justice or anyone involved in it.

"But, at a personal level, I can say the lads, we spent many and many a great year celebrating many trophies and that's something that, whatever happens, they can't take away from us because we've experienced them nights."

Walker admitted it is not an easy subject for former City players to discuss.

The 36-year-old added: "It's something that we probably don't want to talk about because we want to be looked upon as winning them trophies and winning them the right way.

"It's very difficult because we've worked very hard for them, and not just us, I look at the fans that have travelled up and down the country, travelled abroad to Istanbul when we won the treble, and they deserve that night as well."

A City statement released last Friday read: "The club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions relating to this case."

Sports.title: Fury vs Joshua key questions: What we know and what we don't
Sports.content:
Sky Sports considers the key questions ahead of the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua mega-fight.

It's happening?

It is happening. After years of waiting, nursing a rivalry for near enough a decade, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will fight on December 11 at the Principality stadium in Cardiff.

Why have we waited so long?

Fury and Joshua, both British heavyweights, both former world champions, have long been linked to fighting. But they held off from actually boxing, unable to come to an agreement. They didn't manage to make the contest for the undisputed crown when they were both reigning champions and then lost their titles to Oleksandr Usyk.

Even the negotiations to finally reach this moment, in the autumn of their respective careers, have been fraught, with Madison Square Garden emerging as a potential venue before the bout was eventually set for the Principality stadium.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tyson Fury was quick to shut down any idea that Anthony Joshua is his 'landlord'!

Why are promoters feuding?

The vast resources of Saudi financier Turki Alalshikh has brought this fight together and it was announced that Alalshikh's The Ring and American combat sports promoter Dana White were staging the contest.

However Eddie Hearn, who promotes Joshua, has publicly claimed the American cannot be involved.

But with tickets going on sale on Friday it's inconceivable that promotional wrangling could torpedo the fight. It remains on.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Anthony Joshua came up with the perfect response to Tyson Fury during their press conference ahead of their fight on December 11.

What time will the ringwalks be?

To cater for an international audience, notably in the US, the main event ringwalks are expected to take place at 1am local time with the stadium remaining opening afterwards until 3.30am.

Is there a world title on the line?

It's been reported that the WBA will put their 'super' heavyweight world championship, the belt vacated by Oleksandr Usyk, on the line even though they already have a 'regular' champion in Murat Gassiev. Sky Sports has contacted the WBA for confirmation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tyson Fury reveals to AJ how he plans to beat him on December 11!

Who's on the undercard?

This has not yet been set. For the time being we can only speculate.

What's the musical act?

We know that there will be a musical act shortly before the main event, and that it won't be Dua Lipa, but we don't know who it will be.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tyson Fury joined Lennox Lewis, Frank Bruno & Scott Welch in giving Anthony Joshua words of wisdom just after he had won gold at London 2012, and was looking to turn over to the professional ranks.

Will there be a second fight?

This is a one-fight deal with no rematch clause in the contract. So a second bout is not guaranteed, but that doesn't mean one can't be negotiated. Public demand for it though will depend on what happens in this first fight.

Who will win?

Well, we'll have a better idea around 1.30am on December 12. Fury and Joshua at their peak offered a fascinating blend of styles. In recent bouts Fury has appeared to be the better preserved of the pair but Joshua has always been a very heavy puncher indeed. There's only one way to find out…

Sports.title: James: England must keep looking forward in quest for World Cup place
Sports.content:
Lauren James says England cannot do anything about the situation they find themselves in and just need to beat Greece in their play-off double-header in an effort to secure their place at next summer’s World Cup.

England face Greece home and away after finishing second in qualifying Group 3 behind Spain on goal difference.

If they progress past Greece, Sarina Wiegman's side will face the winner of the Slovakia vs Ukraine tie, with the team that comes through that securing qualification for next summer's World Cup in Brazil.

"We can't change what happened and that's where we are now," James told Sky Sports News.

"I think we have to just try to look forward to win these games.

"That's always our goal at the end of the day, and the position we're in at the moment is, we have to win in order to get to somewhere.

"The World Cup's a massive tournament that you always want to be a part of and it's everyone's dream from a little kid.

"So, to go there and get another opportunity again, it's obviously something we're all trying to aim for."

James, who signed a new contract earlier this year, is in good form at club level, with second-placed Chelsea dropping just two points from five league games this season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at some of Lauren James best goals for Chelsea in the Women's Super League

But the forward, who was Chelsea's player of the year in 2024, insists her best is still to come.

"I'm always looking forward to coming into camp with England and getting another opportunity to play games for the country," said James.

"I think it always helps massively when you're doing well with your club, which obviously is why you get called up for your country. Hopefully I can just build the momentum and keep going.

Image: Lauren James celebrates after scoring against Manchester United

"Every time I put on a shirt, whether it's for club or country, I always want to just show what I'm made of.

"The more you play, the more you have rhythm and I like to just play free. And I think the best is still yet to come.

"I'm just trying to enjoy my football and look forward to the things that are coming up."

Potter was 'really surprised' by England call

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lexi Potter lauded the impact of her Chelsea midfield partner Keira Walsh following her first England call up

Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter admits she was "surprised" to earn her first England call-up ahead for the World Cup play-off fixtures.

The 20-year-old has enjoyed a bright start to the campaign after being given a run of starts under Blues boss Sonia Bompastor.

Potter has played a part in all four of Chelsea's victories this season in the Women's Super League and got herself on the scoresheet in a 2-0 win over Birmingham last month.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Pitch to Pod, Nikita Parris and Jordan Nobbs discuss Lexi Potter's 'mature' WSL performance

The youngster learned of her call-up while in her bedroom at her family home, before sharing her delight with her mother.

"I've been really lucky and grateful for the opportunities I've been given at Chelsea and when I got the call, I was really surprised," Potter said.

"I like to stay focused every day and be the best version of myself and don't like to think too far ahead.

"I was at home, I still live at home so I was just in my room watching my phone a bit and then when I got the call I was really happy and went downstairs and told my mum and she was really proud of me."

Sports.title: 'Void of leaders' - The problems for bottom-side Spurs after winless start
Sports.content:
When Aston Villa went 1-0 up in north London, it felt inevitable that Tottenham would head into the international break winless in the Premier League.

That's because it has been nearly two years since Spurs have won a match after conceding the opening goal in any competition. Last month's 3-2 home loss to Villa was the 47th game in this dismal run (D11 L36).

"It is a worry, certainly at home because that's where you need the minerals," former Tottenham boss Tim Sherwood told a special Sky Sports Spurs podcast.

"That's where you need the characters and leaders to come forward, and at the moment, they're void of any leaders and characters.

"I'm not sure there's anyone really losing their head or galvanising the players to try and arrest [it], which is a poor trend, in not fighting back from losing positions.

"The manager is. He certainly looks like he doesn't lack in any passion. But you need that within the pitch and within the dressing room and within the training pitch every single day, and I'm not sure the characters are there."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On a special Sky Sports podcast, Tim Sherwood and Michael Bridge believe Spurs have a lack of leaders in the side

With Spurs accumulating the fewest points (18) among ever-present Premier League sides in 2026, Sky Sports News' Tottenham reporter Michael Bridge aired his concerns over leadership too.

He said: "When Roberto De Zerbi chose his five captains [Micky van de Ven, Pedro Porro, Ben Davies, James Maddison and Archie Gray], and I asked him in the press conference, Andy Robertson wasn't one of the five.

"Archie Gray was, but Archie Gray's not going to be in the team much, so I am a little bit worried about leadership in that camp.

"How many of the players are really going to grab each other by the scruff of the neck?

"Cristian Romero maybe went too far in terms of aggression, but there were times when you did want him on your side, so I need to see a bit more aggression from some of these players as well."

Sherwood unimpressed by new signings

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On a special Spurs Sky Sports podcast, former manager Tim Sherwood questions the club's latest signings

A winless start to the Premier League season has left Tottenham bottom of the table, and their worst start to a Premier League season after five games has already raised questions over Spurs' lavish summer spending.

So, have any of the 10 new players that cost over £330m impressed Sherwood?

"No, no one," he insisted. "I can't say anyone's really impressed me, and anyone would have done a better job than anyone who was there last season.

"They've underachieved, they really have. We always judge on results, so I don't look at any individual player and think, 'Well, you're coming out of some credit here', because the team's losing, and I'm not sure there's been any outstanding performers."

Manchester United

Tottenham Hotspur Saturday 10th October 5:00pm Kick off 5:30pm

The lack of success from Spurs' signings before this summer worries Sherwood about the latest recruits.

"Probably the last four or five years, the track record of Tottenham signings has not been fantastic," he said.

"It's been a very long time since they've made a decent signing. Now, I'm not saying they're poor signings; I'm saying that they haven't done it yet, and there's still a lot of time to be able to get some confidence and show what they can really do.

"We've seen them in fits and starts and little cameos for other teams, but it's a different kettle of fish playing for Tottenham."

He added: "I've seen more nos than yeses at the moment over the last five years in the transfer market.

"I think the best signing they've made in recent history would have to be (Heung-Min) Son - and we're going way back there! We're talking about a real success.

"Maybe (Dejan) Kulusevski, but then he's picked up the injury. But other than that, I can't say there have been too many outstanding successes in the transfer market.

"But it's up to Roberto De Zerbi to develop them players, and hopefully some of these players we've seen in recent years can be unrecognisable."

'Spurs still need a striker'

With Spurs having scored just two league goals, the spotlight for Bridge is on Omar Marmoush to deliver.

The summer signing from Man City is yet to score in his first five Spurs appearances in all competitions, having missed one big chance and had two shots on target from his 10 attempts.

Bridge said: "I think the one for me is Omar Marmoush. How good is this guy?

"I really liked glimpses of him for City, but they were only glimpses; clearly a very talented player. He really showed it in the Bundesliga [with Eintracht Frankfurt].

"But can he do it consistently for Tottenham Hotspur, where he's going to be given a clear run of games.

"Were Tottenham right to spend as they did on Savio and Marmoush? So the jury's going to be out with these players."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' Michael Bridge takes a look at the problems at Spurs

With Dominic Solanke struggling for form and Richarlison frozen out against the backdrop of Spurs academy graduate Will Lankshear scoring freely in the Championship, Spurs' firepower is a problem.

Bridge said: "I think they need a striker - an actual number nine - but how many are there out there?

"It doesn't help that Will Lankshear is scoring every week for Middlesbrough because he looks like a proper old-fashioned centre-forward and he's young and English. That's my worry.

"I'm also not one hundred per cent sure if Antonin Kinsky is a Tottenham number one for years to come.

"If you've spent that amount of money and you still need, for me, a goalkeeper and a number nine, then there's still a way to go."

Is De Zerbi under pressure?

Tottenham aim for their first league win of the season at Manchester United on Saturday, live on Sky Sports.

But should their winless run continue, then Roberto De Zerbi would become just the second Spurs boss in Premier League history to fail to win any of the opening six games of a campaign.

Juande Ramos was the first, and he was sacked after Spurs had two points from eight games. But both Sherwood and Bridge are confident that De Zerbi will not follow the same fate as the Spaniard.

Spurs' games before November international break Saturday: Man Utd (A) - live on Sky Sports

Oct 19: Coventry (H) - live on Sky Sports

Oct 24: Chelsea (A) - live on Sky Sports

Oct 31: Crystal Palace (H) - live on Sky Sports

Nov 7: Leeds (A)

Ex-Spurs boss Sherwood said: "I'm not sure he's under pressure because they've given him everything he wanted, so they must have full trust in him.

"He's proven that he's a very good Premier League manager, albeit he's never been at a club the size of Tottenham Hotspur, with the scrutiny which is upon the club, but he looks like a character who can handle that scrutiny, and he just needs a win."

Bridge said: "I don't think Roberto De Zerbi is under much pressure at all.

"He was tracked by the club for some time. He's on a very good and long contract, and unless he's the one that initiates the departure, I don't see any change for the foreseeable."

But what has to change is Spurs' bouncebackability in games if De Zerbi is to ensure the pressure does not mount.

Sports.title: FIA introducing measures to avoid ‘software bug’ chaos repeat
Sports.content:
The FIA will introduce further changes to wet-weather engine software from the United States Grand Prix after completing a review into the "software bug" that further delayed the start of last week's rain-hit race in Malaysia.

Several cars slowed or briefly stopped on the rain-hit laps to the grid last Sunday due to what the governing body after the race described as an "unprecedented combination" related to both the slow speed the cars were travelling in the wet and the sector configuration of the Sepang lap.

The start procedure was abandoned and the Grand Prix eventually started 48 minutes later after a software update was issued by the FIA to all teams and power-unit manufacturers.

Having promised an investigation into what happened, the FIA delivered its findings and next steps on Thursday ahead of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.

"The review concluded that some cars running on low engine RPM in certain circuit sectors where a 250kW power reduction was applied experienced a loss of power beyond the original intent and that could not be recovered in those sectors," read the statement.

"As a result, the configuration established for the Sepang event will be reinstated for the Singapore Grand Prix should similar weather conditions be expected. Additionally, a further update to the wet weather software will be released for the United States Grand Prix on October 25.

"The review also recommended that measures would be implemented for testing of the software, recognising that opportunities for testing are limited, to make it robust as possible.

"The FIA , together with the teams and Power Unit Manufacturers (PUMs), will continue to strengthen Power Unit software testing and verification capabilities, enhancing the overall validation process through independent assessment and collaborative feedback, including input from the supplier of the standardised Electronics Control Unit (ECU)."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the Sepang International Circuit

The governing body also dismissed suggestions that there had not been testing of the wet-weather software before the issues at Sepang.

"The FIA would like to address comments suggesting that the software had not been tested prior to its deployment," the statement added.

"Before implementation, teams and Power Unit manufacturers conducted simulation exercises to validate the software package, which was subsequently tested in full-scale running during Free Practice 1 sessions at both the Belgian Grand Prix and the Dutch Grand Prix."

The governing body also detailed the timings for how the issues in Sepang were resolved, confirming its technical team had identified the cause of the issue and released software update configurations to teams and power-unit providers within five minutes of the race-start suspension.

Sports.title: Pettersen bounces back on LET return as England's Humphreys moves second
Sports.content:
Suzann Pettersen marked her first round on the Ladies European Tour in four years with an even-par 72 at the Aramco Korea Championship as England's Lily May Humphreys earned a share of second place.

Pettersen, 45, retired after sinking the winning putt for Team Europe in the 2019 Solheim Cup at Gleneagles, with her only appearance since the 2022 Aramco Team Series event in Jeddah.

The Norwegian - who captained Europe at the 2023 and 2024 Solheim Cups - was three over after six holes in South Korea, bogeying the third and double bogeying the sixth.

But the two-time major winner rallied with birdies at eight, 13 and 15 - picking up a shot at the last of those holes with a monster putt - and went bogey-free on her back nine.

Image: Pettersen marked her first round on the Ladies European Tour in four years with an even-par 72

Humphreys: I had quite a lot of good fortune go my way

Humphreys - who won her sole Ladies European Tour title to date at the 2023 Joburg Ladies Open - carded a five-under 67 to sit one shot behind leader Patricie Mackova.

Like Pettersen, the 24-year-old dropped shots at three and six, but she registered five birdies as well as an eagle at the par-five 13th to match the rounds of Miyu Yamashita, Sarah Kemp and Olivia Cowan.

Humphreys said: "I played very nicely and I had quite a lot of good fortune go my way which you need around here to shoot a low number. The course doesn't give you anything. You need to earn every birdie and some pars.

"I holed an insane amount of long putts and the hole-out for eagle which was a nice way to start the afternoon"

Sports.title: Khaldoon al-Mubarak: the tightrope walker who made rare misstep over City charges
Sports.content:
No one better understands the precarious tightrope Abu Dhabi walks when it tries to balance its relationships with western Europe while weighing the complex geopolitics of the Gulf region than Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. He was eight when his father, ambassador Khalifa Ahmed Abdel Aziz al-Mubarak, left the family Paris apartment for work on 9 February 1984 and was assassinated on the street in cold blood by a Palestinian terrorist.

And no one outside the emirate’s royal family could be more wrapped up in the project of making and maintaining Abu Dhabi as a significant and secure world power and the dominant member of the United Arab Emirates, a nation state still only 55 years old. His paternal grandfather, Ahmad Bin Abdul Aziz al-Mubarak, was chair of Abu Dhabi’s Sharia judicial department and senior adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan al-Nahyan, the founding president of the UAE. As such, Ahmad Bin Abdul Aziz was the James Madison of the UAE (the founding father, not the Spurs player) in that he crafted the Islamic legal framework of the new nation in the 1970s.

Khaldoon’s father was assassinated by a group led by Abu Nidal which, according to the CIA, was “the most dangerous and effective of all terrorist groups [and] the best organized of the radical Palestinian terrorist groups” before the emergence of Hamas. The murder was justified in a phone call saying that the UAE “had expelled Palestinian and Arab residents and was linked with American imperialism”. In essence, they were accused of being too soft on the west, not radical enough for Palestinians.

Both al-Mubarak’s grandfather and father have streets named after them in Abu Dhabi, with his father honoured as a martyr of the state. It is fair to say the City chair has honoured the family tradition as chief adviser to the UAE president and Abu Dhabi ruler, Sheikh Mohamed Bin Zayed al-Nahyan, for whom he first worked after graduating from Tufts University in Massachusetts. Given his father’s martyrdom, the royal family is said to have looked out for al-Mubarak as a quasi-adopted son. According to a source in the Financial Times, al-Mubarak is “diplomatically in charge of the UK file as well as the China file … and he’s the main liaison with the US administration” and has diplomatic immunity in the UK. That said, he appears to have made a rare misstep with his belligerent tone on Manchester City

According to Manchester City’s lawyer Simon Cliff, it was al-Mubarak who dictated the aggressive confrontational stance City have taken with football authorities. As far back as 2014, when City were fighting their first Uefa charge, Cliff wrote, according to leaked documents first published by Der Spiegel: “Khaldoon says he would rather spend £30m on the 50 best lawyers in the world and sue them [Uefa] for the next ten years than agree a financial penalty.”

View image in fullscreen Khaldoon al-Mubarak with Pep Guardiola after Manchester City’s Premier League title win in 2021-22. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

He backed down on that occasion, along with the co-accused Paris Saint-Germain, both clubs agreeing a small fine and minor transfer restrictions with Uefa. It is extraordinary that City kept fighting thereafter, whereas the Qatar-owned PSG accepted their punishment, cozied up to Uefa – with the club’s president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, becoming chair of the European Club Association (now European Football Clubs) and chief opponent of the breakaway Super League – and built the most exciting and successful team in Europe, bringing admiration for the Qatari brand among observers willing to ignore human rights abuses. Al-Mubarak, in fighting to the end with City, appears to have broken an ambassador’s cardinal law: don’t embarrass your boss. Should City lose their appeal against an independent commission’s finding that they were guilty of multiple breaches of financial rules, al-Mubarak may be instructed to organise the sale of the club.

“I’m sure that’s the case with Man City,” says Christopher Davidson, author of Abu Dhabi, Oil and Beyond. “More than that, I’ve been told by some [in Abu Dhabi] that it will be the case. I can’t see any reason why they would stick around and try to rebuild the reputation after this. It’s embarrassing the royal family now. I can’t think of any example where things have gone wrong [for Abu Dhabi] and they’ve just kept plugging money into it. I think they’ll play out the appeal – nothing to lose with that – but once that’s done, it’s all about how to get out before the owners are declared unfit, a far worse outcome. There are very clever people involved in Abu Dhabi who I’m led to believe will very strongly counsel this needs to be a quiet retreat because the longer they stay in the game, the more damaging it is and it will unravel any kind of soft power Abu Dhabi managed to gain.”

In June al-Mubarak said “these sorts of jewels, you don’t sell” and that there was “only intention to keep growing this”. As for the wider threat to UK-Abu Dhabi relations, Davidson believes it is overstated. “Some of the reporting perhaps has portrayed Abu Dhabi as a bit monolithic. There are entire big and growing sections of Abu Dhabi state economy that are outside al-Mubarak’s remit. Some of Abu Dhabi’s biggest investments in the UK in recent years have been in renewable energy and the windfarms of Scotland from Masdar energy, which is chaired by Sultan al-Jaber, who’s another key lieutenant of the ruler.”

Davidson also cites the International Holding Company (IHC), which has huge biotech, shipping, healthcare and retail investments in the UK, including the Ivy restaurants, and is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy ruler of Abu Dhabi and brother of the UAE president and Sheikh Mansour. “It’s inconceivable that these investments would be withdrawn,” says Davidson.

View image in fullscreen Khaldoon al-Mubarak (left) alongside City owner Sheikh Mansour at the then City of Manchester Stadium in August 2010. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/Reuters

In May this year the UK signed a free trade agreement with Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE which it said could be worth £3.7bn a year to the UK economy. “The UAE was a major force behind getting that and it was a major accomplishment on both sides, so there’s no prospect any of this is going to be interfered with,” Davidson says.

Al-Mubarak will probably emerge from this fiasco largely untarnished, because City are a tiny part of his portfolio. “He can’t possibly have known what’s going on in every part of his empire,” says Davidson. “My gut feeling would be that it’s the layers below him. It’s all about your legal counsel. I think the Qataris had very clever people working for them. This has been a case of poor advice being given to the senior Emiratis involved, a misreading of UK politics and a misreading of the Premier League and its bigger picture as a rules-based institution.

“I think the statements al-Mubarak has made, including the one early last summer that ‘We will not sell’ are the product of poor advice delivered to him and ultimately to Sheikh Mansour. It may be important to us in the UK but Man City has been a peripheral project [for Abu Dhabi].”

Sports.title: Women’s Super League faces wait until 2029 for full-time referees despite funding boost
Sports.content:
Women’s Super League clubs have agreed to a major funding increase for match officials but the wait for full-time referees in the English top tier is set to continue until 2029, the Guardian has learned.

The extra investment, decided at the latest WSL Football board meeting, will focus on enhancing officials’ education, analysis and physical performance, it is understood.

Although none of the parties involved are ruling out progressing to full-time WSL referees earlier, 2029-30 is the campaign that has been agreed for when the officials will be employed by Pro Ref, the official body, formerly known as PGMOL, responsible for match officials across English professional football.

Calls for fully professional WSL match officials have grown since the English women’s top tier became full-time for players in 2018-19 and more so since the top two divisions were taken over by the independent WSL Football in 2024. A further three-year wait is likely to divide opinion.

According to multiple sources, WSL and WSL 2 clubs – the primary shareholders of WSL Football – were told at the all-club meeting this month of the three-year funding plan to transition to full-time match officials for the 2029-30 campaign. Insiders have told the Guardian there was initially a mixed response, with some clubs hoping the move would happen sooner, before the funding plan was voted on and approved.

One WSL club’s senior executive, who did not want to be named, told the Guardian it was “about time” that there was a specific timeframe but that they were disappointed it was three seasons away.

Another senior WSL club source welcomed the commitment to funding the education and training needed to improve the quality of officiating.

At the board meeting, it is believed clubs the league and clubs discussed balancing the desire to have full-time officials as quickly as possible with a need to enhance standards and provisions.

Many of the officials working in the WSL hold other full-time or part-time jobs. It is understood the new deal followed extensive discussions between WSL Football, the Foootball Association and Pro Ref.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The WSL has repeatedly stated its “intention” to move to having full-time officials but this is believed to be the first time a timeline has been agreed.

In 2021, the FA said it had no immediate plans to introduce full-time referees to the top two divisions of English women’s football.Referees in the English men’s game became full-time professionals in 2001 across the Premier League and the EFL.

There is a seat for a WSL representative on the Pro Ref board for the first time this season, after the launch of Pro Ref this summer, giving the WSL a greater say in the decision-making processes, alongside Premier League and EFL representatives.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta’s new contract reflects where the power now lies at Arsenal | Ed Aarons
Sports.content:
If anyone doubts Mikel Arteta’s status as No 1 at Arsenal in the week he committed his future to the club until 2030, just ask Win the dog. The chocolate labrador who played a starring role in the celebrations when Arsenal were crowned Premier League champions in May has become part of the family at the training ground in Hertfordshire since being introduced by Arteta in May 2023.

Kai Havertz, David Raya and Mikel Merino, who issues commands in Spanish and has spoken about spending time with Win when out for three months with a foot injury, are particular favourites. But, according to sources close to Win, a therapy dog trained not to bark, there is no contest when it comes to her preferred human: Arteta.

The manager is understood to have taken Win home for Christmas last year, having been instrumental in her arrival a few days after his side had finished as runners-up to Manchester City for the first time. Cuddly replicas are available in the club shop. The real version spends most days at Arsenal’s training centre, with her primary carer a full-time member of staff based there.

“I carefully chose the dog and in my opinion it’s the perfect representative of who we are right now,” said Arteta in 2023. “Win needs accountability from us because we have to look after her as well; her emotions and what she needs.”

It is an example of Arteta’s attention to detail that has helped to transform Arsenal from also-rans into champions. Ominously for the rest, the Spaniard promised on Wednesday when he signed a new four-year contract understood to be worth more than £20m a season that this “is only the beginning” of what Arsenal hope could be a trophy-laden dynasty under his leadership.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Arteta ended Arsenal’s wait for a Premier League title last season and has designs on further silverware. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

The length of deal was significant given that it would take Arteta, who will mark his seventh anniversary in the job in December, past a decade at the helm – even if he still has some way to go to match Arsène Wenger’s record almost 22 years in charge. Wenger’s first day was 30 years ago last week and he quickly assumed control at the club. The influence of Arteta, made Arsenal captain by Wenger in 2014, has grown steadily since he was appointed after a stint as Pep Guardiola’s assistant at Manchester City.

Arteta, upgraded from head coach to manager in September 2020 having won the FA Cup six months after replacing Unai Emery, has seen various executives depart as his power has increased. The 44-year-old, who became the second-youngest manager after José Mourinho to win the Premier League, has a direct line to the co-chair Josh Kroenke and is able to exert a major say over most big decisions – on and off the pitch.

Arsenal’s announcement this week that they had decided against a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium came after Arteta is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would be caused by any temporary move to Wembley or elsewhere. The owner, Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, is also thought to have been put off proposals to increase the capacity to 70,000 owing to the cost, despite agreeing a record $4bn (£3bn) deal to buy Major League Baseball’s Los Angeles Angels last month.

That did not stop KSE from making Arteta the best-paid manager in the Premier League with a hefty salary increase from the £10m plus £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League that he agreed in 2024. Only Atlético Madrid’s Diego Simeone is thought to earn more globally.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Arteta is understood to have had the final say on not to pursue interest in Malick Fofana after the Belgium forward was offered in the final days of the transfer window because he wanted to ensure the 16-year-old phenomenon Max Dowman would not be denied opportunities. He may regret not bringing in another forward after Christos Tzolis sustained a hamstring injury with Greece that is expected to keep him out for at least three weeks, but it is clear Arteta has been calling the shots even since the arrival of Andrea Berta as the sporting director in March 2025.

Such is the intensity Arteta brings to the job that it remains to be seen whether he can last as long as Wenger, although there are few signs that operating in such a high-pressure environment has affected him physically.

The odd grey hair aside, he barely looks different from the day he was announced in his first managerial role. With the twin motivations of making Arsenal back-to-back league title winners for the first time since the 1930s and European champions after coming so close last season when they lost to Paris Saint-Germain in the final on penalties, Arteta appears to be here to stay.

Sports.title: Are Brighton genuine contenders to qualify for the Champions League?
Sports.content:
Wingerless, without Danny Welbeck and third in the Premier League. Brighton spent the summer losing some of their best players; they are dealing with a growing injury list; and their outstanding player this season has been a 35-year-old they signed in January for £1.7m. In spite of that, five games into the new Premier League season, they have scored more goals than any other team (16), they have the best goal difference in the league (+11) and they have dismantled the champions, beating Arsenal 3-0 before the international window.

This could have been a transitional season for the club. After finishing eighth in the Premier League last season and qualifying for the Conference League, they sold or loaned out 20 players. There were some headline departures: Carlos Baleba to Manchester United for £70m, Jan Paul van Hecke to Tottenham for £52m, and Danny Welbeck, their top scorer last season with 13 league goals, to Chelsea for £5m.

If the transfer activity had not given Fabian Hürzeler enough of a headache, his two starting wingers – Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh – picked up injuries. To make matters worse, forwards Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter joined them on the treatment table. The lineup beat Arsenal was not the one Hürzeler would have envisioned when drawing up his plans in pre-season, but Brighton have shot up the Premier League, booked their place in the group stage of the Conference League and knocked Manchester United out of the League Cup. They have played eight games in all competitions so far, keeping five clean sheets.

With so many players either sold or injured, a void opened up. Into ​this stepped Pascal Gross, who returned to the club from Borussia Dortmund in January for just £1.7m. The deal read more like a nostalgia play than business that would shape a season, but no Premier League player has been involved in more goals this season than Gross, who has scored three and set up three more.

His importance cannot be overstated. In a squad that has lost much of its creative output, he has been the glue. He can drop deep alongside the defence to help Brighton build from the back, float into spaces to create, or break into the box as a late runner. With Chema Andrés doing the defensive work behind him, Gross can roam, dictate attacks and lead the press from higher up the pitch. He works tirelessly. He has created more chances than any other player in the league this season (15) and, perhaps most impressive given he is 35, he has covered the second most distance (59.7km).

“You can really trust him and he makes the teammates around him better,” said Hürzeler after the Arsenal win. That trust is becoming increasingly important as so many of the old-guard at Brighton have left. Welbeck, Joël Veltman, Solly March and Adam Webster moved on, and James Milner retired. Lewis Dunk, Jason Steele and Gross are the last of a dying breed of Brighton veterans.

View image in fullscreen Pascal Gross celebrates after scoring for Brighton against Manchester United in the League Cup. Photograph: Nigel French/Getty Images/Allstar

Hürzeler knows the importance of these players. When asked how his new-look team had settled so quickly this season, he said: “It comes back to the players. I have to give them a lot of praise. I call Jason Steele, Pascal Gross and Lewis Dunk ‘social leaders’. They are important because they integrate the new players quite fast.” With 290 appearances over two spells at the club under four different managers, Gross is one of the few people left at the club who players – and his young manager – can look to for guidance.

But Gross is not an exception to how Brighton have coped with the squad overhaul. In true Brighton fashion, the players waiting in the wings have stepped effortlessly into the team. Maxim De Cuyper, originally signed as a left-back, has covered for Mitoma at left wing. The 25-year-old has three goals and three assists in all competitions this season. He does not have the same dribbling ability that Mitoma does, but his running power and delivery bring a different type of threat.

Further up the pitch, 19-year-old Charalampos Kostoulas has six goal involvements, twice as many as he managed last season. Ferdi Kadioglu has switched to right-back. Olivier Boscagli has covered at left-back while Malick Yalcouyé, Yasin Ayari, Hinshelwood and the teenage Luka Vuskovic, a £46m club-record signing from Tottenham, have played important roles.

Brighton have nine different scorers in the Premier League this season. Their goals and position in the table are the obvious markers of their fast start, but the more telling numbers come from what happens when they do not have the ball. Despite the summer upheaval, Hürzeler’s demand for intensity has remained unchanged, and Brighton are pressing as intently as ever. No side in the league averages fewer passes allowed per defensive action than Brighton’s 7.4. And no team has recorded more high turnovers than their 56 this season.

Their off-the-ball work was most evident against Arsenal, who could not play their usual controlled game. Brighton made nine final-third regains, the most by any Premier League side against Arsenal since Liverpool also managed nine in December 2023.

Bart Verbruggen, speaking after the game, suggested that intensity is central to what Hürzeler has built. “You could see so clearly his ideas – the way we win the second balls, the way we are in front of our opponents, the way we win our personal duels, how tough it is to play against us when we bring that intensity. That is the DNA of this team and that’s from the gaffer.” Whoever Brighton have on the pitch, Hürzeler demands his players work tirelessly to make life difficult for opponents. It reaped its reward against Arsenal, forcing a side that had conceded once all season into an afternoon of hurried passes and forced mistakes.

When asked after the game if Brighton were involved in the title race this year, Gross replied with a swift “no”. Five games is nowhere near enough evidence to be considering them for a first Premier League title, but qualifying for the Champions League may well be within their reach. They lead the league in goals scored, big chances created, average possession, clean sheets, expected goals and shots on target per match.

There are, however, reasons to keep the champagne on ice. A tough run of fixtures lies in wait: Liverpool and Manchester City away this month, unbeaten Brentford at home – and playing in Europe will add fatigue and injuries. Their injury list will only be tested further. And Gross is 35; asking a player his age to sustain this level of output across a full season is a lot.

In the summer, Brighton looked like a team entering a transition phase. Instead they are riding high in the Premier League. For a side that have lost their top scorer, both first-choice wingers to injury, and most of their senior leadership group in a single summer, that is a remarkable achievement. Being third is something else entirely.

This is an article by WhoScored

Sports.title: Laos footballer arrested in connection with alleged match-fixing for betting syndicate
Sports.content:
A Laos international has been arrested in connection with allegations of match-fixing during the 2026 Asean Championship after the country’s football federation referred suspected bribery, illegal gambling and match manipulation to the authorities.

Soukphachan Lueanthala, a winger who featured for Laos during the tournament and plays in his homeland for Salavan United, is understood to have been accused of helping to organise the alleged operation on behalf of a betting syndicate believed to be from Vietnam.

Quick Guide How do I 

According to sources close to the Laos team, he was arrested after several squad members were questioned by police after returning from their last match at the tournament for south-east Asian nations, away to Myanmar, at the start of August. The arrest has not been confirmed by the federation (LFF) or Lao police, but the Guardian has established that the player is in custody.

The game against Myanmar ended in a 7-2 defeat and followed three other heavy losses during the group stage: 5-0 to Thailand, 4-0 to Malaysia and 4-1 to the Philippines.

The LFF confirmed in a statement on 7 August that it had opened an investigation before referring the case to police. According to a source familiar with the allegations, who did not want to be named, Lueanthala was suspected of giving instructions to other squad members and acting as a link between those involved.

Laos, managed by the Serb Vladica Grujic, failed to match the results achieved two years earlier when they scored seven goals and conceded 11 in four games, pulling off surprise draws against Indonesia and the Philippines, who both sit far higher in the Fifa rankings. The case comes against a background of previous match-fixing scandals involving Laos that led the Asian Football Confederation to impose a life ban on Thipphonexay Inthavongsa in 2020 after finding him guilty of conspiring to manipulate the result of a 2017 international against Hong Kong.

The AFC was contacted for comment about the latest allegations and whether it was assisting the Lao authorities, but did not respond. Neither did the LFF.

The source, who has extensive experience inside Lao football, has alleged that match-fixing has been a long-running problem involving players and potentially officials. Players are particularly vulnerable because of their financial circumstances. “Until last year, they were getting $10 per day when they were joining the national team,” he said.

One player allegedly told him he had fixed three matches for “$10,000” each time. He claimed suspected fixing had damaged Lao football more broadly, with experienced players disappearing from the national team and younger players taking their places. “There is such talent,” he said. “They deserve so much better than this.”

Sports.title: Havertz, Isak, Dorgu … spate of injuries with national teams leaves sour taste for top clubs
Sports.content:
A four-match international break has presented a stress test. “The intensity of the squad, the athleticism of it, really, I think it’s designed for the elite,” said the Wales head coach, Craig Bellamy, on the completion of four matches in 11 days. Elite club coaches would disagree. The Nations League and the wider set of international games staged across the globe have been accompanied by a daily list of casualties, club officials viewing matches through their fingers as players pull up and gesture to the bench.

Hamstring and muscle problems have been rife. Sunderland, for example, will be without Brian Brobbey, a key striker, and Dan Ballard, a defensive mainstay, because of strains picked up playing for the Netherlands and Northern Ireland respectively. Bournemouth, yet to win a Premier League match, have lost Alex Scott for up to two months. His performance for England in their 7-0 victory against Croatia won rave reviews, a young player taking his chance and outshining Luka Modric. It came at a heavy cost. A quadriceps injury that had been diagnosed pre-match worsened. “There was zero risk taken from our side,” said Thomas Tuchel. The Bournemouth coach, Marco Rose, is unlikely to see it that way.

The break had begun with a new phrase entering the football lexicon. Cole Palmer, despite missing the World Cup, would be absent, for reasons of “load management”, said the briefing. The phrasing, also offered for Declan Rice’s absence, is borrowed from the NBA, where basketball’s star players are asked to negotiate an 82-game regular season before the playoffs. Elite football is making similar demands: Rice played 69 matches during the 2025-26 season, 5,394 minutes in total.

Arsenal still had 17 players called up for internationals. Mikel Arteta, given a long time to stew over a 3-0 defeat by Brighton, is counting them back into training with concern. Ezri Konsa’s withdrawal from the England squad on Monday followed injuries for Christos Tzolis and Kai Havertz. Playing for Greece against the Netherlands, Tzolis pulled his shirt over his head after injuring a hamstring. Against the same opponents, playing for Germany, Havertz suffered a similar problem, another setback for a player too often denied to Arteta. A further scare came when Max Dowman, playing for England Under-19s, left the field after taking a heavy tackle.

There is better news for Martin Ødegaard, the recipient of a hefty challenge from Portugal’s Bernardo Silva when playing for Norway on the first Sunday of the break. “Nothing dramatic” in the X-ray was the verdict from the Norwegian camp before Ødegaard returned to face the same opponents. That second encounter with Portugal was marked by concern for Erling Haaland when he requested to leave the field. It was all part of the plan, with the Norway head coach, Ståle Solbakken, saying: “For those who play in the Champions League and have had little vacation, it’s more brutal than for the others.” Haaland will be centre stage when Manchester City travel to Liverpool for their first match since the club was found guilty of 100-plus breaches of Premier League financial regulations. The club have given him a brief, though required, rest.

Almost certainly to the disquiet of Enzo Maresca, City’s Elliot Anderson and Marc Guéhi were, alongside Harry Kane, the only England players to start all four Nations League matches, with Nico O’Reilly withdrawing halfway through. Liverpool’s problems appear to run deeper, with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo, early successes for the Andoni Iraola regime, sustaining injuries with Sweden and the Netherlands respectively. Jérémy Jacquet, another bright spark this season, reportedly strained a hamstring with France.

View image in fullscreen Patrick Dorgu faces a spell on the sidelines after injuring a hamstring with Denmark. Photograph: Liselotte Sabroe/Ritzau Scanpix/Reuters

The Premier League weekend’s other headline clash, Manchester United hosting Tottenham in a derby of fading dreams, will also be without key personnel. United’s Patrick Dorgu pulled up with a hamstring injury when playing for Denmark. Another option at left-back, Noussair Mazraoui, took a knock playing for Morocco against Lesotho. Bruno Fernandes, who has been playing through an injury described by his national coach, Jorge Jesus, as a “complicated problem”, is likely to push through the pain barrier. Spurs’ relief that Micky van der Ven’s hand injury was not serious was tempered by Jan Paul van Hecke’s foot injury, while the World Cup winner Pedro Porro missed Spain’s assignments and will not return in time for the trip to Old Trafford.

The injuries are not confined to English football. Elite European players are affected, too. Bayern Munich have lost Jamal Musiala to the torn muscle in his right thigh sustained on international duty with Germany. Jürgen Klopp’s selection of 44 players for his first camp was partially designed to lower the load yet still delivered casualties.
