skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Even the very best get hurt. Kylian Mbappé sprained his knee in the second match of Zinedine Zidane’s France reign, though appears on the road to recovery judging by social media pictures of a cycling expedition. How José Mourinho received that can only be speculated on, given Real Madrid’s manager said this week of players in downtime: “You cannot ride a bike. You fall off your bike, and you don’t play three matches maybe, or maybe worse, maybe you break a leg.”

Mourinho is not alone in having his mood darkened by this extended international break.

Sports.title: How the Kop’s chants propelled Andy Burnham to fight for Hillsborough justice
Sports.content:
Since dawn, visitors from as far afield as Australia had been laying flowers, scarves and messages underneath Anfield’s Eternal Flame. These Hillsborough memorial anniversary services were usually subdued and respectful affairs, with 10,000 mourners sitting on the Kop to give themselves and the families support on the most difficult of days.

But on the afternoon of 15 April 2009, the 20th anniversary of the disaster, it felt different. There was an edge in the air. An hour before the service began the Kop was full and the numbers in the three other stands were starting to swell. By the time I had walked with the families from the meeting place in the Centenary Stand to our seats at the front of the Kop, 29,000 people inside Anfield stood to give them the loudest and most heartfelt of ovations. After two decades in which a new generation had been born and reached adulthood, the wounds of Hillsborough were still gaping, the anger still raw at the lack of admission of guilt from above.

The players of ’89, their furrowed brows and downcast expressions hinting at their inability to shed the mental scars they endured back then, when they were forced to turn from athletes into bereavement counsellors, took their seats behind us to warm applause. They were joined by the current stars, including Steven Gerrard, who lost his 10-year-old cousin Jon-Paul Gilhooley in the disaster, and Jamie Carragher.

After 20 years, you’d have thought all the crying had been done, but when 96 candles were lit in the Kop goalmouth and the names were read out by clergy, streams still flowed down the cheeks. You still felt a cold sweat and weak limbs at the two-minute silence broken only by babies’ cries. Outside the ground where the city’s buses, trains and ferries had come to a standstill, church bells signalled the end of the silence, a comforting sign to the families that the wider world had come to a halt to remember a day it should never forget.

Andy Burnham, scouse-born and Evertonian, who was then secretary of state for culture, media and sport, had controversially been invited to speak by Margaret Aspinall, who’d lost her 18-year-old son James at Hillsborough and was by then chair of the Family Support Group. “We had never allowed an MP to speak at the service because we hadn’t really had any meaningful support from any of them. But I wanted to give Andy a chance,” she told me.

Burnham agonised over whether to accept, knowing that Gordon Brown’s Labour government had nothing new to offer the families. But the man who, on the day of Hillsborough had been at Villa Park watching Everton play Norwich in the other FA Cup semi-final, knew he would never forgive himself if he bottled out of giving a speech. His main worry was whether he could get through it without breaking down. He was right to feel worried as he stood before an emotionally charged Kop that day because there was a strong sense of betrayal from a Labour government that had been in power for 12 of the 20 years since the disaster and had done nothing to facilitate calls to unearth the truth.

View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham said he ‘half-expected’ the ‘justice’ chants during his speech at Anfield on the 20th anniversary of Hillsborough. Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Burnham started well. When he told the Kop that Britain’s worst sporting disaster was “man-made” and praised the actions of the fans that day, he received nods of approval and a ripple of applause. But when he said he brought a message from the prime minister that the victims would never be forgotten, for the first time ever at one of these memorial services pockets of the Kop began to boo and jeer, there was a shout of “When do we get justice?” and a scream of “Hypocrite.” It shocked us all and stopped Burnham in his tracks. He looked startled and tongue-tied and stared nervously at the Kop, unsure what to say for the best. Which was when, from the back of the Kop, a chant of “Justice for the 96” broke out, which quickly spread across the rest of the stand and the entirety of Anfield. The message was simple: words are easy, actions hard. You are a senior member of a Labour government which has ruled out the possibility of a fresh inquiry into Hillsborough. Don’t patronise us with easy soundbites. Because you not only insult the living, you insult the dead.

Wisely, Burnham nodded at the Kop with an “I get it” expression. Margaret Aspinall, who was sitting directly in front of him, told me: “I was on eggshells throughout Andy’s speech. When the Kop began chanting for justice our former chairman Trevor Hicks looked at me as if to say: ‘What have you done, Margaret? Let’s say something.’ But I thought: ‘No, let them carry on, don’t say anything. Let the Kop tell the government and the country how angry we all feel.’” Her instincts were right. The dramatic scene of a cabinet minister being barracked during a memorial service led every news bulletin for the rest of the day and made every front page the next.

Burnham later told me: “When the first justice chants rolled off the Kop, I was not surprised, as I half-expected them. And, actually, I wanted the country to hear them. The people on the Kop that day were right to barrack me. I don’t hold anything against anyone who shouted at me. It helped me find the political courage to do something.” He urged Gordon Brown to heed the Kop’s calls and despite some cabinet opposition the prime minister backed him. By the end of 2009 a Hillsborough Independent Panel had been set up, appointing experts to scrutinise hundreds of thousands of unseen documents relating to the disaster. Its final report in 2012 highlighted a litany of calamitous mistakes by police and emergency services, showed how dozens of lives could have been saved and revealed a massive cover-up. Tory prime minister David Cameron had to give a grovelling apology to the families and to Liverpool fans from the floor of the Commons, the original inquest verdicts of “accidental death” were quashed, and new inquests put in place. In 2016 they would return 96 verdicts of “unlawful killing” and exonerate the fans of all blame.

“We would never, ever have got the verdicts of ‘unlawful killing’ without the support of the Kop,” said Margaret Aspinall. “The fans played a vital part over the years in supporting us and getting accountability. But the turning point definitely came when those chants of ‘justice’ came at Andy Burnham. That day the Kop changed everything.”

Five years later Burnham was invited to address the 25th anniversary service. This time it wasn’t snarls, boos and chants of “hypocrite” he faced on the Kop but a banner that read “Thank You, Andy Burnham”. He told them: “Five years ago things changed, not because of me but because of all of you. You made your voices heard and thank God you did. Your voices carried off this Kop into every living room in the land and into the heart of the establishment. I knew you were right and they were wrong. With that chant of ‘justice’ the dam burst. You were asking the most profound question about our country and how it is run. How can it be that an entire city shouted injustice for 20 years and no one was listening? There is still an uncertain road ahead but the country is with you now. The families will prevail because of all of you. You have made this city stronger and you will make our country fairer. You have given hope to people the world over. What was your call five years ago is my call today; justice for the 96.”

This is an extract from The Kop: A Fan’s History of Football’s Most Famous Stand by Brian Reade (Quercus, £25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

Sports.title: Declan Rice close to agreeing new £350,000-per-week deal with Arsenal: England star set to become club's joint-highest earner with Bukayo Saka
Sports.content:
Declan Rice is closing in on a new long-term deal at Arsenal believed to be worth around £350,000 per week.

The contract will put Rice, 27, on a level footing with Bukayo Saka at the top of the club's salary list.

Rice joined Arsenal in 2023 and has established himself as the fulcrum of their midfield, helping steer them to the Premier League title last season.

He played 55 games in all competitions last season as the Gunners reached their first Champions League final since 2006, but lost out to Paris Saint-Germain.

His contract talks have been ongoing for a long time – at least since March – but are reaching a head. Rice's current deal expires in 2028.

Arsenal's £105million fee to sign him from West Ham is looking a far wiser investment than most other footballers who have been bought for over £100m.

Declan Rice is close to signing a new £350,000-per-week long-term contract with Arsenal

Premier League's highest earners 1) Erling Haaland, Manchester City - £525,000 2) Virgil van Dijk, Liverpool - £350,000 3) Enzo Fernandez, Manchester City - £350,000 4) Bukayo Saka, Arsenal - £350,000 5) Declan Rice, Arsenal - £350,000 *contingent on new deal 6) Bruno Fernandes, Manchester United - £320,000 7) Dominik Szoboszlai, Liverpool - £320,000 8) Cody Gakpo, Liverpool - £310,000 9) Phil Foden, Manchester City - £300,000 10) Marcus Rashford, Manchester United - £300,000

Rice has also become highly influential for England and manager Thomas Tuchel said in June: 'I’m proud to be his coach.

'He is one of the very best midfielders in the world. He’s humble, ready to be a team player, ready to give quality and energy to the group. He learns every day in his career.'

Tuchel also said separately: 'He has a high football IQ. He takes care of the formation and structure, the adaptation, and the rhythm of our game.

'He's had two outstanding seasons with Arsenal - one of their main players in their Champions League campaign. He's one of the best midfielders in Europe at the moment, full of confidence. That's why he is my vice-captain.'

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta said of him last season: 'He can adapt to anything that you throw at him.

'But at the moment that forward thinking and anything that is in front of him is probably much more positive for the team.

'He has earned the right to increase that role, to be more and more important, to be very present in everything that we do.

'He’s in the leadership group, which is very important as well, and it’s a real presence. Sometimes you don’t need to just wear the armband to feel really connected, really powerful and really important in the team.'

Sports.title: Furious French tennis star chucks racquet towards crowd in on-court meltdown but AVOIDS disqualification - after bad boy Daniil Medvedev was defaulted for hitting a spectator
Sports.content:
New footage has emerged showing French tennis star Terence Atmane throwing his racquet into the crowd while playing his opening qualifying round at this year's Shanghai Masters.

Despite the violence with which Atmane recklessly chucked his racquet towards a packed stand of spectators after losing a point to opponent Bernard Tomic, the 24-year-old remarkably avoided being defaulted.

Instead, Atmane retired down 5-3 to Tomic in the third set to hand the Australian the win, in his second-consecutive deciding-set retirement of this autumn's Asian swing.

Former Cincinnati Masters finalist Atmane cut an explosive figure for the duration of the match, repeatedly crashing his racquet down into the net when upset with his uneven form and hitting balls out of the stadium.

But although he will likely receive a hefty fine from the tournament for his meltdown, Atmane's on-court display raises questions over fairness in tennis' rules around racquet abuse.

Daniil Medvedev was defaulted on the same day as Atmane in his Beijing semi-final against Novak Djokovic for hitting a ball into the stands unthinkingly, where it caught a man in the face.

Siguen apareciendo más imágenes de la actitud de Atmane contra Tomic.



Hizo todos los méritos para una descalificación pero no pasó nada. https://t.co/74D6P5WVJX pic.twitter.com/3FEYkEJMQc — Ariel Fernández (@AFD7L) October 7, 2026

Terence Atmane flung his racquet into the stands in a dangerous meltdown while qualifying for this year's Shanghai Masters

On the same day, Daniil Medvedev was defaulted for hitting the ball into the stands and injuring a spectator

Although the man escaped serious injury, he was taken to hospital as a precaution. Medvedev, who was deeply apologetic and did not protest his sanction, later sent the man one of his racquets signed with the message 'I am sorry'.

With his default, Medvedev was stripped of all of his prize money won for reaching the final four, and any ranking points gained - a bitter blow as the current world No9 battles for a place at this year's end-of-season ATP Finals next month.

The wording of the rule is clear that players shall not 'violently, dangerously, or with anger hit, kick or throw a racket or other equipment' on court, but its application is dizzyingly inconsistent.

Atmane's slingshotted racquet is far weightier than a loose ball and was tossed with more aggression than Medvedev's misdirected but ultimately reckless shot. But unlike the combustible Russian, Atmane did not injure anyone in the crowd.

Critics of the rules' application believe however that this should not be a barrier to a player getting defaulted, as without the high stakes of lost points and earnings, players might not change their on-court behaviour.

Certainly, there are recent examples of near-misses like Atmane's where players have skirted punishment. Earlier this year at the Hamburg Open, Daniel Altmaier was only handed a code violation for kicking his racquet into the crowd, where it was caught by quick-thinking fans.

Like Medvedev, 12th-seed Belinda Bencic accidentally hit a spectator without looking at this year's US Open during her match against Yulia Putintseva but was deemed by the umpire to have done so 'unintentionally'.

Her opponent argued that she had still 'hit someone' but the chair umpire's decision appeared to hinge on whether the person was injured. They weren't, and Bencic stayed on-court.

There is no consistency between tournaments either. Djokovic made for a sympathetic opponent for Medvedev - not least because it helped him on his way to claiming a seventh-straight China Open title - having been penalised at the 2020 US Open for accidentally striking a line judge in the throat with a loose ball hit in frustration.

'It's a bit of a shock to be honest. I hope that person is not badly injured,' he said in the aftermath of his unorthodox victory. 'I also feel sorry for Daniil. I know exactly how he feels to be disqualified in a big match.

'I am sure that Daniil did not want to do this intentionally.'

Lorenzo Musetti however escaped punishment for the same offence at the 2025 French Open when he kicked a ball which struck a line judge on the shoulder.

Last year at a tournament in China Atmane threw his racquet to the back of the court - and was allowed to continue

Monday's incident confirmed too that Atmane continues to struggle keeping his temper in check.

At the 2024 French Open during his first-round clash with Sebastian Ofner, he was forced to apologise for hitting a fan with an angry ball - another instance where he was allowed to stay on-court.

A year later, at a Challenger event in Guangzhou, he threw his racquet to the back of the court. But he was allowed to continue, and won the match.

Following his defeat to Tomic, Atmane explained that his outbursts had stemmed from his insecurity of dropping out of the top 100.

'Being inside the top 40 a month ago and seeing myself almost out of the top 100 made me way more stressed and pressured than I could possibly imagine,' he admitted. 'It doesn't excuse me for my bad behaviour, and after considering what happened on court for these past weeks, I've decided to take a step back and rebuild myself from 0.'

Hinting at health issues which were physical rather than 'mental', Atmane also shared that he is considering ending his season early.

Sports.title: Guilty of cheating? We're not bothered! Man City's Erling Haaland and grinning manager Enzo Maresca give the thumbs up as they return to training after rule-break talks
Sports.content:
Guilty of cheating? We're not bothered! Man City's Erling Haaland and grinning manager Enzo Maresca give the thumbs up as they return to training after rule-break talks

Manchester City stars have returned to training for the first time after the club was found guilty of all serious financial breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations nearly two weeks ago.

Manager Enzo Maresca was the first to arrive shortly after 9.30am, grinning widely for the waiting photographers and giving them an enthusiastic thumbs-up.

He was followed after midday by superstar striker Erling Haaland, who adopted a similarly positive pose. England star Marc Guehi and Croatia's Josko Gvardiol cut a more low-key profiles.

The majority of Maresca's squad spent time on international duty during the fortnight break, with the manager himself only returning to the Etihad Stadium on Monday ahead of meeting up with his group for the first time.

Preparations are set to begin for the toughest possible initial test - a trip to face Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, with international football awaiting their response to the charges on the pitch.

Man City lodged their appeal against the charges, which found that the club had artificially inflated commercial revenues by over £830million between 2009 and 2018, last Thursday evening.

Erling Haaland looked upbeat as he arrived at Manchester City for the first time since their

Manager Enzo Maresca was the first to arrive this morning and he similarly gave waiting photographers the thumbs-up

Marc Guehi kept a low profile as he drove into Man City's training ground for the first time since September

The independent commission came to their decision over three years after the Premier League first brought charges against the club, with its 10-week hearing taking place in late 2024.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters claimed in a statement released alongside the bombshell core decision that the club 'systemically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade' with their use of 'sham' contracts.

The club also repeatedly breached duties of 'co-operation and utmost good faith towards the League' by failing to help with the investigation. In the core decision, the independent commission deemed evidence given by a number of Man City's witnesses called on behalf of the club to have been 'untrue' and 'dishonest'.

If Man City fail in their appeal, they will face severe sanctions which could include expulsion from the Premier League, future points deductions, stripping of titles and transfer bans.

But goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma's agent Enzo Raiola revealed the Italian - and likely his team-mates - was been given assurances by the club, who still insist on their innocence in the wake of the damning verdict by the independent commission.

He told Radio Napoli Centrale, per Calciomercato: 'Can the Manchester City chaos change anything? No, it won't change anything for us or for Gigio. News comes out periodically.

'The club has spoken to Gigio, and everyone is calm. Now there are important matches against Liverpool and PSG, and then sporting justice will take its course. But Gigio has received reassurances from Manchester City.'

Ahead of Sunday's return to Premier League action, Daily Mail Sport reported on Wednesday that Merseyside Police are braced for fan trouble with some Liverpool fans preparing a hostile 'welcome' for Man City's team bus.

One social media post is advertising a ‘Bus Greeting’ around two hours before the 4.30pm kick-off on Anfield Road.

Fans are asked to bring ‘flags, banners, pyros, flares, kopparbergs’. A wink emoji is placed after Kopparberg, which is a popular cider served in a bottle.

Josko Gvardiol returned to Manchester after facing off with England for Croatia at Wembley

Summer signing Elliot Anderson arrived around lunchtime after returning from England duty

Antoine Semenyo and Ayyoub Bouaddi were also on parade as they returned to their club

Police are aware of the poster and have said that they will have ‘an appropriate policing plan in place’.

Next Wednesday, City will play their first game at the Etihad since they were found guilty and Pep Guardiola will be in attendance in a show of solidarity.

The former manager, who left the club at the end of last season, previously shared a message of support for his ex-employers, telling fans: 'We will get through this together. I love you all.'

Guardiola will be joined at the Etihad Stadium by the City board, including chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, for the club’s first home European match since his summer departure.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta's bizarre management techniques started on DAY ONE at Arsenal: Boss reveals how he destroyed an office - and ordered staff to put it back together again in just two minutes
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has long been known for his unusual ways of testing the Arsenal squad.

From hiring a pickpocket to steal his own player's wallets to directing travel disruption during pre-season, the Arsenal boss turns heads with regularity with his training-ground methods that are designed to keep the champions one step ahead of the pursuing pack.

Arteta was famed for his use of speakers in training (not just blasting You'll Never Walk Alone before a 4-0 defeat at Anfield in 2021) and has even brought in a team dog named Win.

Now, in the wake of agreeing new terms with the Gunners that have made him the Premier League's highest-paid boss, Arteta has revealed that his quirky practices began on his very first day on the job back in December 2019.

The then 37-year-old claimed he 'destroyed' an education centre at Arsenal's training centre, throwing 'the computers, the laptops, the cables' on the floor. He then requested his staff to reorganise the office in no time at all in order to prove their togetherness.

In an interview with The Athletic, Arteta explained: 'I said, "Listen, this is what I heard. I don’t know if it’s true. But from a lot of different people, the sentiment is that this is how they feel about working in the organisation. I’m here to help you enjoy your profession and your life and the passion that we all share. If you want me to help you to do that, you have two minutes to put this in order and at least to be ready to work together’. And I left.

Mikel Arteta has agreed terms on a lucrative new deal that keeps him at Arsenal until 2030

Arteta has admitted that his first bizarre mangerial method was put into action on his first day in the job back in 2019

'That could have been my managerial career because if that would have stayed the same way, I had no job anymore!'

Arteta then outlined how he came back moments later and everything was 'immaculate'.

'Everyone was silent and had their eyes open and they were ready to listen. I said, "This is just the start. It’s something that we have to be in daily. Whatever we want to accomplish, we’re going to have to do it together. I cannot do it by myself. The issue that we have is much deeper than that, but the opportunity is infinite".

While peculiar, these methods are a core reason why Arteta has been able to propel Arsenal back to the top of English football.

The 44-year-old wanted to inspire all of his players and staff to become one unit, an us-against-the-world mentality. He believed that by being all together as one, 'we can create a monster’, and that is what he has managed to do during his seven years at the helm.

'What I decided the day I accepted this incredible opportunity was I’m going to give my life, my soul, all my knowledge, and my best ability to deliver a dream - to connect this football club from top to bottom.

'Then I made a commitment with myself. I need to enjoy the journey and I’m going to the journey. Because I didn’t know how tough it was going to be, I had no experience, I never did it before. I have to be so alert, so curious, and just go day by day.'

After taking the club from tenth position in 2019 to Premier League champions, as well as reaching the Champions League final, Arteta has been rewarded with a lucrative new deal which boosts his salary – which was worth up to £15million with bonuses.

Arteta is famous for his unusual training methods and once blasted 'You'll Never Walk Alone' at his players in training ahead of their trip to Liverpool back in 2021

Arteta's new contract is understood to be worth around £20m per year and makes him the league's best-paid manager. Unai Emery, Andoni Iraola, Enzo Maresca and Roberto De Zerbi are all thought to earn in the £10-12m bracket annually, with Oliver Glasner not far behind.

The Spaniard's contract was due to expire next summer, but this new agreement shuts down any speculation over his future, running until 2030.

Arteta said: 'It's a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal. This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue.

'We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.

'I'm extremely grateful to Stan and Josh (Kroenke) for their trust and support, and feel honoured to be leading this club through such a special period in its 140-year history.

'This is such a proud moment for me and my family. I feel the love and respect from our fantastic supporters, and they have mine – and ours – in return.'

Sports.title: Fuming Paul Scholes renews old rivalry with Martin Keown - as he tells Arsenal legend to 'do one' after demanding a medal off Manchester City
Sports.content:
Fuming Paul Scholes renews old rivalry with Martin Keown - as he tells Arsenal legend to 'do one' after demanding a medal off Manchester City

Paul Scholes has doubled down on his view that Manchester City's Premier League winners should have to hand over their medals.

And the Manchester United legend even told Martin Keown to 'do one' when the Arsenal hero disagreed with his view.

Manchester City were blasted by the Premier League last month for making 'sham' agreements to manipulate their financial accounts to the tune of £900million between 2009 and 2018, during which time they won eight trophies.

City insist they are innocent and are appealing the verdict, which found them guilty of 114 of 115 charges.

Last week, Scholes posted on Instagram: 'Keep hearing ex-teammates say they want trophies taken off them, but they don't want their medals [to be handed over].

'F*** that, I'm a greedy b******, I want my medal.'

Paul Scholes wants another Premier League medal off Manchester City - and has told Martin Keown to 'do one' for disagreeing with him

His old rival, Keown, was unimpressed with Scholes' demand and criticised it on talkSPORT

Scholes lost out on the Premier League title to City on the final day of the 2011-12 season, the one enshrined in the country's collective memory with Sergio Aguero's late goal.

But Keown and Simon Jordan were unimpressed with the 51-year-old's opportunistic moaning, and took shots at him on talkSPORT.

Regarding his demand for extra medals, Keown hit out: 'How many does he need? He’s got a dozen or so already, but I can’t tell him how to behave or think.

'For me, I just think it should be void. I think if we’re going to take away Man City’s trophies throughout that period it should be made void.'

Jordan added: 'I always thought Paul Scholes was a very balanced individual who made sensible points.

'Maybe his experience in management at Oldham has corrupted his thinking because all of a sudden he’s got a podcast and he feels that he and Nicky [Butt] have got to say controversial things. I think he’s a bit better than that, really.'

Scholes did not take kindly to their criticism, responding to a clip on Instagram: 'Pot, Kettle, Black, Simon.'

The Premier League confirmed that Manchester City are guilty of the most serious financial rule breaches

He then clapped back at Keown: 'And you can do one with that "void season" nonsense.'

Scholes's grievance is understandable, given the scale of City's apparent cheating.

In September, Daily Mail Sport reported how City had been found guilty of 114 of 115 charges against them.

In a lengthy statement, the Premier League say City arranged 'sham contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on "sham" agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs'.

It also says the club falsely altered the financial picture at the Etihad to the tune of £900m. The club had agreed exorbitant sponsorship deals with a number of companies but those sponsors only paid part of the fee.

The rest was propped up by the Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

As the Premier League note, this allowed City to 'artificially inflate the club’s revenues' and therefore spend more under Premier League rules. The higher the revenue a club records, the more they are permitted to spend.

Moreover, further 'sham' deals, funded by ADUG, allowed the club to 'record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred'.

The Premier League say that revenues were inflated and costs reduced to the tune of £900million in an attempt to comply with spending rules. The result was that the club 'filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators'.

It added that the club was 'significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits' during the time period in question, 2009-2018 when it won eight major trophies.

Had City reported accurately 'it would have been in breach of both the League's and UEFA's spending limits by a very substantial amount'.

The panel also found that City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and good faith in that it failed to assist the Premier League's four-year investigation, triggered by the emergence of club emails obtained by a hacker.

Indeed, City had 'made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation'.

Sports.title: Mexican wrestler arrested on manslaughter charge after veteran referee is killed in tragic stunt gone wrong
Sports.content:
A Mexican wrestler has been arrested on suspicion of manslaughter or negligent homicide after a stunt went horribly wrong and killed a referee during an event.

The pro wrestler, known as Hijo De Fishman, was arrested in Mineral de la Reforma in Hidalgo after referee Gerardo German Pineda, known as El Buho, died on Wednesday night.

According to reports, Hijo De Fishman performed a pre-planned 'piledriver' move on Pineda, 75, as part of a skit following his match against a rival at the 'Deslealtades' event.

But the move on Pineda, a 15-year wrestling veteran, went horribly wrong and he was left motionless on the floor.

Pineda lay on the floor unattended for several minutes because those inside the area assumed he was feigning injury as a result of the planned move.

When paramedics finally arrived, Pineda was pronounced dead and Fishman was then arrested on suspicion of manslaughter or negligent homicide.

Mexican wrestler Hijo De Fishman has been arrested on a manslaughter charge after a stunt went horribly wrong and killed a referee during an event

Hijo De Fishman performed a pre-planned 'piledriver' move on referee Gerardo German Pineda

Pineda, a 15-year wrestling veteran, was left motionless on the floor after the move went wrong

According to Superluchas, a hearing is scheduled to take place in the next 48 hours to decide if Fishman will be released or charged.

If he is found guilty of manslaughter, he could be facing a prison sentence of up to 15 years.

El Patron Espectaculos, the promotion behind the 'Deslealtades' event, later said in a statement they are helping Hijo De Fishman with 'legal assistance.'

The company said: 'We are attentive to the developing situation and have arranged accompaniment and legal assistance for Hijo De Fishman, so that the corresponding process is carried out in accordance with the law and before the competent authorities.

'The lawyer and legal representative of the company maintains contact with the family of Mr. Gerardo Germán Pineda, "El Buho", and with his legal representatives, to handle the case in the best way and guarantee respect for all parties involved.

'The legal process is still ongoing, so, out of respect for the authorities and due process, this company will refrain from issuing additional information that could interfere with or prejudice the facts.

'We ask the fans, media and members of the guild to act with prudence, discretion and respect, and avoid the spread of rumors or unconfirmed information, so as not to hinder the investigations and out of respect for all parties involved and their families.

'We deeply regret the loss of a life and express our solidarity with his family, friends and colleagues in the wrestling business.'

Sports.title: Southampton's classless response to spying manager Tonda Eckert escaping an FA ban over Spygate scandal
Sports.content:
Southampton's classless response to spying manager Tonda Eckert escaping an FA ban over Spygate scandal

Southampton have been blasted for an 'embarrassing' lack of class after their manager Tonda Eckert escaped a ban for last season's Spygate scandal.

The Championship club - who sit 13th at the moment - made jokes and picked fights with Middlesbrough fans on social media after the verdict.

Eckert is free to continue managing Saints despite Daily Mail Sport's revelation last season that they had spied on Middlesbrough before their play-off semi-final clash. The South Coast club were thrown out of the play-off final as a result.

Their manager has been handed a six-week ban, but it is suspended until the end of next season, meaning he would have to reoffend to serve any of it. He has also been fined £28,000.

Southampton's response on social media has been bullish. They posted a video of Eckert, 33, doing fist pumps to the stands with the caption: 'Just don't think you understand' - which was later deleted.

They also taunted Middlesbrough supporters who had replied, posting a clip of Will McKenzie from The Inbetweeners and asking: 'You still got notifications on?'

Southampton posted a video of Tonda Eckert celebrating after he escaped a ban (X: SouthamptonFC)

Their view is that they have been punished enough. For spying breaches against Boro, Oxford United, and Ipswich Town in 2025 and 2026, they were booted out of the play-offs, costing them a place in the Premier League worth a potential £200m. Boro went on to lose the play-off final in their place to Hull City, who were promoted.

They were also deducted four points coming into this season.

'Southampton Football Club welcomes the outcome of the FA hearing into the events at the end of last season,' a statement read.

'We hope this now brings a conclusion to a regrettable period of our history and measures have been put in place to ensure that such errors in judgement never happen again at our club.

'We want to take this opportunity to thank the supporters for their unconditional backing throughout this process. Our fan base is unmatched, and we are excited to move forward together towards a bright future.'

The FA said that Eckert was the only witness their panel, which included two KCs, heard from and added that he was ‘exceptionally impressive’.

Explaining the Oxford incident, Eckert said that their opponents had sacked Gary Rowett as head coach and appointed Craig Short as interim and that he wanted to see if they were going to play with a back four or a back five so sent someone to watch them train.

In the Ipswich incident, he agreed to receive CCTV footage of them training at National League Eastleigh, ahead of their fixture with his Saints.

Eckert's Spygate scandal last season saw Southampton thrown out of the play-offs

With regards to Boro, Eckert told the panel that in a preparation meeting he asked whether it would be possible to find out if Hayden Hackney had resumed training.

‘One of the assistants informed me that Middlesborough FC’s [sic] training ground is located on a golf course which is accessible to the public,’ he added.

‘I said that we should send someone there to see if Hayden Hackney was training. Nobody expressed any reservations or objections to this proposal.

'The exchange took a matter of minutes and then we continued with the meeting. To confirm I did not ask for any videos to be taken of Middlesborough FC’s [sic] training sessions and I did not identify any particular individual to travel to Middlesborough [sic] to identify if Hayden Hackney was training. I do, however, accept that I was wrong to ask for any kind of observations.’

An intern was sent to the venue, who was subsequently spotted by Boro – who complained to the EFL – but not before Eckert had been ‘provided a breakdown of the videos… including the predicted line up.

‘I had already finished preparing for the match,’ he said, ‘but I watched the videos’.

The panel praised Eckert, 33, for his ‘genuine contrition’. He had argued that during his time in Germany and Italy, spying on training sessions of opponents was ‘commonplace’, that he was unaware it was against the rules in England and said that allegations he had bullied younger members of staff into spying were ‘extremely upsetting’, adding that he would never have forced anyone to do anything to which they had a moral objection, let alone a breach of the rules.

The panel found there was no ‘systemic or organised course of action’ with regards to spying, and found ‘considerable mitigation’ with regards to Eckert who had shown ‘deep and meaningful’ remorse and ‘learned lessons’.

TIMELINE: THE SPY-GATE SAGA May 7 — Daily Mail Sport reveals the spying allegation Daily Mail Sport reported that a Southampton first-team analyst had allegedly been caught hiding in bushes near Middlesbrough's training ground while recording a session ahead of their Championship play-off semi-final. The incident became known as 'Spygate 2.0'. May 8 — Southampton are charged by the EFL The EFL charged Southampton with breaching regulations requiring clubs to act in 'the utmost good faith' and prohibiting them from observing an opponent's training within 72 hours of a match. The report identified the suspected spy as a junior intern and said he had allegedly deleted footage before leaving the site. May 10 — Southampton manager refuses to discuss the affair Manager Tonda Eckert walked out of a tense post-match press conference after refusing to answer questions about the spying allegations, while Middlesbrough's manager publicly criticised Southampton. May 13 — Evidence emerges of the suspected operation Daily Mail Sport published an image apparently showing the Southampton analyst hiding behind a tree and filming Middlesbrough's training. The report also raised questions about a possible paper trail linking the operation to the club. May 14–15 — EFL signals Southampton could be removed from the play-offs The EFL confirmed that Southampton could be expelled from the play-offs, with a disciplinary hearing scheduled just days before the final. Middlesbrough then called publicly for Southampton to be removed from the competition, describing expulsion as the 'only appropriate response'. May 19 — Southampton are expelled from the play-off final An independent disciplinary commission expelled Southampton from the Championship play-offs and imposed a four-point deduction for the following season. Southampton admitted spying on Middlesbrough and two other opponents — Oxford United and Ipswich Town — while Middlesbrough were reinstated to face Hull City in the final. May 20–21 — Southampton lose their appeal and player anger surfaces Southampton's appeal against expulsion was rejected, confirming that Middlesbrough would take their place in the Wembley final. Southampton players publicly expressed their anger and disappointment, while the potential loss of promotion bonuses prompted reports that some could consider legal action against the club. June 1–2 — Leaked messages intensify scrutiny of the club A leaked WhatsApp exchange appeared to show an intern being praised after a spying mission, with the message: 'You legend. Manager loved it!'. The revelations raised fresh questions about pressure placed on junior staff and Eckert's knowledge of the operations. July 22 — The FA charges Tonda Eckert The FA charged Eckert with three breaches of its misconduct rules relating to spying on opposition training. Daily Mail Sport reported that he was expected to cooperate with the investigation and could face a lengthy ban if found guilty. September 21 — Southampton seek leniency ahead of the FA hearing Southampton asked the FA to take into account the punishment already imposed by the EFL — expulsion from the play-offs and a four-point deduction — as Eckert's disciplinary hearing approached. The club acknowledged that staff had been sent to observe Oxford, Ipswich and Middlesbrough training sessions. October 7 - Eckert is handed a suspended six-week ban by the FA

Southampton owner Dragan Solak added: 'I'm pleased that the independent panel has come to a decision and that we have an outcome. We have already suffered enough, and we appreciate the panel's recognition of that.

'We are confident the manager has learned from this matter, and a suspended sentence allows him to continue in his role. I firmly believe that Tonda is one of Europe's most exciting young coaches, and with this distraction removed, I am confident he can lead the team to a successful season.

'I'd like to thank our fans for standing by us and showing the team so much support during a time when we have needed them more than ever.

'The FA process has been a positive experience. Tonda has been given the opportunity to be open and honest with the panel, and the panel has been able to see that he is simply a good person who made poor decisions.

'The same cannot be said for the EFL process, and the way they have subsequently treated us is not something we will forget. However, now is the time to look forward to what I believe will be a great future for our club.'

Before the verdict, Southampton had already lined up former Wolves and Middlesbrough boss Rob Edwards to potentially step in if Eckert's ban was lengthy.

Eckert had pleaded for sympathetic handling, telling the BBC this week that the club have already had a 'big, big punishment' while Saints chief executive Phil Parsons said: 'What we hope as a club is they (the FA panel) actually recognise where we are at the moment, and what we've already been through, because I think it has to be taken into account.

'I really feel like we've taken enough. We've been hurt. I think it's one of the largest sanctions ever when it comes to football, or even sporting, history.'

Sports.title: Attack coaches explain why PREM is now a try-fest with Saints and Bristol leading the way - and how it could help England: Tackle height changes, dynamic back threes, the cat-and-mouse maul and the jackal clampdown
Sports.content:
Attack coaches explain why PREM is now a try-fest with Saints and Bristol leading the way - and how it could help England: Tackle height changes, dynamic back threes, the cat-and-mouse maul and the jackal clampdown

One of Brendan Venter’s early moves as returning Saracens boss was to blast an intimidating chorus of howling wolves over the sound system as his players ran out for their first home game of the season against Sale on Sunday.

It was a nod to the club’s period of dominance, before the salary-cap scandal, when their gameplan was defined by their feared ‘Wolfpack’ defence. Venter is a trendsetter – not a trend follower – and he has ambitions to break the PREM’s cycle of attacking supremacy. The eccentric South African may be on a one-man crusade.

In the opening 10 games of this season, the winning team has scored 38 points on average. The number of tries is higher than ever and, if you ask PREM attack coaches, that should be a fillip for Steve Borthwick’s England.

Tweaks to the game’s laws mean 97 per cent of points now come from tries and conversions. Kicking for three points no longer stacks up. Northampton and Bristol lead the way with their high-intensity attacks but their rivals are catching up.

So, what has led to the PREM becoming a try-fest? Is it good for England? And can Venter stop it?

RULE CHANGES

‘There are loads of little governance changes that have made the game quicker,' Northampton attack coach Sam Vesty tells Daily Mail Sport.

Tommy Freeman of Northampton goes over to score in what has been a try-fest of a PREM season so far

Louis Rees-Zammit of Gloucester is top try-scorer with four so far

‘For example, a few years ago, you could stand with one foot off the pitch and one foot on to catch the ball and it would be out. You get a breather. They switched that rule so it's impossible to take the ball out now. Therefore, the ball's on the pitch for that little bit longer, there's more fatigue and more space to go and attack.

Tackle height plays a part too.

‘If you tackle high, you are now highly sanctioned,' Vesty adds. 'Therefore, people are tackling a bit lower. If you tackle lower, the player being tackled has their hands free and the ball is available to offload easily.

‘Plus, historically, people would say you're overplaying if you had the ball around the halfway line. But now we say keep playing because you're going to create something. It’s more productive to have the ball deeper on the pitch than it is to kick it away.

‘And then there's the offside line. It is being refereed more harshly than it has been previously. Therefore, there's a little bit more space.

'If you think 10 years ago, when Saracens were winning lots of stuff, a lot of that would have been based on a high kick game and a very good defence. The game has changed a lot since then and it’s refereed very differently as well.’

Freddie Steward of Leicester offloads the ball in the tackle. The lower tackle height means it is easier for players to keep the ball alive

ATTACKING INTENT

Financial pressure put the brakes on PREM clubs recruiting the biggest and most powerful players. Many instead moved to France or Japan in search of bigger salaries. There are fewer bulldozing carriers and a greater premium on movement, skill and sleight of hand. High-possession teams are thriving.

‘I watch all the line breaks and tries in the league every week,’ says Gloucester attack coach James Lightfoot-Brown, who has been named in the England A management team for this autumn.

‘There's a real intent to score from every possession, which maybe you wouldn't have seen before. Firstly, you have to credit the cohesion and the accuracy.

'Defences have not just stopped defending. Now teams are attacking with 15 players. Look at some of the movements off the ball from the back three to create numbers and then some of the speed off the floor from forwards.

‘There’s a desire to work. Modern back three players don't just stand on the wing anymore. When we played Exeter two weeks ago, Manny Feyi-Waboso was everywhere. Popping off nine, popping up on the other wing.

'We want to see the number on the back disappear from a back-three perspective when we have the ball. How quickly can we get an overload? How quickly can we get our best players on the ball?

'There are different nuances. These guys are no longer just runners. They can link, they can pop up on shoulders and get an additional pass or an offload. Northampton are the best at it. They are so fluid. If players want to get to the next level, they’ve got to get involvements.'

Exeter winger Manny Feyi-Waboso does not stick to the touchline but roams the park to get his hands on the ball

Rees-Zammit celebrates going over for another try

Bath’s new attack coach, Mike Prendergast, agrees.

‘Teams are looking for space and playing to edges,' he says. 'When you get into that opposition 22, a lot of tries are being scored on the edges. That’s quite an interesting trend.

‘There’s a huge amount of speed here. England have got a lot of very good, quick back-three players. I’ve seen that first hand over the last couple of weeks, including some of our own players at Bath.

'There are some exceptional athletes, especially out wide. A lot of the ball in play has been quite high in the first two rounds, which is great in terms of a spectacle.’

Teams have also been adapting their selection to maximise player output. Louis Rees-Zammit, for example, is the league's top try-scorer with four and has been prolific since he was shifted back to the wing by Bristol from full-back.

RISK-TAKING

‘Teams are taking more risks,' Lightfoot-Brown continues. 'They are running from deep and putting defences under pressure all the time. We used to see a couple of phases of probing, seeing what the defence is going to do.

'There's no probing going on at the moment. Teams are trying to score or they're kicking the ball. There's no middle ground, which makes for an exciting product.’

The warm weather conditions have promoted ball-passing and fast-track pitches which also help explain why 94 tries have already been scored.

‘The time of the year has an effect,’ says Prendergast. ‘The good weather means we’ve generally been playing with dry balls.'

'The time of the year has an effect,’ says Bath coach Mike Prendergast. ‘The good weather means we’ve generally been playing with dry balls'

BROKEN-FIELD BONUSES

The bulk of attacking opportunities now come from broken-field situations.

Last season, 29.3 per cent of attacking chances came from kick returns and 16 per cent from turnovers. Attack coaches have been encouraging their teams to react to unstructured defences, with harsher officiating of the breakdown ensuring the attacking team has the advantage.

‘Referees are not rewarding negative defensive actions as much as they used to,’ adds Lightfoot-Brown. ‘It’s becoming very clear that the jackal attempt has to be a genuine positive action. No hands on the floor.

'It can't just be a post-tackle effort to slow up the ball. We always want to reward good defensive work on the floor, but they’re not letting teams cynically slow things down.’

CAT AND MOUSE MAUL

But the most significant change this season has been around the maul. Defending forwards now have less freedom to disrupt the set-piece play, which means they have to commit more players to stop the drive. The byproduct has been additional space to attack.

‘The maul has come back into the game,’ says Prendergast. ‘Outside of the 22, the maul probably went away. Now we’re seeing a lot of mauls around the halfway line and up.

'The forwards coaches are looking to get it moving forwards or moving in towards the 15 so you can create space on the edge. The defence has to put numbers in to negate it or keep numbers out on their feet.

'It’s a bit of cat and mouse at the moment and everyone is trying to figure it out. It’s certainly something teams are looking to exploit.’

Nathan Michelow of Saracens controls the maul during the match against Leicester Tigers at Welford Road

SO, IS IT GOOD FOR ENGLAND?

Bigger collisions, better jackallers and stronger set-piece all change the game at international level but there seems to be a consensus that the level of PREM attacking play should boost the national side.

‘People follow what has been successful,’ says Vesty. ‘People look at the way Bordeaux and Toulouse keep the ball alive and score loads of points. The high tempo game has been successful so people go after that.

Marcus Smith scores a try for England - but can the PREM's attacking instincts rub off on Steve Borthwick's national team?

‘New Zealand are playing in a quite PREM style at the moment. Because the Springboks have so much power, if you try to take them on at that you are going to come second.

'The All Blacks have been high speed and high possession and they look really good at it. People talk about high numbers of phases but if you do it well then you don’t need loads of phases. They would rather have a crack as a first option and use a kicking game to move up the field as almost a second option.

‘The PREM is a better product but we need to make sure it doesn't become a basketball-style try-fest. The beauty of the game is that you can win in a lot of ways. If it just turns into a basketball, you score, we score, you score type affair, it gets a bit boring. We’re not there yet but we need to be mindful.’

As autumn descends and Venter gets his claws in deeper, the PREM will find out if the Wolfpack can make defence fashionable again.

Sports.title: In The Saddle with David Probert: 'I want to land that elusive Group 1 prize'
Sports.content:
In The Saddle with David Probert: 'I want to land that elusive Group 1 prize'

The Welshman from Bargoed in South Wales's Rhymney Valley has ridden more than 1,500 winners, notably as a stalwart member of the Andrew Balding stable

View 4 Images David Probert: takes part in our Q&A (Image: Hong Kong Jockey Club)

David Probert is one of British racing's most respected and consistent Flat jockeys. Hailing from Bargoed in South Wales’s Rhymney Valley, he rose through the pony racing ranks before joining Andrew Balding's Kingsclere operation.

‌



‌



Since sharing the Champion Apprentice title in 2008, Probert has ridden more than 1,500 winners, claimed the All-Weather Championship in 2021-22 and established himself as a trusted rider at the highest levels of the sport, with a reputation for professionalism and tactical awareness.

‌



Probert, who has finished second in both the 2,000 Guineas and Derby from limited opportunities, has become a stalwart member of the Balding stable, steering Never So Brave to victory in the Group 2 Summer Mille last year, shortly before taking up an end of year stint in Hong Kong.

‌



Best advice you have been given? When you get knocked down, get back up

What would you say are your main attributes in the saddle? I enjoy making the running on horses - I feel I have an idea about pace

You were one of the busiest jockeys in Britain in 2021 when you rode 1,227 times. What gave you that drive to keep going at such a prolific rate? I love my job and love riding horses and winners are always a good bonus

‌



If you could ride one race again, what would it be? I remember riding Side Glance in the Summer Mile at Ascot – where I was locked up with nowhere to go.

View 4 Images Tronada was David Probert's 1,000th winner (Image: PA)

Best moment in the saddle? My two Royal Ascot winners

‌



What are your main ambitions in racing? To achieve as much as I can and try and get that elusive Group 1

Hardest jockey to beat in a finish? Oisin Murphy Best horse you’ve sat on? Crystal Ocean

View 4 Images Crystal Ocean (left): the best horse David Probert has ridden (Image: Getty)

‌



Favourite Course? Ascot/Chester Favourite Festival? Royal Ascot

A race you haven’t won – that you would love to win? The Derby

If you hadn’t been a jockey, what would you be? I would more than likely be working on a farm somewhere

‌



Proudest moment away from racing? Getting the keys to my house

Biggest passion away from racing? Playing golf

What is your most treasured possession? My St Christopher travels everywhere with me

‌



View 4 Images Actor Owen Wilson (Image: Getty Images)

Who would play you in a film? Owen Wilson

What would your superpower be? The ability to teleport

‌



A trait you most value in others? Kindness

What is your guilty pleasure? Eating too much

Biggest sporting idol outside of racing? Tiger Woods

What is your death row meal? Pepperoni Pizza

If you could only listen to one song again, what would it be? Sing like Madonna - Sebastian Schub

Sports.title: Liverpool get worrying injury update on Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo from Andoni Iraola
Sports.content:
Liverpool get worrying injury update on Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo from Andoni Iraola

Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo both returned early from international duty after suffering injuries and Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola says they are doubtful to face Manchester City

View 2 Images Andoni Iraola has given an injury update (Image: Gaspafotos/MB Media, Getty Images)

Andoni Iraola has admitted that Liverpool duo Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo are "both injured" and are major doubts to face Manchester City this weekend.

‌



‌



Liverpool have their players back from international duty and are preparing to face City in the Premier League on Sunday afternoon at Anfield. City come into the game top of the league, having won all five of their games, and Liverpool's task has been made harder by injury concerns.

‌



Isak picked up a thigh injury while playing for Sweden, while Gakpo had to withdraw from Netherlands duty after being on the receiving end of a strong tackle. The duo are key attackers for Liverpool and Iraola did little to reassure fans ahead of the return to club football.

‌



"I think Alex Isak and Cody Gakpo both have had to leave the national teams with injuries," he said. "Now it's a matter of if they are going to recover in time to help us in the next game or not. But right now they are both injured."

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Isak was injured while playing for Sweden against Romania on September 25. His manager Graham Potter didn't sound too concerned when he explained the issue.

“He’s got a small problem with his thigh,” Potter said. “It’s not a big one but because of the amount of games we’ve got in a small space of time, he won’t be able to make those.

“It was during the game. Like anything, you sometimes get bumps and bruises in the game, you might think it’s a bit of a dead leg or something. But actually as the 24 hours, 48 hours after the game, not quite what you think.

‌



“Unfortunately after getting it checked out, it’s a little bit more than what you think during the match. He has to miss the rest of the camp."

View 2 Images Cody Gakpo picked up an injury on international duty (Image: Roy Lazet/Getty Images)

Gakpo had to be substituted after a nasty challenge by Serbia midfielder Sasa Lukic. He has two goals and four assists in six games for Liverpool this season and would be a big miss for Iraola, who has also benefited from four goals in five Premier League games from Isak.

‌



Liverpool host Manchester City on Sunday looking to take advantage of the uncertainty surrounding their opponents following their guilty verdict. Iraola knows the size of the task facing them against Enzo Maresca's side.

"We've been unbeaten but they've won all of them, so it makes a big difference in their side," he added. "I think we need to be very, very good if we want to beat City because they've been especially offensively scoring a lot of goals lately.

"We know the names that are very dangerous. But I think also we've shown good defensive improvements lately and I hope we can defend the threats that they have and also hurt them on the other side."

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo eviscerates Simon Jordan as brutal text message leaked
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo eviscerates Simon Jordan as brutal text message leaked

Cristiano Ronaldo has been at the centre of controversy during the international break after walking out on Portugal's international duty

View 2 Images Personal text messages from Cristiano Ronaldo have been revealed. (Image: Getty Images)

Piers Morgan has revealed Cristiano Ronaldo launched a harsh, personal attack on talkSPORT heavyweight Simon Jordan, where he called on him to 'stop using Botox' in a savage text message. The TV presenter has been at the defence of the five-time Ballon d'Or winner once again after Ronaldo's latest spat.

‌



‌



The 41-year-old stormed out of international duty with Portugal under new manager Jorge Jesus after being left on the bench against Norway. Ronaldo walked out on the eve of the win over Denmark after being an unused substitute in Oslo, and in a subsequent statement, it was claimed that Jesus told him that he would play him for 30 minutes against Norway, ultimately going back on his word.

‌



Ronaldo has since apologised for his actions and asked the Portuguese Football Federation to punish him and spare any leniency, yet the latest high-profile incident involving the iconic footballer has divided the footballing sphere, with Rio Ferdinand and Morgan rushing to his defence.

‌



Why Pep Guardiola is returning to Man City for the first time since guilty verdict READ MORE :

Cristiano Ronaldo pays surprise tribute to Lionel Messi after final Argentina game READ MORE :

Speaking on the Football Uncensored segment of Morgan's show, the 61-year-old revealed that he exchanged messages with the former Manchester United and Real Madrid attacker, one of which included a clip from talkSPORT with Jim White and Jordan.

Morgan said: "I want to give you a cheerful note to take back to your workstation. I sent Cristiano the clip of me with Simon Jordan this morning, and he texted back, 'That blonde guy, tell him to stop with the Botox, he looks like an apple'.

"That's my breaking news. Breaking news from Cristiano Ronaldo, Simon Jordan you are an apple. You suspiciously smooth-faced apple."

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

It came after Morgan's appearance earlier in the day on talkSPORT alongside Jordan and White. The pair became locked in a back-and-forth verbal match on the topic of Ronaldo's actions and behaviour since the international break flashpoint.

Jordan said: "I know you work on the premise that everything is a bleeding filibuster, other people can have an opinion. In your objective, rounded mind, is there not a common denominator of fallouts might be some of Ronaldo's behaviour?

‌



"Is there a possibility in your balanced, shell-like, kissing Ronaldo's backside mentality..." Morgan interrupted Jordan's question with a series of no answers."

View 2 Images Piers Morgan revealed Cristiano Ronaldo's harsh, personal attack on Simon Jordan. (Image: Uncensored/YouTube)

Jordan continued: "Well, you're a bloody fool then aren't you? In your wide experiences of managing players and understanding dynamics behind the scenes, you can't see beyond the end of your nose that there might be a common denominator when problems occur that might be Ronaldo's behaviour. No? OK."

‌



In light of Lionel Messi's emotional farewell from international football with Argentina, doubts have been cast over Ronaldo's future on the world's stage at the age of 41. Ronaldo accused Jesus of broken promises in his lengthy statement to his 679 million Instagram followers.

The former Benfica manager worked with the forward at Al-Nassr in the Saudi Pro League but says he will respond to the statement once he has had time to read it.

Jesus was at an under-21s game when the statement was released and reporters were waiting for him upon his return home. But Ronaldo has apologised for his actions and for stepping away from duty with the national team.

Article continues below

He said: "Never, at any moment, have I interfered in any technical or tactical decision of any coach or national team manager in almost 25 years of career. I accept, for better or worse, what they propose that I do. I respect the decision, and when they break their word to me, I feel that my place is not there.

"I felt that, from that point on, my remaining would only harm the working group, and I did what I have always said I would do if I did not feel useful: I packed my bags and left."

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo pays surprise tribute to Lionel Messi after final Argentina game
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo pays surprise tribute to Lionel Messi after final Argentina game

Cristiano Ronaldo has always been a rival of Lionel Messi during their careers, but he put aside their history to send him a touching message upon his international retirement

View 2 Images Cristiano Ronaldo has been a long-time rival of Lionel Messi (Image: Alexander Hassenstein - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

Cristiano Ronaldo has sent a classy message to Lionel Messi after his long-time rival retired from international football.

‌



‌



Messi scored a penalty in his last game for Argentina against Benin on Wednesday. His 126th goal for his country came in his 208th appearance on an emotional night in Buenos Aires.

‌



The 39-year-old got an incredible send-off at the Estadio Monumental, with a drone show celebrating his best moments in an Argentina shirt after the match. Messi then delivered a tear-filled speech to his team-mates, describing his international career as “the most wonderful thing that can happen".

‌



Messi was instrumental in Argentina's World Cup win in 2022, their first title since 1986, and his goals helped Lionel Scaloni's side reach the final once again this summer, although they were beaten by Spain. His legacy as one of the greats of the game is undisputed and shown by the message from Ronaldo.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Writing on Instagram, Ronaldo said: "Leo, so many years defending your country and a history that will last forever. All my respect for what you have achieved with Argentina. A hug."

‌



The 41-year-old's words came under Messi's statement, which read: "Yesterday was my last game and I already miss wearing blue and white. I know I'm making the right decision. It was an incredible road, filled with joys and also some sorrows, but I'm clear that it was worth every step I took.

"And I'm left with a lot to say. It is impossible for me to express everything I feel in a few words or in a post. This trip would have been impossible without my family, who always stood by my side and supported me, especially during the difficult times, when I needed it most.

View 2 Images Lionel Messi bowed out of international football in Buenos Aires (Image: Marcelo Endelli/Getty Images)

‌



"They were also indispensable my friends, all the colleagues and technicians I had, along with their technical bodies. I don't want to forget Diego, who put our country where it deserved to be and who, as I always say, I know that he helped us being here with us and also from heaven, in every step we took.

"Thanks to the clubs I played in, for always respecting my feelings and allowing me to dedicate myself to my country when it was time to put on the national team shirt. And, of course, thank God: without His guidance and His will, we wouldn't even be dreaming of having come this far.

"I am a grateful person. I love you so much, I will miss you and I will always thank you for being by our side, by my side."

Article continues below

While he has waved goodbye to Argentina, Messi will continue playing club football, with his Inter Miami contract running until the end of the 2028 season. He has already laid the groundwork for when he does retire, buying Spanish minnows UE Cornella as well as becoming the owner of second-division side CD Eldense.

Sports.title: Harry Kane urged to follow in David Beckham's footsteps in MLS before taking on the NFL
Sports.content:
Harry Kane urged to follow in David Beckham's footsteps in MLS before taking on the NFL

Harry Kane spoke recently about his desire to become an NFL kicker and the head of Major League Soccer Don Garber has urged him to use the league as a stepping stone

View 3 Images Harry Kane is already planning the next step of his career (Image: Joe Klamar / AFP via Getty Images)

Harry Kane has been given an open invitation to move to Major League Soccer.

‌



‌



MLS commissioner Don Garber says they would “love” to welcome England captain Kane as the next high profile signing. Kane, 33, revealed last month that he already had a career plan mapped out as he is set to sign a new deal with Bayern Munich, then move to the United States and finish as an NFL kicker.

‌



MLS chiefs have already had David Beckham and Lionel Messi as mega stars to boost football in the US and Kane looks set to follow when he eventually leaves Bayern. Garber said: “I mean, I'd love for him to do that. For me, it is the fulfilment of the dream that we have built a proper soccer league that would drive a soccer nation.

‌



“We wanted to create something that would have the Harry Kanes of the world say, I'd kind of like to play in MLS. And I think Messi proved that, too. That was a competitive process. Working to ensure that we had a dynamic that would be better than going back to Barcelona?”

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Kane would have no shortage of offers from MLS clubs and there are also seven club owners who also run NFL teams, so there is the chance of a crossover. While there has been nothing formal in place, there is an open door for Kane to move after his next Bayern deal which is likely to expire in 2029 when he puts pen to paper.

Garber has been MLS commissioner since 1999 and guided the league from being seen as “quirky” into being a set-up to compete with major European leagues. A huge part of that was built on the “Beckham effect” when the former England captain left Real Madrid to join LA Galaxy.

That was a game changer but Garber admits that it's hard to choose between Beckham and Messi as who had the biggest effect on MLS and its development. Messi said farewell to Argentina in his final game on Tuesday night but is still going strong for Inter Miami.

‌



View 3 Images Lionel Messi is the MLS' biggest star at Inter Miami (Image: Michael Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Garber said: “Beckham or Messi? I don't think I would say one is more important than the other. That's a good question. David put this league on the path to credibility and respect. And in the prime of his career, he came here to LA. We were talking in 2006 a couple years before we were going, managed out of bankruptcy, discussions.

“I remember the opening party that we introduced him, and every top actor and celebrity in L.A. was welcoming him then, and he played well. He showed the world that this league can be competitive, it could be respected, it could be fun. It could have great players. It attracted Thierry Henry and many, many other players right after that.

‌



“So without David, there's probably no major league soccer. That being said, Major League soccer would not be the global phenomenon and not be, sort of, on the hearts and minds of just about anybody in the world without Leo Messi. He is so competitive and plays to such a high level as he showed in the World Cup and that proves how important MLS is.”

Garber has put MLS firmly on the map. He takes pride in the development of the US national team, how many MLS players were at the World Cup and the latest step is falling into line with the international calendar for its fixture list.

View 3 Images David Beckham helped make the MLS what it is today (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Antoine Griezmann was a big signing for the MLS and now, Garber says, there are more live football matches shown in the States than any other sport which shows how the game has grown. Garber will stand down from his current role on January 1 with Larry Berg set to take over with no regrets and just pride at his legacy.

Garber added: “We went from being sort of the quirky kids in the back of the room to now. We are not at the front of the classroom, and we're certainly not teaching the class. But we're walking around in a way where there's much more respect for what's going on in America. I think MLS has been a huge part of growing that.

“And the World Cup just delivered on everything we thought our country would be able to be a proper soccer nation, with packed stadiums and passionate fans, and an understanding of what the game means globally, and its inculcation into the culture of our community.

‌



“And it's been a great full circle. I'm great. Somebody said recently: ‘How you doing?’ I said: ‘I couldn't be better.’ And I walked in realising that maybe these guys were wondering how I was feeling about the whole thing.

“I said: ’It’s not as if the high school prom queen kicked me out. You know, I kicked her out. I had the greatest job in sports, and I just thought it was the right time after the World Cup.”
