Ghana News.title: PAC Ranking Member accuses Health Ministry of ‘organised crime’ over GH¢10m outstanding car loans
Ghana News.content:
Ranking Member on Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee (PAC), Samuel Atta Mills, has criticised the Ministry of Health over the alleged failure to recover about GH¢10 million in car loans, describing the arrangement as “organised crime”.

Mr Atta Mills made the remarks when officials of the Ministry of Health appeared before the Public Accounts Committee on October 8 to respond to concerns over vehicles provided to officials under a car loan arrangement.

According to the Ranking Member, some beneficiaries who, in his view, did not qualify to drive official vehicles based on their salaries were nevertheless provided with cars under arrangements that allowed them to determine when and how they would repay the loans.

“We know these people don’t qualify to drive cars because of their salaries, and then we bypass the system. We give them their cars, and they choose when and how they are going to pay,” he said.

He questioned the rationale behind the arrangement and expressed concern over the ministry’s approach to recovering outstanding amounts from beneficiaries.

“If this isn’t organised crime, I don’t know what else it is. This is organised crime, being encouraged by the Minister of Health,” Mr Atta Mills said.

Questions over retired and deceased beneficiaries

The Ranking Member also raised concerns about beneficiaries who have either retired from public service or died without fully settling their car loans.

He demanded a comprehensive list of such beneficiaries, suggesting that some vehicles could still be in the possession of relatives despite outstanding payments.

‘Put a stop to it’

Mr Atta Mills called on the Minister of Health to take immediate steps to recover the outstanding vehicles and funds.

“This is organised crime, Minister of Health. Put a stop to it,” he said.

His concerns centred particularly on the recovery process and the responsibility of the Ministry of Health to ensure that vehicles issued under the arrangement are either fully paid for or recovered where beneficiaries fail to meet the terms of the arrangement.

Ranking Member challenges DVLA explanation

The PAC Ranking Member also rejected an explanation that the list of beneficiaries or vehicles had been forwarded to the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA).

He questioned why the DVLA should be expected to resolve a matter that originated from the Ministry of Health.

“Was it DVLA who gave them those cars? Was it DVLA who organised that crime?” he asked.

According to Mr Atta Mills, responsibility for recovering the vehicles rests primarily with the institution that provided them.

He therefore called for the establishment of a dedicated recovery unit or team within the Ministry to pursue beneficiaries who have failed to honour their obligations.

“What you need to do is you need to have a recovery unit, or a recovery team who will go and collect all these cars,” he said.

Calls for aggressive recovery

Mr Atta Mills argued that the Ministry must take stronger measures to retrieve vehicles where beneficiaries obtained them without meeting the applicable requirements or have failed to repay the associated loans.

He suggested that a dedicated recovery team should be empowered to identify vehicles and take steps to retrieve them where necessary.

“Somebody who will stop you in the middle of the highway and take the car away from you because you got it fraudulently,” he said.

He accused the Ministry of shifting responsibility to other institutions instead of directly addressing the recovery of the vehicles.

“You organised this crime, and then you blame everybody else. Whilst you are the criminals,” he added.

The confrontation at the Public Accounts Committee highlights concerns over the management and recovery of government-backed vehicle loans, particularly where beneficiaries have retired, died or allegedly failed to meet repayment obligations.

Ghana News.title: GAUA strike disrupts student registration at University of Ghana
Ghana News.content:
The ongoing strike by the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) is disrupting administrative services at public universities, with students facing difficulties completing registration and other admission-related processes.

GAUA has been on strike for more than two months following failed negotiations with the government over the payment of negotiated and approved allowances. The university administrators are also demanding action to address what they describe as disparities in allowances and other conditions of service.

At the University of Ghana, several administrative services, including student, legal, financial and library services, have been affected by the industrial action.

The disruption has also affected first-semester registration for the 2026/2027 academic year.

A notice from the University of Ghana, signed by Pro Vice-Chancellor Professor Gordon Awandare, informed Level 100 and continuing students that registration had been put on hold due to the ongoing strike by university administrators.

“Management of the University of Ghana wishes to apologise to our cherished students, Level 100 and continuing students, for the current challenges with online registration for the first semester of the 2026-2027 academic year, which are caused by the ongoing industrial action by the university administrators,” the notice stated.

Checks by JoyNews at the University of Ghana showed that some students are struggling with course registration, accommodation arrangements and access to the university portal.

Some parents also said they had been trying to access the portal for several days but had been unable to complete the registration process.

The disruption comes as concerns grow over the impact of industrial actions on instructional time and the smooth running of Ghana’s education system.

The ongoing teachers’ strike has already affected teaching and learning in some basic and secondary schools, with some pupils reportedly staying home.

Parents say the situation is putting additional pressure on families, particularly those who have invested heavily in their children's education.

One parent expressed his frustration. “I have invested a lot for my kids, and honestly speaking, I feel so much sad for this outcome, that after all the investment, my child will not go to school to learn. It is so pathetic for me,” the parent said.

The parent urged the authorities to urgently resolve the disputes to prevent students from losing more instructional time.

Ghana News.title: Tema is regaining its industrial glory days as Ghana’s industrial city – Mahama
Ghana News.content:
President John Mahama says Tema is regaining its glory days as Ghana’s industrial city, citing the expansion of the Tema Port, the return of the Tema Oil Refinery and ongoing efforts to revive VALCO.

Speaking at the commissioning and inspection of Nestlé Ghana’s expanded evaporated milk production line in Tema, he said the progress and the expansion of industries such as Nestlé is helping to restore Tema’s position as a key industrial centre.

“Kwame Nkrumah planned Tema as Ghana’s industrial city, and I am pleased to say that Tema is regaining its glory days”. President Mahama said.

He stated that industries operating in the Tema enclave depend on efficient infrastructure, including the port, roads and reliable electricity, to serve markets beyond Ghana.

President Mahama said his government accepts the responsibility of providing the infrastructure needed to support industrial expansion.

“My government accepts that obligation without reservation, and we are committed to meeting it,” he said.

He also urged Nestlé to leverage Ghana’s position as the headquarters of the African Continental Free Trade Area to expand its reach across the continent.

“Ghana is the headquarters of the African Continental Free Trade Area, and we must take advantage of this to make Ghana Africa’s production powerhouse,” he said.

President Mahama said the expanded Nestlé production line provides the company with the capacity to contribute to that ambition.

“This expansion gives Nestlé Ghana the capacity to do exactly that, and I urge the company to seize the opportunity with boldness and carry the words ‘Made in Ghana’ into every market across the length and breadth of Africa,” he said.

He also warned that the increased domestic production capacity would come with greater attention to illicit imports and customs evasion.

“Having built the capacity to make these cans ourselves, we will take an equally close interest in illicit imports and customs evasion,” President Mahama said.

President Mahama declared that Ghana was open for business and outlined measures his administration was taking to improve the business environment.

“Ghana is back and Ghana is open for business. Ghana is working again. My government is your partner.” he said.

He said government was reforming customs procedures, revising the tax incentive framework and digitising public services to make doing business in Ghana faster, simpler and more predictable.

President Mahama assured Ghanaian businesses that his administration would continue to provide the enabling environment, financing and infrastructure needed to support their growth.

He said Ghana’s renewed confidence was being built through the work of businesses and workers across the country.

“The confidence we are rebuilding today is not borrowed from anyone. It is earned factory by factory and production line by production line through the labour and dedication of Ghanaian workers,” he said.

Ghana News.title: FBI says more than 130 detained in Ghana over scam operation targeting US victims
Ghana News.content:
FBI Director Kash Patel says a scam operation in Ghana has been dismantled as part of the bureau's global Operation Blackout targeting transnational fraud networks.

In a post on X on Thursday, October 8, Patel said the Ghana operation had so far identified nearly US$10 million in losses and 89 victims, while more than 130 people had been arrested or detained.

OPERATION BLACKOUT: this FBI’s global scam center fraud demolition. Another takedown this week out of Ghana: -Nearly $10 million in identified losses so far -89 victims identified -130+ individuals arrested or detained (including victims who will be repatriated to home country) -300+ devices seized Investigation is ongoing. These scam compounds target American citizens and destroy lives - and this @FBI is crushing them in every corner of the world. More to come. Operation Blackout totals so far: -Roughly $17 BILLION seized -Hundreds of alleged scammers arrested -Thousands of trafficked workers freed -10,000+ Americans warned before losing their money -$670 MILLION in estimated losses prevented — FBI Director Kash Patel (@FBIDirectorKash) October 8, 2026

He also said more than 300 devices had been seized during the operation.

“These scam compounds target American citizens and destroy lives – and this FBI is crushing them in every corner of the world. More to come,” Patel said.

The FBI Director said the investigation remains ongoing.

According to Patel's account, some of those detained in Ghana are victims who will be repatriated to their home countries.

The identities of those arrested or detained, the locations of the operations and the specific Ghanaian institutions involved have not been disclosed in Patel's post.

It is also not yet clear whether any of those arrested will face prosecution in Ghana or extradition proceedings in the United States.

The Ghana operation forms part of Operation Blackout, which the FBI describes as a global effort targeting scam compounds involved in fraud against Americans.

Patel has previously said Operation Blackout has resulted in roughly US$17 billion in fraud-related assets being seized.

He has also said the initiative has led to hundreds of arrests, the freeing of thousands of trafficked workers and efforts to warn potential victims before they lose money.

The FBI's separate prevention effort, Operation Level Up, has reportedly contacted more than 10,000 potential victims and prevented hundreds of millions of dollars in losses.

Patel has described scam compounds targeted by the operation as large, fortified facilities where trafficked workers are allegedly forced to conduct fraud against victims abroad.

He has also said criminal networks are increasingly moving their operations towards Africa as law enforcement pressure increases in Southeast Asia and other regions.

The announcement comes amid growing cooperation between Ghanaian and US authorities over transnational financial and cybercrime.

In July, Ghanaian national Frederick Kumi, popularly known as Abu Trica, was extradited to the United States to face charges over his alleged involvement in a romance-fraud network.

The US Department of Justice said Kumi, 31, was accused of being part of a network that targeted more than 80 elderly victims in the United States and allegedly defrauded them of more than US$8 million.

Kumi was arrested in Ghana in December 2025 and extradited to the US on July 9, 2026. He faces charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy.

The US authorities acknowledged the cooperation of several Ghanaian institutions in securing his arrest and extradition, including the Attorney-General's Office, Economic and Organised Crime Office, Ghana Police Service, Cyber Security Authority, National Intelligence Bureau and the FBI Legal Attaché Office in Accra.

Patel ended his announcement on the Ghana operation by saying “More to come,” suggesting the bureau's campaign against international scam networks is continuing.

The FBI has not provided further details on the identities of those arrested in Ghana or the precise location and nature of the operation.

Ghana News.title: BlaKid reflects on Shatta Wale collaboration and TGMA recognition
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian artiste BlaKid Music says working with Shatta Wale taught him valuable lessons about consistency, confidence and work ethic.

The singer was speaking on Prime Time with George Quaye. The discussion centred on his breakthrough, recognition at the Telecel Ghana Music Awards (TGMA), and his feature on Shatta Wale’s projects.

BlaKid described getting the call to work with Shatta Wale as a turning point in his career. According to him, being in the studio and on projects with the multiple award-winning dancehall artiste was more than just music, it was a masterclass in consistency, confidence and work ethic.

He said Shatta Wale taught him the importance of believing in his sound and staying true to his craft, even when the industry gets tough.

“Working with Shatta Wale opened my eyes. His energy, his drive, how he treats music like business, I learnt a lot. He encourages young artistes to push and not wait for anyone,” BlaKid said.

He added that the collaboration has introduced his music to a much bigger audience and given him credibility among industry players.

Reflecting on his TGMA experience, BlaKid said earning recognition at Ghana’s biggest music awards night was both humbling and motivating. He described the night as a celebration of hard work and noted that for a young artiste like himself, just being mentioned on that platform is a win.

He admitted, however, that the journey has not been easy. From funding his own productions to getting airplay and breaking through a saturated market, the challenges are real.

“The industry is not easy for upcoming artistes. You need to invest a lot, you need a good team, and you need to stay consistent. But awards like TGMA show that people are watching your work,” he stated.

BlaKid, who is known for blending Afrobeats with Highlife and Dancehall influences, said he is currently working on new music and hopes to drop a project in the coming months.

His focus now, he said, is to build on the momentum from the TGMA recognition and the Shatta Wale feature to reach audiences beyond Ghana.

He also thanked his growing fan base for their loyalty and urged other young creatives not to give up.

“To every young artiste out there, keep working. Your time will come. Don’t stop because of the challenges,” he added.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Two killed after building partially collapses in Turkiye’s Istanbul
World.content:
Eight survivors rescued from the rubble as fears of further collapse slow operations in Istanbul’s Maltepe district.

Share Two killed after building partially collapses in Turkiye’s Istanbul on social media

At least two people have been killed after a seven-storey building in Turkiye’s Istanbul partially collapsed, officials said.

Emergency crews were trying to reach at least two people who were believed to be trapped, authorities said on Thursday.

The cause of the collapse was not immediately known, and an investigation was under way.

The building’s three lower floors, including a ground-floor shop, caved in before dawn in the district of Maltepe, on the Asian side of Istanbul, a city that is bisected by the Bosporus Strait.

Residents from the upper floors were safely evacuated while search teams rescued eight more people from the rubble.

The rescuers recovered two bodies and were trying to reach two people still believed to be inside, according to the Istanbul governor’s office.

Earlier, Istanbul Governor Davut Gul said rescuers had made contact with a 6-year-old trapped in the rubble. It was not immediately clear if the child was among those rescued.

He warned that the building was at risk of further collapse, hampering the rescue efforts. Nearby buildings were also evacuated for safety, the governor said.

Istanbul and other parts of Turkiye are undergoing an urban transformation programme that aims to replace old and earthquake-prone buildings with safer housing.

World.title: South Korea to recall Ukraine envoy in diplomatic row over POWs
World.content:
South Korea and Ukraine embroiled in a diplomatic row after President Zelenskyy revealed alleged transfer of two North Korean soldiers.

Share South Korea to recall Ukraine envoy in diplomatic row over POWs on social media

South Korea says it will recall its ambassador to Kyiv following a recent revelation by Ukraine of a transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The South Korean announcement on Thursday came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologise over the revelation.

“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

“The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end.”

South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his United Nations General Assembly address last month.

South Korea accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement relating to the transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.

The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers have expressed their desire to resettle in South Korea because they could face persecution if repatriated to North Korea.

South Korea had said it would accept them because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

South Korean officials said the nondisclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North.



There have been no comments from North Korea’s state media on the soldiers’ transfer. But the North has previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and its key ally, the United States, and focused on bolstering its nuclear programme since 2019.

South Korea has provided $445m in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100m in aid to Ukraine during a meeting with Zelenskyy.

World.title: UK’s Burnham ‘open’ to Germany joining GCAP fighter jet programme
World.content:
GCAP pact between the UK, Italy and Japan to build a new fighter jet welcomed Canada as an ‘observer’ in July

Prime ⁠⁠Minister Andy Burnham says the United Kingdom is open to Germany ⁠⁠joining the GCAP programme, a partnership with ⁠⁠Italy and Japan to build a new fighter jet, after meeting Chancellor Friedrich ‌‌Merz in Berlin.

“I’ve indicated to the Chancellor … our openness to Germany joining GCAP,” Burnham told a news conference on Thursday.

“That is something ⁠⁠that we seek ⁠⁠to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy ⁠⁠and Japan.”

There has been growing speculation that the ⁠⁠founding countries of the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) could open the door to ‌‌Germany after a rival Franco-German fighter programme collapsed in ‌‌June.

The GCAP pact to build a sixth generation fighter jet welcomed Canada as an “observer nation” in July.

As western nations seek to maintain air superiority over rival powers, the new warplanes will be equipped with AI, next-generation sensors and other technology.

Burnham is on his first official visit to Germany since becoming Britain’s prime minister in July. The leaders are also expected to confirm a new UK-Germany joint security partnership to counter sabotage, cyberattacks and other hybrid threats from adversaries.

“Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat. They reach into people’s homes and workplaces and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided,” Burnham said in a statement ahead of the visit.

Burnham’s office singled out the threat posed by Russia in a statement on Thursday, but stressed that the partnership would confront security threats regardless of their origin.



As part of the agreement, the UK and Germany will share security information and work together to monitor, deter and disrupt threats.

British MPs have raised concerns in recent months about the potential threats posed by Russia, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warning last month that Russia and its President, Vladimir Putin, were the biggest threat to the country’s security.

Germany has also raised concerns about what it sees as a growing security threat posed by Moscow. Last month, Berlin accused Russia of being behind a failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Moscow denies any wrongdoing.

Reporting from Berlin, Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane said the security partnership is “supposed to send a message to several countries” about the intention to increase European security.

“It’s a way of demonstrating German and British intent in so far as Ukraine is concerned, but also more broadly about where Europe goes next, remembering of course that the United States plays a role in so far as NATO is concerned,” Kane said.

“We know that Merz and Starmer [Burnham’s predecessor] and we can assume Burnham want to show to the Americans, as much as to the Russians, how much European security means to them.”

Burnham and Merz are also expected to discuss other key issues for Europe, including ongoing support for Ukraine in its war against Russia and disruption to global trade routes, including through the Strait of Hormuz.

The leaders are also expected to formally ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty. The accord commits both countries to deepening cooperation on science, technology, defence, security and economic growth.

World.title: Italian law to give election winners bonus seats: Why that’s controversial
World.content:
Critics say the proposed law is undemocratic, potentially granting a winning coalition disproportionate power in parliament.

Italy’s parliament is voting on Thursday on a new electoral law that would make it easier for election winners to form a majority government.

The law, proposed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, would award extra seats to any party or coalition that obtains more than 42 percent of seats in both parliamentary chambers, ensuring it holds a majority.

Meloni has framed the legislation as a route to greater stability in Italy’s political system, which has often been run by fragile coalition governments. Her critics, however, say the move is actually aimed at boosting her own chances in elections next year.

Here’s what we know about the electoral law and what it means for Italian politics:

What is Italy’s current electoral system?

Italy currently has a mixed electoral system for its 600-seat parliament, with about 36 percent of members of parliament elected directly in constituencies where the candidate with the most votes wins, and the rest decided through proportional representation.

The system, called “Rosatellum”, has been in place since 2017. It encourages coalition-building but can produce fractured results that make a governing majority hard to forge.

What would the new law change?

The new legislation would replace the mixed electoral system with a fully proportional one, as well as awarding extra seats to the party or coalition that wins the most seats if it secures at least 42 percent in both chambers.

The bonus would be as many as 70 seats in the 400-member Chamber of Deputies, the lower house, and up to 35 seats in the Senate, which has 200 elected members.



That means if a party or coalition meets the 42 percent share threshold in both chambers, it would have stronger power to govern. If no party or coalition meets the threshold, representation would be decided proportionally.

The new law would also force coalitions to announce their candidates for prime minister before the elections. Rado Fonda, head of research at Italian pollster SWG, told the Reuters news agency this provision could “prove problematic for the centre-left, potentially forcing an early leadership contest and exposing divisions that could weaken the bloc”.

Meloni, who currently leads the country’s longest-serving government since World War II, has said the reform will help stabilise the country rather than serve any one political group. “Whoever wins the elections will have the numbers to govern,” she said.

What stage is the legislation at?

The proposed law has already been approved by the Senate and must now undergo a final secret-ballot vote in the Chamber of Deputies.

Giovanni Orsina, a political scientist at Rome’s Luiss Guido Carli University, predicted that the law is “extremely likely” to pass.

If it fails, Meloni has said she will resign.

Why is the legislation controversial?

Opponents say the law is undemocratic because it could potentially grant a winning coalition a disproportionate level of power in parliament.

They also say that the legislation is intended to favour Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy party (Fdl) is bracing for a tough election battle next year.

Riccardo Magi, head of the liberal More Europe party, who is on a hunger strike to protest the proposed reform, has called it an “anti-democratic law” that risks giving a minority bloc a huge majority in parliament.

Senator Matteo Renzi, who leads the Italia Viva party, has accused Italy’s governing coalition of pushing the electoral reform due to a fear of losing power.

Other critics have pointed out that the law would do little to stabilise the political system if no party or coalition reaches the 42 percent threshold in both chambers – a relatively high bar.

“This could produce a hung parliament, making post-electoral negotiations necessary to form a government,” Vincenzo Emanuele, a political science professor at Luiss Guido Carli University in Rome and a member of the Italian Center for Electoral Studies (CISE), told Al Jazeera. “Even relatively small changes in coalition composition could make the difference between a clear parliamentary majority and a situation of political deadlock.”



When are Italy’s next elections, and what do the polls show?

Italy’s next general election must be held by December 22, 2027, although the government can call elections earlier if it wishes.

Currently, Meloni’s Fdl is polling ahead of all other parties, with 27 percent support, according to Politico’s polling aggregator. Her coalition partners, Lega and Forza Italia, have a combined 12 percent support, according to Politico, bringing the coalition share to 39 percent.

Fdl’s polling has been dented by support for a new far-right group, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), Reuters reported. It currently has 7.8 percent support, according to Italian polling institute SWG.

In opposition, the Democratic Party (PD) has 21 percent support, the Five Star Movement (M5S) has 12 percent and the Alliance of Greens and Left (AVS) has 6 percent, according to Politico. The Italy Viva (IV) and More Europe parties have 2 percent support each.

Emanuele said the current landscape means the proposed electoral law would not necessarily favour Meloni and could even benefit the opposition.

He said recent simulations by the CISE have shown that a centre-left coalition including the PD and M5S could potentially reach 44 percent of the vote, securing a “comfortable parliamentary majority”, though that could change if Meloni allies with National Future.

“The reform does not inherently favour the incumbent government: Its effects will depend crucially on how the competing coalitions are formed,” said Emanuele.

World.title: Why has Iraq devalued its currency, and why are some MPs against it?
World.content:
The move gives Baghdad more dinars for every dollar it earns from oil, at a cost MPs say will fall on ordinary Iraqis.

Share Iraq devalues its currency but some MPs oppose it on social media

Iraq has devalued its national currency again, undoing the previous government’s move to strengthen the Iraqi dinar and prompting calls in parliament to reverse the decision.

The cabinet approved new exchange rates for the dinar on Tuesday, following an emergency recommendation from Finance Minister Falih al-Sari and the governor of the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI).

From Wednesday, banks and exchange companies have been selling dollars to the public at 1,520 dinars each, 200 higher than the previous price.

MPs who opposed the move had the agenda for Wednesday’s session of parliament cancelled in order to debate it instead.

The finance minister and the central bank governor are due to appear before parliament on Thursday to discuss the devaluation.

Here is what we know.

Why has Iraq devalued the dinar now?

Right before instituting the devaluation, Iraq’s government adopted its annual budget for 2027. It plans to spend 217 trillion dinars (about $166bn) next year, and expects a deficit of more than 40 trillion dinars ($30bn).

The massive shortfall reflects the difficult financial situation Iraq faces as a consequence of the US war on Iran. Since fighting began in late February, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been severely disrupted.

Iraq’s oil exports – the majority of which must transit Hormuz to reach global markets – have fluctuated throughout the war, at one point falling by 90 percent to a trickle. In August, they were at 2.34 million barrels a day, far lower than their pre-war average of 3.6 million.

Last month, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said his country was “facing extraordinary economic challenges”, having lost about $60bn in oil revenue as a result of the disruption.



Oil revenues pay for more than 90 percent of Iraq’s federal budget. The lost income has made it harder to pay state salaries and the CBI’s foreign currency reserves fell from about $106bn before the war to roughly $80bn by late August.

Speaking to the Reuters news agency, Iraqi analyst Mohammed al-Saffar said the measure “gives the government more dinars for each dollar of oil revenue, but raises import costs and reduces households’ purchasing power”.

Why are some MPs opposing devaluation?

Iraq’s Central Bank described the decision as a “strategic step” to steady the country’s finances. But many MPs have urged the government to reverse the change, saying it will raise the cost of living for Iraqis.

In a joint statement on Wednesday, dozens of MPs opposed to the move said they had not been told how or why the decision came about – and that the CBI should have explained it to parliament before it was taken.

Speaking on their behalf, MP Aziz Nasser al-Shammari, who sits on the Iraqi parliament’s integrity body, denounced the move, saying that they had been “surprised” by the decision. “Waging war on the poor like this is wrong,” he declared.

Hassan al-Asadi, leader of the al-Nahj National Alliance bloc, rejected the measure and suggested alternative methods to balance the budget, such as cutting unnecessary spending.

MP Saba al-Saadi was also among those who rejected using a weaker dinar to plug the budget gap. She blamed the Finance Ministry and the CBI for what she called financial mismanagement and vowed to bring the matter before parliament for review.

What does it mean for ordinary Iraqis?

A weaker dinar against the dollar means that imports will become more expensive for Iraqis, raising costs that have already been elevated by regional instability.

Iraq relies on imports for much of what it consumes, from food and medicines to raw materials for industry. Last month, Iraqi consumers and business owners told Al Jazeera that prices had already risen significantly since the Iran war began, on top of delays and disruption to seaborne imports.

Opposing MPs criticised the adoption of the measure at a time when Iraqis were already facing rising prices, import fees, taxes, unemployment and delays in government salary and welfare payments.

Al-Asadi called attention to a growing gap between the official and parallel price of dollars in the country, warning it could “inflict severe harm on the poor and vulnerable”.



After the new official rate took effect on Wednesday, the rate of the dollar on the parallel market rose as well, with the gap between them widening.

In practice, most Iraqis cannot get dollars at the official rate and pay the parallel market price instead.

Has Iraq done this before?

Yes. In December 2020, Iraq devalued the dinar to 1,450 per dollar from about 1,182, after a crash in oil prices left the government short of cash.

A leaked draft budget had set out the move alongside salary cuts, prompting an outcry from state employees.

At the time, Mohammed al-Daraji, a member of parliament’s finance committee, said the weaker rate would help cover the budget gap but warned of steep price rises unless the government helped poor families.

Recalling that devaluation, al-Asadi said private banks and currency speculators, not the state, had profited from the difference between what the CBI and private banks charged for dollars.

In January 2023, after the dinar slid to about 1,670 per dollar amid US curbs on dollar flows, then-Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani replaced the central bank governor. His government later strengthened the dinar, setting the rate for the public at 1,320.

The MPs who issued Wednesday’s joint statement also asked how citizens would be affected by the dollar rate being cut under the previous government, only to be raised again.

World.title: Can emergency reserves ease the diesel crisis?
World.content:
The G7 plans to release emergency fuel stocks as diesel shortages raise transport costs and squeeze household budgets.

From delivering goods to harvesting crops, much of the world’s economic activity depends on diesel fuel.

When it becomes scarce or expensive, the impact reaches far beyond the pump to food prices, household budgets and economic growth.

Right now, prices have hit record highs.

Supply has tightened as the United States-Israel war on Iran disrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Ukrainian attacks damage Russian refineries and China reportedly curbs its exports.

The Group of Seven has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from its emergency stockpiles over four months. That amount equates to about one day of global oil demand.

World.title: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
World.content:
At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.

Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.

Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.

Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."

In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."

Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.

Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.

According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.

In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, meeting Zelensky in Kyiv on Thursday, said the attack in Pryluky showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".

He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".

World.title: US and Lebanon protecting wanted Syrian general, BBC finds
World.content:
A former Syrian general wanted for crimes against humanity, external is being bankrolled and protected by the US and Lebanese authorities, a BBC News investigation has found.

Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons programme and was a senior adviser to former President Bashar al-Assad, is being harboured in Lebanon following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024.

An investigation by the BBC and the US broadcaster NPR has discovered that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI, and other US and Lebanese authorities. This is because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, we have been told.

Last month the BBC revealed Tice's abduction had been a planned operation, with Hassan in the chain of command.

Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government have told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial, but that US authorities want him kept in Lebanon, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this.

We asked the FBI, the CIA and Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security to comment on our findings. Only the FBI responded, declining to comment and instead directing us to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return.

In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family said: "If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive.

"This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice and he should be returned to stand trial."

World.title: Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate, Israel says, as Miliband says 'vital services' to remain
World.content:
Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission".

"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the consul general would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will "work with the Palestinian people".

Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.

The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.

The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.

It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions.

"The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," he wrote on social media.

However, the British flag could still be seen outside on Thursday morning, and several staff were seen entering.

Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel."

But Saar acknowledged that the building is "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate in the building.

As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel".

Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London - raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations.

This agreement is a compromise of sorts and means - for the moment - the heat has been taken out of a dispute that could have further worsened UK-Israel relations.

Israel can claim that the British Consulate is "closing its operations". A score of British diplomats, including the consul general, are leaving.

But Miliband says they are going only temporarily and only for their safety and security. He continues to insist Israel has no legal right to close the consulate.

"The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory," Miliband wrote in a statement.

Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building "will not be closing" and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday.

However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises".

"Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added.

The Foreign Office said the seven UK diplomats who remain will be "independent and operational" and continue to deliver vital services. Israel said they will provide "only a limited scope of activity".

FCDO sources described the deal as a "good outcome" because the entire operation was not closing, as had been threatened. They said that maintaining a UK presence would help build back the mission in the future.

Speaking to the Today programme, Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty explained: "The building remains open. We retain our presence, we continue having staff able to do important work engaging with the Palestinian Authority... and we are engaging in ongoing conversations with Israel on this matter."

Asked if this was a political fudge, Doughty said "you can see what's changed in terms of a name but crucially our presence remains", adding that the "policies towards this Israeli government, which we fundamentally disagree with" would continue.

The foreign secretary made clear the UK reserved the right to take what he called "reciprocal action" but said he would not do so while "discussions are under way and credible". That means any UK retaliation is unlikely before Israel's elections later this month.

World.title: Christa Pike now walking after failed US execution, lawyer tells BBC
World.content:
Christa Pike is "up and walking" while in hospital after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, a member of her legal team says.

Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented.

Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but that he had learned she was moving around her hospital room for the first time while still being mentally "foggy".

Earlier, a court ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.

That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

The failed execution was branded a "mess" by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death.

Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.

Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

World.title: Italy overhauls electoral system after fiercely contested debate
World.content:
Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.

Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.

Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of flouting democracy.

Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.

Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.

The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.

Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.

A party or coalition which emerges with the largest share of the votes - provided this exceeds 42% - will be awarded 105 additional seats in parliament (70 in the lower house and 35 in the senate), which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.

In a debate ahead of the vote, centre-left members accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules.

"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.

World.title: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
World.content:
A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.

The incident - a rare attack deep inside the Gulf - happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal with casualties reported, the UKMTO said.

Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers. On Saturday it was reported as sailing towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.

Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.

At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).

The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.

This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.

Also on Thursday, Vanguard amended an earlier report that had said there was a fire on board another tanker in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.

The company clarified that there were no indications a fire occurred on the vessel, which it had identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

World.title: Teacher who sexually abused pupil back in Indonesia jail after BBC investigation
World.content:
A former teacher who sexually assaulted a student has been returned to jail in Indonesia after a BBC investigation revealed he was secretly released early.

Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2022 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a female student at his father's prominent Islamic boarding school in East Java, where he worked as a teacher.

A BBC Eye undercover investigation revealed he was secretly released on parole in August 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The woman he had been convicted of assaulting had not been informed - despite her legal right to know.

On hearing he was back in prison, she cried with relief.

"I pray that this doesn't happen to anyone else and that, going forward, the law will be applied justly in Indonesia," the former student, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC.

The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections previously told the BBC that Bechi was released because of sentence reductions granted in accordance with regulations.

But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review.

That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison.

Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions".

"We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said.

World.title: Residents airlifted to safety after flooding in central Chile
World.content:
Police in central Chile have airlifted several residents to safety after rising floodwaters left them trapped in their homes.

Recent torrential rains caused the Mapocho river to burst its banks, flooding large parts of the city of Talagante, 35km (22 miles) south-west of the capital, Santiago.

Santiago has seen 74mm of rainfall in the first seven days of this month, making it the rainiest October for the area in 76 years, meteorologists have said.

They have warned that this year's unusually strong El NiÃ±o climate phenomenon will likely continue to bring unusually wet weather, powerful winds and storms to the region during the southern hemisphere's spring.

Officials said one person had been found dead in a flooded underpass in the city of San Bernardo, south of Santiago, although they have yet to confirm the cause of death.

In Talagante, police used helicopters to rescue people and pets living on the banks of the Mapocho who had been surprised by the fast-rising waters overnight.

Dirt roads turned into rivers in the riverside community which, unlike in July's storms, had not been evacuated ahead of the heavy downpours.

World.title: Asaba Massacre: Obasanjo urges forgiveness, reconciliation
World.content:
Former President Olusegun Obasanjo has urged survivors and families of victims of the 1967 Asaba Massacre to embrace forgiveness and reconciliation.

Mr Obasanjo made the call on Wednesday while participating virtually as chairman of the occasion at the 59th anniversary memorial of the massacre in Asaba.

He described the massacre as one of the most painful and terrible aspects of the Nigerian civil war.

Mr Obasanjo said the war was an unfortunate event that should never happen, adding that he wept after receiving documents on the massacre from Chuck Nduka-Eze, the Isama Ajie of Asaba and convener of the Asaba Massacre Memorial.

“To all of you assembled: let us keep one thing in mind, forgiveness, forgiveness, and forgiveness again,” Mr Obasanjo said.

He urged the people of Asaba to forgive and work toward reconciliation, enphasising the need to prevent such tragedies from recurring.

‘We may not forget, but we have to forgive’

Responding to the appeal, the Asagba of Asaba, Epiphany Azinge, said the people could forgive but would not forget the tragedy.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Azinge, a professor, said there would be no closure or healing until a sitting president publicly apologised to the people of Asaba.

“We may not forget, but certainly, we have to forgive,” Mr Azinge said, adding that former military Head of State, Yakubu Gowon, apologised while out of office.

“We need a sitting president to apologise to Asaba people; that will bring closure,” the traditional ruler said.

He also questioned Mr Obasanjo’s “never again” appeal, recalling that the Odi killings occurred during Obasanjo’s administration as president.

“Coming from him, I was a bit taken aback. How long do we say ‘never again’? But it happened at Odi,” he said.

The Asagba urged Nigerians to continue remembering the victims, saying, “From the going down of the sun till the morning, we will always remember them.”

He said the people had moved on, but stressed that remembrance, justice and reconciliation remained necessary as Asaba prepared for the 60th anniversary of the tragedy.

Despite the demand for a presidential apology, Mr Azinge made a significant reconciliation gesture by publicly proclaiming forgiveness for the family of Ibrahim Taiwo.

“On behalf of the Asaba community, and as the prescribed authority, the Asagba of Asaba, I hereby publicly proclaim that we have forgiven the Taiwo family,” he said.

He said the community had accepted the apology offered by the retired Major-General Ahmed Taiwo, son of Mr Taiwo, who was a colonel in the Nigerian Army during the incident.

Mr Taiwo had expressed regret and apologised on behalf of his father and family for any act, omission or commission that led to the massacre.

‘Killing of unarmed civilians can never be justified’

Meanwhile, Governor Sheriff Oborevwori of Delta State said researchers and community historians estimated that more than 1,000 people died in the massacre.

Represented by the Secretary to the Delta State Government, Kingsley Emu, Mr Oborevwori said, “Let us speak clearly: the killing of unarmed civilians can never be justified.”

The governor pledged continued support for national recognition of the massacre and the establishment of a fitting national memorial.

Also speaking, the Isama Ajie of Asaba and Convener of the Asaba Massacre Memorial, Mr Nduka-Eze, said preparations were underway for the 60th anniversary next year, with efforts intensified to establish a permanent memorial centre.

“The message we’ve been sending about the Asaba Massacre is that Nigerian lives matter,” he said.

He said the 60th anniversary would provide an opportunity to further tell the story of the massacre to Nigeria and the world.

Enotie Ogbebor, son of then-Colonel Paul Ogbebor, who was credited with intervening to save lives during the tragedy, said the massacre should be remembered globally.

He said the proposed memorial site would remind humanity that no innocent life should be lost unfairly for any reason.

The Obi of Onitsha, Nnaemeka Achebe, also spoke on restitution, reconciliation and forgiveness at the memorial.

(NAN)

World.title: Nigeria at 66: Understanding its politics of the supernatural, By Ayo Akerele
World.content:
But I must also urge you to remember this: Nigeria’s problems are not only political and economic… They carry deep, far-reaching spiritual dimensions that can only be decisively addressed by a superior spiritual force; one wielded by men and women with an unwavering commitment to righteousness, and above all, to the Lord Jesus Christ. This is where the Nigerian church is most urgently needed.

One of the most unsettling visions I received about Nigeria came during the administration of President Muhammadu Buhari. In it, I watched his presidential motorcade being intercepted, deliberately cut off, by a group of politicians. They produced what appeared to be a document and, under armed supervision, compelled him to sign it. Then the vision ended.

Not long after, something unmistakable began to unfold in the natural realm. Buhari’s most vocal supporters began abandoning him, one by one, consumed by disillusionment as Nigeria descended into a catastrophic spiral of insecurity and economic suffering. What most people did not realise, what they could not see, was that the foundation for that collapse had already been laid in the spirit realm. Agreements had been struck. Bargains had been sealed.

The forces I saw in that vision were not ordinary political actors. They were spiritual powers operating through human vessels, powers determined to use the Buhari administration as a vehicle to entrench the ideology of Jihad in Nigeria; advancing it through the deliberate displacement of ethnic communities and the systematic economic subjugation of non-dominant groups.

This is a truth that must be stated plainly: the spirit controls the natural. It is not primarily politics that determines the direction of a nation, it is the totality of the spiritual climate and the spiritual allegiances of its leadership.

A Nation on the Verge of Breaking

On a separate occasion, I was shown another quick but deeply sobering vision; a map of Nigeria. Before my eyes, it cracked and split apart, from the upper right to the lower left. The vision was brief. But its weight has never left me.

Taken together, these revelations, along with many other messages the Lord has entrusted to me over the years, have driven me to one unavoidable conclusion: Nigeria is in the deliberate plan of God for a strategic shift. But that shift will not come through politics alone, nor through spiritual activity divorced from the realities of governance.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It will require both, the supernatural and the political working in concert.

Politics determines who leads and the policies they pursue. The supernatural determines the environment in which those leaders either rise or fall. One without the other is incomplete.

When the Supernatural and the Political Converge: A Warning From American History

Dr Perry Stone, in his prophetic work on the supernatural dimensions of American politics, documented a striking and sobering pattern in one of his books, Deciphering Endtime Prophetic Codes.
