World.title: Liberia: Errors, Contradictions Cloud Drug Case Against Ex-VP Taylor as she and several others Named in indictment
World.content:
MONROVIA – When officers raided a compound on Cement Road in the VOA Community on July 21, they found 3,971 “plates” of the drug, packed in 157 bags and valued at about US$317 million.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Two foreign men were arrested on the spot. Eleven weeks later, the State has gone much further. A 55-page indictment now names 20 people, among them senior security officers, an aviation official and the woman who was once a heartbeat from the presidency, former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor.



But a close reading of the document tells a messier story. Dates shift from page to page. Payments grow or appear out of nowhere. The indictment gets Taylor’s own term of office wrong, and the court that filed it is not the court that ordered the arrests.

Taylor’s lawyer, Cllr. Gbawou Kowou, says the case against his client rests on the word of one man, co-defendant Sheik Bashiru Kante.

“The entire indictment of Jewel is nothing more [than] the same ‘Sheikh say,'” Kowou told FrontPageAfrica, playing on the word “hearsay.” The government’s evidence, he said, “as referenced and narrated in Numbers 12, 29 through 31 of the indictment, clearly show[s] the same ‘Sheikh say’ reliance on which the case against Jewel is built.”

He also accused prosecutors of lumping strangers together. The State, he said, “placed everyone in one group, most of whom are not connected or known to each other.”

None of the allegations have been tested in court, and every defendant is presumed innocent.

An office she no longer held

The State’s theory is simple. In 2021, it says, Taylor agreed to use her power as Vice President to protect a cartel moving cocaine through Liberia to Europe. In return, money flowed to her and to her charity, the Jewel Starfish Foundation.

On that theory, she faces seven of the 11 counts: conspiracy, importation, transportation, trafficking, exportation, facilitation and money laundering.

The trouble starts with the calendar. The indictment says she served as Vice President until January 2023. In fact, the Weah–Taylor government left office on January 22, 2024. And nearly everything the cartel is accused of actually doing in Liberia happened after that date: the aircraft bought in August 2025, the beach scouting at Marshall that September, the land at Royesville, the May 2026 convoy and the July seizure.

Nowhere does the indictment say what protection a former Vice President could offer in 2025 or 2026. It does not describe a single phone call, order, or favor she gave the network at any time. “High-level political assurance and cover” is the phrase it uses, again and again, without saying what that cover was.

Even the story of how she was recruited changes. In one paragraph, two cartel men meet her at her Congo Town home in October 2021, and she flies to Dubai to meet their boss that November. In another, the introduction happens “in 2022,” and she is already called the “former” Vice President, though she was then in office. A third paragraph moves the Dubai meeting to November 2022.

The money moves too. A US$27,000 travel payment and a US$75,000 gift to her foundation appear early. A US$45,000 “shopping-gift bag” turns up only in the money-laundering count, 52 pages in. The 2021 payments are called “proceeds of the cocaine,” though no cocaine deal before them is described.

There is also a question of law. The 2021 conduct is charged under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act of 2023. Liberia’s Constitution, in Article 21(a), forbids punishing anyone under a law that did not exist when the act took place. Prosecutors may answer that a conspiracy is a continuing crime. That argument is much harder to make for the other counts.

One export charge even ties her to a cocoa shipment that left the Freeport of Monrovia on October 12, 2021, weeks before the Dubai meeting at which she was supposedly recruited. No cocaine was ever reported found in those containers.

Only the 2021 shipment and Dubai meeting fall inside her term. Everything else the indictment describes came after she left office.

The tapes, and the man in the middle

The newest evidence against Taylor is a set of WhatsApp voice notes she allegedly sent Kante on August 31, 2026. That is six weeks after the cocaine was seized and the first arrests made.

On the recordings, as quoted by prosecutors, she sounds like a politician short of cash. “You know things are really crazy on our end,” she says. “So please ask Nicholas if he could send me some help.” She thanks Kante for US$15,000, worries about a child’s school fees, and talks of party conventions and campaign vehicles across the 15 counties.

What she never mentions is drugs. The talk of “the 19 kilos” and “19 million or whatever that was” is put in Kante’s mouth, not hers. Her most suspicious-sounding line, “So maybe [they are] being hidden somewhere until a better time,” carries two words in brackets that the prosecution added.

The law asks more than whether she took money from Ivancic. For money laundering, the State must show she knew or suspected the money came from crime. The indictment says she knew who sent it. It does not say how she knew where it came from.

Nor does it explain how the recordings were obtained, or from whose phone. One of the files is even labeled an “Image,” though it is described as audio.

This is where Kowou’s “Sheikh say” argument bites. Read paragraphs 12 and 29 to 31, the ones he cites, and Kante is everywhere. He meets the cartel men in a Dubai nightclub. He promises them protection from top officials. He brings them to Taylor’s home, travels in her Dubai delegation, and receives her voice notes.

The indictment lists only three witnesses, all police officers, plus unnamed documents. It names no one outside the defendants who saw Taylor agree to anything. If the 2021 story rests on Kante, a man charged in the same case, his credibility will decide much of it.

Kante arranged or attended every meeting Taylor is accused of. The indictment never says she met, called, or paid anyone who ran the 2025–26 operation, which is the heart of Kowou’s complaint that strangers were lumped together.

A document at odds with itself

The problems are not confined to Taylor. The indictment itself was filed before Criminal Assizes “A” and Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie. The writ ordering the arrests came from a different court, Criminal Court “C” under Judge Ousman F. Feika, which describes the case as its own. The writ also misspells the former Vice President’s first name as “Jowel.”

The grand jury’s sign-off raises its own questions. There are 11 counts but only six “True Bill” endorsements, with no word on which counts they cover. The closing paragraph mentions only one crime, illicit trafficking. And on the copy FrontPageAfrica reviewed, the date beside the foreman’s signature appears to read 2025, a year before the seizure.

Perhaps the most striking gap is the cocaine itself. Drug charges in Liberia are graded by the type and amount of the drug, yet the indictment never gives a weight. It counts “plates” in one place and “bags” in another. It calls the substance lab-confirmed cocaine on one page and “suspected cocaine” on others.

The smaller details wobble too. One defendant is said to have “lived in” the Royesville house until his arrest, though he was arrested at a different address, on Cement Road. Former NSA official Gerald Folley Smith is paid “millions” in one paragraph and “more than US$80,000” in another. One co-defendant’s conduct is dated 2015, six years before the conspiracy began. Three NSA agents are described as knowingly escorting cocaine for cash, yet none of them is charged.

Each pair comes from the same 55-page document. May 30, 2026, was a Saturday.

What happens next

None of this means the cocaine was not real or that no crime took place. Two men were caught with the drugs, and the case against them looks direct. For the rest, prosecutors’ strongest ground is the conspiracy count, which needs only an agreement and a single act by any member.

The other charges against Taylor are harder to square with the text. They accuse her of importing, moving and exporting cocaine, but describe nothing she did beyond meetings in 2021 and money she received. Expect her lawyers to press on the dates, the 2023 law, and the two courts as soon as the case is called.

World.title: Liberia: Saudi Rice Trial Moves to Final Arguments As Evidence Phase Ends
World.content:
MONROVIA — The long-running trial involving the alleged misappropriation of Saudi-donated rice has entered its final stage, with the prosecution and defense scheduled to deliver closing arguments before the jury on Friday, October 9, 2026, at 8:00 a.m.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The development followed Wednesday’s sitting before Criminal Court “C,” where the prosecution presented its final rebuttal witnesses, bringing the evidentiary phase of the trial to a close.



With no further witnesses expected, the court ordered both sides to proceed to final arguments on Friday.

The court also directed the prosecution and defense to submit their respective post-trial memoranda to the Clerk of Court, outlining the legal authorities and citations they intend to rely upon in support of their positions.

Both parties and their legal counsel have been ordered to appear for Friday’s proceedings.

The transition to final arguments marks a critical juncture in a case centered on the handling and distribution of 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice donated by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to Liberia.

The prosecution has alleged that a substantial portion of the donation was unlawfully diverted, while the defense has challenged the State’s accounting of the rice, its movement among government institutions and the alleged criminal responsibility of the accused.

A Trial of Conflicting Accounts

Throughout the trial, prosecution witnesses sought to establish how the Saudi donation moved from its receipt into government storage and subsequently to various institutions and beneficiaries.

The State has maintained that 25,054 bags were at issue in the indictment after accounting for quantities it considers to have been legitimately supplied, placing the alleged value of the disputed rice at approximately US$425,918.

The defense, however, has questioned the State’s calculations and the evidentiary basis for some of the quantities presented during the proceedings.

A central issue has been the movement of the rice from the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) to warehouses operated by the General Services Agency (GSA).

Former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf, who also chaired the NDMA Board, previously testified that the transfer was an institutional decision and rejected suggestions that former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah directed him to move the rice.

Former GSA Director Genera Mary T. Broh, who also testified during the trial, provided evidence concerning the involvement of various government agencies in the movement and distribution of the commodity.

Kemayah Maintains His Defense

Kemayah, one of the defendants, has consistently denied the allegations against him.

Testifying in his own defense, the former Foreign Minister said he did not steal any of the Saudi-donated rice and maintained that his involvement was connected to his role in facilitating the donation between Liberia and Saudi Arabia.

His testimony challenged the prosecution’s characterization of the movement of the rice, particularly the role of government institutions responsible for receiving, storing and distributing the commodity.

The defense has argued that administrative decisions involving the rice should not, by themselves, constitute evidence of criminal conduct.

Prosecution Gets Final Rebuttal

Wednesday’s sitting provided the prosecution its final opportunity to respond to the defense through rebuttal evidence before both sides rested their cases.

With the evidentiary phase now closed, neither side is expected to present additional witnesses when proceedings resume Friday.

Instead, the focus will shift from testimony and exhibits to legal and factual arguments, with each side expected to present its interpretation of the evidence before the jury.

The prosecution is expected to argue that the evidence presented during the trial establishes the offenses charged and links the defendants to the alleged wrongdoing.

Prosecution, Defense Set to Face Jury Friday in Case Over 29,412 Bags of Saudi-Donated Rice

The defense, meanwhile, is expected to challenge that conclusion, pointing to what it considers inconsistencies, evidentiary gaps and unanswered questions in the State’s case.

Court Seeks Post-Trial Legal Arguments

The court’s order requiring post-trial memoranda is expected to further narrow the legal issues arising from the evidence presented during the trial.

The memoranda will contain the legal authorities and citations on which the respective parties intend to rely as the court moves toward the next stage of the proceedings, including jury instructions.

For the jury, Friday’s final arguments will provide the prosecution and defense with their last opportunity to directly interpret the evidence and make their respective cases before jurors are instructed by the court and retire to deliberate.

The case has therefore moved beyond the competing accounts presented by witnesses on the stand.

The central question now is whether the evidence presented throughout the trial, measured against the applicable law and the State’s burden of proof, is sufficient to sustain the charges against the defendants.

Criminal Court “C” has ordered all parties and their respective legal counsel to be present at 8:00 a.m. Friday, October 9, for final arguments.

The defendants remain presumed innocent unless proven guilty according to law.

World.title: GTMS Liberia Disowns ‘General Manager’ and PR Executive, Says Appointments Came from Unknown ‘Director’ Linked to UK Firm in Liquidation
World.content:
GTMS Liberia Inc. has disowned Presley S. Tenwah and Elvis D. Johnson, who it says have been posing as its General Manager and Public Relations Executive. The company says the two were appointed by a self-styled “Director,” Sahr H. W. Ngegba, who has no position in its corporate structure. It insists it has no ties to GTMS-UK, a firm it says is in liquidation and under investigation in Britain, and has warned the public not to deal with the two men. It has also instructed its lawyers to pursue civil and criminal action.

Monrovia – Global Tracking & Maritime Solutions Liberia Inc. (GTMS Liberia Inc.) has publicly disowned two men who have been presenting themselves as senior officials of the company. The company says their appointments were made by a person who holds no position in its corporate structure.

In a press release issued Wednesday, October 7, GTMS Liberia said it had learned that Mr. Presley S. Tenwah and Mr. Elvis D. Johnson had been named General Manager-Liberia and Public Relations Executive & Operations Manager, respectively. The appointments were reportedly made by a Mr. Sahr H. W. Ngegba, who claims to be a Director of the company.



GTMS Liberia said it has no one by the name of Sahr H. W. Ngegba on its staff list or in its corporate structure, “let alone any position of Director held by such person.” The company described the appointments as “wishful thinking.”

Link to UK Firm Denied

At the center of the dispute is GTMS-UK, which GTMS Liberia says is currently in liquidation in the United Kingdom. The Liberian company said it is neither a partner nor a subsidiary of GTMS-UK.

In its release, GTMS Liberia alleged that the appointments were “a brazen attempt to mislead the public” and to conceal what it called administrative failings and financial fraud at the UK entity. The company claims British authorities are investigating GTMS-UK. It also accused the UK firm of trying to use the GTMS Liberia name “to shield itself from accountability.”

Lawyers Issue Formal Disclaimer

In a separate letter dated October 7, AFDASA Global Consultancy Inc., which says it has been retained by GTMS Liberia, wrote directly to Mr. Tenwah. The letter accuses him of “an escapade of misinformation” by “parading” himself as General Manager-Liberia. It says his appointment letter was dated September 10, 2026, and signed by Mr. Ngegba.

The letter, signed by AFDASA’s Corporate Administrative Manager, Joseph Papie Mulbah, says Mr. Tenwah’s appointment was structured under GTMS-UK, an entity with “no direct connection, affiliation, or partnership” with the Liberian company. It calls the appointment “a complete figment of the imagination of Mr. Ngegba,” with no force or effect on GTMS Liberia’s operations.

AFDASA advised Mr. Tenwah and “your benefactors” to stop immediately any actions suggesting he is an official, agent or representative of GTMS Liberia. The letter warned that the company “will not take kindly to any youthful exuberance for undue publicity.” It said Mr. Tenwah should act “to avert future embarrassment and to avoid both civil and criminal liability.”

The letter was copied to Ms. Aminata Bangura, Managing Director of GTMS Liberia Inc., and Cllr. Sayma Syrenius Cephus, Global Lead Counsel.

Public Warned; Legal Action Planned

GTMS Liberia warned customers and the public not to do business with Mr. Tenwah or Mr. Johnson in the company’s name “in any form, manner or shape.” The company said the two men “should be regarded as imposters.”

The company said it has instructed AFDASA Global’s Global Lead Counsel to begin civil and criminal proceedings against both men. It accused them of misleading the public and creating “a serious corporate crisis” that has disrupted its operations over the past few days.

World.title: Liberia: As Climate Change Gathers Pace, Monrovia Sees Another Destructive Rainy Season
World.content:
Flooding inundates school roads forcing students to walk in water to school, in Lofa Community. Photo: Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon.

Summary

Heavier and less predictable rainfall, intensified by climate change, is combining with clogged drains and construction in wetlands to worsen flooding across Monrovia’s low-lying communities.

Nearly 20,000 families have been affected, displaced, disrupted schooling, lost income, illness and with 7 deaths as floodwater surrounds their homes and remains for days in two counties.

Residents want blocked waterways reopened, while officials call for stronger forecasting, better drainage, wetland protection and increased disaster-response funding.

By Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon, climate and environment reporter with New Narratives

LOFA COMMUNITY, Montserrado County – Paulina Manloh knows the water is coming before she sees it. She has lived in the Lofa community since 2019, long enough to recognize the pattern: rain falls, and within hours the ground around her home disappears beneath brown water.



When the rain is very heavy things get even worse.

“The water can get full until sometime entering the house,” she said, sitting near the swamp that has come to define six months a year of her family’s life. “So now we’re not able to get outside to go look for food or do other activities.”

Across Monrovia, seasonal flooding is becoming a persistent threat to thousands of families. An estimated 5,950 people in Lofa Community alone are affected by flooding, according to the community leader, while families face displacement, disrupted schooling, lost income, illness and death as floodwater surrounds their homes and remains for days. Scientists and government officials say climate change is bringing heavier and less predictable rainfall to a city already struggling with decades of unplanned growth, clogged drains and weak enforcement of environmental laws.

This year Kawi Badio, director for risk and early warning at the National Disaster Management Agency, the body responsible for coordinating disaster preparedness, emergency response and recovery efforts, said 19,986 people have already been affected by flooding across Montserrado, and Grand Cape Mount with seven deaths recorded.

Authorities warn that the crisis will worsen unless the government acts. Anthony Saah Tengbeh, chairperson of the Department of Environmental Studies and Climate Change at the University of Liberia, said flooding in Monrovia and its environs is not caused by climate change alone. He said heavier rainfall is colliding with inadequate drainage, blocked waterways, construction on wetlands and poorly planned urban development, leaving fewer places for floodwater to go.

Some families are displaced for a week at a time. Children cannot reach school, and parents cannot reach work. In June, Harris S. Quoiduo, a block leader in the Lofa community estimates that flooding affects about 85 percent of the roughly 7,000 people living across the community’s four blocks. A four-year-old girl drowned after she was swept from a flooded bridge while crossing to find her mother.

“It makes the community feel very, very sad,” he said. “Just imagine your child was not sick, you left the child home just to go and come back, and then you find out the child drowned.”

For Manloh, the consequences are immediate. She has five children, and when the water rises, their world shrinks to whatever dry ground remains. School stops. Errands stop. Sickness moves in. “It can really make me feel bad,” she said. “You struggle for money, pay your children’s school fees, but the water does not allow them to go to school.”

In Monrovia’s 13th Street community in Sinkor, Lansanah Mbawo, a 25-year-old teacher, described in July a newer version of the same problem. Water near his home no longer drains, he said, after a shop was built over what residents believe was the community’s drainage channel.

“We did not use to walk in water,” Mbawo said. “But now it is not really easy.” He said neighbors have fallen ill after wading through stagnant water to reach food, work or family.

Following repeated complaints to the Ministry of Public Works, the structure was eventually demolished.

A resident affected by flooding makes her way home through standing water on 13th Street, Sinkor, Monrovia last month.

A City Built on Water

Much of the damage can be traced to where and how Monrovia grew. “Monrovia was built not for the population that dwells in it today,” said Ansu V.S. Dulleh, the agency executive director. The drainage network installed decades ago was designed for a much smaller city.

As informal settlements expanded into wetlands and swamps, homes, shops and roads blocked the natural routes water once used to escape. “You know the water is very jealous,” Dulleh said. “Once the rain comes down, the water will try to find a way to its original inhabitants.” Until the city redesigns its drainage system and stops construction in wetlands, he said, flooding will continue.

A ClimSA/PUMA2025 system used to forecast weather at Roberts International Airport. Photo credit: Liberia Meteorological Service

Emmanuel Urey Yarkpawolo, executive director of the Environmental Protection Agency, put it more bluntly: “Monrovia is a sinkhole” – low-lying, where water naturally collects. The EPA can issue fines and enforce wetland protections, he said, but a land-starved population continues to push into swamps that flood every rainy season.

Enforcement is also constrained by limited resources.

Wetland destruction is part of the worsening flooding situation

Tengbeh said wetlands, (also known as mangroves because of the plants that grow there) act as natural storage areas for excess rainwater. But construction on top of them across the city is reducing their ability to absorb floodwater.

“When we build on the wetland, we build in the swamps, the swamp now will not play its role as a sponge.” Then the consequence: “And that excess water that should be absorbed by the swamp will now go to the dry land and now start to cause problem for us.”

But stopping construction in wetlands remains difficult. The EPA depends on police to carry out eviction orders, Yarkpawolo said, and officers can act only when they have sufficient manpower and logistics.

“Monrovia is overcrowded,” Yarkpawolo said. “The land space in Monrovia is not enough.”

Uncollected trash is also a major issue. With no money to hire heavy equipment, residents have tried to clear the clogged waterways themselves, sometimes with their bare hands and without gloves or boots. Quoiduo said the government should send two or three excavators to reopen the channel.

“That is the most important thing,” he said. “Giving an individual money will not help. They will give the money today, you use it, and the next day you experience the same thing.”

Flooding in Lofa Community left homes surrounded by water for days. Photo credit: Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon

Rainfall Is Becoming Harder to Predict

Residents’ sense that the weather is changing is supported by government forecasters. Albert Momolu Sherman, director of meteorological services at the Ministry of Transport, said Liberia’s historical data shows rainfall becoming more intense even as its timing grows less predictable.

“What we used to experience previously, we do not have now,” Sherman said. “It is like two to three days of rainfall falling in a few hours.” Liberia’s drainage systems were not engineered for that intensity, he said.

Tengbeh said researchers at the University of Liberia are studying whether Liberia’s traditional understanding of two seasons still accurately reflects changing weather patterns.

He holds the view that Liberia has more than three seasons, “all we need to do is to take into consideration the climatic condition over a number of years and have consistent data to determine what is happening in our country.”

The country also lacks the computing capacity to model storms independently. Forecasters instead rely largely on international satellite data supplied through the African Union and European Union. That gives them about two or three days’ warning before a major storm.

That is enough time to issue an alert, Sherman said, but not enough to constitute a complete national early-warning system. He said the deeper problem is institutional. Liberia does not have a fully resourced national service. Responsibility for weather-related work is scattered across several ministries.

FrontPage Africa/New Narratives documented suspected corruption and a lack of capacity under the Weah administration that led to four-year delays in the US$10 million Climate Information System project, which was funded by international donors and intended to warn communities about hazardous weather.

The Boakai administration began the work to move the project forward, but it has faced obstacles. “That project also has its activities to make sure that the met service and the hydrological service go autonomous. We still have yet to see that project kicking off fully,” said Sherman.

Living With Standing Water

Still, the broader frustration remains: forecasts are issued, ministries meet and officials visit, but the same low-lying neighborhoods flood year after year. The disaster agency, created in 2016, coordinates the national response but relies on a small, mostly volunteer workforce.

Dulleh said only 30 to 40 volunteers serve nationwide, and the agency’s budget is too small for the scale of the problem. He is pressing the World Bank to help establish a national disaster trust fund.

Flooding is only one of the hazards the agency is tracking. This year, windstorms have also torn roofs from homes in Gbarpolu, Bomi, Bong and Nimba counties. When floodwater does not recede, Dulleh said, disease often follows, creating additional demands for health workers, food assistance and relocation support. “We cannot continue to go in a cycle,” he said. “Every time there is flooding, we move there.”

Residents Want Waterways Clear, Not Money

Residents living with the water say they are not asking first for relief packages or temporary compensation. They want blocked waterways reopened before the next storm.

“When they open the waterway, it will help us,” Manloh said. Residents repeatedly clear the channel near Lofa, she said, only to see it blocked again by new construction. “I want the government to help us open the waterway,” she said. “The main problem is the waterway.”

The worst may not be over. Dulleh said the seasonal forecast points to especially heavy rainfall through September, with Montserrado, Bomi and Lofa counties among the most exposed. Flash flooding has already affected West Point, Clara Town and Doe Community in Monrovia.

No deaths had been confirmed in those communities this season, he said, but families had been displaced and officials were preparing for disease outbreaks linked to standing water.

World.title: MultiChoice Group, a Canal+ Company, Teases the New Era of DStv
World.content:
MONROVIA — A major transformation is brewing for television screens across Liberia, and the continent’s biggest entertainment player is dropping its biggest hint yet.

MultiChoice Group, operating under Canal+, has begun teasing a sweeping overhaul of its satellite television service—rallying under a bold new tagline: “DStv Expect More.”

Rather than a simple refresh, the company promises a complete reinvention of the DStv platform built entirely from the ground up. The vision? A hyper-customized viewing experience designed around how people actually watch TV today.



While full details remain under wraps, MultiChoice hints that a brand-new suite of tailored packages is on the horizon. Whether you live for live sports on the pitch, binge-watch movies and series, or try to keep a crowded household happy, a custom-built DStv experience is heading your way.

“This is the next evolution for Africa’s most loved storyteller,” the company teased in a recent statement, promising subscribers more choice, greater value, and control over their screens.

What these newly designed packages look like, which channels are making the cut, and how localized pricing will shape out for the Liberian market remain closely guarded secrets for now. Viewers across the country will just have to sit tight and stay tuned as MultiChoice prepares to reveal the full picture in the coming weeks.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-Mines Minister Paye Says Liberia Must Adopt “Resource Sovereignty” to Break Mining Cartels, Stop Reliance on Foreign Loans
World.content:
MONROVIA – Former Minister of Mines and Energy, Wilmot Paye, has called on the Liberian government to adopt a policy of resource sovereignty, arguing that the country cannot substantially benefit from its natural wealth unless it breaks the hold of cartels and outside influence over the minerals sector.

By Obediah Johnson

Mr. Paye spoke on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, as a guest on Voice of Liberia 104.1 FM in Monrovia.



Cartels and “extended influence”

Mr. Paye said Liberia is more richly endowed with natural resources than other countries in the region, but that its minerals sector continues to be threatened by cartels and extended influence. He recalled that during the previous administration, the mining cartel was very strong and powerful in the country.

He said many African countries are already promoting resource sovereignty and are taking charge of their own destinies instead of depending on others for survival. Liberia, he said, should do the same.

According to Mr. Paye, a sound policy approach, effective implementation and the removal of hurdles and outside influence would make the energy and minerals sectors more vibrant for the benefit of citizens.

“While I was in government I believe in it, while I’m out I believe in it and I will continue to believe in it,” he said of resource sovereignty, adding that Liberia needs to change its approach and mindset.

“Not relief agencies”

The former minister cautioned that mining companies operating in Liberia are not relief agencies. If steps are not taken to promote resource sovereignty, he warned, such companies could deplete the country’s resources without bringing significant benefits to citizens.

Against reliance on loans

Mr. Paye argued that Liberia should stop treating loans and borrowing as the answer to its difficulties, given the abundance of its natural resources. He said that by promoting resource sovereignty, the country would not need loans from the World Bank or other international financial bodies to fund its development programs.

He identified minerals as a very significant part of the country’s natural wealth, but said greed among some past and current public officials, whom he did not name, is a contributing factor depriving the nation of the benefits.

Allegations of “double standards”

Mr. Paye noted that Liberia’s new mineral law prohibits public officials, employees and agents of the Ministry of Mines and Energy from holding mining licenses. However, he said some of these officials continue to play double standards to influence the sector.

He observed that some public officials interfere in the sector by being awarded contracts by companies operating in it. He did not provide specific names or examples.

China-Liberia mineral survey

Mr. Paye also disclosed that China and Liberia reached an agreement and carried out a mineral resource survey across the country as part of efforts to strengthen bilateral relations after years of strained ties.

He said the survey was conducted jointly by the Ministry of Mines and Energy, during his tenure, and the China Geological Survey, with support from the Wuhan Center in China. It provided additional insights into Liberia’s mineral potential and identified more than two dozen minerals found in the country, he said.

“Liberia is a resource-rich country; there is no country in our region that is as blessed as Liberia,” Mr. Paye said, adding that the country’s potential spans forest, mineral, renewable and non-renewable resources.

Court cases during his tenure

Mr. Paye recalled that his administration at the ministry rejected unfavorable requests from influential people inside and outside government that were not in the interest of the country and its citizens. He said his firm stance on carrying out the ministry’s statutory responsibilities led to the ministry being taken to court on numerous occasions.

The claims in this article are those of Mr. Paye. The officials and companies he referred to were not named, and no response from the government was available at the time of publication.

World.title: Liberia: Founder of Change Agent Network Eric Wowoh Charged by Police Over Alleged Land Fraud Involving US-Based Couple
World.content:
According to the charge sheet, investigators reviewed bank transfers, Zelle, Cash App and other electronic payments showing the couple paid US$18,741 toward the price. Mr. Wowoh, however, admitted to investigators that he received only US$9,200 from Mrs. Acquah as part payment, the charge sheet says

MONROVIA – The Liberia National Police has charged Eric W. Wowoh, founder and executive director of the civil society organization Change Agent Network, with theft of property, receiving money under false pretences and criminal conveyance of land, in connection with a land transaction involving a couple based in the United States.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]



According to a police charge sheet dated October 6, 2026, Mr. Wowoh was arrested on September 16, 2026, by Detective Joseph S. Nagbe at the LNP headquarters in Monrovia. The document lists no accomplices and says the case is to be forwarded to court.

Complaint filed through lawyer

The case stems from a complaint filed on September 11, 2026, by Mrs. Rebekah Acquah and her husband, Mr. John Acquah, who reside in Rhode Island. They reported the matter to the police’s Crime Services Department through their lawyer, Atty. Stephen B. Lavelah of the Kailando and Associates Law Firm.

The couple alleges that Mr. Wowoh, who is associated with the organization, received US$18,741 toward the purchase of a property valued at US$30,500. The property consists of two lots of land with a structure under construction in the Rock Church Community, Duazon, Margibi County.

How the deal allegedly unfolded

Police say the Acquahs approached Mr. Wowoh in 2024 to help them find land in Liberia. In December 2024, he allegedly agreed to sell them part of his own property: US$5,500 for the two lots and US$25,000 for the house, totaling US$30,500.

According to the charge sheet, investigators reviewed bank transfers, Zelle, Cash App and other electronic payments showing the couple paid US$18,741 toward the price. Mr. Wowoh, however, admitted to investigators that he received only US$9,200 from Mrs. Acquah as part payment, the document says.

Police say that in February 2025 Mr. Wowoh handed the couple the legal documents for the property, including the administrator’s deed, warranty deed and transferred deeds. The charge sheet describes the deed as valid and legitimate.

But investigators allege that he later secretly retrieved the same documents and sold the property to another buyer, acting with criminal intent to resell it. The charge sheet also notes that Mrs. Acquah paid US$482.34 in taxes to the Liberia Land Authority (LLA) for the property.

Charges and legal basis

After its investigation, the police resolved to charge Mr. Wowoh with theft of property/receiving money under false pretense and criminal conveyance of land. The charges are brought under Chapter 15, Subchapter A, Sections 15.5 and 15.23 of the Revised Penal Code of the Republic of Liberia.

Concerns for civil society

The charge against the head of a civil society organization is likely to draw attention to the conduct of leaders in Liberia’s non-governmental sector. The charge sheet does not say the alleged transaction involved the organization’s funds or activities, and it does not accuse the organization itself of wrongdoing.

The document was signed by Commander-in-Charge R. Smith. It records Mr. Wowoh as a Liberian of Lorma descent, born in Fissibu Town, Lofa County. Mr. Wowoh could not be reached for comment.

World.title: Kasama records increase in GBV cases
World.content:
The number of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) cases is on the rise in Kasama District of Northern Province.

Kasama One Stop Center Psychosocial Counselor, Matilda Mbalamweshi has revealed that the centre is receiving between six and nine Gender Based Violence cases every day.

Speaking in an interview with the media, Ms Mbalamweshi has cited sexual and physical assaults as among the majority cases being reported.

She said about three of the cases recorded daily are usually sexual assault cases.

“We are receiving about six to nine GBV cases every day, and among these, about three are usually sexual assault cases,” she said.

“We also attend to physical assault and other forms of abuse, and all these cases have increased,” she added.

She has since called on stakeholders to strengthen efforts aimed at preventing Gender Based Violence and ensuring that survivors receive the necessary support.

“I call upon stakeholders to come on board and work to help fight gender-based violence and ensure that survivors receive the support they need,” she said.

And Bakashana Basambilile Gender Programme Officer, Mercy Chizyuka has called on traditional leaders to take an active role in the fight against Gender Based Violence in communities.

Ms Chizyuka said traditional leaders are key gatekeepers in their communities and can play an important role in preventing Gender Based Violence.

“Traditional leaders are gatekeepers in our communities, they understand the effects of Gender-Based Violence and the impact it has on individuals, families and communities, it will be easier for organisations to work with them in addressing these cases,” she said.

She indicated that stronger collaboration with traditional leaders will help organisations reach communities more effectively and strengthen awareness on the dangers of Gender Based Violence.

World.title: Siame calls for nullification of Mwenzo MP’s election
World.content:
Losing United Party for National Development (UPND) Mwenzo Candidate in Nakonde District, Musingwa Siame has asked the Chinsali High Court to nullify the election of Lucas Simumba as Mwenzo Member of Parliament.

Mr Siame is alleging widespread corruption, electoral malpractice and violence during the August 13th 2026 general election.

The losing candidate said Mr Simumba of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) issued money and ball pens to voters during voting day.

He said the alleged incidents happened at Tenga Junction, Mwenzo Primary School, Musyani and Waitwika Village.

Mr Siame further told the court that he saw about 30 people forcing their way through the gate at Nakonde Civic Centre, which was locked, as they attempted to gain entry into the premises.

Mr Siame said this in his presentation before Lusaka High Court Judge Twambo Musonda who is sitting in Chinsali District.

This is in a case in which Mr Siame of the UPND has petitioned for the election of Mr Simumba of the NRPUP as Mwenzo Member of Parliament.

However, during cross-examination, James Kayula, who was representing the Member of Parliament questioned Mr Siame whether he had made any complaints to the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) or the police concerning the alleged violence or electoral malpractice.

Mr Kayula also questioned Mr Siame on whether he had evidence showing that Mr Simumba was the one distributing money and whether voters were turned away from voting.

Mr Siame responded that although he alleged that electoral malpractice was widespread and affected the majority of voters, he had not identified any voter who was allegedly prevented from voting.

He also admitted that he had no written document evidence from police showing that the money and pens allegedly distributed to voters came from Mr Simumba.

Meanwhile, petitioner’s witness, James Mumba told the court that Mr Simumba went to the Civic Centre on August 5th with a group of people.

Mr Mumba said one person in the group pushed him while attempting to gain access to the premises.

When asked whether Mr Simumba was the person who pushed him, he admitted that Mr Simumba was not the person who pushed him and that he did not identify the person who allegedly pushed him.

Mr Mumba said Mr Simumba’s visit to the Civic Centre concerned the recruitment of polling staff, particularly the exclusion of Nakonde residents.

He said Mr Simumba went to the Council Secretary’s office, where the Council Secretary explained the recruitment procedure to him.

Another petitioner’s witness, Anold Simwinga, told the court that he had a conversation with Mr Simumba on August 12 concerning an alleged plan to cause commotion and that he was going to be paid K50,000.

He said he had worked for Mr Simumba in 2021 by causing commotion at polling stations.

Mr Simwinga said Mr Simumba gave him K1,000 for a drink, which he accepted.

Mr Simwinga also alleged that Mr Simumba gave him five catapults, which he received but never used.

When asked whether there was an independent person present when the issue of the K50,000 was discussed and whether he had reported the matter to ECZ or the police, Mr Simwinga said no independent person witnessed the conversation and that he had no written evidence of the alleged promise.

He admitted that he did not report the matter to ECZ or the police and had no documentary evidence showing that he had reported the allegation.

NRPUP candidate Lukas Simumba obtained 9,002 votes against UPND candidate Nathan Musingwa Siame, who received 4,075 votes.

Trial continues today.

World.title: Chilengi urges enhanced health delivery at UTH
World.content:
Minister of Health Roma Chilengi has instructed University Teaching Hospital (UTH) Management to fix long-standing water supply challenges at the highest referral hospital in the country, aimed at improving the provision of health care services.

Professor Chilengi has also called for infrastructure upgrades at UTH, in order to enhance service delivery.

The Health Minister was speaking when he toured the health facility this morning.

“There is an urgent need to ensure speedy rehabilitation and upgrading of the water reticulation system, to improve health service delivery, it is not okay to run the health institution without water, so we need to ensure that this problem is solved quickly,” Professor Chilengi stated.

And Professor Chilengi has also issued strict directives to the management of the UTH to address systemic inefficiencies and improve direct patient care.

“If you do not have enough doctors, do the jobs yourselves, go in the wards and work, “he told them.

Professor Chilengi has further directed management to recruit qualified engineers who will be repairing or servicing heavy-duty commercial and hospital laundry machinery so that they are in constant operation.

“You cannot have only one machine working, whilst others are down, what if the one working breaks down what are you going to do? Then the whole institution is crippled, please, employ engineers immediately,” he told management.

The Minister also called for solar power installations at the largest public health institution, meant to back up the 1000 kilovolt genset, after staff complained that it consumes 80,000 liters of diesel per hour.

Professor Chilengi however, expressed delight that UTH has embarked on a comprehensive facelift project, aimed at improving infrastructure and enhancing service delivery.

Meanwhile, Professor Chilengi warned that hospital staff caught vandalising public assets will be held accountable.

World.title: Kasenengwa polls marred with errors, irregularities-Daka
World.content:
Kasenengwa Constituency returning officer, John Daka has confirmed before the Chipata High Court that the August polls in Kasenengwa were marred with a lot of errors and irregularities.

This is in a matter where UPND losing candidate, Levison Ziwa petitioned the election of NRPUP’s Philemon Twasa as Kasenengwa Member of Parliament.

Mr Daka, 35, said after a recount as directed by the court, it was established that some rejected ballots were found in Mr Twasa’s sealed envelope which was not supposed to be the case.

He, however, mentioned that counting is done at the polling station in the presence of some electoral stakeholders but a returning officer is never present.

Mr Daka further confirmed that even some ballot papers for the other candidates that contested the seat were also found in Mr Twasa’s envelope.

When asked by the petitioner’s lawyer, Obadiah Munsanje why those errors happened, Mr Daka said only presiding officers could give reasons as he was not physically present when counting was done.

The returning officer further denied assertions that the ballot papers could have been tampered with as they are guarded 24/7 by the Zambia Police stating that the container was only opened during the recount.

He also added that he felt threatened before he could officially announce the results for the polls as Mr Twasa in the company of his supporters stormed the totaling centre pressuring him on why he was taking longer than necessary to announce the results.

Mr Daka said he had to display a screen in the totaling centre for the stakeholders including Mr Twasa to appreciate the process that had to be done before results are announced.

On September 22, 2026, Chipata High Court Judge, Elita Phiri Mwikisa ordered for a recount for the Kasenengwa parliamentary polls and High Court Registrar Yvonne Nalomba who witnessed the exercise has since submitted a report before the court to form part of the evidence.

During the recount, Mr Ziwa got 14, 693 votes while Mr Twasa got 12, 907 showing a difference of 1, 786 votes.

Following the conclusion of trial, Justice Mwikisa has since set November 25th, 2026 as a date for judgement.

World.title: 2026 Africa Decentralisation Day set for Oct 15th
World.content:
The 2026 Africa Decentralisation Day has been set for October 15th in Mumbwa District, Central Province, under the theme: “Empowered local governments for sustainable water and sanitation: advancing resilient, inclusive and sustainable territories towards agenda 2063.”

This is according to a statement issued to the media by Management Development Division Permanent Secretary at the Cabinet Office, Alfred Sakwiya, who says the day provides African Union (AU) Member States an opportunity to assess progress and share experiences in the implementation of decentralisation reforms.

The Permanent Secretary added that it will also help raise awareness of the critical role of local governments in strengthening democracy, enhancing citizen participation, improving service delivery and driving sustainable development.

And Mr Sakwiya noted that this year’s theme underscores the important role of local governments in ensuring access to sustainable water and sanitation services, strengthening resilience to climate-related challenges and promoting inclusive development in line with the aspirations of agenda 2063.

“The observance is anchored on the principles of the African charter on the values and principles of decentralisation, local governance and local development, which promotes citizen participation, accountability, subsidiarity and sustainable local development as essential components of good governance and democratic development across Africa,” he added.

He reiterated the government’s commitment to implementing the national decentralisation policy and advancing the devolution programme as a means of bringing development and public services closer to the people.

He explained that through these reforms, local authorities continue to play an important role in planning, coordinating and delivering development interventions that respond to local needs and priorities.

Meanwhile, Mr Sakwiya disclosed that, as part of the programme, outstanding local authorities will be recognised for their performance under the water and sanitation development scorecard and related indicators aligned with the four thematic areas of the commemoration.

He has since invited all stakeholders and members of the public to participate in the event and join the country in reaffirming its commitment to empowered local governments, improved service delivery and sustainable development for all citizens.

World.title: Pray for him, encourage him — Mwewa’s mother
World.content:
Florence Mwewa, mother of newly installed Lusaka Mayor Chitambala Mwewa, has called on Lusaka residents to pray for and encourage her son as he begins leading the capital city.

Florence said her son had taken on a huge responsibility and would need the support of residents to succeed.

Speaking shortly after Mwewa’s installation yesterday, she said she was confident that God would help her son overcome the challenges that came with the position.

Florence said the most important thing residents could do was to stand behind the Mayor and encourage him as he worked to improve the city.

“All we have to do is pray for him, encourage him because he needs that encouragement,” she said.

The Mayor’s mother also reflected on the Lusaka her late husband, Simon Mwewa, led as Mayor, saying the city was much cleaner at the time.

“I can assure you when my husband was a Mayor, this city was very clean. I don’t know where the people went wrong,” she said.

She said she was pleased that her son had taken up the challenge of restoring cleanliness in Lusaka.

“And I’m glad my son has taken up that battle to try, and I’m sure there’s nothing hard that God can’t do,” Florence said.

Meanwhile, during his investiture ceremony, Mayor Mwewa said taking over an office once occupied by his late father had been a surreal experience.

Mwewa said his late father served as Mayor of Lusaka and later as Governor, making his own journey into the same office particularly emotional.

He recalled that in 1979, the late Tom Bradley, who was then Mayor of Los Angeles in the United States, visited Zambia while his father was serving as Mayor of Lusaka.

According to Mwewa, Bradley gave his father four coasters bearing his name as a personal gift.

Mwewa said that after being elected Mayor and entering the Mayor’s office, he discovered that the same coasters were still there.

“Standing here in front of you is very surreal for me because, as many of you know, my late father served as Mayor of this amazing city. He also served as Governor,” he said.

“When I was first elected Mayor and I was ushered into the Mayor’s office, looking around the office, I noticed the same coasters that he had gifted my father were the same ones that he left in the Mayor’s office when my father was the Mayor,” Mwewa recalled.

Mwewa was yesterday sworn in and later installed as Lusaka Mayor during a colourful investiture ceremony held at Lusaka Civic Centre.

He takes over from immediate past Mayor Chilando Chitangala, with a stated aim of restoring sanity and cleanliness to the capital city.

World.title: Banda gets UPND ticket for Mandevu by-election
World.content:
The United Party for National Development (UPND) has adopted former independent parliamentary candidate Adrian Banda to contest the Mandevu Constituency by-election scheduled for November 5.

UPND National Chairperson for Elections Likando Mufalila announced Banda’s adoption yesterday, alongside Anderson Banda, who will contest the Lumezi Constituency by-election, and Felix Mulwanda, the party’s candidate for the Nambala District Council Chairperson seat.

Mufalila said the party received eight applications from aspiring candidates for the Mandevu parliamentary seat.

He urged all those who had expressed interest in the various positions to rally behind the adopted candidates and work together for the success of the party.

Banda’s adoption comes days after he officially rejoined the UPND on October 2, describing the move as a return to his political roots.

He started his political career with the UPND in 2011 before later joining the Patriotic Front.

Before entering parliamentary politics, Banda served as Ngwerere Ward 22 local government councillor in Mandevu Constituency for more than a decade.

He contested the August 13 general election as an independent candidate for Mandevu and was among the top contenders alongside UPND candidate Christopher Shakafuswa and Resolute Party candidate Jean Kapata.

However, the Mandevu parliamentary election was declared inconclusive after criminals attacked the constituency results aggregation centre on August 18.

The attackers assaulted electoral staff and destroyed results transmission kits and election materials, including ballot papers.

The incident left the Returning Officer unable to verify and declare the final results, prompting the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) to order a fresh election.

Following his adoption, Banda called on youths and party structures to rally behind the UPND government, saying Mandevu Constituency should have one party.

He thanked the party for adopting him and said his work in the constituency had started immediately.

“I’m grateful that the UPND has adopted me and my work in the Constituency starts now,” he said.

“Through the UPND, I will make sure to deliver what people want.”

The ECZ has set October 8 as nomination day, with campaigns scheduled to run from October 10 to November 4.

The Mandevu Constituency by-election will be held on November 5.

World.title: COUNCIL POLICE NEED TO BE EQUIPPED – MWEWA
World.content:
Newly installed Lusaka Mayor Chitambala Mwewa says the Lusaka City Council Police need to be better equipped to help restore order and cleanliness in the capital.

Mr. Mwewa, who is the son of Lusaka’s first Zambian indigenous mayor, the late Simon Mwewa, has taken up office after winning the mayoral election.

Speaking during his investiture ceremony yesterday, Mr. Mwewa said the council police are an important part of his administration’s efforts to make Lusaka cleaner, better organised and safer.

He said the unit needs greater capacity to effectively carry out its duties and support the council’s enforcement work.

Mr. Mwewa said adequately equipping the council police would enable them to perform their duties more effectively for the city and its residents.

The Mayor said his administration would focus on restoring order and cleanliness through proper systems, infrastructure and enforcement.

He said his office has already embarked on Operation Clear Path, an initiative aimed at restoring order and cleanliness in Lusaka.

Mr. Mwewa said the capital has lost much of its cleanliness over the years and needs more than calls for residents to keep it clean.

He said the council must first put systems in place to make Lusaka clean before residents can be expected to maintain it.

Meanwhile, Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister Mulambo Haimbe, who graced the event, said Government supports efforts to improve the cleanliness and functionality of Lusaka.

Mr. Haimbe said residents expect clean streets, efficient waste management, reliable street lighting, safe markets and functioning drainage.

He said keeping Lusaka clean is a shared responsibility involving Government, the council, businesses and residents.

Mr. Haimbe assured Mr. Mwewa that Government would work with the Lusaka City Council to strengthen service delivery and modernise urban infrastructure.

He also urged the council to ensure that public resources are used transparently and provide value for money.

Mr. Mwewa was yesterday sworn in and later installed as Lusaka Mayor during an investiture ceremony held at Lusaka Civic Centre.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 8, 2026
World.content:
press review

10 Quarantined After Kenya's First Ebola Case

Kenya is facing its first confirmed Ebola case after a man who travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo died in a Nairobi hospital. Health officials have quarantined ten people who came into contact with him, while tracing 57 others who may have been exposed. Concern is growing over screening measures after it emerged that the patient, who had reportedly been ill for about a month, travelled through several cities in DR Congo, crossed into Uganda and flew to Kenya without being detected. Kenyan authorities said that surveillance has been intensified at airports and border crossings, with more than 650,000 travellers screened and 267 samples tested so far. Health officials have also designated four hospitals to manage suspected Ebola cases, while the Africa CDC is working with countries in the region to strengthen their response.

Eritrean Troops Reportedly Move Into Ethiopia's Tigray Region



Eritrean soldiers are reportedly moving into northern Ethiopia's Tigray region as renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and Tigrayan forces raises fears of a wider conflict. Residents in Adigrat said that they had seen convoys of Eritrean military trucks travelling south towards areas where clashes have been reported. The developments come amid worsening relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea and accusations from Addis Ababa that Eritrea is supporting the Tigray People's Liberation Front, which Asmara has denied. The reported return of Eritrean troops has caused anxiety among Tigray residents, many of whom remember alleged atrocities committed during the 2020–2022 civil war.

UN Allocates $160m for Global Humanitarian Crises

The United Nations has allocated US$160 million from its Central Emergency Response Fund to provide life-saving assistance in 12 of the world's most underfunded humanitarian crises across Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Middle East. Of the funding, US$150 million will support emergency responses in countries including Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Cameroon and Afghanistan, as well as the occupied Palestinian territory, Cuba and Yemen. A further US$10 million will support people with disabilities and make humanitarian assistance more accessible and inclusive. The UN says the funding forms part of a wider effort to reach 87 million people facing severe humanitarian needs this year, while stressing that political action is also needed to secure humanitarian access to affected populations.

African Union Launches First Regional Credit Rating Agency in Mauritius

The African Union is launching the Africa Credit Rating Agency, the continent's first regional credit rating agency, in Mauritius, in an effort to provide an alternative perspective to the major global rating agencies. The agency will assess sovereign governments, financial institutions and private companies, with the AU saying it will draw on African data, expertise and economic realities to provide more context-specific assessments. African leaders have long criticised major international rating agencies over what they see as unfair assessments of African economies, although the agencies reject accusations of systemic bias. The AU says AfCRA could help improve investor confidence, market transparency and access to capital, particularly as African countries face rising debt-service costs and 23 economies currently lack ratings from the major global agencies.

Nigerian Authorities Launch Probe After Passenger Dies on Kenya Airways Flight

A passenger has died aboard a Kenya Airways flight from Nairobi to Lagos after becoming unresponsive about 20 minutes before the aircraft landed at Murtala Muhammed International Airport. The airline said its crew administered first aid and followed emergency procedures before medical personnel met the aircraft on arrival and confirmed the passenger had died. Nigerian aviation authorities said the passenger had reportedly been denied entry into Madagascar. He was being returned to Nigeria when complications arose during the flight. Authorities said the passenger had allegedly become aggressive, attempted to enter the cockpit and later tried to open a rear aircraft door before being restrained by crew members. Police have taken over the investigation, obtained statements from the crew and placed the body in a morgue in Ikeja. The passenger's identity and cause of death have not been disclosed.

Close 

Zambia Set to Sign $1.5bn U.S. Health Deal

Zambia is set to sign a U.S.$1.5 billion health funding agreement with the United States after resolving a dispute over the sharing of sensitive health data. The agreement will provide U.S.$1.5 billion in U.S. funding over five years. Zambia is expected to contribute U.S.$2.1 billion towards health programmes. Zambia had initially rejected the deal over concerns about requirements to share medical information and biological samples. However, officials said that the data-sharing provisions have now been narrowed to information needed to monitor and evaluate U.S.-funded programmes, with a clause allowing access to patient specimens removed. Meanwhile, Zimbabwe and Ghana have rejected similar U.S. funding terms over concerns about sovereignty and sensitive health data. Zimbabwe particularly warned against unrestricted access to epidemiological data and biological samples.

World.title: South Africa: Anti-Immigration Groups Promise More Disruptions - South African News Briefs - October 8, 2026
World.content:
press review

Anti-Immigration Groups Vow to Disrupt Durban Home Affairs Centre

Anti-illegal immigration groups have vowed to continue disrupting operations at the Home Affairs Refugee Reception Centre in Durban, reports EWN. About 1,000 foreign nationals seeking asylum and other immigration services were chased away by demonstrators carrying sticks and sjamboks. The protests follow a Home Affairs directive allowing all foreign nationals to apply for asylum, regardless of their legal status. This comes after a Constitutional Court ruling found restrictions on such applications unconstitutional.

10 Killed in Minibus Taxi Crash in Durban

Ten people have died in a minibus taxi accident on the MR385 Road in Cato Ridge, Durban, reports SABC News. Preliminary reports indicate the taxi lost control and collided with a tree. The KwaZulu-Natal Department of Transport said that a Road Traffic Inspectorate and road safety team have been deployed to the area. Increased traffic law enforcement is planned across the province during Transport Month.

State Links AKA Murder Weapon to Accused

The State has begun presenting its case in the murder trial of rapper Kiernan "AKA" Forbes and Tebello "Tibz" Motsoane by seeking to link the alleged murder weapon to the accused, reports EWN. Seven men are on trial at the Durban High Court over the February 2023 killings. The first witness, a retired police officer, testified about a firearm recovered after a May 2022 shooting in Mayville, which the State says was later linked to the AKA and Tibz murders.
