World.title: Africa: World Cotton Day - The Real Value of Africa's Cotton Comes After the Harvest
World.content:
World Cotton Day should measure more than output. It should ask how much manufacturing, employment and African-owned value the continent creates from every bale it grows.

A cotton boll is light enough to sit in the palm of a hand. The economy wrapped around it is not. Before cotton becomes a shirt, a uniform, a designer collection or a roll of industrial fabric, it can pass through farms, ginneries, spinning mills, weaving plants, dye houses, garment factories, logistics companies, retailers and digital marketplaces. At each stage, value is added. Across much of Africa, too many of those stages still happen elsewhere.

That is the contradiction World Cotton Day should bring into focus. Africa produced about 7.5 per cent of the world’s cotton in 2022, according to the Cotton to Cloth World Cotton Day data pack. Yet estimates compiled in the same document show that most African cotton leaves the continent before it is transformed. The precise share varies by source: UNCTAD places raw-cotton exports at 70 per cent, UNESCO cites an International Cotton Advisory Committee estimate of 81 per cent for sub-Saharan Africa in 2022, while the World Trade Organization estimate is higher still. The methodologies differ, but the industrial message is remarkably consistent: Africa grows cotton more successfully than it converts cotton into prosperity.

The imbalance becomes clearer at the other end of the chain. Drawing on the World Bank’s World Integrated Trade Solutions database, UNESCO reports that Africa exports about $15.5 billion worth of textiles, clothing and footwear each year but imports $23.1 billion, leaving a $7.6 billion deficit. This is not simply a trade statistic. It describes factories that could have been operating, skills that could have been acquired, brands that could have been built and incomes that could have circulated through African economies.



Raw cotton is valuable. What happens after the harvest is more valuable still. Ginning separates fibre from seed. Spinning turns fibre into yarn. Weaving and knitting create fabric. Dyeing, finishing, cutting, sewing, branding and retailing multiply the commercial possibilities. The African Development Bank estimates that ownership of the cotton value chain can generate a 600 per cent increase in economic value. That figure explains why the central question is not whether Africa should grow more cotton, but whether it can retain more of the value created from the cotton it already grows.

Benin offers an early indication of what the shift can look like. Cotton farming accounts for roughly 12 to 13 per cent of the country’s economy. The emergence of the Glo-Djigbe Industrial Zone has enabled about 30 per cent of Benin’s cotton to be processed locally, with annual output estimated at seven to ten million finished garments. Faki Adje, the zone’s deputy general manager, has said the wider effort to activate the cotton value chain could support 300,000 formal industrial jobs by 2030. These are ambitions, not guarantees, but the direction matters: the cotton field is being linked deliberately to the factory floor.

That link changes the development equation. A farmer’s productivity still matters, but so do electricity tariffs, water, freight costs, machinery finance, technical training, quality standards and the reliability of customs systems. Cotton policy cannot stop at agriculture ministries. It must reach finance ministries, trade authorities, power utilities, universities, logistics operators and the private investors who decide whether a mill is commercially possible.

The opportunity is also social. Cotton provides income to an estimated 3.5 million African farmers, although only about 17 per cent are women. Further down the chain, women make up between 70 and 90 per cent of the continent’s formal garment workforce. That contrast should shape policy. If value addition expands without deliberate attention to ownership, pay, skills and progression, women may remain concentrated in the least secure parts of the chain. If it is designed well, cotton industrialisation can widen women’s access not only to jobs, but to management, enterprise and capital.

The market is no longer hypothetical. Clothing and footwear sales in sub-Saharan Africa were valued at about $31 billion in 2020. Online commerce is widening the route to consumers: the share of active e-commerce shoppers in Africa rose from 13 per cent in 2017 to 28 per cent in 2021, reaching an estimated 334 million users. For African designers and manufacturers, digital distribution can shorten the distance between workshop and wardrobe. But a marketplace cannot compensate for an absent production base. The product still has to be made competitively, consistently and at scale.

Scale is where the African Continental Free Trade Area becomes central. A complete textile ecosystem need not be duplicated in every country. Cotton grown in one market can be ginned or spun in another, woven elsewhere, cut and sewn where specialised capacity exists, and sold across the continent. The advantage lies in connecting capabilities. Yet intra-African trade in textiles and apparel is valued at only $2.7 billion, about 8 per cent of continental imports. The AfCFTA is projected to lift intra-African trade by 11 per cent, but tariffs are only part of the obstacle. Slow borders, incompatible standards, costly transport and fragmented payments can erase the advantage of regional production.

Close 

World Cotton Day should therefore be less a ceremonial tribute to a crop than an annual industrial audit. Is Africa processing a larger share of its fibre? Are mills operating closer to capacity? Are farmers earning more predictable incomes? Are women progressing through the value chain? Are African manufacturers supplying African retailers? Are designers building brands that can compete at home and abroad? Are governments removing the costs that make local production uncompetitive?

Cotton is grown as a primary cash crop in 37 of Africa’s 54 countries. That reach gives the continent a foundation few industries enjoy: raw material, farming knowledge, an existing workforce, creative talent and a large consumer market. What remains uneven is the machinery that joins them together.

The cotton field should not be treated as the end of an export story. It is the beginning of an industrial one. The true measure of success will not be the number of bales Africa sends abroad, but the amount of skill, enterprise, manufacturing and wealth it builds before a single garment reaches the customer.

World.title: Africa: United States Accused of Exploiting Migrant Suffering With Africa Deportations
World.content:
U.S. Transferees arriving at the Robert International Airport in Monrovia (file photo).

The United States is violating international law by deporting migrants to African countries where they have no ties, NGO Human Rights Watch said on Thursday, accusing Washington of using deportation to remote destinations as a deterrent to immigration.

United States deportation policy has expanded sharply since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, with his administration striking agreements with governments in Africa, Latin America and the Pacific to receive foreign nationals who cannot legally be returned to their own countries.

More than 500 people have since been deported from the US to African countries other than their own, according to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) data cited by Human Rights Watch.



A separate investigation published by the Forbidden Stories journalism consortium in September estimated that around 25,000 people had been deported to destinations worldwide under the third-country deportation programme.

Human Rights Watch said the policy "violates international human rights law and is designed to instrumentalise human suffering as a deterrent to migration".

Inside the US system deporting migrants through African countries

'The point is to scare people'

The organisation said it interviewed 24 people who had been deported from the US to six African countries - Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan.

Some described being kept in chains during flights of up to 18 hours and said they were not told where they were being taken.

The rights group also cited an unnamed US official who told a US Senate hearing that the choice of distant destinations was intended in part to frighten other migrants.

"With countries like Palau or Eswatini, the point is that the administration can threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere," the official was quoted as saying. "The point is to scare people."

Human Rights Watch said Washington had also deported at least a dozen LGBTQI+ people to African countries where same-sex relations are criminalised or heavily repressed.

The group warned that transferring people to countries where they face persecution or serious abuse could breach the international legal principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits states from sending people to places where they face severe human rights violations.

Many of the agreements underpinning the programme remain secret or only partly disclosed, Human Rights Watch said, making it difficult to establish the conditions under which migrants are accepted or what incentives are offered to participating governments.

Close 

The global machinery built to carry out Trump's mass deportation drive

The growing network of deportation agreements has also drawn attention to the pressure Washington is placing on African governments to cooperate with its migration policies.

An investigation by French news agency AFP earlier this year found that the US had used diplomatic and economic leverage in negotiations, including threats of higher tariffs, restrictions on the issuing of visas and cuts to development aid.

Burundi became the latest country to sign up this month, becoming the 15th African nation to agree to receive US deportees despite facing severe economic and humanitarian pressures of its own.

(with newswires)

World.title: Zambia: Zambia Finalises U.S.$1.5 Billion U.S. Health Funding Deal As Zimbabwe Rejects Terms
World.content:
President of the Republic of Zambia, Hakainde Hichilema.

Zambia is set to sign a US$1.5 billion health funding agreement with the United States this week after resolving a dispute over sensitive health data-sharing requirements.

Zimbabwe and Ghana, however, will miss out on the funding after rejecting the terms over concerns about the sharing of sensitive health data.

The development comes as both countries grapple with health funding challenges that cannot be fully addressed through their own national budgets.

Zambia had initially rejected the deal, with Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe criticising what he described as a US attempt to link health funding to American economic interests by connecting the agreement to a separate deal granting Washington access to critical minerals.



However, in an update on Tuesday, Zambian authorities confirmed that they had overcome obstacles encountered earlier this year over a US request for access to medical data and would now proceed with the agreement.

"The government is pleased to announce that it will sign the agreement on Thursday," Health Minister Roma Chilengi said.

Chilengi said the agreement would see the US provide US$1.5 billion in health funding over five years, while Zambia would contribute US$2.1 billion.

The United States is already a major supporter of Zambia's HIV/AIDS, malaria and public health programmes.

Like several other African countries, Zambia had raised concerns over an initial US condition requiring the sharing of broad sets of medical data in exchange for financial support.

Chilengi said the data-sharing provisions had since been narrowed.

He explained that data-sharing would now be "limited to providing information required to monitor and evaluate US-funded health programs."

"A previously proposed clause, which would have required Zambia to share patient medical specimens upon request, has been removed," the health official said.

Earlier this year, Zimbabwe rejected a US$367 million US health funding proposal, describing its terms as "lopsided" and a breach of national sovereignty, particularly over the sharing of sensitive health data and biological samples.

The United States had demanded unrestricted access to epidemiological data and citizens' biological samples for research and commercial purposes.

With the US set to end all bilateral health funding to Zimbabwe by the end of September, just before the start of the malaria season, the country faces significant gaps in its health budget.

Researchers have warned that, "as a consequence of full PEPFAR withdrawal and no additional government or international support," Zimbabwe could record more than 75,000 new HIV infections within a year.

World.title: Malawi: Mutharika's Fifth Private Trip to South Africa - 'No Need for Concern'
World.content:
A political analyst has moved to calm growing public unease over President Peter Mutharika's repeated unexplained trips abroad, insisting there is nothing sinister to worry about as the president jets off to South Africa for the fifth time this year.

The reassurance comes after Mutharika once again left Malawi for the Rainbow Nation, with government officials offering no explanation whatsoever for the purpose behind the mysterious trip -- the latest in a string of similarly unexplained visits that have fuelled mounting speculation back home.

Political analyst George Phiri attempted to put minds at rest, insisting Malawi has robust constitutional structures in place to handle any handover of power should the need ever arise during the president's time away.

But in a revealing admission that will do little to quiet the rumour mill, Phiri conceded that Malawi simply does not have strong enough laws to force authorities to disclose the president's actual health status to the nation.

The stark admission comes amid swirling speculation over Mutharika's wellbeing, with opposition figures previously demanding proof of his physical fitness, and the president's repeated, unexplained dashes to South Africa doing little to put those concerns to rest.

With government continuing to offer nothing beyond the bare minimum each time the president departs, many Malawians are likely to remain unconvinced by assurances that there is "no need for concern" -- particularly given the absence of any legal requirement compelling officials to come clean about exactly what is going on.

World.title: South Africa: Home Affairs Slams Disinformation On Asylum Application Case
World.content:
A member of the vigilante group stands outside the Home Affairs gate. Police moved the group from inside the gate after the harassment of several asylum seekers.

The Department of Home Affairs (DHA) has condemned disinformation about the Constitutional Court's 7 July 2026 judgment in the Scalabrini Centre of Cape Town matter, which concerns the processing of asylum applications.

"Despite it being public knowledge that this case was vigorously opposed by the department and that it led to a binding ruling of the Constitutional Court, nefarious actors have launched a large scale disinformation campaign targeting the Minister of Home Affairs and other officials, claiming that the decision to suspend good cause interviews was taken at the initiative of the Minister, the department or political parties. This is categorically false," the department said in a statement on Wednesday.

In July, the DHA said it would study the judgment handed down by the court in the matter between the Scalabrini Centre and the Minister of Home Affairs.

The Scalabrini Centre is a non-profit organisation that assists migrants, refugees and local South Africans.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The case between the centre and the Minister concerns the constitutionality of certain provisions of the Refugees Act relating to the asylum application process. The Constitutional Court confirmed the Western Cape High Court's declaration that these provisions were unconstitutional and invalid.

The court declared sections of the Refugees Act, which allowed for immigration officials to deport an asylum seeker if they are in the country without a transit visa, unconstitutional. A transit visa is issued at a port of entry to allow a person to travel to a refugee reception centre and apply for asylum.

The Scalabrini Centre, represented by Lawyers for Human Rights, challenged the Minister of Home Affairs regarding practices related to asylum seekers and the "good cause" interviews required for their applications. If applicants failed to meet these conditions, they had to provide immigration officers with a valid reason and show "good cause" for lacking the required visa. "Good cause" interviews were conducted to determine whether someone, who did not have the required documentation, could proceed with an asylum application.

READ | Home Affairs notes Constitutional Court judgment

The case was brought to the Western Cape High Court, where the applicants argued that certain provisions of the Refugees Act unjustly barred individuals with irregular immigration status from seeking asylum, violating their constitutional rights and international non-refoulement principles.

On Wednesday, the DHA said the Constitutional Court judgment is binding, adding that the "department is constitutionally obliged to implement".

"An operational directive was subsequently issued solely to give effect to that judgment, as is standard practice to ensure compliance with rulings of the highest court in the land. Claims that this judgment by the Constitutional Court grants asylum seekers citizenship or provides for the blanket legalisation of foreign nationals are also categorically false.

Close 

"Respect for binding court judgments is fundamental to the rule of law and our constitutional democracy," the DHA said.

The department said it will continue to fulfil its constitutional obligations, irrespective of whether it was successful in the litigation concerned.

"The matter will be referred to the Independent Electoral Commission for further action in terms of the newly published Code of Conduct on Countering Disinformation," said the DHA.

The Code provides rail guards for the conduct of political parties, candidates and anyone acting on political parties' or candidates' instruction, authority or for reward across all election-related communication, whether online or offline, paid or unpaid. The Code protects legitimate debate and robust debate.

The department further called on South Africans to help combat the growing scourge of disinformation and incitement by verifying information.

World.title: Uganda: Govt Renews Push to End Child Labour As 6.2 Million Children Remain Affected
World.content:
The government has renewed its call for urgent action to eliminate child labour, slavery and trafficking in Uganda, with officials urging stronger coordination and practical interventions to protect children.

The call was made during the 13th meeting of the National Steering Committee on the Elimination of Child Labour held at Hotel La Vena in Seguku on Wednesday.

The Acting Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development, Alex Asiimwe, said child labour continues to undermine national development by denying children access to education, health and protection while perpetuating poverty and vulnerability.

His remarks were delivered by Judith Auma, Manager of Labour Inspections and Enforcement at the ministry.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and UNICEF, nearly 138 million children were engaged in child labour globally in 2024, including 54 million in hazardous work.

The latest estimates show that child labour has declined globally since 2020, but progress remains too slow to meet the target of eliminating child labour by 2025.

In Uganda, the 2021 Uganda National Labour Force Survey found that 6.2 million children aged 5 to 17, equivalent to about 40% of children in that age group, were engaged in child labour, excluding household chores.

The survey found a slightly higher proportion among boys than girls.

Asiimwe urged the steering committee to review progress from previous engagements, identify implementation gaps and agree on practical measures with clear responsibilities and timelines.

He also called for stronger links between national policies and implementation at district, community and workplace levels, while emphasising responsible business practices and human rights due diligence in supply chains.

"Identification of a child labour risk should lead to corrective action and effective remediation, rather than simply termination of a supplier relationship or displacement of the affected child from one form of work to another," Asiimwe said.

He said addressing child labour requires interventions that protect affected children rather than simply removing them from one workplace and leaving them vulnerable to exploitation elsewhere.

Asiimwe reaffirmed government's commitment to using recommendations from the meeting to guide the review and implementation of the National Action Plan on the Elimination of Child Labour (NAP II), which covered the 2020/21-2024/25 period.

He also pledged continued coordination among government institutions, particularly the ministries responsible for education, finance, local government and social protection.

The National Steering Committee brings together representatives from government ministries, departments and agencies, development partners, civil society organisations and other organisations involved in efforts to eliminate child labour, slavery and trafficking.

Close 

The meeting comes as Uganda seeks to strengthen implementation of measures addressing the economic and social factors that push children into work, including poverty, limited access to education and vulnerabilities within agricultural and other supply chains.

World.title: Trail cam captures buck walking around with another deer's antlers dangling from its rack
World.content:
Some wild nature footage has surfaced online.

Buck captured on trail cam with another deer's antlers dangling from its rack

World.title: Ithaca council halts Cornell event permits amid scrutiny over handling of rape allegations
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Ithaca Common Council voted late Wednesday night to stop issuing city permits to Cornell University and affiliated student groups, including fraternities, following widespread criticism of the Ivy League school's handling of rape allegations made by a former student.

After hours of debate, the council voted 9-1 in favor of a moratorium, which temporarily bars Cornell from obtaining new permits for assemblies, parades and special events at the Ithaca Commons and activities requiring noise permits, citing public safety concerns.

The measure drew support from numerous Cornell students and Ithaca residents, although some graduate students raised concerns that the restrictions were overly broad and could disrupt activities unrelated to Greek life.

CORNELL PROTESTERS SWARM CAMPUS TO SUPPORT JANE DOE, CALL FOR UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT'S RESIGNATION

One graduate student warned that the moratorium could result in canceled or delayed events, lost deposits, reduced access to venues and disruptions to conferences.

The moratorium will stay in place until Nov. 5, unless the council extends it at a later date. The measure also includes an amendment that requires Cornell to refer investigations involving sexual and violent crimes to the Ithaca Police Department, though its unclear how that will be enforced.

The moratorium comes after the student, identified as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit in September accusing seven former Chi Phi fraternity members of drugging and raping her on the night of Oct. 19, 2024, and into the following morning.

In the lawsuit, she alleges she arrived at the frat house already intoxicated, after which the men pressured her into taking ketamine and other substances. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated.

CORNELL PICKS FORMER DEPUTY US ATTORNEY GENERAL TO REVIEW SEX ASSAULT RESPONSE

The fraternity was suspended on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe reported sexual assault allegations to campus police, according to Doe's civil complaint.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who initially declined to pursue charges, has said Doe's Nov. 2024 sworn statement did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang-raped and, instead, described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

However, CBS New York obtained the transcript of the Cornell police interviews with Jane Doe on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, during which she told investigators: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

Van Houten said he was never provided the full transcript. Late last month, he announced his office was reopening the case because the allegations contained in Jane Doe's lawsuit differed from her sworn statement nearly two years earlier.

BAR NAMED IN CORNELL RAPE LAWSUIT DISPUTES ACCUSER'S ACCOUNT, SAYS SHE WAS NEVER SERVED ALCOHOL WHILE UNDERAGE

In an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday, Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said Cornell police led her to believe the criminal investigation remained active even though Van Houten had decided against filing charges just days after she first spoke with investigators.

Van Houten has said he instructed Cornell police to inform Jane Doe that charges would not be pursued, but acknowledged he never spoke directly with her or her attorney.

Gov. Kathy Hochul effectively took the investigation out of Van Houten's hands on Oct. 1, by appointing Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor on the case.

"Newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute an alleged sexual assault on Cornell University's campus in October 2024," Hochul said in a statement.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

She added: "This has, in turn, undercut my faith, and the public's faith, in the District Attorney's ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time."

On Wednesday, one of the men named in Jane Doe's lawsuit petitioned a court to remove James from the case, accusing her of bias over a social media post she made days before her appointment in which she called what Doe allegedly endured "horrific and unacceptable," The Associated Press reported.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: California woman accused of spying for China fights detention with $820K in proposed security
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A California real estate agent accused of gathering intelligence on a relative of Taiwan's president for the Chinese government sought release from federal custody Wednesday, offering more than $800,000 in property equity and financial guarantees while disputing prosecutors' claims that she posed a flight risk.

Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine, argued through her attorney that her American citizenship, family ties and history of returning from overseas trips demonstrated she would appear for future court proceedings, according to a nine-page defense filing obtained by Fox News Digital.

Zhang was arrested Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport while preparing to board a flight to China. She faces a federal charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.

FEDS SAY US CITIZEN GATHERED INFORMATION ON AMERICAN TARGETS FOR CHINESE COMMUNIST PARTY

Her attorney, Craig Harbaugh, told the court that Zhang came to the United States in 2014, became a naturalized citizen in 2020 and has worked in Orange County real estate for approximately a decade.

She lives with her husband and their two daughters, ages 8 and 5, according to the filing.

The defense proposed using an Irvine residence with at least $700,000 in equity to secure her release, along with $120,000 in financial guarantees from her husband, his sister, his father and a family friend.

Harbaugh also proposed GPS-monitored home detention, surrendering travel documents, electronic-device monitoring and restrictions on entering airports or contacting individuals connected to the case.

The defense acknowledged that Pretrial Services recommended detention over concerns about Zhang's potential failure to appear in court, but argued that strict release conditions would adequately address those concerns.

Zhang's lawyers also disputed the significance of her one-way ticket to China, arguing that she frequently booked international trips using separately purchased outbound and return flights.

According to the filing, Zhang had traveled to China, France and Japan during the past year and returned to the United States after each trip.

The defense said her planned October trip was intended to visit her mother and had been postponed until after her daughters' birthdays.

TAIWAN ANALYSTS SAY TRUMP-XI SUMMIT PRODUCED NO POLICY SHIFT BUT REAL TEST LIES AHEAD

The underlying criminal complaint alleges Zhang participated in a September 2025 surveillance operation outside the Seattle-area residence of a close relative of a Taiwanese government official.

According to an FBI affidavit, investigators reviewed security-camera footage allegedly showing Zhang and another individual photographing the person and family members near their home.

Federal authorities also alleged that Zhang transmitted photographs, video and vehicle information to a suspected Chinese government official through electronic communications.

Investigators said Zhang attended China's University of International Relations in Beijing, which the FBI described as closely associated with China's intelligence apparatus.

Zhang's attorneys contest the charge and maintain that she intends to establish her innocence.

She faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in federal prison if convicted.

World.title: Weaponizing the charge of genocide fuels an increasingly dangerous antisemitism
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Genocide, the intentional annihilation of a group of people, is the gravest of crimes. As malicious actors weaponize the term and endanger Jews everywhere, meticulous use of the charge is more essential than ever.

We are honored to serve as the current and former chairs of the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, an institution memorializing history’s most well-documented genocide: Nazi Germany and its collaborators’ attempt to systematically murder every Jewish man, woman and child in Europe. They almost succeeded. Two-thirds of European Jews – 6 million – were killed. The global Jewish population has yet to recover, with fewer Jews alive today than in 1939, when World War II began.

Holocaust survivors fervently hoped antisemitism would wither when Germany was defeated and its crimes exposed. Yet, they knew from centuries of persecutions long before the Nazis, this ancient hatred is impossible to eradicate. Even so, after World War II, antisemitism became socially unacceptable. The shocking reactions from many quarters to Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack on Israel, three years ago, show this is no longer the case.

DANNY DANON: FROM OCT 7 TO FLIGHT 1073: THE RESILIENCE THAT KEEPS ISRAEL STANDING

On that day, Hamas terrorists invaded Israel intending to murder as many Jewish people as possible, bringing about the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust. As Israel defends itself, we reiterate our wholehearted conviction that Israel has not committed genocide, reflecting the United States government’s consistent and prevailing view.

At the same time, we cannot forget the terrible tragedy many innocent Gazans have experienced as a result of the war. The loss of tens of thousands, including many children, is horrific.

'NOBODY WANTS THIS': CONSULTING RABBI CALLS OUT STAR'S 'IGNORANT' TAKE ON 'GENOCIDE' IN GAZA

As we mourn so many innocent lives lost, we cannot ignore that Hamas puts civilians in harm’s way as a central part of its strategy to demonize Israel. Despite this deadly strategy, Israel has made efforts to warn civilians when to evacuate, provide food and relief, and facilitate vaccine distribution.

Israel, like any country, is not exempt from criticism. And yet, whether out of ignorance or malice, people from all walks of life, often with little knowledge or legal expertise, including in the specific definition of genocide, continually wield the term. Others weaponize it to delegitimize the world’s only Jewish state. Regardless of their intention, the impact is a terrifying eruption of antisemitism and a more dangerous world for Jewish people everywhere.

ISRAELI PRESIDENT HERZOG CALLS ANTISEMITISM A 'CONTAMINATION OF SOCIETIES' AS HATE CRIMES SURGE

Furthermore, state actors like Iran, Qatar, China and Russia spread antisemitic and anti-Israel conspiracy theories and Holocaust denial to stir hatred of Jews and sow chaos in democracies. They are succeeding. Antisemitism is no longer lurking at society’s fringes. It is marching openly through its institutions. Violent antisemitism is at levels not seen since the Holocaust. From Pittsburgh’s Tree of Life synagogue to Bondi Beach in Australia, to Manchester, England, and far too many other places, Jews are under deadly attack. And every day, Jews face relentless harassment and threats on streets, campuses and online.

The Holocaust teaches the dangers of unchecked antisemitism and how hatred began with the Jews but did not end with the Jews – it infected all of society. It is a sad truth that as Jews desperately tried to flee Nazi Europe, the rest of the world did not want them, including our own nation.

History shows some Jews who survived returned to their homes only to face further deadly violence from their former neighbors. Knowing Europe was a Jewish graveyard, survivors desperately wanted to build new lives where they could feel secure – primarily the United States and their ancestral homeland, what is now Israel, which was then under British colonial rule.

The Holocaust also teaches other lessons about humanity. As the Nazis and their collaborators hunted Jews, in every country some remarkable individuals chose to help, rising above the propaganda, hatred and threats to their own safety. And the survivors showed remarkable resilience as they rebuilt their lives, perhaps wondering if there had been a Jewish state, how many of their lost family members might have been saved.

Even so, after World War II, antisemitism became socially unacceptable. The shocking reactions from many quarters to Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack on Israel, three years ago, show this is no longer the case.

Even today, principled individuals are risking all to stand against this age-old hatred. Holocaust survivors, people who have seen the worst humanity has to offer, continue to demonstrate a strength and courage we can only marvel at as they share their testimony. We need this courage from all of society.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

History has taught us what happens when antisemitism is excused, normalized or allowed to masquerade as something more respectable. We cannot make that mistake again. "Never Again" cannot be something we say about the past. It must be a promise of what all of us are willing to do in the present.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

We owe that to the 6 million. We owe it to the Holocaust survivors still among us. And we owe it to the generations of Jews who must never again be taught that hatred is simply something they are expected to endure.

Ambassador Stuart Eizenstat served as chair of the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum under President Joe Biden.

World.title: What strangers can learn from your political donation
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Search your name in the Federal Election Commission's contribution database or on a campaign finance site such as OpenSecrets.org. If you have given enough to trigger federal disclosure requirements, you may be surprised by how much information can be connected to your donation. Depending on the record, that can include your name, mailing address, employer, occupation, donation amount and the political committee that received your money.

This is not a data breach. It is part of federal campaign finance disclosure law. And once information about you is public, it can potentially be combined with personal details found elsewhere online. Here's what your political donation can reveal, how that information can be used and what you can do to reduce the rest of your exposure.

Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.

See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com.

DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT MAKES DAMNING ADMISSION AS GOP PROBES FOREIGN DONATION ALLEGATIONS

What's actually in your political donation record

Federal campaigns generally must itemize an individual's contributions once that person's contributions exceed $200 in the aggregate during the applicable election cycle. For PACs and party committees, the reporting period can be based on the calendar year.

An itemized federal contribution can include:

Your full name

Your mailing address

Your employer

Your occupation

The date of the contribution

The amount you contributed

The candidate or committee receiving the contribution

One contribution may not seem revealing on its own. The privacy concern grows when those details can be connected with information already available through people-search sites, public records and data brokers.

Pay particular attention to your employer and occupation. A people-search profile may already include addresses and relatives, while a campaign finance record can add another verified detail about where you work or what you do. Want to see how much of your personal information is already exposed online? Use the free data exposure scanner at CyberGuy.com to check.

How public donation information can add to your online profile

A campaign finance record alone provides only part of the picture. Other public sources and people-search sites may reveal much more. Sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can contain address histories, possible relatives, phone numbers, email addresses and property information. When information from several sources lines up, someone researching you may be able to build a much more detailed profile. Here is how those pieces can connect.

Step 1: They can confirm who you are

Names are rarely unique. An address, employer or occupation can help distinguish you from another person with the same name. That makes publicly available information useful for confirming that someone has found the right person.

Step 2: They can look for your family

Once someone has your name and location, people-search services may make it easier to identify possible relatives. Your political donation record does not normally list your family members. However, information found elsewhere can connect your identity with a spouse, adult child, parent or other relative. That can create opportunities for impersonation scams and highly personalized phishing attempts.

HOW HURRICANE CHARITY SCAMS TARGET YOU BEFORE STORMS HIT

Step 3: Your workplace can make a scam more convincing

Knowing where you work gives a scammer another detail that can make an email, text or phone call feel legitimate. A phishing message that mentions your actual employer or professional role can be more convincing than a generic message because it contains information you recognize. That is why limiting the amount of personal information available across the web can reduce what criminals have to work with.

Step 4: Be cautious with personalized donation requests

Scammers frequently imitate legitimate organizations, charities and fundraising groups. The FTC warns that fraudulent fundraisers may use familiar-sounding names, pressure people to act quickly or falsely claim someone donated before. There is also an important legal protection around federal campaign finance data. Information copied or obtained from FEC reports about individual contributors cannot legally be sold or used to solicit political or charitable contributions or for commercial purposes. Criminals do not always follow the law, of course. Still, you should be suspicious of any unexpected fundraising request that seems unusually familiar with your personal history.

What if you donated through ActBlue or WinRed?

Using an online fundraising platform does not automatically make a federal contribution private. For earmarked federal contributions exceeding $200, reporting requirements can include the contributor's name, mailing address, employer, occupation, date and amount.

State campaign finance rules are different. Disclosure thresholds and the information made public vary by state, so a contribution that is not itemized under federal rules could still be subject to separate state reporting requirements.

What data removal services can and cannot remove

This is an important limitation to understand. A data removal service generally cannot erase legally required government records such as federal campaign finance filings. That means an FEC filing is not something a removal service can simply delete. What these services can address is the personal information surrounding that public record.

Your campaign finance record might identify your name, mailing address, employer and occupation. Meanwhile, data brokers may have phone numbers, email addresses, relatives, previous addresses and other personal information. Removing those additional profiles can make it harder for someone to connect separate pieces of information about you into one detailed profile.

Some data removal services automatically send opt-out requests to data brokers and continue checking for information that may reappear. Others also offer custom removal requests for websites where your personal information is exposed. However, legal and technical restrictions still apply, especially when the information comes from government records or other sources that are required to remain public.

You can also submit removal requests yourself. The process takes more time, but reducing the amount of personal information spread across people-search sites and data brokers can make it harder for strangers or scammers to build a detailed profile about you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

What to do right now

Here are several steps I would take to see what information about you is already exposed.

Search your political contribution history

Start by searching your name through the FEC's campaign finance records and OpenSecrets.org. Look closely at what information is associated with your contributions. Do not assume every result belongs to you, especially if you have a common name.

THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET

Understand the $200 federal threshold

For federal candidate committees, individual contributions generally become itemized once your aggregate contributions exceed $200 during an election cycle. PAC and party committee reporting rules can use a calendar-year threshold instead. Also remember that some committees voluntarily disclose contributions below the amount they are required to itemize.

Check your state records separately

State disclosure laws vary significantly. Your state may use a different reporting threshold or disclose different information than the federal system, so check the campaign finance database maintained by your state election authority.

Be skeptical of personalized fundraising messages

Do not assume a message is legitimate because it mentions a candidate, organization or contribution you recognize. Instead of clicking a link in an unexpected email or text, visit the organization's official website independently. Also be wary of anyone pressuring you to donate immediately or asking you to pay through gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency.

Reduce the personal information surrounding your public records

You may not be able to remove a legally required campaign finance filing, but you can reduce the additional information available about you through data brokers and people-search sites. You can submit opt-out requests yourself or use a data removal service to handle many of those requests for you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Kurt's key takeaways

I think the surprising part here is how much information can become connected to something as simple as making a political contribution. Federal disclosure rules can make your name, mailing address, employer, occupation and contribution history publicly available once you cross the reporting threshold. You cannot erase a legally required FEC filing with a data removal service, but you can reduce the other information surrounding it. I would search my own name, see what is visible and then work on removing the people-search and data broker profiles that make it easier for strangers or scammers to fill in the rest of the picture.

How much personal information do you think should become public when someone makes a political contribution? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: Olivia Rodrigo calls women-focused festival ‘one hundred percent’ political, tells critics to not buy a ticket
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Grammy-winning singer Olivia Rodrigo said her women-focused music festival Daisy Chain Fields was "one hundred percent" political, saying critics who disagree with her message "don’t have to buy a ticket."

Headlined by Rodrigo, the one-day music festival in Irvine, Calif., featured an all-female lineup including performances by Chappell Roan, Sarah McLachlan and Stevie Nicks.

Net proceeds from Daisy Chain Fields were directed toward nonprofit organizations "dedicated to advancing and advocating for women and girls," including Planned Parenthood, the Center for Reproductive Rights, Baby2Baby and the Black Mamas Matter Alliance.

The festival raised $20 million for the women-focused charities and Rodrigo made it clear that she planned the festival with politics in mind.

PLANNED PARENTHOOD ACROSS MIDWEST AT RISK DUE TO LACK OF FEDERAL FUNDS AFTER 3 FACILITIES CLOSE IN MICHIGAN

"One hundred percent, yes," she told The Hollywood Reporter when asked whether Daisy Chain Fields was political.

"But I think it’s also about joy," she added. "I think the two things can exist at the same time, they kind of have to … I think young people have lost hope in our leaders and lost hope in each other. I really wanted to galvanize people and be evidence of what can happen when you come together and are part of something and contribute."

The "Drivers License" singer also stated that those who don't agree with the festival's political message don't have to buy a ticket.

"Everyone is welcome to come to Daisy Chain. But if you don’t agree with the message that we’re sending, then you don’t have to buy a ticket," she said.

ED SHEERAN CONCERTGOERS WARN ARTISTS ABOUT SHARING POLITICAL VIEWS: 'YOU'RE GOING TO ALIENATE' FANS

Daisy Chain Fields was inspired by Lilith Fair, an all-female traveling music festival launched in the late 1990s by McLachlan, who was frustrated over the lack of female representation in the music industry.

Rodrigo, 23, argued that women had more rights in the 1990s than they do in 2026.

"When Lilith Fair was happening 30 years ago, women in America had more rights, had more autonomy over their bodies," the singer said.

"I’ve always felt really protective of my young fans, and when I play a show and I look out into the audience and see young girls with their friends or their moms or their families, I feel such a kinship with them," she continued. "And if I could be a small part in making the world a safer and better place for them to grow up and live, that’s what I want."

SUPREME COURT TEMPORARILY BLOCKS APPEALS COURT RULING ON ABORTION PILL, RESTORES WIDER ACCESS TO DRUG

Rodrigo released her song "Serena Joy" just before the festival. The single is named after a character from "Handmaid’s Tale" who promoted an oppressive regime that eventually deprived her of her own power.

Lyrics including "a tower we built, painted gold on the walls" and "now go bother your neighbors while we do what we wish" have prompted speculation that the song takes aim at President Donald Trump, though Rodrigo declined to confirm that interpretation.

"It’s basically a song about complacency," the singer said. "It’s about how an attack on one person’s human rights is an attack on all of our human rights. It’s something I’ve been thinking about a lot."

Rodrigo's decision to incorporate politics into her performances drew praise and criticism from political commentators, some of whom argued that her approach alienates fans who do not share her views.

Podcast host Ben Ferguson told Fox News Digital that the festival represented the "breathtaking hypocrisy of Hollywood," arguing that Rodrigo was treating her audience like "political minions."

SPRINGSTEEN, OTHER STARS SHARE STAGE WITH HARDCORE LEFTIST GROUPS AT MUSIC FEST

"These celebrities love preaching tolerance, diversity, and inclusion right up until someone dares to disagree with their politics. Then suddenly it’s, ‘Don’t buy a ticket.’ Apparently, everyone is welcome as long as they think exactly like Olivia Rodrigo," Ferguson said. "That’s not inclusion. That’s political arrogance wrapped in a concert tour."

But Rodrigo’s willingness to openly embrace politics has also won praise from Democrats, including strategist Kaivan Shroff, who said celebrities who don’t speak out on current events can be viewed as "inauthentic."

"This is not some niche artist trying to cultivate a fanbase by leaning into cheap politics. She is making politics part of the art, part of the live show and part of the brand, and at least she is being honest about that and owning it," Shroff told Fox News Digital.

"I actually think ‘if you don’t agree, don’t buy a ticket’ is cleaner than pretending the politics are incidental. But there is a tradeoff," he continued. "The minute you tell people the show itself carries a political message, disagreement with that message becomes part of the consumer experience too. You cannot make politics central to the product and then act surprised when the product gets judged politically."

Rodrigo has previously sparred with the Trump administration, condemning the Department of Homeland Security in 2025 after it used her song "All-American b----" in a social media post encouraging illegal immigrants to self-deport from the country. She has also criticized Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for being "barbaric and cruel."

Film critic and Hollywood in Toto founder Christian Toto echoed Ferguson’s concerns, telling Fox News Digital: "In these contentious times, getting hyper political and alienating large swathes of your audience is less than ideal."

World.title: DNC sues administration over taxpayer-funded pro-Trump TV ads
World.content:
The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration Wednesday over its taxpayer-funded s that portray President Donald Trump in a favorable light, alleging the ads violate federal laws on government spending and propaganda.

The DNC cited a measure Trump signed into law this year that says funds appropriated by Congress can’t be used “for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress.”

The lawsuit also cites the Anti-Deficiency Act, which bars spending government money that hasn’t been appropriated by Congress, and the Purpose Statute, which says taxpayer funds can be used only for the specific purposes approved by Congress.

The DNC said the administration’s use of taxpayer dollars for “campaign-style s” deprived Democrats “of a fair electoral process by adding public funds to the resources available to support Republican candidates.” The use of public funds places Democratic candidates at an electoral disadvantage, it argued.

The watchdog group Common Cause filed its own suit making similar legal arguments, alleging the administration had violated appropriations statutes.

The ads, launched last month, sparked criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, many of whom questioned their legality.

Trump reversed course Monday, announcing on Truth Social he would no longer use government funds for the ads and saying he and his PAC, MAGA Inc., would foot the bill moving forward, instead. He didn’t say whether the government would be reimbursed for the ads that already ran.

Reached for comment on the lawsuits, the White House pointed NBC News to Trump’s Truth Social post. The Department of Homeland Security and the Office of Management and Budget, which are named as defendants in addition to Trump and the White House, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.

Since Trump’s announcement, several of the ads have continued to run with the disclaimer that they were paid for by the U.S. government.

Asked by NBC News whether those were paid for before or after Trump pledged to cover the costs, the White House wouldn’t say either way.

A person familiar with the ads said that the ad buy for the spots, placed before Trump’s Monday announcement, will end this week. Afterwards, the person said, outside groups will begin paying for the ads.

NBC News has reported that a $20 million contract was awarded to a Maryland firm for the ad campaign. AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm, estimated that at least $10 million had been spent to air the ads through Monday.

Attorneys for the DNC asked a federal judge in Washington to find that the administration acted unlawfully “by developing and airing the propaganda ads using Congressionally appropriated funds” and to prevent it from using those funds to develop and air the ads in the future.

DNC Chair Ken Martin condemned the administration for using taxpayer dollars as Americans struggle with a rising cost of living.

“Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes,” he said in a statement Wednesday.

Omar Noureldin, Common Cause’s senior vice president of policy and litigation, said in an interview with NBC News Wednesday that the group is bringing forth the suit “because we want to make sure that no president, regardless of party, can hijack public funds to fund political self-promotion without congressional approval.”

“It appears that the $20 million that had been contracted for this has not all been spent yet, and so they will continue to run ads paid for by taxpayer dollars, and so we think we need to stop that now, and not another dollar of taxpayer dollars should be spent on these ads,” Noureldin said.

The federal money for the ads came from funds intended for Customs and Border Protection, an arm of DHS. NBC News reported that CBP leadership was cut out of the decision to run the ads.

Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, said last week that the ads didn’t merit FCC review, arguing that they weren’t “anything at all out of the ordinary.”

The White House has defended the ads by calling them “clearly not political” and claiming they were about “reminding Americans to love their country.” It has also pointed to other administrations’ use of public safety announcements.

World.title: At least 30 people killed in Russian bus bombing in Ukraine
World.content:
At least 30 people were killed when a Russian bomb struck two buses in the Ukrainian frontline city of Kramatorsk Thursday, local officials said, as Moscow’s intensifying attacks grow ever more deadly.

Another 18 people were wounded when the bomb hit a street in the city at 10 a.m. local time (3 a.m. ET), Ukraine’s National Police said in a statement.

Kramatorsk’s Regional Governor Vadym Filashkin accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians, sharing images of a charred bus wreckage and bodies and body parts on the road next to it. Filashkin said he was shutting down public transport in the city and neighboring Sloviansk in light of “the sharp deterioration of the security situation.”

The bloody aftermath left debris and body parts strewn across a road in the eastern city. Ukrainian National Police

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement on X that Russia struck “an ordinary public transport stop” in Kramatorsk with an aerial bomb.

In a later post, he said doctors were fighting to save the lives of those injured and “some of those killed have still not been identified because of the severity of their injuries.”

Kramatorsk is close to the active frontline and part of Ukraine’s industrial Donbass region, which has been central to President Vladimir Putin war plans.

Civilian casualties have surged as Russia intensifies attacks across Ukraine, and the country Ukraine runs low on air defense munitions. There has also been an uptick in daytime attacks in recent weeks, creating a round-the-clock threat to civilians.

On Wednesday, a missile strike on a residential building in the north of the country killed 22 people, including five children.

Moscow has repeatedly denied that it deliberately targets civilians in Ukraine.

World.title: Oil prices hit $105 and stocks tumble as Trump considers renewed strikes on Iran
World.content:
The price of oil jumped sharply Thursday, as President Donald Trump weighs whether to resume large-scale U.S. military operations against Iran in the coming weeks.

Brent crude oil rose more than 5% to more than $105 per barrel in early trading, while U.S. crude oil rose almost 5% to nearly $93 per barrel. Benchmark diesel futures jumped 4.5% in European trading. Heating oil, a proxy for jet fuel, rose more than 4%.

The move higher in oil prices also pushed up bond yields. The 10-year Treasury yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, jumped to 5.35%. That level effectively reversed a drop in yields seen late Wednesday. The yield on every other Treasury bond also rose.

U.S. stock futures dropped in response. S&P 500 futures fell 0.6% and Nasdaq 100 futures slid 0.8%. Futures for the Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium-sized companies, fell 1%.

No decisions have yet been made yet about resuming combat operations in Iran, people familiar with the discussions told NBC News.

But with the midterm elections less than a month out and early voting underway, any substantial action by the Trump White House in the coming weeks would be likely to have at least some impact on voter attitudes.

A return to large-scale U.S. strikes on Iranian targets would represent a significant escalation in the war and an end to the uneasy stalemate between Washington and Tehran that has held for three months.

The prospect of U.S. forces resuming strikes on Iran was first reported Wednesday by The Atlantic.

Smaller-scale Iranian attacks on commercial shipping have reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery for global oil supplies, to just a fraction of prewar levels.

From Sept. 28 through Oct. 4, daily traffic in the strait averaged fewer than 23 ships a day, according to data from MarineTraffic. Before the war, hundreds of ships per day passed through the waterway delivering crude oil and related products to global markets.

Oil and commodities market experts have repeatedly warned that any escalation in the fighting in Iran will cause oil prices to trend even higher.

“The market remains exposed to significant risks,” Bank of America’s head of global commodities, Francisco Blanch, wrote in early September. If skirmishes curbing oil flows continued into the year’s end, he wrote, Brent could trade in a $95-$120 per barrel range.

“Meanwhile, a broader conflict resulting in major energy infrastructure damage may spike prices” as high as $150 per barrel, he added.

The cost to ship crude oil from countries that are not directly impacted by the closure of the strait has also reached new highs, as producers scramble to meet demand.

It now costs $77 million for a crude carrier to move U.S. oil to Asia, according to Bloomberg, which cited data from the Baltic Exchange in London. The average price for the same route in 2025 was just $9.2 million.

The continued elevation of crude oil prices has caused gas prices to remain higher for consumers, with just weeks until polls close in the midterm elections. On Thursday, the national average price for regular unleaded gas was $4.36 per gallon. That price is more than 45% higher than when the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28.

Diesel fuel prices have soared even more, spurred on by recent escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war. At $6.28 per gallon, diesel has risen almost 70% since Feb. 28.

World.title: Ithaca council passes moratorium on new Cornell events permits
World.content:
The Ithaca Common Council voted Wednesday night to pass a temporary moratorium on special events permits at Cornell University and called on the school to hand over investigations into "violent sex crimes" to the Ithaca Police Department.

The moratorium will apply to Cornell University, its residential and nonresidential sorority and fraternity organizations, general student organizations, and university student affiliations, according to Ithaca's mayor, Robert Cantelmo.

Effective immediately, the city will not issue new permits to the affected parties for assemblies, parades, special events and noise. The moratorium, which is set to expire on Nov. 5, passed by a 9-1 vote and is designed so that the council can choose to renew it on a monthly basis.

Cantelmo said the council adopted the moratorium "based on substantial concerns for the safety, health, and welfare of the residents of, and visitors to, the city of Ithaca."

The council also amended the moratorium Wednesday night to include a resolution "that the city calls upon Cornell to hand over investigation of violent sex crimes" to the Ithaca Police Department.

Cantelmo said the city is demanding the school do more to "punish, monitor transparently and prevent sexual violence on campus."

The mayor proposed the moratorium on campus events in the wake of a civil lawsuit filed last month by a former Cornell student, Jane Doe, who alleged she was drugged and gang-raped by seven fraternity brothers at the Chi Phi house in October 2024.

She reported the alleged assault to the Cornell University Police Department three weeks later. The department turned over a summary of her allegations in a sworn statement to the district attorney, who decided not to pursue charges. Ithaca Police say they were not informed of the case.

In response to an investigation by Cornell's Title IX office, the school said that two of the men were expelled, two were suspended for at least two semesters, one had already graduated before any punishment could be handed down, and two were found not to be responsible for sexual misconduct.

After the woman filed her lawsuit and details of the allegations became public, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to review the case.

On Cornell's campus, students have held rallies and protests to express anger with the school administration's handling of the allegations, and to stand in solidarity with sexual violence survivors. On Monday, over 1,000 people, including students, professors and local Ithaca residents, gathered to demand change from the school. On Wednesday, more than 100 students staged a seven-hour sit-in at a dining hall.

A 2025 survey conducted by Cornell found that more than one in three undergraduate women reported nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since entering the school. More than 49% of respondents reported harassment. The survey identified campus-affiliated settings like residence halls and fraternity houses as the location of most incidents.

Cecily Cox, a graduate student at Cornell who opposes the moratorium, addressed the council Wednesday night at the meeting where it passed.

"Parties do not cause sexual violence," Cox told CBS News.

She took issue with the moratorium's "ambiguity" and said it will affect more students than necessary.

It "should not be for all students and should not punish all students who have nothing to do with what is going on with the sexual assault case," Cox said.

Cantelmo said the moratorium is not intended to be applied in a way that would infringe on any student's right to exercise freedom of religion, speech or peaceful assembly.

Other students, including Sam Poole, believe the moratorium is an opportunity for the city to put pressure on the school.

"Cornell's already feeling this pressure, and we need the city to keep this moratorium in place until they actually make structural change," said Poole.

"Cornell will not protect survivors unless somebody forces them to," Poole added. "I think the city of Ithaca has the power by threatening the thing they care about, which is their events."

World.title: Isaias becomes first hurricane of 2026 Atlantic season, threatens Gulf Coast
World.content:
Hurricane Isaias was intensifying early Thursday and is expected to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, threatening parts of Mississippi, Alabama and the western part of the Florida Panhandle. It became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season after strengthening from a tropical storm late Wednesday night.

A hurricane warning is in effect for the northern Gulf Coast, from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, across Alabama to Florida's Bay/Gulf County line.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in his state, and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties.

Maps show hurricane's path

Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," had maximum sustained winds of 80 mph at 8 a.m. ET, and its core was located about 385 miles south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, according to the National Hurricane Center. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 15 miles from the storm's center, and tropical-storm-force winds extended outward up to 90 miles.

Map shows the potential path of Hurricane Isaias as it heads toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

"Additional strengthening is expected through early Friday, and Isaias should remain a dangerous hurricane as it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday night," the center said, emphasizing that "preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds along the warning area of the Gulf Coast should be rushed to completion."

Mandatory evacuations have been ordered in parts of Florida's Okaloosa County, in the panhandle, which were set to take effect Thursday at 12 p.m. ET. Voluntary evacuations were in place for coastal spots in southeastern Alabama, with officials in the city of Gulf Shores urging non-residents to leave the area to "help reduce congestion, support emergency operations, and ensure the safety of those who may be most vulnerable during the storm."

Along with the hurricane warning, a tropical storm warning was issued from Louisiana's Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line to west of Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and from east of the Bay/Gulf County line to Florida's Aucilla River. A storm surge warning was issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Steinhatchee River in Florida, and a storm surge watch was in effect from Steinhatchee River to Florida's Yankeetown.

Map shows the strength of the wind Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring to the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 7 inches of rain and as much as 10 inches in some places along the coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see heavy rainfall.

Map shows amounts of rain expected through Saturday in some regions of U.S. CBS News

The latest for a first hurricane since 1905

Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.

The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.

An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late-June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early- to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.

Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.

World.title: U.K. police release 7th man arrested over RAF Fairford incident on bail
World.content:
A 22-year-old man arrested in London earlier this week on suspicion of a terror offense has been released on bail, British counterterrorism police said. He is the seventh man arrested in connection with a security incident that British authorities have linked to Iran against RAF Fairford. American bombers had used this base to strike Iran during the ongoing war.

The man, a British national, was arrested Tuesday in the Westminster area of central London on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006. He was released from custody under "strict bail conditions," police said.

All seven men arrested in the investigation, each in their 20s, now remain on police bail while "specialist teams continue to pursue all lines of enquiry," police said. Officers are appealing for anyone with information to come forward.

The decision to bail the first six men drew criticism last week from President Trump. He had said Iran "might be" involved in the incident, telling reporters on Sept. 28 that U.S. and British authorities worked "very closely" on the matter.

"We would not have released them," he said.

Concrete blocks were installed near the RAF Fairford main gate on Oct. 1, 2026, in Fairford, England, amid increased security measures following a major incident near the air base. David Bown / Getty Images / DAVIDBOWN

Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near RAF Fairford, about 100 miles west of London, early on Sept. 27, as armed police and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant, gasoline, in three vans linked to the first five suspects, but no explosives.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident, without saying why or what the nature of the suspected plot was.

Iran denied involvement in the incident but previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. American bombers have used Fairford to strike Iran during the ongoing war.

The U.S. moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from the base on Sunday, though it's unclear whether or how the move was connected to the arrests.

Mr. Trump told reporters Monday he didn't want to tempt "the enemy" by having the bombers there.

"We had a threat, and if we're going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that," he said, adding that those behind the unspecified threat "would be linked to Iran," without offering details.

World.title: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
World.content:
South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute

toggle caption i Seth Wenig/AP

SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.

Sponsor Message

South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.

The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.

North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.

Sponsor Message

It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.

Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.

South Korea has provided $445 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100 million in aid to Ukraine in a meeting with Zelenskyy,

World.title: South Korea test-flies its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon
World.content:
South Korea test-flies its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon

toggle caption i Jeon Heon-kyun/EPA POOL via AP

SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea flight-tested on Thursday its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defense systems, bringing Seoul closer to what it says could be game-changing weapons capabilities.

There was no immediate response from North Korea, which last week tested its own hypersonic missile that landed in the waters near Japan.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attended the test, saying it's a major step in strengthening the country's conventional defense capabilities, according to a statement. It did not elaborate where the test took place.

Sponsor Message

The statement said the weapon separated from its booster rocket at the planned altitude, then descended and maneuvered both vertically and horizontally before hitting a test target. It said once developed, the weapon would be able to strike key targets by surprise in the "Korean Peninsula theater of operations."

Lee stressed that South Korea "must secure our security through our own strength," and also inspected the country's most powerful Hyunmoo-5 ballistic missile on Thursday, his office said. It did not mention any direct comments by Lee on the North.

Tensions between the Koreas have increased in recent weeks after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border.

The South's military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South's demands for an apology.

North Korea has also stepped up weapons testing activity as its leader Kim Jong Un expands his military nuclear program while taking an increasingly hard line toward Seoul.

Kim has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump's calls to revive their diplomacy that broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its "hostile" policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for its denuclearization as a precondition for talks.

Sponsor Message

The tensions have been a setback for Lee, who favors engagement with North Korea and has tempered his rhetoric toward the North even as public anger grows over the mine blasts.

Lee has also called for strengthening South Korea's conventional defense capabilities while reducing its reliance on the United States, which unilaterally decided to scale back a major military exercise with the South in August, with Trump citing his "very good relationship" with Kim.

In its latest weapons test on Oct. 3, North Korea launched what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that it said flew more than 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). Japan said the missile landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone.

South Korea said it detected the missile flying more than 700 kilometers (435 miles), while Japan's Defense Ministry said it assessed that the missile flew about 680 kilometers (422 miles).
