The U.S. Department ⁠of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether the agency planned to set up screening there.

A spokesperson from Health and Human Services said there are about 200 individuals per year from the Siberian region who travel to the United States. Direct flights between Russia and the United States have been suspended ​since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022.

World.title: Layoffs at Stelco underway, and will roll out over 3 weeks, says union president
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Layoffs at Hamilton's Stelco steel plant are underway and expected to roll out over three weeks.

Not all workers have been formally notified, said Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, which covers Stelco workers in Hamilton. But he said "people have a general idea" of whether or not their job is on the line.

Wells said Wednesday that a batch of layoffs is expected this week, with another the following week and a final group the week after that. One worker, Jordan Williams, told CBC Hamilton that he received his notice on Wednesday, coming into effect Sunday.

In total, Wells expects 300 to 350 layoffs in Hamilton, with more at Stelco's Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, which is covered by a different union local.

Wells explained that new rules in Ontario's Employment Standards Act mean the company doesn't have to give advance notice of a temporary layoff shorter than 35 weeks, so people could get their notice and be laid off on the same day.

Ron Wells, president of USW Local 1005, says he is 'disgusted' by the decision to lay off approximately 350 workers. (Meagan Fitzpatrick/CBC)

"If it becomes permanent, like after 35 weeks, they would have to add those 12 weeks to any severance pay owing," he told CBC Hamilton, adding that the laid-off workers would retain their medical benefits for the time being.

"People are obviously worried about the future. How you going to pay the bills?... But the overriding emotion is anger," Wells said. "I think almost all the workers I've talked to, they feel that this shutdown and layoff isn't necessary. There's a market out there for our product and we're being used as pawns in a political game."

Wells believes Stelco owner Cleveland-Cliffs, whose CEO Lourenco Goncalves has expressed support for tariffs and for U.S. President Donald Trump, is eager to make it appear as though Trump's tariffs are working, ahead of midterm elections in the U.S.

"I hope, basically, the federal government makes an example out of them," Wells said. "We just want to make sure they … follow through with it."

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly warned on Monday that Stelco had five business days to share a plan to keep jobs or the government would launch legal action under the Investment Canada Act.

In a previous interview with CBC News, Goncalves defended his right to idle production.

"We had the ability to sell into the United States," he said at the time. "That was an underlying condition for me to acquire Stelco.

"I would not have acquired the Stelco if I knew that Canada and the United States would become what they became — enemies in trade."

CBC Hamilton contacted Stelco to ask if the company plans to meet the government's deadline, but did not hear back.

Local tradespeople eye impact of layoffs, look to help

Wells said that for every unemployed steel worker, there are up to five other jobs that could now be on the line. Bernard Tompkins, who works for a contractor that does equipment maintenance at Stelco, said Wednesday that people who work in various trades are worried.

"Working on site gives me a perspective on how much further the impact can reach beyond the Stelco employees who are directly being laid off," said Tompkins in an email on Wednesday.

"It’s not just the direct employees — it also affects other building trades, contractors, suppliers, technicians and companies whose work depends on maintaining and supporting those operations."

Tompkins, a boilermaker who is running for Hamilton council in Ward 2, said his union is looking into creating internship opportunities for some of the displaced Stelco workers "considering the amount of work currently available in [the] trade.

"From what I was told, those kinds of conversations were already taking place," he said. "I really feel for the workers and families going through this hard time and unfortunately Christmas is just around the corner."

Job retraining available for 75 laid-off workers

On Tuesday, the federal and provincial governments announced $203,000 toward job retraining for 75 "steel and manufacturing workers," to be delivered by Learning Connections Hamilton.

"Ontario will deliver the funding through Skills Advance Ontario, which partners with employers and training providers to help workers transition into in-demand careers," said a release from the province.

"The training will provide participants with skills assessments, individualized training plans, digital skills upgrading, training referrals, case management and support accessing certifications and short-term training required for employment."

Affected workers can access support through the United Steelworkers Action Centre by calling 905-548-9197 or visiting in person at 1031 Barton St. E.

Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said Wednesday that her "Head of Lake Ontario" tariff-response plan will help laid-off Stelco workers by keeping property tax increases below inflation and allowing for emergency tax and fee deferrals for people who can't pay their city bills.

"When the news on Stelco broke, I immediately called on the federal and provincial governments to push them to save these jobs through negotiation or enforcement, and to immediately release relief funding for impacted workers and their families," she said in an email statement to CBC Hamilton on Wednesday.

"I can’t control Trump's actions, but I can control how we respond."

World.title: How NATO is prepping in the Baltic skies for a possible confrontation with Russia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

NATO is strengthening its air defence and border security in the Baltics in response to escalating Russian sabotage and drone threats. A CBC News team gets an up-close look at the alliance’s readiness and the Canadian military’s contribution.

How NATO is flexing in the face of Russian aggression

When Latvians cast their ballots in a national election this past weekend, many did so without realizing that three countries — Turkey, Spain and Italy — all had fighter jets patrolling the grey skies high above them for any overt Russian attempts to disrupt the vote.

"Nothing flies without authorization in the alliance airspace," said Capt. Antonio Moncebo, a Spanish F-18 pilot whose squadron was operating out of a base in Estonia next door.

So when NATO identifies a possible threat, "we trigger a scramble, and we seek them and shoot them down."

Spanish fighter pilot Antonio Moncebo spoke to CBC News at a NATO airbase in Lithuania. (Jason Ho/CBC)

NATO’s high-altitude vigilance with its "sky shield" is no longer just a routine drill.

While many NATO military planners believe Russia is unlikely to deliberately start a war with the Western alliance, if Russian President Vladimir Putin decides he wants to test NATO’s resolve with a lower-threshold provocation, the Baltic states could be vulnerable.

From suspected Russian arson attacks at high-tech defence facilities in Estonia to a foiled cargo plane bombing plot in Germany, Putin's intelligence services are increasingly pushing past traditional red lines in an effort to weaken Western resolve to aid Ukraine.

NATO jets from Italy, Spain and Turkey fly in a tight formation above Latvia, as part of a demonstration by the alliance's air command. (Adrian Di Virgilio/CBC News)

Justin Bronk, with the British military think-tank RUSI, says Putin may believe there's an opportunity to exploit U.S President Donald Trump’s often antagonistic relationship with Europe.

"Clearly at the moment, there's a lot of concern about the potential for Russian direct aggression against NATO members in order to presumably try … to demonstrate that the alliance won't come to the military aid of one of its member states," said Bronk.

Members of the media, including a CBC videographer, perch at the edge of the ramp in the back of a Lithuanian military aircraft to photograph NATO jets in the sky. The photographers were tethered with harnesses so they wouldn't fall out. (CBC)

Whether NATO is prepared to counter potential Russian aggression is an existential question.

Lieut.-Gen. Guillaume Thomas, who commands the air operations over the Baltic states, dismisses any talk that a Trump-led U.S. can’t be relied upon.

"I am completely confident in the support of U.S. forces in protecting the alliance. I have no doubt every day I can see the development of the U.S. force and I have no doubt about their support, their continuous support."

To prove its readiness, NATO, which is anchored by the principle of collective defence, recently invited a small group of media, including CBC News, to witness the air shield over the Baltic states first-hand.

High above Lithuania, aircrew lowered the back ramp of a military transport plane in mid-flight, allowing journalists a dizzying, close-up view of Italian Eurofighters, Spanish F-18s and Turkish fighter jets flying wing to wing.

Thomas says such tight formations are a visual manifestation of a deeper, more profound shift in how the alliance secures its eastern flank.

Spanish and Italian fighter jets fly in a tight formation next to a Lithuanian military plane carrying members of the media. (Adrian Di Virgilio/CBC)

"It was a shift in mindset to go from an air policing mission to an air defence mission," he said. "That enabled us to be more reactive, more flexible, more agile, to demonstrate our ability to protect our air spaces."

Building a 'drone wall'

But NATO’s air shield remains a work in progress.

Russia’s successful and repeated use of highly destructive jet-powered drones in Ukraine has forced Baltic nations to rapidly rethink their own domestic defences.

Latvia is now actively constructing what it calls a "drone wall" along its heavily forested eastern border.

"It consists of integrated radar, interceptors and command-and-control systems so that we're able to detect and intercept, if needed, a hostile drone," explained Airis Rikveilis, state secretary for the Latvian Ministry of Defence.

Police officers stand at the site of a Russian drone strike on the North Bridge in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 4. (Reuters)

NATO planners admit that building a flawless shield is mathematically impossible.

While heavy fighter jets can intercept larger threats, they represent a severe cost mismatch when deployed against tiny, low-flying surveillance drones.

On the tarmac in Lithuania, crews flew a new Latvian-designed anti-drone system called Blaze. It features a propeller-driven interceptor equipped with cameras and a high explosive warhead that can be used to crash into Russian drones as far as 10 kilometres away.

But Blaze is only just being introduced and its use at the moment isn't widespread.

Rikveilis, the Latvian defence official, acknowledges more work is needed to complete preparations but denies drone defence is a NATO weak spot.

The threat of Russian drones "is a new one, it's an evolving one, but at the same time it is being taken care of."

The Canadian connection

Holding the vulnerable ground underneath any of NATO's defensive gaps falls squarely on Canada.

Over the last decade, Ottawa’s commitment to the region has quietly scaled up from a localized battle group to full brigade leadership, placing up to 3,000 Canadian troops right on Russia’s doorstep.

As commander of Task Force Latvia (TFL), Canadian Brig.-Gen. Mason Stalker oversees Canada's military presence in the Baltic region. He is also deputy commander of Multinational Division-North (MND-N). (Adrian Di Virgilio/CBC)

For the newly appointed Canadian commander in this theatre, the immediate focus is keeping the multi-nation force integrated and lethal.

"My concern always is making sure that we have the combat power necessary to basically make sure our NATO commitments are adhered to," says Canadian Brig.-Gen. Mason Stalker.

"And we do. We can surge as required."

While military commanders and fighter pilots project absolute confidence in the skies, the reality for Latvians on the ground is more complex.

With its towering stone column, the historic Freedom Monument in Latvia's capital, Riga, is a reminder of a nation that fought hard to break free from foreign rule.

A large poster depicting Russian President Vladimir Putin with a skeletal, skull-like jaw is displayed across the road from the Russian Embassy in Riga, Latvia. (Chris Brown/CBC)

For many people walking past it on cobblestone streets, the memory of Soviet occupation is not ancient history but a lived experience.

With Russia’s brutal war against Ukraine now in its fourth year, this history creates a persistent, low-grade anxiety.

"We just have a history with Russia, so I'm thinking that something similar can happen again," said Leva Rosenberg, a 20-year-old music student in Riga who spoke to CBC News.

"I am scared about it every day, but I'm just living and hoping our government will save us."

That daily fear represents exactly the kind of psychological vulnerability Vladimir Putin’s hybrid campaign aims to exploit.

For others in Riga’s Old Town, the visible presence of NATO and Canadian troops on the ground and allied jets in the sky provides an ironclad sense of security that their grandparents never had.

"Latvia is part of NATO," said Lina Valaine. "So I think if something happens... then NATO will be involved, and I don't think Russia needs that at the moment. So, I don't think anything is going to happen."

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Mayor from Colombia’s north claims De la Espriella’s armed men intimidated him
World.content:
The mayor of Sincelejo claimed Sunday that armed men intimidated him during a meeting with Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a video message, Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña said that armed men positioned themselves behind him while the president accused the mayor of corruption and threatened to pull municipal funds.

The accusations were partly published on the social media pages of the president, who accused Acuña of being “a person who, like you, faces 13 corruption charges, has a video in which he explains how to embezzle funds from the PAE, and, on top of that, is set to stand trial in the Supreme Court of Justice on charges of illicit enrichment.”

So let’s see what we do with Sincelejo, but I do not work under your scheme of corruption. And if you think you can continue engaging in those practices, know that someone has arrived who is going to prevent it and that I am going to concentrate on it. This money, mister mayor, I will take care of it, and to take care of it I have to keep it away from your control. President Abelardo de la Espriella

In his response, Acuña claimed that De la Espriella’s video “has been edited and digitally manipulated.”

I ask you, please, to show the full video, where you can see how disciplinary and criminal codes are being violated in Colombia, where you can see how a mayor is being intimidated with rifles in the hands of civilians. How can a mayor be constantly flanked—for the entire duration of an event—by a person armed with a rifle, with the sole purpose of intimidating him? Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

Investigative journalist Laura Ardila said on social media platform X that sources from the province confirmed Acuña’s allegations.

Sources from the department who were present say—fearing they might be named—that they left the scene terrified. They claim that Acuña was indeed surrounded by heavily armed men in civilian clothing, that the president’s office was recording the entire time, and that, based on details like these, they believe it was a scene staged in advance to go viral. Journalist Laura Ardila

The mayor subsequently pointed out that the investigations into his alleged corruption existed before the presidential campaign, during which the De la Espriella campaign may have violated electoral laws, according to Acuña.

Among other things, the mayor said that he had been approached by De la Espriella’s parents to support the far-right president’s campaign and that local print shops may have received unreported campaign funds.

Since this needs to be clarified, mister President, it would be a good idea for the oversight agencies to investigate whether any printing shops in Sincelejo incurred campaign expenses that have not yet been reported to the National Electoral Council, whether there was campaign financing, and where that campaign financing came from, Mister President. Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

The mayor also pointed out that two members of the De la Espriella administration are being investigated on corruption charges and that the president had ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

The president has repeatedly used corruption allegations to target political enemies.

World.title: Colombia’s top corporate lobbyist resigns over reported tensions with president
World.content:
The director of one of Colombia’s most powerful business associations, Bruce Mac Master of the ANDI, resigned amid tensions with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a letter to the ANDI, Mac Master said that “it is time for me to step down from my role as head of the National Association of Entrepreneurs of Colombia.”

According to the former ANDI boss, “unexpected and troubling circumstances” made working for the association “particularly complex” and ‘multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously.”

In recent weeks, unexpected and troubling circumstances have arisen that have made the Association’s operating environment particularly complex, with potential adverse effects on its members and staff. Multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously. In the face of these challenges, I have sought to act with firmness and prudence, always prioritizing institutional channels and placing the interests of the ANDI above any personal considerations, in an effort to resolve this situation. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master’s resignation followed news suggesting that De la Espriella instructed his cabinet of boycotting the ANDI chief.

According to political news magazine La Silla Vacia, the rift between the ANDI and the government was because De la Espriella’s law firm was never allowed to join the ANDI and the association’s donations in response to the august 10 earthquake bypassed the First Lady’s newly founded and very controversial foundation.

“The General Board of Directors, its Executive Committee, and I did everything in our power to facilitate a solution and create conditions that would allow the Association to fully fulfill its role, seeking to keep channels of dialogue open and to continue contributing,” but “all of those attempts were unsuccessful.”

I deeply regret this, because I have always believed in collective intelligence and in the need for the government, the private sector, and institutions to work together—even in the face of differences—with respect, independence, and a sense of national responsibility. We tried, but we were unsuccessful. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master said that he hoped that his resignation would restore “collaboration between the national government and the business community—as represented by the General Board of Directors, the members, and the various divisions of the Association.”

The former ANDI chief had been trying to represent the business interests of its approximately 1,600 members since 2013.

World.title: Colombia seeks to tighten checks on public protests
World.content:
Colombia’s government published a draft decree that seeks to tighten regulations on public protests.

The draft was published weeks before labor unions and social organizations plan regional anti-government protests ahead of a national strike that is set for November.

The draft seeks to update the Decree #3 of 2021, which was issued months before a national strike that was violently repressed by the police and the military.

In an attempt to prevent another bloodbath, the decree seeks to regulate authorities’ response to protests and the coordinated use of force in response to acts of vandalism and violence.

The decree regulates dialogue between the protesters and law enforcement authorities to promote the peaceful nature of protests.

The decree additionally limits the use of police intelligence against those organizing and participating in the protests.

Last but not least, the decree seeks the effective prosecution of those arrested during protests through increased surveillance and a permanent police presence.

The decree comes amid social tensions that surged after the far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and announced counterrevolutionary measures that seek to undo reforms by his leftist predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro.

Swelling student protests have been publicly accused of being fueled by insurgencies and De la Espriella has warned that police may enter universities if they find evidence they are used to prepare acts of vandalism or terrorism.

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Why Argentina's Falklands sanctions do not automatically reach Sea Lion's operator
World.content:
Why Argentina's Falklands sanctions do not automatically reach Sea Lion's operator

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:29 UTC Full article

Photo: Raphael WOLLMANN / Getty Images

The sanctions Argentina has imposed on companies involved in the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands target specific entities rather than entire corporate groups, so the subsidiary currently operating the field is not automatically covered, according to a legal analysis by specialist site Diplomacy & Law.

Argentina's Energy Secretariat declared Rockhopper Exploration plc's activities illegal in 2012 and barred it from operating in the country for 20 years in 2013. In 2022 it imposed a similar sanction on Navitas Petroleum LP. But the project's current operator is Navitas Petroleum Development and Production Ltd, a UK subsidiary of the Israeli group. “A sanction imposed on Navitas Petroleum LP does not automatically become an identical sanction against every affiliated company,” writes the author, Edmarverson A. Santos, unless the law expressly provides for it or a new measure is adopted.

Argentina's legal framework nonetheless reaches beyond licence holders. Law 26,659 of 2011 prohibits direct or indirect participation in hydrocarbon exploration or exploitation that the country regards as unauthorised on its continental shelf, with bans of five to 20 years. Subject to its conditions, it covers shareholders, service providers, financiers, logistics operators and technical advisers. Law 26,915 of 2013 added penalties for directors and companies.

The decree signed by President Javier Milei on September 3 designated the foreign ministry as the enforcing authority, set short deadlines for proceedings and required compliance declarations from those applying for the large-investment incentive regime or hydrocarbon permits in the country. That mechanism explains the effect on companies with business in Argentina: Halliburton, SLB and Baker Hughes have said they will not work on Sea Lion, and Halliburton said the authorities raised criminal and civil enforcement with it.

The analysis distinguishes between making rules and enforcing them. Argentina can deny permits and benefits and sanction those under its jurisdiction, but it cannot exercise coercive authority in the archipelago or another state without an independent legal basis or that country's cooperation. For companies with no ties to Argentina, the risk is mainly reputational or commercial.

None of these measures resolves the underlying question. “Falkland licences cannot establish British title to the islands, and Argentine administrative resolutions cannot establish Argentine title,” the author concludes. The United Kingdom maintains that the activity is legitimate and governed by the archipelago's legislation in accordance with international law; Argentina maintains its sovereignty claim and holds that the licences are invalid.

World.title: What could happen when Argentina's Sea Lion ultimatum to the UK expires
World.content:
What could happen when Argentina's Sea Lion ultimatum to the UK expires

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:18 UTC Full article

Milei ordered on September 28 the start of arbitration and said that, if London does not act, Argentina will seek provisional measures from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea

The two-week deadline Argentina gave the United Kingdom to halt the Sea Lion oil project in the North Falklands basin expires around October 12. Its expiry will not in itself suspend the project or establish a British breach of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, according to a legal analysis published by specialist site Diplomacy & Law.

President Javier Milei ordered on September 28 the start of arbitration under Annex VII of the convention and said that, if London does not act, Argentina will seek provisional measures from the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. The analysis's author, Edmarverson A. Santos, stresses that the deadline was set by Argentina and does not derive from the convention, and that the government's instruction and the formal start of proceedings are separate steps: arbitration begins with written notification to the other state, accompanied by the claim and its grounds. There is no record that this has been sent.

The Annex VII route reflects both countries' choices. Under Article 287 of the convention, Argentina chose the Hamburg tribunal as its first preference and the United Kingdom the International Court of Justice; where the parties do not coincide, the dispute goes to arbitration. Beforehand, Article 283 requires an exchange of views on how to settle the dispute, something a tribunal would have to assess.

If Argentina seeks provisional measures, the Hamburg tribunal could order them while the arbitral tribunal is being constituted, provided it considers that the latter would have prima facie jurisdiction and that the matter is urgent. Such measures would be provisional, not a ruling on sovereignty or the merits.

The main obstacle is jurisdiction. Convention tribunals can only rule on its interpretation or application, not on territorial title. In the 2015 arbitration between Mauritius and the United Kingdom over the Chagos Islands, the tribunal declined to rule on a claim whose real subject was sovereignty; in the 2020 case between Ukraine and Russia, it excluded claims requiring a decision on Crimea, though proceedings continued on the rest. In addition, both countries have made declarations under Article 298: Argentina excluded maritime delimitation disputes, among others, in 1995, and the United Kingdom made exclusions in 2003 and, according to the analysis, again in 2020.

“Argentina would need to formulate claims capable of adjudication under UNCLOS without requiring the tribunal to decide, expressly or implicitly, sovereignty over the Falkland Islands,” the author concludes.

The United Kingdom rejected the arbitration on September 30 and maintains that the activity is governed by the archipelago's legislation in accordance with international law. Sea Lion, developed by Navitas and Rockhopper, has had a final investment decision since December 2025.

World.title: Flávio Bolsonaro proposes constitutional reform to overhaul the courts and lower the criminal age
World.content:
Flávio Bolsonaro proposes constitutional reform to overhaul the courts and lower the criminal age

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:10 UTC Full article

The candidate said he intended to use his party's legislative weight to choose the presiding officers of both chambers and “amend the Constitution, to redemocratise the country”

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who will face Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil's presidential runoff on October 25, has said that if he wins he will use his Liberal Party's congressional bloc to push a constitutional reform that would change the judiciary, lower the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 and abolish presidential re-election.

On Tuesday, at an event in Goiânia, the candidate said he intended to use his party's legislative weight to choose the presiding officers of both chambers and “amend the Constitution, to redemocratise the country, so that institutions once again respect the Constitution”. Amid concern over the remark, he set out the scope of the reform in Brasília on Wednesday and responded to those fearing an authoritarian turn: “I've seen people saying that now, with a majority, Flávio will do what his father didn't. Stop that. Let's come back down to the real world.” His father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup.

A constitutional amendment in Brazil requires three fifths of each chamber in two votes: 308 of 513 deputies and 49 of 81 senators. According to the newspaper El País, the Liberal Party won 121 seats in the Chamber of Deputies on Sunday, 20% more than in 2022, and with its allies would hold around 50 in the Senate. Those elected include the former president's wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, and his son Carlos, as senators.

Bolsonaro this week won the backing of two first-round candidates. Ronaldo Caiado, a former governor of Goiás who won around 2.2% of the vote, endorsed him at the Goiânia event: “I'm here to defeat the PT.” Former Minas Gerais governor Romeu Zema, with less than 1%, did so on Monday. São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas, re-elected on Sunday, also attended.

Bolsonaro, who won 47% of valid votes to Lula's 45%, had already announced on Monday plans to cut the number of ministries and appoint at least four Supreme Federal Court justices. Lula held no public events on Monday or Tuesday and met his campaign team in Brasília, which has said the president will seek direct confrontation in the runoff.

World.title: Stuart Lawrence, for three decades a captain of Britain's Antarctic ships, has died
World.content:
Stuart Lawrence, for three decades a captain of Britain's Antarctic ships, has died

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:07 UTC Full article

He was awarded the Polar Medal in 1983 and appointed MBE in 1998. He retired in 2003 after 33 Antarctic voyages and 42 years at sea, with a farewell from the Ernest Shackleton in Stanley

Captain Stuart Lawrence MBE, who for more than three decades commanded the British Antarctic Survey vessels RRS Bransfield and RRS Ernest Shackleton, has died suddenly, according to the National Coastwatch Institution in Gosport, southern England, where he served as a volunteer watchkeeper.

His calling began at the age of five in Grimsby, where he lived on the same street as a Cunard liner captain. He entered the HMS Conway training ship at 13 and spent his seventeenth birthday as a Canadian Pacific cadet. He was about to join the Royal National Lifeboat Institution when its head, Admiral Egg Irving, urged him instead to sail to the Antarctic. He joined the British Antarctic Survey in 1970 and remained until 2003.

After two voyages on the John Biscoe, he moved to the Bransfield, taking temporary command in 1972 and permanent command in 1974. He took her every year to Halley, the organisation's most southerly station, through the Weddell Sea. In 1984, the UK Antarctic Place-Names Committee named Lawrence Channel, on the Antarctic Peninsula, after him. From 1999 he commanded the Ernest Shackleton.

Days before the 1982 Argentine invasion, he hosted a reception on board in Stanley. He sailed on March 31 and, halfway to Tierra del Fuego, learned of the invasion from Patrick Watts' radio broadcasts and alerted the organisation's headquarters in Britain. By his own account, he later had to restrain part of the crew, who wanted to return and scuttle the ship at the entrance to Stanley Harbour.

Ships under his command were regular visitors to Montevideo on voyages to Stanley and Antarctica, according to those who sailed with him.

He was awarded the Polar Medal in 1983 and appointed MBE in 1998. He retired in 2003 after 33 Antarctic voyages and 42 years at sea, with a farewell from the Ernest Shackleton in Stanley. His wife, Sue, had died months earlier.

He later worked for the UK Hydrographic Office and as an ice master on cruise ships, and from 2017 volunteered at the Gosport coastwatch station. “A watch with Stuart would be one of professionally recording every detail and aspect of incidents at sea, interspersed with tales of the Antarctic and any number of anecdotes,” the institution wrote.

World.title: What was the world's largest penguin colony has lost nearly two thirds of its nests
World.content:
What was the world's largest penguin colony has lost nearly two thirds of its nests

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:54 UTC Full article

Photo: Nicole Richters

The chinstrap penguin population on Zavodovski Island, in the South Sandwich Islands, has fallen by almost two thirds since 2011, according to a study by the British Antarctic Survey. The island, described that year as the world's largest penguin colony, has lost that title.

Researchers recorded 63% fewer occupied nests in 2025 than in 2011. That year, the same organisation estimated that some 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nested on the island. For the new study, a team sailed for 15 days to Zavodovski, a volcanic island north of the Antarctic continent administered by the United Kingdom, and used drones, aerial photography, satellite imagery and tracking devices fitted to 20 birds.

According to the study's lead, Professor Norman Ratcliffe, the cause is ocean warming. “With waters warming, the krill the chinstrap penguins eat have moved southwards. Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food,” he said. The researchers believe the species may now qualify as officially endangered.

The team ruled out other explanations. The island's volcano, Mount Curry, last erupted significantly in 2016, while the decline has been steady since 2011. Nor do they attribute the fall to competition for krill from humpback whales, which in turn help boost krill production.

By contrast, the macaroni penguin population increased markedly. Tracking data show they forage in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where they are likely supplementing their diet with fish and other crustaceans. Ratcliffe described the shift as “the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica” and as “further evidence of how rapid warming is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems”.

The world's largest penguin colony is now at Cape Adare, in the Ross Sea, more than 5,000 kilometres away on the other side of the Antarctic continent.

The study comes days after Antarctic sea ice recorded its third-lowest winter maximum since satellite measurements began this year.

World.title: On the war's third anniversary, 5,600 children are waiting to be evacuated from Gaza
World.content:
On the war's third anniversary, 5,600 children are waiting to be evacuated from Gaza

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:53 UTC Full article

Some 5,600 children are waiting to be evacuated from Gaza for medical treatment, according to the territory's Hamas-run Health Ministry, as three years pass since the group's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which killed around 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage and triggered the war.

To leave the Strip, patients need a referral from the Health Ministry, acceptance by a host country and Israeli security clearance. Among those recently evacuated is Raseel, a six-year-old girl injured at the al-Mawasi displacement camp in July, who travelled to Egypt in late September with support from the World Health Organization. Witnesses attributed the strike to an Israeli helicopter; the Israeli military said it had no record of a strike at that time and place.

Doctors warn that antibiotic-resistant infections are complicating the recovery of the wounded. A study shared with the BBC World Service, based on almost 80,000 bacterial samples collected at 11 hospitals between 2015 and 2025, found widespread resistance to key antibiotics. It was carried out by Gaza-based researchers with support from Imperial College London and the American University of Beirut; it has not yet been peer-reviewed and its findings are preliminary. “We will see the number of amputations rise, even if the war stops,” said Awni al-Jaafarawi, a Médecins Sans Frontières doctor at Nasser hospital.

The researchers link the problem to the destruction of water and sanitation. According to the UN, almost 90% of that infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged, and more than 80% of families face water insecurity. Cogat, the Israeli body that manages access to Gaza, says the water supplied exceeds the UN humanitarian threshold and that medicines, including antibiotics, enter without restriction.

Gaza's Health Ministry puts the number of Palestinians killed since the war began at more than 74,000, and at 1,421 since the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025. Israel disputes the figures and says it acts to minimise harm to civilians.

World.title: FAO Food Price Index rises in September amid weather concerns and transport disruptions
World.content:
FAO Food Price Index rises in September amid weather concerns and transport disruptions

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:37 UTC Full article

The FAO Cereal Price Index increased by 5.1 percent from August, averaging 17.2 percent higher than its September 2025 level.

FAO’s benchmark measure of world food commodity prices increased in September, due mostly to transportation disruptions and weather concerns that constrained availability as well as to higher quotations for crop-based commodity groups, according to new data released by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).

The FAO Food Price Index, which tracks monthly changes in the international prices of a basket of globally-traded food commodities, averaged 136.0 points in September 2026, up 1.5 percent from August and 5.8 percent from a year ago.

“We are seeing a persistent and increasingly broad based build up in global commodity prices, as disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea combine with climate shocks, putting pressure on energy, transport and key food commodities,” said FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero. “If sustained, these pressures will soon pass through to consumer food prices, especially in food and energy import dependent countries.”

The FAO Cereal Price Index increased by 5.1 percent from August, averaging 17.2 percent higher than its September 2025 level. World wheat prices increased by 6.3 percent, due to logistical constraints in the Black Sea region and dry weather in parts of North America ahead of sowing, while global maize prices rose by 5.6 percent from the previous month due to concerns over yields in the United States of America, reduced export availability in Brazil and disruptions to Black Sea trade. Ongoing uncertainty over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz provided additional support to prices of biofuel feedstocks such as maize.

The FAO All Rice Price Index increased by 1.4 percent, as Indica quotations rose amid weather concerns and seasonally tighter supplies.

The FAO Vegetable Oil Price Index increased by 0.9 percent from August, reflecting higher world palm oil prices associated with strong global import demand and concerns over the impact of dry weather on production prospects in Southeast Asia.

The FAO Meat Price Index declined by 1.1 percent, as pig and poultry meat prices fell amid abundant exportable supplies. Brazil’s bovine meat export quotations increased, supported by stronger import demand by United States, while ovine meat prices remained largely stable.

The FAO Dairy Price Index dipped by 0.1 percent in September, as declines in cheese prices slightly offset increases in milk powder quotations, and butter prices changed little.

The FAO Sugar Price Index increased by 6.1 percent from August, driven by expectations of tighter global sugar supplies in the 2026/27 season. Contributing factors included lower expected sugar production in Thailand, concerns over crop prospects in India due to below-normal rainfall and strengthening El Niño conditions, heavy rains in Brazil’s Centre-South growing region, and a decline in the area planted to sugar beet in the European Union.

World.title: British Army exploring military working horses: US used them against Taliban and Russia in Ukraine
World.content:
British Army exploring military working horses: US used them against Taliban and Russia in Ukraine

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:37 UTC Full article

When you hear of horses being used in battle, you could be forgiven for thinking back to the First World War or even the Napoleonic era. However, the British Army, specifically The Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment (HCMR), is exploring how Military Working Horses could contribute to future operations.

“We are platform agnostic. Whether it's a Challenger 2 or a horse, it doesn't really matter,” says Lieutenant Colonel Ben McNeil, HCMR's Commanding Officer.

The regiment is taking inspiration from other armed forces around the world, including Russia. In an era where drones are ripping up the playbook of modern warfare, the need for a war horse may seem redundant, however they bring many benefits.

For starters, horses and mules are an effective way of moving troops and cargo across rugged terrain. They can also carry more weight and travel further distances than troops on foot, saving soldier energy for the fight.

Horses are also low-cost, low-maintenance and can be procured even in remote locations – all qualities an armored vehicle or tank does not possess.

One of the big advantages horses and mules can bring to the battlefield lies in their genetics. They have a surprisingly small heat signature, making them great at evading drone detection.

Lt Col McNeil added: “A horse in a forest is a normal context to be in, and that plays to our advantage versus an armored vehicle, which has a very mechanical profile to it and thermal profile with it, as well as sound.”

These advantages are why we've seen horses used by Russia in the Ukraine war for frontline logistics and transport where regular vehicles are vulnerable. Videos circulating online even show Russian soldiers attaching Starlink terminals to horses to get internet on the frontline.

“It shows the utility of them,” said Lt Col McNeil. “Whilst we give our soldiers the opportunity to do something different and they really enjoy it and are enthused by it, it could grow into a capability that the British Army could use in the future.”

Forces closer to home use horses too. “We're learning an awful lot. Our Spanish, our Italian, our German colleagues, our French colleagues in the Gendarmerie, are using them in all sorts of ways, whether that's in ground-holding roles or whether that's in more reconnaissance-related or resupply elements.

”It's about applying a platform, as we are platform-orientated soldiers, into the environment that works.”

Household Cavalry soldiers split their time between the Mounted Regiment – the ceremonial side in London, which involves escorting the King. Then there's the operational side, which involves carrying out reconnaissance in tanks and, eventually, the Ajax armored fighting vehicle, if all goes to plan.

Should these horses ever be used in war, there could come a time when the troopers would need to engage the enemy from the saddle (Picture: MOD)

You don't have to look as far back as you might think for examples of horses used in war. US special forces from Operational Detachment Alpha 595 were sent to the mountains of Afghanistan to fight successfully against the Taliban on horseback, just after the 9/11 attacks in 2001.

Their efforts were depicted in the Hollywood movie 12 Strong and America maintains a mounted capability today.

The first experiment for The Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment took place during their annual summer camp on Longmoor Training Area. Soldiers learned new skills like emergency first aid for horses and tested using camouflage nets on the animals.

As the experimentation continues, we could see the world-famous cavalry horses go from trotting up and down The Mall to finding enemy locations on military operations.

World.title: Jalisco governor announces water-rationing plan for Guadalajara amid contamination crisis
World.content:
Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus has announced a water-rationing plan for the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area (ZMG) amid growing concerns over citywide water contamination.

“The city is going through an unprecedented drinking water crisis,” Lemus said in a video posted on his official social media channels. “And like in any crisis, the first step is to acknowledge it in order to solve it.”

The temporary measure, expected to last approximately six months in its first stage, will involve withdrawing up to 2.5 cubic meters per second from the distribution network by no longer using water from the Las Pintas dam and the old Chapala system.

According to the newspaper La Jornada, water consumption in the ZMG stands at between 10 and 11.5 cubic meters per second, so the decrease would represent around a quarter of the supply.

Gov. Lemus acknowledged in his video announcement that the move means less water during the rehabilitation project — hence the rationing — but what flows will be cleaner.

The plan does not mean that homes will be without water for six consecutive months. Rather, service rotations, low-pressure episodes, and interruptions during one or two days are expected in the most affected areas.

Further details about how the program will operate will be announced by the Intermunicipal Potable Water and Sewerage System (SIAPA) and the municipalities on Oct. 12.

State Chief of Staff Alberto Esquer told the newspaper El Informador that authorities are analyzing the volume of water that can be distributed without drawing from the Las Pintas source. This calculation will make it possible to determine service rotations and conditions while the planned works are being carried out.

“We call on residents for patience; we are working on this, and we acknowledge the problem,” Esquer said.

Poor water quality affects at least 342 metropolitan neighborhoods. Lemus attributed the problem primarily to the aging Chapala supply system and illegal discharges into the Las Pintas canal, where the water coming from Chapala mixes with the drainage from the south of the city.

To restore the supply, authorities will fast-track the La Calera diversion aqueduct and the first phase of the expansion of Water Treatment Plant No. 1 one in Miravalle. They will also establish a permanent working group with metropolitan mayors to monitor water supply and quality.

As a long-term solution, Lemus proposed building a replacement Chapala–Guadalajara aqueduct, with an estimated completion time of two years. He added that President Claudia Sheinbaum agreed that the federal government would carry out and fund the outstanding works required for the El Zapotillo system to operate at full capacity.

Lemus said that the announced measures would not entail public debt, increases in SIAPA rates, or privatization of the water service.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: No Atlantic hurricanes hit Mexico throughout September. That’s not normal
World.content:
The eastern coast of Mexico made it through September without a hurricane as the Atlantic basin recorded its first hurricane-free September in more than three decades.

On the country’s Pacific side, however, the storms kept churning.

Through Wednesday, the Pacific basin — which stretches from the Americas westward to the International Date Line — had produced 20 named storms and nine hurricanes during a 2026 season that began May 15.

Three of those hurricanes reached Category 5: Hurricane Genevieve, well off Mexico’s Pacific coast in July; Hurricane Lowell, which formed in the Eastern Pacific in August and moved toward Hawaii; and Hurricane Polo, which pounded the Baja Peninsula and the Sonora coast in September.

Meanwhile, no Atlantic storm had reached hurricane strength through Oct. 1, although the current Tropical Storm Isaias could change that.

A major driver is a “super” El Niño creating exceptionally warm equatorial Pacific waters.

According to specialists at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), warmer water from the central equatorial Pacific is shifted by El Niño toward the northeastern Pacific off Mexico, providing more energy for cyclones to form and intensify. Plus, El Niño tends to reduce vertical wind shear in the eastern and central Pacific, making conditions more favorable for hurricanes.

In the Atlantic, El Niño tends to increase vertical wind shear — changes in wind speed or direction with altitude — which can tear apart developing storms.

The contrast was forecast months ago, when Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN) projected 18 to 21 tropical cyclones in the eastern Pacific and 11 to 15 in the Atlantic.

September further illustrated the contrast.

Historically the statistical peak of the Atlantic hurricane season, September was hurricane-free in the Atlantic for the first time since 1994.

The only other such Septembers since 1950 were in 1972 and 1962, according to Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach.

All of that being said, the 2026 Atlantic lull might be over.

Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the southwestern Gulf of Mexico, north of Veracruz and west of the Yucatán Peninsula, and was forecast to become the season’s first Atlantic hurricane. Its maximum sustained winds were charted at 45 mph at 9 a.m. Mexico City time Wednesday.

The National Hurricane Center (NHC) forecast Isaias to reach hurricane strength, with winds of at least 75 mph, early Thursday and peak early Friday at 110 mph, near the top of the Category 2 range.

Though increasing wind shear could weaken Isaias before landfall, the NHC expected it to reach the southern U.S. late Friday or early Saturday.

Before that, the storm could bring 5 to 10 centimeters (2 to 4 inches) of rain around the Bay of Campeche and the Yucatan Peninsula.

Both hurricane seasons run through Nov. 30.

With reports from El Horizonte, Smithsonian magazine, KABC and BBC

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: State competitiveness, electric scooter rules and SIAPA director scrutiny
World.content:
This week we look at where and how Jalisco’s competitiveness ranking has fallen in 2026 in relation to other states, what the new SIAPA director has been up to in lieu of briefing the state Congress, and long-awaited new rules for electric scooter riders.

Jalisco falls to 6th place in state competitiveness rankings

Jalisco is losing competitiveness in its ability to generate, attract and retain investment and talent, according to the recently released 2026 Urban Competitiveness Index (ICE).

Prepared by the Mexican Institute for Competitiveness (IMCO), the ICE study ranks all 32 Mexican states for competitiveness, based on 53 indicators across six categories.

In 2026, Jalisco fell two spots to 6th place, down from 4th in the 2025 study. The state’s worst performance came in Political System and Government, at 16th out of 32 states (falling from 9th last year). Jalisco also did poorly in Law, ranking 15th, and Society and Environment, at 13th.

Weakness in the political system and government ranking this year is attributable to the public’s declining confidence in the public sector, with 86% of state residents believing that corruption is “frequent” or “very frequent” in Jalisco.

Another factor negatively impacting Jalisco’s competitiveness ranking this year is its poor performance in the Legal category — ranking 29th out of 32. Relative to other states, Jalisco’s notarial services are very limited, with only 1.3 notaries per 100,000 inhabitants.

Finally, Jalisco also underperformed in the Perception of Security indicator, ranking 18th. In 2026, the study found that only 21.5% of state residents over the age of 18 feel safe living here.

Offsetting these shortcomings, Jalisco performed well in its ability to develop and attract skilled labor, improving to 3rd place from 8th last year, and in economic innovation, where it ranked 3rd in 2026.

Commenting on Jalisco’s performance, Israel Macías López, an economics professor at the Pan-American University, told El Mural that the state cannot rely solely on its economic strengths any longer, adding, “This ultimately serves as a wake-up call for the state government.”

The top five states in the 2026 ICE rankings are Mexico City, Querétaro, Nuevo León, Coahuila and Baja California Sur, in that order. A year ago, the top five were Mexico City, Baja California Sur, Nuevo León, Jalisco and Aguascalientes.

With reporting from El Mural.

New regulations approved for e-scooter riders in Guadalajara

In recent years, walking or biking around the metropolitan area can sometimes feel like a death-defying maneuver, as scooter riders zoom every which way without warning. New regulations just passed by the Jalisco Congress seek to bring some order to the chaos.

A motion sponsored by two legislators of the Movimiento Ciudadano party, Alejandra Giadans and Mónica Magaña, passed with 20 votes in favor, 14 against, and one abstention.

The new law bans scooters from sidewalks as well as main avenues, tunnels, bridges and overpasses across the city, where traffic speeds exceed 50 km per hour. Scooter usage will now be limited to bike paths at speeds not to exceed 25 km per hour. In pedestrian zones, scooter users will be required to walk with the device instead of riding it.

According to Magaña, “This initiative incorporates elements to promote a cultural transformation towards a more humane and inclusive city, where the protection and safety of all people is a priority, considering pedestrians as the most vulnerable users.”

Each municipality covered by the new law will be responsible for defining penalties for the misuse of scooters in their jurisdiction. They now have a six-month window to adapt their local transit rules to the new law, with full enforcement expected to begin sometime next year.

With reporting from El Informador.

SIAPA’s new director yet to address Congress after 6 months on the job

Miguel de la Rosa Figueroa, leader of the Morena caucus, and deputy Mariana Casillas Guerrero, who oversees the Planning, Territorial Organization and Water Management Commission of the Congress, late last month called on State Water Ministry (SIAPA) Director Ismael Jáuregui Castañeda to attend a hearing before the Congress of Jalisco to talk about water quality issues and the agency’s plans to address them.

Jáuregui has been at the helm of the embattled water agency for almost six months and has yet to appear, despite numerous invitations from state legislators.

For his part, in a letter to Congress, Jáuregui cited the need to prioritize pressing hydraulic projects — such as work to overhaul the La Calera system and Miravalle Water Treatment Plant — over attending meetings with state officials. He has also indicated he would appear before the legislature only after Governor Pablo Lemus submitted a formal request for SIAPA’s new budget.

While Jáuregui clearly has his hands full, lawmakers’ frustrations are beginning to mount. Opposition groups have characterized his failure to appear as an act of disrespect and defiance in the face of the water quality crisis affecting Guadalajara.

With reporting from the University of Guadalajara press.

World.title: Latest Citi poll of Mexico-based analysts sees weakened peso through 2027
World.content:
The “super peso” that strengthened the Mexican currency’s exchange rate to under 17 per dollar for more than a week in late August and early September won’t be returning any time soon, according to the Citi Survey of Expectations published on Tuesday.

The prevailing opinion of the Mexico-based analysts consulted is that the peso will trade at 18 pesos per dollar at the end of 2026, a half peso weaker than was suggested in the early September Citi forecast, published at the height of the super peso. It is seen weakening further to 18.50 by the end of 2027, although some of the survey responders see it approaching 20 to the dollar.

If proof is needed that economics is not an exact science, one can note that predictions from the consulted institutions range from 16.80 to 18.80 pesos per dollar by the end of the year. Several financial institutions, including Barclays, BNP Paribas, Bx+, Citi, Bank of America, Santander México, and Itaú BBA, expect a more favorable outcome, while Masari Casa de Bolsa and Bankaool expect the peso to depreciate more quickly.

The analysts mainly agree on the peso weakening even further against the dollar in 2027, but not on how much.

“By the end of 2027, the consensus expects the exchange rate to be at 18.50 pesos per dollar, down from 18 pesos per dollar two weeks ago, with expectations ranging from 17.00 to 19.80,” the Citi Survey stated.

On Sept. 4, the peso traded at 16.89 pesos per dollar before depreciating throughout the rest of September, finally inching above 18 after losing 46 centavos against the dollar between September 28 and October 2. During September, the peso was the worst-performing currency against the dollar, falling 6%.

The dollar fell back under 18 pesos on Tuesday, but most analysts don’t foresee the peso remaining so strong, amid heightened global risk aversion and concerns about inflation and interest-rate differentials.

In the survey, 25 of 37 respondents said they expect the Bank of Mexico’s interest rate to remain at 6.5% through the end of 2027, a major factor in the pessimistic prognosis of the peso’s value.

Minutes from the U.S. Federal Reserve’s latest policy meeting, due Wednesday, could provide greater insight into interest rates and the U.S. central bank’s policy plans, informing future forecasts.

With reports from El Financiero, Informador and Reuters

World.title: Mexico’s trade surplus with the United States is up more than 20% this year
World.content:
Mexico’s trade surplus with the United States increased more than 20% year over year in the first eight months of 2026, climbing to almost US $156 billion as Mexican exports to the U.S. reached a record high.

The U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis reported Tuesday that Mexico’s exports to the United States totaled $419.34 billion between January and August, while its imports from the U.S. were worth $263.47 billion.

Mexico thus recorded a trade surplus of $155.87 billion, an increase of 21.2% compared to its surplus with the U.S. in the first eight months of 2025. In August, Mexico recorded a trade surplus of almost $27 billion with its northern neighbor.

Of all countries around the world, Mexico recorded the second-highest surplus with the U.S. between January and August, behind Vietnam.

According to the Bank of Canada, “[a] trade deficit is not necessarily bad, and a trade surplus is not necessarily good.”

In Mexico’s case, a large and growing trade surplus with the United States is arguably not desirable at a time when the Mexican government is seeking to reach a trade deal with the Trump administration, which in July announced that it had decided against renewing the USMCA free trade pact in its current form. U.S. President Donald Trump frequently rails against the United States’ deficits with Mexico and other countries, saying last month, “We lose with Mexico $195 billion a year.”

He has even said that Mexico and Canada should become U.S. states given that the United States runs large deficits with the two countries.

Mexico’s exports to US surge 18% between January and August

Mexico shipped goods worth a record high $419.34 billion to the U.S. in the first eight months of 2026, an increase of 18.3% compared to the same period of last year. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. in August were worth $60.63 billion, a record for any month and a 34.2% year-over-year increase.

Mexico remained the largest exporter to the United States in the first eight months of 2026, taking a 17.4% share of the U.S. $2.41 trillion import market in the period.

Mexico’s share of the market increased 2.1 percentage points compared to the first eight months of 2025. Most Mexican exports enter the United States tariff-free as the USMCA remains in effect, despite the U.S. government’s decision not to renew the trilateral pact for an additional 16 years. However, some important Mexican exports — including vehicles, steel and aluminum — do face tariffs when entering the U.S.

Mexico’s export revenue and share of the U.S. import market has increased as Mexican exporters ship much larger quantities of tech products, including AI servers, to the United States to support that country’s data center boom. Such products typically have low levels of Mexican value added as much of their content is imported, especially from Asia.

Still, the increase in Mexican — if not wholly “Made in Mexico” — exports to the U.S. has allowed Mexico to further consolidate its position as the top exporter to the world’s largest economy.

Canada’s share of the U.S. import market remained broadly steady at around 11.2% in the first eight months of 2026, while China’s share fell to 7.6% from 9.5% between January and August 2025. Canada and China are the second and third largest exporters to the United States.

Mexico’s imports from US increase 16.6% in first 8 months of 2026

Mexico imported U.S. goods worth $263.47 billion in the first eight months of 2026, an increase of 16.6% compared to the same period of last year. In August, Mexico imported U.S. goods worth $33.65 billion, a 15.3% increase compared to the same month of 2025.

Mexico was the world’s largest importer of U.S. goods in the January-August period, receiving 16% of all U.S. exports (based on their value).

Canada was the second largest importer of U.S. goods in the first eight months of the year, receiving 14.4% of all U.S. exports (by value).

Mexico-US trade accounts for around 1/6 of total US trade

Two-way trade between Mexico and the United States totaled $681.82 billion in the first eight months of 2026, accounting for 16.8% of total U.S. trade with all countries around the world. Mexico was easily the United States’ largest trade partner in the period.

The United States’ second largest trade partner between January and August was Canada, with trade between the North American neighbors worth $505.61 billion. That amount is equivalent to 12.5% of all U.S. trade in the period, which totaled $4.05 trillion.

The United States spent $2.41 trillion on imports between January and August, while U.S. exports were worth $1.64 trillion. Consequently, the U.S. recorded a trade deficit of $773.93 billion.

Mexico recorded a trade surplus of $9.86 billion between January and August, according to data published by the national statistics agency INEGI last week.

With reports from El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: El Jalapeño: Bomb squad heroically ‘defuses’ suspicious churros found on Mexico City Metro
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Emergency protocol gave way to quick-thinking heroism on Metro Line 7 Friday afternoon after elite bomb disposal units successfully neutralized a highly volatile cardboard box containing dozens of freshly fried, cinnamon-sugar-dusted churros.

The high-stakes incident began when an alert commuter flagged an unattended package sitting isolated on a southbound train traveling from El Rosario toward Barranca del Muerto. Within minutes, officers from Mexico City’s Policía Bancaria e Industrial (PBI) established a safety perimeter at the Mixcoac station, donning heavy protective gear to approach what tactical analysts classified as an imminent threat to local waistlines.

“Initial field assessments indicated a dangerous combination of crispy exteriors, soft doughy interiors, and a dusting of sugar that presented a clear and present hazard,” said lead bomb technician Commander Arturo Gómez, wiping a trace of cajeta filling from his chin during a press briefing. “Standard procedure dictates controlled detonation, but given the golden-brown quality of the target, our team made the tactical decision to neutralize the threat orally, piece by piece.”

Witnesses reported that the multi-stage defusal operation took approximately six minutes, with officers systematically consuming the pastries alongside small tactical cups of warm champurrado supplied by a nearby platform vendor. According to official police logs, all units involved displayed exemplary discipline, ensuring that not a single drop of chocolate sauce was left on the train car floor.

Metro authorities praised the rapid response, citing it as a testament to the department’s unwavering commitment to public safety and street-food preservation. Officials confirmed that while the owner of the box was not located, the vendor’s lost inventory had been thoroughly and safely processed and deemed entirely non-lethal, albeit slightly heavy on the digestion.

“In operations of this nature, every second counts before the dough loses its crunch,” Gómez added, adjusting his tactical vest. “We urge the public to remain vigilant, report any suspicious, freshly baked goods immediately, and allow trained professionals to handle the situation before the churros go cold.”
