World.title: Rebeca Grynspan Leads UN Secretary-General Vote for Fourth Time
World.content:
Former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan on Wednesday topped a United Nations Security Council “straw poll” for the fourth time in the race to become the next UN secretary-general, according to a diplomatic source. Uncertainty remains over the outcome, however, because the possibility that a major power could veto her candidacy has not been ruled out in the complex and opaque process used to select the future head of an organization increasingly strained by divisions among its members.

Four women and three men are currently seeking to succeed Portugal’s António Guterres, 77, who will complete his second five-year term as UN secretary-general on December 31. During Wednesday’s closed-door vote, the 15 members of the Security Council anonymously assigned each candidate one of three ratings: “encourage,” “discourage” or “no opinion.”

According to a diplomatic source, Grynspan finished first with nine “encourage” votes, six “discourage” votes and no “no opinion” votes. It was the fourth time she has led the field in five straw polls held since July. Her showing, however, was weaker than in a previous vote held on September 29, when she received 10 “encourage” votes, three “discourage” votes and two “no opinion” votes.

Most importantly, a single opposing vote from one of the Security Council’s five permanent members would be enough to derail her candidacy. Because the straw polls are anonymous, it is not known whether one or more of those countries — France, the United Kingdom, Russia, China and the United States — were among the six members that voted to “discourage” her candidacy.

Later in the process, color-coded ballots will reveal whether any permanent member intends to use its veto. That next round of voting could take place before the end of the month, according to several diplomatic sources. It also remains entirely possible that another candidate could enter the race.

“In 1995, Kofi Annan was not a candidate, and he appeared one day before he was elected,” one diplomatic source noted. Grynspan, 70, recently stepped aside from her leadership role at the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, or UNCTAD, which she had headed for slightly more than four years, in order to campaign for the secretary-general post.

Finishing behind her in Wednesday’s vote was Rafael Grossi of Argentina, the current director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, who received six “encourage” votes, seven “discourage” votes and two “no opinion” votes. He was followed by Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, a former foreign minister of Guyana, who received five “encourage” votes, nine “discourage” votes and one “no opinion” vote.

Unless there is a significant shift, Rodrigues-Birkett’s chances of being selected appear to be fading as opposition to her candidacy grows.

World.title: Costa Rica Opens Probe Into Political Ties of Man Wanted by US DEA
World.content:
Costa Rica’s attorney general will investigate whether a naturalized Costa Rican detained for extradition to the United States had political ties or helped finance last February’s presidential campaign, after he was photographed at President Laura Fernández’s election-night celebration.

Guobin Tam Zhang, 54, who also uses the name Juan Carlos Tam Cheong, was detained Oct. 2 in Granadilla de Curridabat at the request of the U.S. government. He is sought by the United States in connection with alleged international drug trafficking, and Costa Rican prosecutors say he also faces a local investigation for alleged money laundering.

The Ministry of Public Security described Tam as one of the main launderers of drug-trafficking proceeds here. According to the ministry, he allegedly coordinated cocaine shipments bound for the United States and then handled payments for those shipments on behalf of the cartels involved.

The arrest was carried out jointly by the Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Drug Control Police, the Fuerza Pública, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the U.S. Treasury Department.

On Monday, the San José Criminal Court ordered two months of provisional detention while the extradition request proceeds, according to Tam’s lawyer, Moisés Chinchilla. Chinchilla said the court informed his client of the DEA file during the hearing, and that the United States must still submit formal documentation and the evidence supporting its request.

The same day, the Ministry of Justice and Peace ordered Tam into the prison system’s high-containment circuit. The ministry said he met the criteria because of his alleged links to criminal structures, and that he will be held in an individual cell with controls on his visits, calls, contacts and personal belongings.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said Monday that prosecutors will open an investigation on their own initiative into any political relationships Tam may have had, with a focus on money laundering and possible illegal campaign financing. Díaz said prosecutors will first await a report from the Supreme Elections Tribunal’s department that oversees political party financing.

Díaz said Costa Rica will prioritize sending Tam to the United States, applying a prosecutorial discretion rule that suspends local cases against an extraditable defendant. He said, however, that anyone found to have assisted Tam, including front men, corrupt officials or party representatives who knowingly accepted illegal money, would face investigation.

The attorney general also said a judge has authorized prosecutors to open five electronic devices seized from Tam, four of them cellphones, and that any evidence of crimes by other people would lead to new cases. Díaz linked the arrest to the second phase of a joint strategy with the DEA aimed at what he calls invisible narcos, people who would not be identified as possible traffickers without an investigation.

The case turned political after a photograph circulated showing Tam beside Pilar Cisneros, a former lawmaker who now advises the presidency on communications, at the Feb. 1 event at the Aurola hotel in San José where Fernández received the election results. Local reports say Tam was inside rooms reserved for campaign staff, party leaders and invited guests. The mother of two of Tam’s children also attended and was photographed with Fernández, according to those reports.

Fernández said Monday that she does not know Tam, has never met with him and does not know what he does for a living. Cisneros said she does not know him either and that many people approached her for photographs that night.

The two have given differing accounts of the photograph itself. Speaking yesterday in Mora, Fernández said she did not know whether the image circulating of Tam with Cisneros was authentic, adding that about 2,000 people attended the celebration and she did not know all of them. Cisneros, however, has confirmed that the photograph is genuine and was taken that night at the Aurola, while maintaining that she has never spoken with Tam.

The ruling Pueblo Soberano party issued a certification from its treasurer, Raúl Zamora, stating that party records show no donations, contracts, transfers or other transactions involving Tam under any of the names he uses. Party president Mayuli Ortega said neither she nor the party has any relationship with him, and secretary general Freddy González said Tam was not on the party’s guest list for the celebration.

Opposition lawmakers have demanded further explanations. Liberación Nacional legislator Marco Badilla said the Legislative Assembly’s Security and Drug Trafficking Commission will examine the case, and fellow party legislator Víctor Hidalgo formally asked the presidency whether Tam was invited to the May 8 transfer of power or has visited executive branch offices.

Frente Amplio leader José María Villalta called on the government and the party to explain Tam’s presence at official events, while Claudia Dobles, head of the Coalición Agenda Ciudadana caucus, asked the Supreme Elections Tribunal to examine campaign financing. Pueblo Soberano caucus leader Nogui Acosta questioned whether the Legislative Assembly should investigate, saying the faction has no relationship with Tam.

In a sworn statement dated Aug. 4, 2025, Tam declared that all his income came from lawful activities, mainly the rental of commercial premises and homes on properties he represents or manages. Public records reviewed by local media show no properties registered in his name or in companies where he sits on the board.

Tam has not been convicted of any crime. His case is one of a series of U.S. extradition requests Costa Rica has handled this year in connection with drug investigations, including the 24 requests under review as of August and the prosecution of former magistrate Celso Gamboa in Texas.

World.title: International News: Trump Administration proposes $70,000 fee for International students seeking work training
World.content:
International News: Trump Administration proposes $70,000 fee for International students seeking work training

By Zoila Palma: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed requiring international students to pay as much as $70,000 for work training authorization in the United States, in the latest move by the Trump administration to tighten restrictions on foreign visa holders.

The proposal was outlined in a government notice published Wednesday, Reuters report.

Under the proposed rules, students holding F-1 visas would be required to pay $70,000 to a certified institution for Optional Practical Training (OPT), which allows eligible international students to gain work experience related to their studies. An additional $30,000 fee would reportedly apply for further work training. Students currently pay about $500 to participate in the program.

DHS said the proposed fees are intended to combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system and protect American workers.

OPT allows eligible foreign students to work up to 20 hours per week while school is in session and for a limited period after graduation, with additional opportunities available to graduates in science, technology, engineering and mathematics fields.

The proposal could face legal challenges and comes as the administration also targets the H-1B visa program, which has long provided a pathway for highly skilled foreign graduates to work in the US.

World.title: Belize Defence Force celebrates Taiwan’s National Day with cultural event
World.content:
Belize Defence Force celebrates Taiwan’s National Day with cultural event

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Defence Force (BDF) celebrated Taiwan’s National Day with a cultural exchange event aimed at promoting greater understanding of Taiwanese traditions and daily life.

The event was hosted by Mandarin teacherYi-Ying Hsiao, with BDF Commander Brigadier General Anthony Velasquez also in attendance.

The event featured cultural presentations that introduced participants to various aspects of Taiwan, including its cuisine, night markets, religious traditions, population and everyday life. The presentations provided students with an opportunity to learn more about Taiwan’s culture and heritage.

A highlight of the celebration was the Taiwan Night Market Challenge, which featured traditional activities such as spinning tops, stilt walking and marble games. After participating in the challenges, students enjoyed popular Taiwanese foods and refreshments, including dumplings, zongzi and bubble tea.

The celebration provided an opportunity for participants to experience Taiwanese culture through interactive activities, food and learning.

World.title: Mile 8 man accused of assaulting police inspector granted bail as daughter alleges harassment
World.content:
Mile 8 man accused of assaulting police inspector granted bail as daughter alleges harassment

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 47-year-old maintenance worker from Mile 8 has been granted bail after pleading not guilty to aggravated assault and threat of death charges involving a police inspector, while his daughter has accused the officer of repeatedly harassing her father.

David Funes, also known as “Bonna,” appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in Belize City on Wednesday, charged in connection with an October 1 incident involving a police inspector who is attached to the Mahogany Heights Sub-Police Station.

According to court allegations, the inspector was performing special duties at CK’s Shop in the Mile 8 community around 7 p.m. when he encountered Funes, who was reportedly drinking a beer outside the establishment.

The inspector alleges that after telling Funes he could not remain at the location, Funes threatened him, saying, “Nuh because you dah police I fraid feh you. You wah dead.”

A physical confrontation reportedly followed, during which Funes allegedly pushed the officer in the chest. The inspector said he grabbed Funes, and a struggle ensued before Funes fell, got up and walked away.

During Wednesday’s arraignment, Funes’ daughter addressed the court, alleging that the inspector had been harassing her father following a previous court case that was dismissed. She claimed the officer had even attempted to prevent her father from visiting the neighbourhood shop, despite the shopkeeper having no objection to his presence.

She also informed the court that her father has a history of mental health difficulties and had previously been prescribed medication. She said she had requested his medical records but was advised they would take approximately one week to obtain.

The Chief Magistrate urged her to secure those records as soon as possible to help the court understand Funes’ condition and determine how to proceed with his case.

Funes was offered bail of $800 plus one surety of the same amount, with no additional conditions imposed. His daughter was advised that she could sign as his surety but would be responsible for ensuring his attendance at subsequent court hearings.

The matter was adjourned until December 14, 2026.

World.title: No more Area Rep visits: New portal opens online access to Education assistance
World.content:
No more Area Rep visits: New portal opens online access to Education assistance

By Zoila Palma: On October 6, 2026, Prime Minister John Briceño said that the government has introduced a new online portal for educational assistance, allowing students and families to apply for support based on need without having to visit their Area Representative.

The PM said that this is part of his administration’s efforts to put more money in the pockets of Belizean families through measures including free education and education assistance programmes.

Briceño said approximately 80 percent of students at the high school and University of Belize levels receive some form of assistance.

“Minister Fonseca set up a portal for educational assistance so you can apply and get assistance through that portal based on need. So, now you don’t have to go to your area rep for assistance,” Briceño said.

The new system represents a shift from a longstanding practice in which families would visit the offices of their respective Area Representatives to request educational assistance.

Through the portal, families can instead submit applications directly for consideration based on their needs.

World.title: World Food Programme concerned that record-strong El Niño could push millions deeper into hunger
World.content:
World Food Programme concerned that record-strong El Niño could push millions deeper into hunger

By Zoila Palma: The World Food Programme (WFP) is warning that the intensifying 2026-27 El Niño could worsen global hunger and food insecurity, with as many as 49 million people potentially pushed into acute hunger.

WFP climate expert Richard Choularton said the current forecasts suggest the El Niño could become the strongest on record, bringing more intense and widespread droughts, floods and storms.

Choularton said initial impacts have already been seen in Central America and Africa’s Sahel region.

In Central America, severe drought during the early growing season caused farmers to lose crops or experience lower yields, with the effects extending beyond agriculture as farmers reduce planting, investment and labour hiring.

WFP estimates that Latin America and the Caribbean, along with large parts of Africa and Asia and the Pacific, could face some of the greatest impacts.

Choularton said he is particularly concerned about countries already facing severe hunger crises, such as Somalia, as well as vulnerable countries in Southern Africa that are still recovering from previous El Niño-related droughts.

He also warned that disruptions to major global trade routes, including the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Black Sea, are contributing to higher food, fuel and fertilizer prices, potentially worsening the effects of drought and reducing agricultural production and incomes.

The WFP is using anticipatory action to help communities prepare before extreme weather strikes, including early warnings, disaster risk financing and community preparedness programmes.

World.title: Stakeholders review proposal to strengthen Belize’s Climate Resilience
World.content:
Stakeholders review proposal to strengthen Belize’s Climate Resilience

By Zoila Palma: The Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT), Belize’s accredited entity for the Green Climate Fund, brought together key stakeholders in Belmopan on October 6, 2026, for a Review and Validation Workshop on a proposed project aimed at strengthening Belize’s climate resilience.

The workshop focused on reviewing and validating the first draft of a funding proposal titled “Strengthening the Belize National Protected Area System (BNPAS) to Provide Resilience and Reduce Vulnerability of Communities against Climate Change.”

Participants examined the proposed project components, outputs and activities as part of the ongoing project development process.

The session included representatives from the Association of Protected Areas Management Organizations, the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management, and the Ministry of Blue Economy and Marine Conservation.

World.title: Team Belize to compete at Dakar 2026 Summer Youth Olympic Games
World.content:
Team Belize to compete at Dakar 2026 Summer Youth Olympic Games

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association (BOCGA) has announced the athletes and officials who will represent Belize at the 4th Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, in 2026.

The Games will bring together young athletes from around the world for a celebration of sport, culture, friendship and the Olympic spirit.

Belize’s delegation will feature two young athletes: Melody Gabourel of Corozalito Village, who will compete in the women’s shot put, and Jaaden Williams of Punta Gorda, who will compete in the men’s triple jump.

The delegation will be led by Chef de Mission Herman Pastor Jr., with Shelmadine Carr serving as Team Official.

Gabourel and Williams were selected by the Belize Athletic Association (BAA) in accordance with the International Olympic Committee’s participation criteria for Belize. The criteria require athletes to meet the under-18 age requirement, include one male and one female athlete in the delegation, and compete in the disciplines allocated to Belize.

Team Belize is scheduled to depart Belize on October 29, 2026, and return on November 14, 2026.

World.title: Time to grow more food and to eat more of what we grow
World.content:
Time to grow more food and to eat more of what we grow

By Hugh O’Brien: The issue with ANY PROBLEM WE HAVE IN BELIZE, including INFLATION and the COST OF LIVING, amongst others, is that our culture is to look outside for solutions and not to marvel enough at our individual resilience. As a people, we look 1st to the International Community for solutions, 2nd to the Government, 3rd to our Area Representatives, City or Town Councils, 4th to our community, friends and neighbours, 5th to our family, and last to each of OURSELVES.

Within ourselves lie the solutions, as when we change and make decisions, we influence our family and friends, then we influence our community, then eventually our approach to local government and national government and ultimately the international way of life.

‘WE CANNOT EXPECT THE CHANGE IN OTHERS THAT WE OURSELVES ARE UNWILLING TO MAKE AND LIVE BY.”

Food prices have risen sharply over the last 5-10 years, and the sad news is that food prices are expected to continue to increase in the next 5 to 10 years – Let’s begin to plant and eat a little more healthy callaloo, chaya, okra, spinach, sweet potato, habanero pepper, leafy onion or chives, cilantro etc in our backyard, and for those living in the villages, let’s plant and consume more coconuts, papaya, banana, plantains, limes, avocado, breadfruit, golden plum, bluggoe, cocoyams, cassava, etc. and grow more local chickens, eggs, a lil sheep or goat here and there etc.

The photo below shows a health patch of callaloo being grown in the yard of a villager in the Cayo District.

World.title: Rent row retreat
World.content:
The Digicel headquarters building in downtown Kingston where the Government has leased space for the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority. (Photo: Observer file)

PRIME Minister Dr Andrew Holness has announced that the Government will initially limit the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) to one floor of the Digicel building, cutting the amount of office space originally planned for the agency following public outrage over the roughly $115-million annual rental cost of its headquarters.

But in an immediate response to the Jamaica Observer on Wednesday, Opposition spokesman on finance Julian Robinson rejected the Government’s decision, saying it did not go far enough.

“My view is that it’s not good enough. I think the lease must be cancelled fully and the Government must find existing office space. The Government has hundreds of thousands of square feet of office space around the country. A lot of it is not being fully utilised and they must use space that exists instead of renting space. There’s no justification for that in this climate,” Robinson said.

He also dismissed the Government’s argument that NaRRA needs a disaster-resilient building to carry out its work, questioning whether that requirement falls within the authority’s mandate.

“Jamaica is in the worst fiscal position we have been in for about 10 years. We are $31 billion below budget. Our borrowing is almost $70 billion more than projected. There are people who are living in Westmoreland, St Elizabeth, and St James and they’re under tarpaulin, and we’re going to spend their money to lease an office and we don’t even reach the cost of NaRRA in terms of staff and all of that. Madness!” he said.

Holness, on Wednesday, said the move is intended to reduce the immediate cost of establishing NaRRA, while allowing the authority to begin its work with a smaller operation.

“Instead of doing the two floors where you would roll out the organisation as quickly as you can, we’ll start with one floor, and people there will have to double up and work fast and earn the credit of the trust,” Holness said during an Office of the Prime Minister retreat at Terra Nova hotel in St Andrew.

The decision follows public backlash over the cost of the five-year lease for NaRRA’s proposed headquarters at 14 Ocean Boulevard in downtown Kingston. The authority announced on Monday that the lease was based on a rate of US$26 per square foot, with an annual cost of US$725,972, equivalent to about $115 million.

The controversy has unfolded as thousands of Jamaicans remain in need of assistance following Hurricane Melissa — which demolished large sections of western Jamaica last October — including people awaiting roof grants and others still without shelter.

Holness said he understood why the cost of the lease had caused concern, particularly when placed alongside the outstanding needs of hurricane victims.

“The announcement of the lease is understandably met with concern. Because it could appear as if the Government is giving expenditure priority to the establishment of NaRRA versus paying the grants and taking care of persons who have not yet received any benefits from the Government or are now currently without shelter,” he said.

Holness maintained, however, that the decision to use the Digicel building was not based on comfort or luxury, but on the need for NaRRA to continue functioning during a disaster.

He said the authority, which is responsible for supporting Jamaica’s reconstruction and resilience efforts, needs headquarters that can withstand hurricanes and earthquakes, remain operational after a disaster, and accommodate its various functions in one location.

He said the Digicel building was originally designed for a utility company and was therefore built to support a high level of operational continuity.

Holness also defended the cost of the lease.

“The price of the building, you know, that is a market reality. When you look at where it fell in terms of the range, it’s average. In fact, before NaRRA could have engaged in the lease, my understanding is that it would have had to be reviewed by the National Land Agency,” he said.

He added that while he believed there could have been further negotiations, the Government ultimately had to reach an agreement because NaRRA needed to begin operating.

The prime minister said the greater concern now was not simply the rental cost, but the effect the controversy could have on public confidence in the new authority.

“I spent a lot of time this morning going through it with [NaRRA CEO] Ambassador [Antony] Anderson and the team, and we have decided to seek a review of the lease with the leasing company to revise the lease, and to also scale the staging of NaRRA,” Holness said.

He shared the Government had initially intended to move quickly with a full launch so that NaRRA could begin delivering projects as soon as possible. However, he said the controversy over the cost of the headquarters could become a distraction and weaken public support for the authority.

Meanwhile, Information Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon, speaking at the post-Cabinet press briefing, also on Wednesday, confirmed that the Government had instructed NaRRA to reduce the amount of space it will use.

She said the change could also mean that the authority hires fewer people at the start and takes longer to reach its intended level of operations.

“Having listened to the sentiments of Jamaicans, there would have been meetings between yesterday and this morning in terms of how to move forward. So the plan is wherever NaRRA is, it will be using less space. Right now it’s looking like it will still be in that same building, but scaling down the scope and the size of space that will be used,” she said.

Morris Dixon also addressed questions about why NaRRA could not use other Government space, including the building previously occupied by the Ministry of Legal and Constitutional Affairs on Fairway Avenue in St Andrew.

She said that the ministry had since been merged with the Ministry of Justice and that the former office space was no longer being used because of problems with the building.

“They had to come out of the lease for that specific space that you’re speaking to, and from my checks this morning, it had to do with issues of leaking in the building, and also significant electrical problems in the building,” Morris Dixon explained.

“So that staff is actually now being housed in a gym in the offices of the Ministry of Justice. So I always say you have to get your information from credible sources. This morning, I had to reach out to the Ministry of Justice to get an understanding of that because I saw that on social media. But that team is no longer in that building because that building was not suitable, even for the team that was there,” she added.

Morris Dixon also said original space requirements for NaRRA were based on an expected workforce of between 100 and 120 employees, along with engineers and consultants who would periodically come to Jamaica as part of reconstruction efforts.

For now, Holness said the Government’s priority was to reduce the immediate cost while ensuring that NaRRA could still begin its work.

“So the public can be assured that we are not wasting your funds. We hear what you say. We will cut it back. It will have an impact on how we will be able to deliver the things you actually want. But we understand that,” he said.

World.title: Enough of the absences
World.content:
PINNOCK... former head of Caribbean Maritime University

Clearly frustrated by disruptions caused by the repeated absence of a defence attorney, Justice Sanchia Burrell on Wednesday told co-accused Fritz Pinnock that he may have to cross-examine a witness himself if no legal representation is present for him when the delay-plagued Ruel Reid fraud trial resumes next Monday.

“I’m expecting that counsel will be here and that you will be assisted or represented in so far as proceedings are concerned. It may, however, be that you will have to apply those doctoral muscles and ask questions in cross-examination,” Burrell told Pinnock, former head of Caribbean Maritime University (CMU).

Pinnock was in the dock alongside his co-accused — Reid, the former education minister; his wife Sharen Reid and daughter Sharelle Reid; as well as Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence (Jamaica Labour Party, Brown’s Town Division).

The five are before the Half-Way-Tree Parish Court in the high-profile $25-million trial.

The judge’s comments followed the departure of a witness, who was placed on hold for the possibility of cross-examination by Pinnock’s attorney Hugh Wildman.

It was highlighted that at least two witnesses have now been deferred for cross-examination by the lawyer.

Burrell, in fielding the Crown’s concerns about the arrangement, maintained that the court could not defer every witness, noting that it impacts how the evidence flows and how the court is organised.

While she impressed upon Pinnock that she would be present to assist him, if necessary, reminding him that she is an independent arbiter, the judge made it clear she expected an attorney to be present to give him the representation he deserved.

“If not, Mr Pinnock, please come prepared to type or write and prepare cross-examination,” she said.

The directive followed statements made by Justice Burrell Wednesday morning about the way in which Wildman was communicating his absences to the court. She described it as piecemeal, disjointed communication that was unhelpful at best.

The trial had resumed Wednesday morning with one attorney, Carolyn Chuck, who represents Reid’s daughter Sharelle, present via Zoom. Oswest Senior-Smith, who represents Brown Lawrence, also joined late during the trial via Zoom.

Chuck briefed Burrell on the absences of several others, including Linda Wright, who represents Reid; Shannen Clarke, who represents Reid’s wife, Sharen; and Wildman, who had asked Chuck the day before to hold for him in the matter.

When she indicated that she was unable, she said Wildman had advised that he would ask another attorney to hold in his stead; but no one turned up.

Chuck went on to share that Wildman had indicated that he could also have challenges with being present next week as he was given time off from the Supreme Court to deal with the arrangements for his mother’s funeral.

Justice Burrell, acknowledging the sensitivity of the matter, extended condolence to Wildman’s family. However, she queried why this had not been communicated before.

“I don’t take lightly that Mr Wildman is making funeral arrangements for his mother, and my condolences go out to him and his family, but early information sharing makes a huge difference,” she maintained.

“I have to be very sensitive because all of us who are here either have a mother or had a mother at some point …but I am not understanding the lack of communication; the lack of communication is very unhelpful,” the judge said.

Emphasising that the case impacts four other accused, Burrell said Wildman and Pinnock are not entitled to an infinite supply of the court’s resources.

The judge’s comments come on the one-year anniversary of the official start of the trial, which has been plagued with scheduling challenges.

“It cannot be that Mr Wildman avoids appropriate and adequate communication and expects to get what he asks for,” she said.

“How can the rights of four other people be expected to continuously and infinitely, at this point in time, … be expected to yield to Mr Wildman’s failure — I am using the word failure — to organise himself?”

The judge impressed upon the court her sympathies for Wildman, but also highlighted that the attorney had secured time off from the Supreme Court, not the Parish Court, making it likely he had not intended to be present in the trial anyway, and that prior communication or arrangements should have been made, allowing the Parish Court to arrange itself accordingly.

“It should not have to be said, but counsel should only take on a workload that their chambers can support,” Burrell said.

The Crown expects to call more than 90 witnesses in the case and Burrell maintained that the witnesses are real people with lives of their own which must also be considered.

Wednesday’s witness, Brown’s Town Community College Principal Claudeth Haughton, shared information on the operations of the school, with the prosecution focusing specifically on whether lunches were provided for certain students.

The principal, who has served in the capacity since 2015, addressed the period of time from 2017 to 2019.

She told the court that the school has a number of courses, including customer engagement operation training.

Questions from the prosecution surrounded whether food was ever provided for the students of this course by the school, to which Haughton responded, “No.”

The prosecution also asked how students would have obtained meals.

The principal responded that students were at liberty to purchase meals from a restaurant, which she identified as operated by a Carol Brown, who rented the canteen on the college’s main campus in Brown’s Town to provide meals to students, staff, and visitors.

The principal confirmed that she had been visited by a police officer on April 9, 2019, after which she gathered certain documents relating to the registration of students in the programme.

While she indicated she knew Kim Brown Lawrence, who was introduced to her only as Kim at the time, Haughton confirmed that the community college had no relationship with either Kim Brown Lawrence, an individual cited as Joseph Martin, or Optimal Customer Service Consultancy.

She indicated that the college had not contracted any of these people to provide meals for the students or for any other purpose during the period 2017 to 2019.

Haughton admitted that there were certain occasions, such as honour roll events, when food would be provided for students and that the restaurateur on campus would’ve been contracted during that period to prepare refreshments.

Senior Smith, who represents Brown Lawrence, during cross-examination, asked whether it was the principal’s impression, based on questions asked by the prosecution, that his client had said she was a supplier of food for Brown’s Town Community College or its students.

The question prompted an objection by the prosecution.

But Justice Burrell allowed the question, and the witness indicated she had not formed any impression based on the questions.

Haughton told Senior Smith that while she was familiar with Brown’s Town in general and Brown’s Plaza, she was not familiar with any restaurants operated by Kim Brown Lawrence and her husband at said plaza.

She also confirmed that the college has, in the past, allowed both major political parties to host events, but indicated that any catering done would have been handled by the parties themselves.

Under further cross-examination by Senior Smith on whether Brown Lawrence had used the premises of the college for a Jamaica Labour Party divisional meeting in early 2018, Haughton said, “I cannot confirm.”

Upon further questioning from Senior Smith, who queried whether she was “not saying it did not happen” the witness repeated: “I cannot confirm that, sir.”

The principal also maintained that she had never been shown any statement purported to be that of Kim Brown Lawrence by police.

More witnesses are expected to be called in the case on Monday.

Brown Lawrence and the other four accused are before the court to answer to allegations that between March 2016 and October 2019 they participated in a scheme with others unknown, which siphoned off a revised figure of more than $25 million from both the Ministry of Education and CMU.

It is alleged that this money was funnelled through transfers to various accounts either owned or controlled by the accused, or handed over in cash, with the recipients either knowing, or reasonably should have known, that it was criminal property, resulting in charges of acquisition of criminal property.

Pinnock and Reid are accused of using their roles as public servants to mastermind and effect a scheme in which individuals were being paid on a regular basis by CMU, without knowledge that they were being paid; and in which invoices for goods and services were generated, but not by the individuals being paid, who did not, at any time, provide the stated services or goods to CMU, resulting in charges of conspiracy to defraud.

The two are also charged with acts of corruption under Section 15 of the Corruption Act.

World.title: Here comes Fudgie…30 years later
World.content:
Mr G

Dancehall artiste and producer Mr G, aka Goofy, credits his breakthrough 1996 hit Fudgie for opening several doors for his career.

The deejay, who started his Young Blood Records label in 1999, went on to score major success as a producer.

“Fudgie changed my life drastically,” he told the Jamaica Observer in a recent interview.

“Mi buss [got the breakthrough] at the end of August and, within months, I signed a deal with EMI/BMG Records in the United Kingdom. Early the next year I was able to purchase my first apartment in Kingston,” Mr G recalled.

Fudgie, produced by Danny Browne of Main Street Records, opened the floodgates for subsequent hits, including I Don’t Give a Damn, Big Man Little Yute with Red Rat, Buff Bay, Normal, Nah Stoop Low (with Chico), and Brush Yuh Teeth from Mawning.

Mr G shared the back story behind the origins of Fudgie and how the song became a hit.

“Me and [recording artiste] Mad Anju were walking along Donmair Road when a fudge man rode by on his bicycle. Mad Anju said, ‘Here comes Fudgie’, and I asked him if I could use the line in a song. My ears always indicated to me when I heard something special,” said Mr G.

He indicated that while it was not easy-going, he always had confidence in the track.

“I always knew Fudgie would have been a hit. I voiced the song three times for three different producers before it became a hit. I did it in 1994 for Junior Fender, who was my first manager, then I recorded it for Collin Fat, but he didn’t release the song,” he said.

He headed over to Main Street Records, a fledgling label at the time that had among its roster the likes of Papa San, General Degree, Richie Stephens, and Lady G. There he presented the song to Browne, who told him that he had a rhythm for up-and-coming artistes to ‘voice on’.

Mr G later accompanied Richie Stephens and General Degree to a stage show that was being held at a nightclub at the foot of Spur Tree Hill heading to St Elizabeth. There he tested the song Fudgie to see what the response would be like.

“The song mash up the show. Monday after the show I went to Arrows [studio] to cut a dub plate for the song and I bought a fudge horn downtown and included the horn in the song. After that, I jumped on a taxi from Spanish Town and went all the way down to Irie FM in Ocho Rios and gave the dub plate to Big A (Ainsworth Higgins). He said the song would change my life. And it did,” Mr G shared.

While travelling in the taxi on his way back to Kingston, Mr G heard the song being played several times. This continued for the next few days and, within a week, a promoter contacted Main Street Records wanting to book Mr G for his very first performance at Orchid Great House in Westmoreland.

“Fudgie gave me my first paid show at Orchid Great House in Westmoreland and, from there, everything fell into place. Hits after hits,” said Mr G.

Last month he released his latest musical juggling, titled I Shall Be Released rhythm, on his Young Blood Records imprint. It features the songs Weh Mi Woulda by Eminoxx, If You Love Me by Little John, Broken Promises by Phalcon, Baby Mother by Renigad, Mind Over Matter by Spanner Banner, You Don’t Deserve by Pinchers, If You Were Mine by Christopher Martin and Jesse Royal, No Substitute by Romain Virgo, and Free Up Di Youths by Mr G and Richie Spice.

I Shall Be Released rhythm is a remake of the beat accompanying the song of the same name by The Heptones, which was released in 1969.

“What I try to do, as a producer, is to preserve our culture and, by preserving our culture, sometimes we revisit some rhythms and give them a fresh sound, a fresh energy, whether it’s the artistes that are established or new artistes. We try to do things that will spark and create that buzz and resonate with people,” Mr G reasoned.

Mr G’s credentials as a producer are impeccable. Among the hits he has produced are 100 Dollar Bag by Beenie Man; Wah Dis Fada, the breakthrough hit for Mad Anju; Eva Clean by Beenie Man; Breath of Fresh Air by Warrior King; Ben Ova by RDX; Oh, My Lord by Chuck Fenda; Wife and Sweetheart by Christopher Martin and Romain Virgo; and Martin’s collaborative hit Leave People Business Alone.

World.title: Scotia going private
World.content:
Scotia Group Jamaica (SGJ) Chairman Vernon Douglas reads the result of the vote at Wednesday’s extraordinary general meeting. Observing from the head table are SGJ executives Audrey Tugwell Henry (left) and Maia Wilson.

Scotia Group Jamaica Limited (SGJ) is set to become a private company in the coming months as minority shareholders on Wednesday approved an offer by Scotiabank Caribbean Holdings Limited (SCH) to acquire their shares for $63.50 billion (US$397.84 million).

The decision was taken at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) called by the financial conglomerate at AC Hotel Kingston under a scheme of arrangement as directed by the Supreme Court of Jamaica.

At the meeting, minority shareholders were asked to vote on the offer by SCH to purchase their shares for $75 per share and take the company private. The vote was reviewed by scrutineers PwC Corporate Services (Jamaica) Limited.

“The resolution was approved by a majority in number of the stockholders being 77 per cent holding 97 per cent of stock units voting in person or by proxy at this meeting, which means preliminarily, the vote has been approved on both counts,” stated SGJ Chairman Vernon Douglas as he delivered the results to a round of applause.

The shareholder meeting was attended by more than 300 people comprising mainly older shareholders such as pensioners and a few young investors. Several shareholders asked about a better offer for their shares, with one older shareholder saying the $75 was not good enough, while another said that SCH should go and find more money for the offer.

However, institutional shareholders, like pension funds and managed funds, voted to support the offer.

There were 334 proxy forms submitted prior to the EGM, with SGJ’s second-largest shareholder, Sagicor Pooled Equity Fund, voting in favour of the scheme.

SGJ disclosed last Tuesday that some institutional shareholders entered into voting support arrangements for the offer, which was adjusted from $61.50 to $75. These shareholders represented 21.12 per cent of the minority shares in SGJ.

“Today’s shareholder support marks an important milestone and validates the strength of the proposal we put forward. This is a decisive statement of the Caribbean’s strategic importance to Scotiabank and of our confidence in Jamaica’s long-term future. Jamaica is a priority market, and we will continue investing in our business, our people, and the communities we serve,” a press release quoted Scotiabank Dominican Republic and the Caribbean President Jabar Singh on Wednesday.

Following the conclusion of the EGM, Scotia executives, including Audrey Tugwell Henry and Maia Wilson, attorney Gina Phillipps Black, and former Scotia Investments Jamaica Limited CEO Lissant Mitchell celebrated with hugs.

With the resolution approved by minority shareholders, SGJ and SCH will now return to Justice David Batts on October 30 for the final court hearing to sanction the scheme of arrangement. If the scheme is sanctioned, the court order would be filed with the Companies Office of Jamaica to make the scheme effective.

SCH would remit the funds to minority shareholders and become the sole shareholder of SGJ. Shareholders must submit a physically signed currency election form prior to the effective date to be paid in United States dollars. Also, shareholders who own more than 13,334 ordinary shares need to ensure that they have an electronic dividend mandate to be paid over $1 million as, since September 1 Jamaica has stopped processing cheques over that amount.

The Jamaican subsidiary will delist from the Jamaica Stock Exchange (JSE) after more than 57 years as a listed company partially owned by Jamaicans. SGJ is currently the most profitable company on the JSE as measured by net profit attributable to shareholders as it reported $16.18 billion.

SGJ represented 10.55 per cent of the JSE Main Market and 9.83 per cent of the entire Jamaican dollar equity market as of September 30. It was worth $226.75 billion as of Wednesday, making it the largest company on the JSE by market capitalisation.

World.title: 200 Cubans back in public health system
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton speaking at Wednesday’s post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House.

THE Government has re-engaged 157 Cuban medical professionals months after the collapse of a long-standing bilateral health-care arrangement with Cuba, bringing the number of health-care workers from the neighbouring Caribbean island now serving here to 200.

Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton made the disclosure at Wednesday’s post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House, saying the latest arrivals had been appropriately deployed across the public health system.

“The renegotiated agreement with our Cuban health-care workers has resulted in, to date, an engagement of some 157 Cuban medical professionals, including doctors and nurses, who have returned to Jamaica to support health-care delivery across the island,” Tufton said.

The largest complement, 69 professionals, has been assigned to the South East Regional Health Authority (SERHA), while 28 have been deployed to the Western Regional Health Authority and 26 to the Southern Regional Health Authority.

Another 25 have been assigned to University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), while nine are serving within the Ministry of Health and Wellness and the North East Regional Health Authority.

The 157 are in addition to 43 Cuban health-care workers who opted to remain in Jamaica after the Government ended the previous country-to-country arrangement and offered them the option of continuing to work under individual contracts.

Tufton said the latest re-engagement brings the number of Cuban medical professionals in Jamaica to 200, compared with 277 before the renegotiated arrangement.

“We basically gave them an offer. We said, we can’t do the arrangement as was the case, but if you return and it’s your option, your choice, we would engage you in a direct contract,” he said.

“So, we are close to where we were, and they have been appropriately deployed.”

The development comes after Jamaica announced that it would discontinue the existing technical cooperation arrangement with Cuba after both governments failed to reach an agreement on the terms of a new framework.

The previous agreement had expired in February 2023, but Cuban medical professionals continued working in Jamaica while negotiations for a replacement arrangement continued. In March this year, the Government said it was willing to engage the professionals individually under Jamaican labour laws to ensure continuity of services.

At the time, the health system had about 260 Cuban health-care workers, with the largest group consisting of 97 assigned to SERHA. Others were deployed across the western and southern regions, UHWI and specialised services, including the Jamaica-Cuba Eye Care Programme.

The end of the bilateral arrangement subsequently exposed staffing gaps at some public facilities. At Cornwall Regional Hospital in St James, for example, 27 Cuban health-care workers, including nurses, doctors and radiotherapists, left with the hospital having to recruit locally and look overseas for specialised personnel to fill some vacancies.

The Cuban programme has been a major component of Jamaica’s public health-care system for decades, with the eye-care programme in particular providing specialised services to Jamaicans since 2010.

Tufton on Wednesday expressed appreciation to the Cuban professionals who had chosen to return.

“I want to thank those who have chosen that option because the system needs them,” he said.

World.title: Golding, Chuck trade blows over Gun Court data
World.content:
GOLDING : I think that must be a critical deliverable of the Ministry of Justice to track how this legislation is impacting the justice system

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck and Opposition Leader Mark Golding clashed in Parliament on Tuesday over data on the Gun Court.

The exchange was sparked after Golding questioned why the justice ministry had not determined whether the 2022 Firearms Act was affecting guilty pleas and case backlogs.

Both legislators also engaged in a joust over Chuck’s response to a question about juveniles and people with no previous convictions who may have received the mandatory 15-year sentence for possessing imitation firearms, with Golding arguing that the minister should have obtained the information from the relevant agencies.

The exchange came during the House of Representatives’ Questions and Answers to Questions segment on Tuesday, after Opposition spokeswoman on Justice Zulieka Jess put seven questions to Chuck about the operation of the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022.

One of Jess’s questions was whether the Government had assessed the extent to which the 15-year mandatory minimum sentence had reduced the incentive for early guilty pleas and what specific effect that had had on the trial backlog in the Gun Court.

Chuck’s answer was brief.

“Answer no,” said the justice minister.

Golding then rose to ask a supplementary question, challenging Chuck over the absence of an assessment on an issue he said should be central to the justice ministry’s work.

“I was shocked by that because I think that must be a critical deliverable of the Ministry of Justice to track how this legislation is impacting the justice system. And I’m asking you, why is it that you don’t have that information? How is it that you don’t have the data as to what impact this legislation is having on the flow of cases through the court system?” Golding queried.

Chuck defended the ministry’s position by pointing to the time it takes for criminal cases to move through the Gun Court.

“First of all, [when] all of these matters come into the gun courts, most of these matters tend to last two or three years before they’re tried. So to say that over the past four years, I should have figures when most of these matters would not even be tried after the Gun Court Act…and with due respect, all the material that would come to the Ministry of Justice would be two, three years.

“They would not be indicating what has been the impact of the 2022 legislation. So you should know that most of these figures would only come after three, four years,” explained Chuck.

Golding, however, pointed to information already being produced by the Court Administration Division, saying the issue was not necessarily whether cases brought under the 2022 law had already been completed, but whether available case-flow information showed an effect on the backlog.

The disagreement then moved to the treatment of juveniles and people with no previous criminal records.

Jess had asked the minister whether any juveniles, or people without prior convictions, were serving or awaiting trial for the mandatory 15-year sentence solely because they possessed an object classified under the law as an imitation firearm.

Chuck initially answered that those statistics were held by other agencies.

But Golding argued that the minister should obtain the information rather than leave the question unanswered.

“You say that doesn’t lie in your ministry. But it’s your obligation to answer the question. So if you don’t have the information in your ministry about sentencing or in the courts, which fall under your ministry, you should get it from whatever source there is,” charged Golding.

Chuck later clarified his position, saying he was aware juveniles might be before the courts, but he had not been informed of any juvenile who had been convicted under the Act and was serving a 15-year sentence.

The explanation was challenged by Golding who argued that Chuck’s response appeared inconsistent with his earlier answer that the information rested with other agencies.

“Your answer was that you can’t provide an answer because that information resides elsewhere. Then, on your feet, you are saying, to the best of your knowledge, there has been no case where somebody has been convicted in those circumstances. So those are two different answers,” argued the Opposition leader.

“…And unless you’re just going to arrogantly dismiss the questions that have been asked, which is really how it felt like, to be honest, you would be expected to find out from whatever ministries… I mean, these questions were tabled just recently, and you’re providing the answers already without any real attempt to find out the information to answer the question, and I think that was unbecoming of a minister of your stature,” Golding added.

Chuck then explained that he had requested more recent information, but had not received it.

He said the ministry’s statistician is a consultant and, to his knowledge, was behind on some of the data.

According to Chuck, even after the information is obtained, the ministry would have to compare recent figures with those from previous years before determining the effect of the 2022 law.

He acknowledged that the comparison had not yet been completed.

The exchange took place against the background of the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, which replaced the previous firearms law and introduced tougher provisions governing firearms offences.

The Act is set to be reviewed by the Government after members of the defence bar staged a protest to push for changes.

World.title: SHALLOW THINKS DEEP
World.content:
West Indies players stand for their national anthem during the ICC Men’s T20 Cricket World Cup Super Eights match against Zimbabwe at the Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai, India, on February 23. (Photo: AFP)

Cricket West Indies (CWI) President Dr Kishore Shallow says stronger Government support could help transform the sport into a more profitable venture for all stakeholders.

CWI recently announced several changes amid its financial challenges, including major salary cuts for international and domestic players as well as the scrapping of several annual competitions and initiatives.

The regional governing body says taking these measures is critical to ensuring West Indies cricket’s financial stability going forward.

Over the years, governments have been criticised for not investing enough in the sport.

This includes Jamaica after opting not to bid to host the 2024 ICC Men’s T20 World Cup.

The Jamaican Government, however, played a significant role in the Jamaica Kingsmen’s debuting in this year’s Caribbean Premier League (CPL) and invested in upgrades at Sabina Park in 2025.

Shallow, who also serves as minister of tourism in St Vincent and the Grenadines, says cricket is too valuable to the Caribbean to be overlooked.

“I don’t think Cricket West Indies over the years has done a good enough job at letting the public know about this but [there are] thousands of jobs created annually in the region because of cricket,” he told the Super Over Podcast.

“There’s nothing close to sports tourism, when you look at all the other sports or events in the region close to what cricket does.

[Not just] hosting the [2024] World Cup but even outside of that hosting series after series after series plus CPL, what it does for the region is it stimulates the economy like nothing else.

However, Shallow says he understands that social and economic issues are a hindrance in Government’s increasing their support.

“It is not a lack of passion for West Indies cricket by the regional leaders.

It’s just that everyone, in terms of the national leaders, has their challenges,” he said.

“Even Caricom, every week there’s another challenge and while they are committed in different forms and have made their contributions to cricket, I suspect once there’s the fiscal room or privilege to do such, it’ll be done.

“I just think that [they’ll] have competing priorities.

So they’ll tell you, ‘Yes, we understand cricket stimulates the economy, but then we could do other things.’ “[They] could invest it in air travel, they could talk about using it to invest in a fund to market the region as a whole better, establishing a regional health system that helps us all and there have been requests from other organisations for [support] so we’re not alone or unique in making this request but again, it’s a matter of competing priorities.” Shallow, however, says increased investment in cricket could strengthen the economies of the countries involved and create greater financial opportunities.

“The reason why I have no doubt or reservation in my mind that the leaders fully appreciate this is when you look at cricket — and this is obviously no bias and I challenge anyone to prove me wrong — there’s nothing else in the region that impacts us like cricket,” he said.

“It is really an investment and maybe Caricom and regional leaders should look at it as an investment into the economy because by boosting cricket, you are ultimately boosting the economy.

There’s so many great opportunities in the game now across the region that I think it is a really responsible thing for the governments to invest in cricket or find ways that will not affect them fiscally, locally or nationally, but that could help the region in cricket.” In August, Sports Minister Olivia Grange said the Government is “doing everything possible to make sure we build back cricket here in Jamaica”, after the return of the CPL to the island.

World.title: Belize minister bullish on Wambugu apple research at CASE
World.content:
Belize Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries Rodwell Ferguson (left) engages in discussion with farm supervisor at the College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) Christopher Honeyghan (second left); managing director of Summit Apple Orchards Latoya Panton; and senior advisor to the minister, Hugh O’Brien, during a visit to CASE on October 1.

BELIZE’S Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries Rodwell Ferguson believes research into the cultivation of the Wambugu apple at the College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) in Portland, could provide a valuable blueprint for other Caricom countries seeking to diversify local agricultural production and strengthen food security.



Ferguson expressed this view during a visit to CASE on October 1, where he inspected the fruit first-hand as part of efforts to assess its potential for cultivation in Belize.

The minister said his interest was sparked by the prospect of cultivating apples in tropical climates, noting that the fruit has traditionally been associated with colder regions and temperate growing conditions.

“I was told apples can only grow in cold temperatures… and so it is always imported from the USA [and] Canada. This would be a significant step forward if we can get it grown in the region. People across the world eat apples… they eat grapes. So, it would be good [if] we could grow [them] in Belize and [make them] marketable,” Ferguson told JIS News.

He was in Jamaica to attend the Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026, which was held at the Ocean Coral Spring Resort in Trelawny from September 27 to October 2.

Ferguson was accompanied on the visit to CASE by managing director of Summit Apple Orchards, home of My Jamaican Food Forest, Latoya Panton, who explained that the company imports and distributes Wambugu apples from Kenya to Jamaica and other Caribbean islands.

“My aim, when I first started bringing these apples in, was to see [them] being grown across the Caribbean,” said Panton.

She indicated that the Wambugu apple has been performing well in Jamaica, with farmers and backyard gardeners successfully cultivating the fruit.

According to Panton, the next step is to scale up production to levels that would support exportation.

“We have been harvesting fruits and, for me, I would just love to see more farmers coming on board and planting… and for us to get to a commercial level with the apple,” she said.

Meanwhile, Ferguson called for increased investment in agricultural research, citing Brazil as an example of how innovation can contribute to food self-sufficiency and export expansion.

“They create the environment to be able to make everything grow. So Brazil is self-sufficient and they are exporting to every part of the world. We can do likewise in the Caribbean… [but] we need to do the research, because whatever is going on in other parts of the world, if we do the research, we can do it in the Caribbean,” argued Ferguson

— JIS

World.title: ‘Targets of terror’: Russia kills 30 in single strike in Donbas
World.content:
President Zelenskyy said Russia was “trying to destroy all life in Donbas” and that the attack would “not go unanswered.”

KYIV — At least 30 people were killed and 18 injured in a Russian attack on two buses in Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s Donbas region Thursday morning.

“At the time of the attack, civilian buses were carrying passengers. People just going by their day,” Kramatorsk city council said in a statement. “For frontline Kramatorsk — where only a fraction of the population remains due to constant Russian shelling and evacuations — every trip across the city is an inherent daily risk. There are few people left here. Yet, even civilian vehicles carrying passengers become targets of Russian terror,” the city council added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said doctors were “fighting to save the lives of people injured” and that the number of fatalities may still rise. “Some of those killed have still not been identified because of the severity of their injuries. My condolences to all their families and loved ones,” he added. Prosecutors have opened a criminal case into the attack.

World.title: Slovakia’s Fico calls nude Trump statue a sign of EU decline
World.content:
The sculpture, titled The Orange Plague, was unveiled Tuesday by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt in the Parliament building in Strasbourg. The 2.6-meter work depicts a nude, gold-leaf-covered Trump perched on a frail man’s shoulders, holding a golf club and scales of justice. A plaque reads: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden.”

POLITICO was present at the unveiling, where visitors clamored for miniature replicas of the sculpture, which were distributed in several colors. The statue stands in a prominent spot at the entrance to Parliament’s Winston Churchill building, before the corridor linking MEPs’ and Commission officials’ offices with the plenary chamber.

Galschiøt said the work was intended to confront Trump’s policies and start a debate about how the U.S. president was “destroying the world’s only chance to counter the climate catastrophe.”

Danish left-wing MEP Per Clausen, who invited the artist, defended the installation in a statement. “If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture … then they have no place on the world stage,” he said.

Fico has cultivated ties with Trump, meeting him at Mar-a-Lago in January to discuss closer cooperation, including civilian nuclear energy. He has praised the MAGA movement as “a vision that urgently resonates not only in the United States but across the world.”

The sculpture was previously displayed at protests in Copenhagen and the COP30 summit in Brazil. It is due to appear at next month’s COP31 conference in Antalya, Türkiye.

Trump has not commented on the installation.

Gerardo Fortuna contributed to this report.

World.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine ambassador in prisoner of war row
World.content:
Seoul accused Ukraine of breaching a non-disclosure agreement over the transfer of two North Korean soldiers to South Korea.

Seoul recalled its ambassador to Ukraine on Thursday, two weeks after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, triggering a diplomatic spat.

“The government hopes that pending bilateral issues will be resolved smoothly and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end,” the South Korean ministry’s statement said.

On Sept 24, South Korean president Lee Jae-myung accused Ukraine of breaching a confidentiality agreement between Seoul and Kyiv after Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of two North Korean soldiers to its neighbour to the south.

World.title: UK and Israel broker compromise over East Jerusalem consulate
World.content:
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the diplomats and their families were being “temporarily withdrawn” to secure their safety, but he said the mission will remain independent, operational and continue to work with the Palestinian people.

“We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence, and we will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible,” he continued, in a statement released as he was visiting Ukraine.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar set out a list of diplomatic actions taken against Britain, adding: “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response.”

Sa’ar said the consulate would be “closing its operations today” and that the “sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed.” Twenty British diplomats, including the consul general, will be leaving East Jerusalem.

But the British flag was still flying on Thursday afternoon. Seven diplomats remain.

The dispute over the consulate has been the latest marker of declining relations between Israel and the U.K. under its Labour government. Israel threatened to close the consulate within 30 days of Sept. 8, in retaliation against Andy Burnham’s government announcing a ban on trade with illegal settlements in the West Bank.

World.title: Will Berlin help Britain rejoin the EU?
World.content:
With conference season in the rear-view mirror, Andy Burnham jets off to Germany for his first European trip as PM – but how much do Anglo-German relations matter right now?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy look ahead to his meeting with German chancellor Friedrich Merz as the countries attempt to align ambitions and maybe find an avenue to rejoin the EU.

Elsewhere, an MP gets in touch to ask whether the government is trying to curb transparency and scrutiny.

World.title: Can Europe finally get tough on China?
World.content:
Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is kicking off his visit to China today — and the stakes are high.

On today’s show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Sarah Wheaton discuss the most important topic on the agenda: Europe’s trade deficit with China. France and Germany are finally on the same page and want Brussels to get tougher on unfair trade. So can we expect results from the meeting?

Next, EU development ministers are meeting in Dublin to discuss the future of Europe’s development policy. But the timing is unfortunate, as governments prepare another round of cuts to the next long-term budget.

Finally, a mysterious death at a Russian anti-plague lab has an unexpected connection to Zoya’s own family.

World.title: Far-right surge threatens Europe’s drive to rearm
World.content:
Roberto Vannacci, a former general and MEP who leads the far-right National Future party, which is increasingly challenging Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, called for a rethink of defense spending. “Let’s evaluate whether this military spending is justified: in my opinion, it isn’t, especially at a time when commodity prices are hitting record highs,” he said last week.

The challenge for Europe’s mainstream parties is how to sustain support for higher defense budgets even if that means competing with welfare and other priorities.

“People are struggling with the rising cost of living across the board … so there’s room for populistic rhetoric about how much should we support Ukraine financially, or how much should we invest in defense,” said Janne Kuusela, permanent secretary at Finland’s defense ministry.

The dilemma is sharpening as several large NATO members, including France, Italy and Poland, face elections in 2027, when far-right parties stand a real chance of coming to power. Many countries are also beginning talks on next year’s budgets.

For NATO, a spending slowdown would complicate efforts to meet the alliance’s target of spending 5% of GDP on defense and security by 2035. Four NATO diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely, said the risk is a growing concern, though some said its effects may not be clear until next year’s budget cycle.

“We’re already in a situation where we need to catch up” with Russia, said a NATO military official. “So far, we’re on a positive trajectory — if someone closes the faucet, there’s a risk of losing capabilities.”
