World.title: Royal Navy sailor faces court over alleged spying for Russia
World.content:
A 24-year-old Royal Navy sailor appeared in a London court on Thursday, accused of spying for Russia.

 

Teddy Young faces two charges under the UK's National Security Act for allegedly obtaining and preparing to share protected information between November 2024 and May 2025, London’s Metropolitan Police Service said.

“The allegation is that while serving as a Royal Navy warfare intelligence rating with high level security clearance and intelligence-system access, Teddy Stanley Greenidge Young accessed and retained sensitive UK defense and intelligence material and engaged in activity consistent with preparing to pass protected information to a foreign power,” the Crown Prosecution Service wrote summary.

Young allegedly used the dark web to try to contact Russian authorities, drafting a message that “sought to make contact with a potential threat actor.”

Court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Royal Navy sailor Teddy Young appearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court in London, Thursday 8 Oct., 2026. AP Photo

Young was not asked to enter a plea during Thursday's brief hearing due to the seriousness of the charges. He will remain in custody until his next court appearance in London on 16 October.

The sailor joined the Navy in April 2024 and is accused of committing the offences during his first deployment, which began on 4 November 2024.

Young was previously arrested on May 21, 2025, and released on bail pending further investigation. His security clearance was suspended at that time and he was removed from his duties.

The Royal Navy issued a statement acknowledging the arrest of a service member.

“As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage,” the navy said.

World.title: Iran strikes tankers outside Hormuz in signs of expanding campaign
World.content:
Iran's armed forces struck two commercial tankers outside the Strait of Hormuz within 24 hours this week, in what appeared to be a deliberate expansion of attacks beyond the strait, as Iranian officials issued a fresh wave of warnings against the United States.

 

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said several projectiles hit the oil and chemical tanker Acers, flagged in Antigua and Barbuda, 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal in Qatar on Wednesday. Casualties were reported.

Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel and said it was heading toward the Strait of Hormuz.

It was the first attack in that area in more than six months.

In a separate incident on Thursday, Vanguard reported a fire on a tanker some 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, which it identified as likely the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalgout.

The UKMTO had not recorded the incident, and the cause of the fire was not immediately clear. NASA's FIRMS fire-detection system confirmed the blaze, and US military aircraft — including two KC-46 tankers, a KC-135, a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and several helicopters — were over the area at the time.

Iran and media affiliated with the IRGC did not officially claim responsibility for either attack. IRGC-affiliated outlets implicitly suggested that Tehran had "extended the scope of its operations against commercial vessels that violate Iranian laws and regulations in the Strait of Hormuz to waters beyond the strait."

Both incidents fall outside the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and gas shipments normally pass. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began in late February, after Iran and the US imposed concurrent naval blockades.

"The distance between you and us is determined by our missiles," Acting Defence Minister Majid Ebn ol-Reza posted on X on Thursday.

"Yesterday the Gulf of Oman, today the Indian Ocean and tomorrow the Bay of Pigs. If you make a mistake, you will see a new set of dividing lines.," ol-Reza added in an apparent reference to a failed, US-backed military landing on the southwestern coast of Cuba from April 1961 aimed at overthrowing the communist government of Fidel Castro.

Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior military adviser to Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, had earlier warned that if the US or Israel attacked Iran again, Tehran could extend the war "as far as the Indian Ocean or other places," adding that Iranian forces had prepared contingency plans for worst-case scenarios.

Ebn ol-Reza was appointed acting minister after Aziz Nasirzadeh, Iran's then defence minister, was killed on 28 February — the first day of the war — alongside several other military commanders. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has nominated Mehrdad Akhlaqi as a permanent replacement, and parliament is due to hold a confidence vote on 18 October.

Iran's army spokesman said separately that its forces were ready to carry out pre-emptive operations, if necessary, to prevent what he described as "any aggression or attack by the enemy."

At a midterm election campaign rally in Nebraska, US President Donald Trump defended the decision to go to war with Iran. "This is a small price to pay for keeping the world and our country safe. They can destroy a city. Let them destroy it. Let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," he said.

At a separate rally in Texas on Wednesday night, Trump walked back those remarks after criticism. "We protect our own cities. We will not allow such a thing to happen," he said.

US President Donald Trump defended the launch of war against Iran at a midterm election campaign rally in Nebraska, stating that "this is a small price to pay for keeping the world and our country safe."

"They can destroy a city. Let them destroy it. Let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," Trump said.

However, in another speech in Texas on Wednesday night Trump responded to criticism of his controversial remarks two days earlier about a possible Iranian attack on Los Angeles and San Diego.

"We protect our own cities. We will not allow such a thing to happen," he said.

World.title: EU presses Russia for more details on suspected plague case
World.content:
The European Commission has stepped up pressure on Russia to provide full details of a suspected plague case in Siberia, echoing calls for transparency from the United States and the World Health Organisation (WHO).

 

Moscow has pushed back,insisting there is no risk of an epidemic.

"Let me say, for the third time this week in the press room: Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible," Eva Hrncirova, the Commission's health spokesperson, said on Thursday.

"We don't have enough information to assess the epidemiological situation, to assess the risks for other countries and to take appropriate measures, if necessary."

The comments came a day after the Commission convened the EU's Health Security Committee, bringing together representatives of the 27 member states, along with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the WHO.

The committee coordinates the EU's response to serious cross-border health threats, allowing national authorities to share information, assess risks and discuss possible measures.

However, Wednesday's meeting ended without any specific decisions because of the lack of reliable information from Russia.

The Commission said it was ready to reconvene the committee at short notice if new information emerged or the situation deteriorated.

"We need information from Russia," Hrncirova said. "It's linked to the Russian membership in the WHO Europe: sharing timely, precise, exact information so that the experts can assess the situation because the situation can have cross-border implications."

The EU delegation in Moscow reached out to the WHO's office in Russia to convey its concerns, the spokesperson said, citing the lack of direct diplomatic contact between Brussels and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"Basically the whole world is waiting for the information from Russia," she added.

The case revolves around a female lab worker at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute, in south-eastern Siberia, who died on 2 October in uncertain circumstances.

Her death was initially attributed to a "pneumonia of unknown aetiology", sparking global alarm and intense scrutiny.

Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, says the lab worker was "vaccinated and had immunity to the dangerous infections she was working with", and that nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no dangerous pathogens.

More than 90% of those who had contact with her have completed medical monitoring after being placed under strict observation, it said.

WHO has requested details to clarify the lab worker's death, the pathogen that triggered the quarantine measures, and a reported second case, which Moscow called "false".

The US has also urged Russia to provide accurate and timely information. President Donald Trump said he had scheduled a call with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to discuss the suspected outbreak.

"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government. We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," a US State Department spokesperson said.

Pneumonic plague occurs when the bacteria responsible for plague infect the lungs. It is the most serious form of the disease and can spread from person to person. Without treatment, its case-fatality ratio ranges from 30% to 100%.

World.title: Germany lifts GDP forecast as economy withstands Iran war
World.content:
Foreign trade is expected to boost Europe's biggest economy this year.

 

Stronger exports helped prompt the German government to more than double its growth forecast for this year on Thursday, as it said the economy had withstood the energy shock caused by the Iran war and was benefiting from the global AI boom.

The improved outlook could take some pressure off Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is facing criticism that he has not done enough to kickstart the long-stagnant economy.

"The German economy proved more robust than projected in the spring," Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said as she announced the new forecasts.

"Despite geopolitical uncertainties, despite a global energy price shock, despite the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and despite tariffs, the economy was able to embark on a path of recovery," she told a press conference.

Germany's economy has faced years of stagnation amid weak export demand, high energy costs, US tariffs and Chinese competition, though recent indicators suggest it is starting to recover.

Reiche said foreign importers had rushed to stockpile German-made goods such as steel, fertiliser and aluminium in the months following the outbreak of the Iran war, supporting growth.

The government expects exports to grow by 3.7% this year, reversing a 0.9% decline in 2025.

German suppliers were also benefiting from the "global trend of investment in artificial intelligence", she said.

The boom in data centre construction has led to a surge in orders for German-made equipment such as lasers, semiconductor machinery and cooling systems, she said.

The economy ministry also raised its forecast for 2027 to 1.1%, from 0.9% previously, and said increased public spending on defence and infrastructure would support the economy in the coming years. Growth is expected to slow to 0.6% in 2028.

But it warned that household consumption would remain subdued as higher energy costs push up consumer prices. German inflation hit 3.3% in September, the highest level in nearly three years.

The ministry expects inflation to average 2.7% this year and rise to 3.0% in 2027, while household spending is forecast to grow by just 0.3% and 0.5%, respectively, after adjusting for inflation.

As in other countries, Germany has seen fuel costs surge amid the Iran war, prompting the government last week to announce a temporary fuel tax cut to provide some relief for drivers.

The official growth forecast for 2026 is in line with recent estimates by Germany's leading economic research institutes.

World.title: 2027 budget reaches parliament with PS backing assured
World.content:
The government on Thursday early afternoon submitted to parliament the draft State Budget law for 2027, two days before the deadline, after approving it this morning in the Council of Ministers.

 

The document was handed over by the finance minister, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, to the Speaker of the Assembly of the Republic, José Pedro-Aguiar Branco.

The third State Budget of Luís Montenegro's government has its approval once again assured by the Socialist Party (PS).

The Socialist secretary-general, José Luís Carneiro, announced last week that the party intends to abstain in the vote on the bill in general terms, scheduled for 28 October, after the prime minister, Luís Montenegro, gave guarantees on four conditions set by the Socialists: a constitutional revision with PS and PSD playing a central role, protection of current and future pensions, funding for investment projects that remain to be carried out after the Recovery and Resilience Plan (PRR), and support for the recovery of municipalities and regions affected by storms.

The detailed debate and vote will take place between 29 October and 24 November, with the final overall vote set for 24 November.

The Communist Party (PCP) and the Left Bloc have already announced that they will vote against the government's proposal. Chega has also threatened to vote against (source in Portuguese)if the prime minister refuses to lower the retirement age, and has made an additional demand: a cut in VAT on fuel and the introduction of zero VAT on a basket of essential foodstuffs. These are red lines the government has already rejected.

The remaining parties have not yet announced how they will vote.

The President of the Republic, António José Seguro, said on Thursday that he expected a "fruitful debate" to improve people's lives "at a very difficult time".

Speaking to reporters in parliament after meetings with the parties on the draft budget, the finance minister, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, refused to estimate how much room there is for negotiations, confirming that the projected surplus for next year will be between 0.1% and 0.2% of gross domestic product (GDP).

The government estimates that the economic measures already adopted, which will continue to have an impact on the public accounts in 2027, will have a 4.8 billion-euro impact next year, not yet counting any new policies to be included in the next budget.

As for the macroeconomic scenario for next year, the government is forecasting economic growth of 2%, in line with the trend of recent years, along with a budget surplus of up to 0.2%.

Pensions, public-sector wages and debt-interest payments are among the main sources of pressure, alongside tax measures such as updating income tax brackets, cutting the corporation tax rate and housing measures.

The finance minister said that the 2027 State Budget provides for a further cut in income tax, through updating the brackets, the specific tax deduction and the minimum subsistence threshold, mechanisms which by law have to be adjusted.

The PSD/CDS-PP government has decided to lower income tax rates in the first to sixth brackets by between 0.3 and 0.5 percentage points, a measure with an estimated impact of 400 million euros that will already be reflected in withholding at source in 2026.

The reduction will be 0.3 percentage points in the first bracket, 0.5 points in the second to fifth brackets and again 0.3 points in the sixth bracket.

The government has also announced a 50-euro increase in the solidarity supplement for the elderly (CSI) in 2027, with the reference amount rising to 720 euros.

The government's programme provides for this amount to reach 870 euros in 2029, compared to the current 670 euros.

A rise in the minimum wage from 920 to 970 euros is also planned. The tripartite agreement on wage increases and economic growth for 2025-2028, signed in October 2024 between the government, the four employers' confederations and the UGT trade union, revised upwards the path of the national minimum wage. The agreement provides for annual increases of 50 euros, with the aim of reaching 1,020 euros in 2028.

In the civil service, the multiannual agreement in force provides for pay rises of 2.30% in 2027, with a minimum increase of 60.52 euros.

If the planned increase in the agreement goes ahead, the minimum basic wage in the public administration should rise to 995.51 euros in 2027.

The same agreement also provides for an increase in the meal allowance, currently set at 6.15 euros, of 15 cents per year up to 2029.

World.title: Scientists in Austria and China create the world’s first nuclear clocks. Here’s why it matters
World.content:
Scientists have invented the world’s first nuclear clocks that they say could unlock the fundamentals of physics.

 

The two devices are the newest atomic clocks, which measure time by monitoring light by using transitions occurring inside the atomic nucleus, involving protons and neutrons.

Atomic clocks have been used to keep precise measures of time and were first created in 1949 and, despite the name, do not use nuclear fusion or fission.

The world's best clocks have relied on electrons jumping between energy levels in atoms but the discovery has shown that the reference for a clock can come from the nucleus itself.

The research teams from China’s Tsinghua University and other institutions in the country and Austria’s TU Wien reported their breakthroughs separately in two papers published in Nature on Wednesday.

The clock uses thorium-229, a rare atom whose nucleus can switch energy states using ultraviolet light from a laser. It is the only nucleus known to work this way.

The team built a laser that makes ultraviolet light at 148.4 nanometres and aimed it at small calcium fluoride crystals containing thorium-229.

The key finding was that the nuclear clocks worked. The laser stayed locked to the thorium-229 nucleus and kept steady time, reaching a precision of about one part in a quadrillion (10⁻¹⁵) over the test period.

While precise timekeeping is vital for everyday technologies such as satellite navigation and telecommunications, nuclear clocks could make these systems more precise

They could also be important in fundamental physics, the paper reads, however, it does not specify the exact use cases.

World.title: Early-onset cancer rising worldwide: Causes, risk, prevention
World.content:
Across Latin America, early-onset cancer rates have risen, with Chile and Brazil seeing the fastest growth, especially of bowel, breast and cervical cancers. But it is a worldwide trend.

The numbers are striking. Some cancer rates have doubled in the past 20 years. It's just not yet clear whether we're seeing a rise in actual cases or whether we're seeing more early-stage cases because of better awareness, diagnosis and treatment in hospitals.

Take, for example, colorectal (or bowel) cancer: In 2001, about one in every 26,000 people under 50 in England were diagnosed with it each year. By 2023, the rate of diagnoses was about one in 12,000. Twice what it was at the turn of the century.

That's according to the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF) , an international network of charities, which analyzed registry data from England, the US and the Netherlands. It found the number of new cancer cases had risen for seven cancers in England alone.

So, rates have doubled, but the numbers overall are still small, said Amy Berrington de Gonzalez, a professor of clinical epidemiology at the Institute of Cancer Research in the UK capital London.

"Cancer is still very uncommon among young people," Berrington de Gonzalez told DW. "Three times a small number is still a small number."

But she and other scientists still want to know why this is happening, because it is a worldwide trend. Latin America is a case in point.

Early-onset cancer rates rising in Latin America

A 2025 study analyzed registry data from 50 countries and territories up to 2017 . It found early-onset colorectal cancer rising in 27 of those regions.

In Latin America, rates rose in Chile, Argentina, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Puerto Rico. Chile's rise — at almost 4% per year — was among the highest.

In Brazil, the evidence comes directly from hospitals. At the A.C. Camargo Cancer Center in Sao Paulo, the number of colorectal cancer patients under 50 grew by 7.6% per year between 2000 and 2023. That's a five-fold increase.

The number of patients over 50 grew even faster — at 8.1% — or about six-fold.

But since the figures come from a single hospital, they do not show whether cases are rising across Brazil. They may only reflect that this one hospital is treating more patients.

"We need better cancer registration systems," said Berrington de Gonzalez, "especially in countries like Brazil and Mexico, where obesity rates have also been increasing."

Marc Gunter, professor of cancer epidemiology at Imperial College London, said he expected Latin America to follow richer countries as diets there become more Westernized and lifestyles more sedentary. "I think it's already happening," he said.

These six cancers affect young adults most

In another study in 2025 , involving 42 countries, Berrington de Gonzalez compared data from two age groups — 20 to 49 years and 50 years and older — between 2003 and 2017.

Six cancers — thyroid, breast, colorectal, kidney, uterine and leukemia — rose among the younger groups in most countries. All but colorectal cancer were seen to rise in older adults, too.

In fact, colorectal cancer stood out. In about a third of the countries, it rose faster in younger adults than in older ones. "It is the one cancer that seems to be increasing in younger people whilst decreasing in older people," said Berrington de Gonzalez.

This has consequences for research. If cancers are rising in all age groups, the causes are likely to be widespread, so studies looking only at young people risk chasing complicated explanations with too little data to test them, she said.

Better awareness could explain the rise in diagnoses

A US study of pancreatic cancer in adults aged 15 to 39 years found the rise was almost entirely made up of early-stage tumors.

Death rates remained unchanged.

The authors said this suggested that instead of the number of cancer cases going up, it was the number of early diagnoses that had gone up. And that can be explained by better awareness in the community, with people getting checked more often.

But the data for colorectal cancer looks different: Some US studies show it rising in advanced stages of the disease as well, which suggests an increase in the number of cases, not just the number of diagnoses.

Bowel cancer rates rising in young people To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The link between cancer and obesity

Obesity is an established cause of at least 13 cancers, according to the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

According to a 2021 review of existing studies, young adults with obesity were almost twice as likely to develop colorectal cancer before the age of 50.

Obesity has also spread fastest among the young. The WHO reports that obesity rates have doubled among adults since the 1990s and quadrupled among adolescents.

What you consume matters:

Processed meat is classed as carcinogenic

Alcohol is also considered a risk factor

Fiber (vegetables, whole grains and pulses) lowers cancer risk

Some also say ultra-processed foods and microplastics cause cancer. But Gunter said the evidence was inconclusive.

"There's a lot of hype," Gunter said, adding that more research was needed. Berrington de Gonzalez agreed: "Diets have changed, but we don't yet know the role they might play."

How young people can lower their cancer risk

Gunter said individuals should not be blamed for living in societies built around convenience foods and desk jobs, and that lasting change needs public health policy.

But he also said young people can lower their cancer risk by maintaining a healthy weight, moving more, eating more fiber and cutting back on processed meat.

"Going for a walk, being more physically active, eating more fruits and vegetables," he said. "Those things are maybe not so trendy, but they are really important."

For a 30-year-old reading this, Berrington de Gonzalez's message was one of reassurance: Cancer at a young age remains relatively rare.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

World.title: Germany news: UK's Burnham visits Berlin for talks with Merz
World.content:
10/08/2026 October 8, 2026 German spy agency BND approved suspect's side job

Germany's foreign intelligence agency reportedly approved outside work by an employee for a former spy chief who is now suspected of illegally obtaining classified information.

According to German news magazine Der Spiegel, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) officially authorized Manfred D. to work for former BND head August Hanning, who became a private-sector consultant after leaving government service in 2009.

Prosecutors allege that Manfred D. supplied Hanning with nearly 2,000 internal BND documents, many of them classified, which the former intelligence chief allegedly used for commercial gain.

Investigators believe the arrangement began around 2010, when Hanning and his former chief of staff allegedly agreed that intelligence would be supplied in return for payment.

Manfred D. allegedly passed the documents to Hanning between 2010 and 2022.

Hanning, 80, headed the BND from 1998 to 2005. He is suspected of offenses including intelligence-agent activity, espionage involving state secrets and attempted treason.

Manfred D., 64, served as chief of staff to several BND presidents from March 2012 until March 2026, a position that gave him access to sensitive intelligence.

He is accused of aiding attempted treason and espionage involving state secrets.

Both men have been held in pretrial detention since this week.

According to Der Spiegel, the BND had known about Manfred D.'s work for Hanning for some time and had issued an official authorization for the secondary employment.

The agency declined to answer questions about when the authorization was granted or what activities it covered, the magazine said.

Hanning's lawyer has denied wrongdoing, saying his client was being prosecuted unjustly.

He acknowledged that Hanning had possessed confidential documents but denied he had passed on information detrimental to Germany or had done so for payment.

World.title: South Korea warns of AI-aided hacking after bank data breaches
World.content:
Seoul is alarmed after a recent breach of South Korean banks' cyber defenses that reportedly involved AI-assisted hacking. Officials warn such methods could be used to also target other sectors and government agencies.

The South Korean government has demanded a comprehensive overhaul of safeguards against hackers after seven of the nation's major financial institutions' cyber defenses were breached last week and the private data of thousands of customers was leaked.

The data breaches go beyond the financial sector, with two of the largest churches in the country and Korea Electric Power Corp. on Wednesday confirming that their online systems had been illegally accessed, although it is not clear whether the same perpetrator was responsible for all the attacks.

On Tuesday, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook called for measures to be taken swiftly to halt any further leaks.

"This is a serious situation because this incident is believed to have taken advantage of artificial intelligence, and if AI is used in phishing attacks, it could lead to secondary damage," Yonhap News quoted Han as saying at a Cabinet meeting.

"It is also a serious situation in that similar hacking methods could spread beyond the financial sector to industries, as well as government and public sectors."

Cyberattacks: How secure are smart devices really? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Threats to other sectors

Han said government agencies, public institutions, the financial sector and private enterprises all need to "remain vigilant."

Early reports from the US-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike suggest that the attack may have originated in China, although South Korea's Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) said it had identified 28 internet protocol addresses in the United States, Japan, Germany and at least 10 other countries that were involved in the bank breaches.

"South Korea officials are being careful about how they are framing their findings," said Aditya Das, an analyst at cryptocurrency research firm Brave New Coin in Auckland, New Zealand.

In the bank logs, investigators found traces of a tool called ARTEX, an open-source "autonomous penetration-testing" agent built by a Chinese developer, he said.

"It is freely available on the internet and officials have said explicitly that a Chinese-built tool doesn't mean Chinese attackers," Das told DW, adding that the use of multiple IP addresses is likely to be "a ploy by the hackers to hide their tracks."

It appears that the hackers exploited weak authentication protocols in portals used by external loan recruiters, employees' mobile tools and sales-support systems.

How much are hackers making? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Data on thousands of customers lost

According to South Korean media reports, data belonging to as many as 68,000 customers was taken, with Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Hana Bank among the worst affected. Names, phone numbers, annual income figures, loan limits and their loan products were accessed, along with a small number of national identification numbers.

Das pointed out that if a scammer has a person's name, phone number, income figure and is aware that the individual has recently applied for a loan, a fake "bank security" call can be very convincing to the unwary. Once a victim has transferred funds to an account specified by the scammer, it is very difficult to get it back.

Hyobin Lee, a professor at Sogang University in Seoul, says the seriousness of the incident goes far beyond the simple exposure of personal information.

"If criminals obtain such information, they may be able to carry out sophisticated financial fraud, identity theft, or highly targeted phishing attacks," she said.

"Another concern is that stolen personal information can be reused or combined with other leaked databases, potentially creating security risks that persist long after the original attack," Lee underlined.

"More broadly, such incidents can undermine public confidence in financial institutions and raise concerns about the security of the financial system as a whole."

While major financial institutions have invested heavily in protecting their core systems, such as internet banking and mobile banking platforms, Lee said they have overlooked other elements of their networks.

"Some auxiliary systems, such as loan agent information portals and internal mobile applications used by employees, appear to have received less security attention," she said, adding that the application of AI by the hackers is another concerning element.

Is AI the new weapon of mass data theft? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AI makes hacking easier?

"In the past, identifying security vulnerabilities, developing malicious code and conducting attacks against financial institutions required substantial technical expertise and considerable time," Lee pointed out. "Today, generative AI tools can assist with writing computer code, analyzing software vulnerabilities, processing large amounts of information and automating certain stages of cyber operations."

AI is "lowering the technical barriers to cybercrime" and making it accessible to more bad actors. At the same time, the technology is ramping up the speed and scale of attacks to overwhelm cyber defenses.

Given those developments, Lee fears that AI-assisted cyberattacks are only going to become more frequent.

"And the risks will not be limited to financial institutions," she said. "Hospitals, government agencies, energy infrastructure, telecommunications networks and other organizations holding sensitive information may also become increasingly attractive targets."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: India news: Opposition doubles down against poll chief after detentions
World.content:
10/08/2026 October 8, 2026 India's opposition alliance plans third day of protest against election chief

A bloc of Indian political parties, in alliance against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP party, is expected to stage a protest in central Delhi on Thursday to demand the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged misconduct.

Opposition leaders including Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Vadra are visibly at the forefront of the protest.

On Tuesday, Gandhi, Vadra, their supporters and over 200 allied Members of Parliament (MPs) marched on the Election Commission of India (ECI) to demand a meeting with Kumar. When blocked by the Delhi police, they began an impromptu sit in which ended with temporary detentions.

On Wednesday, the INC hosted a lunch-meeting in Delhi for about 200 MPs to discuss action against the CEC. Post lunch, they loaded up in buses to move towards the designated protest site of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi. Eventually on foot, the lawmakers were stopped by the police again.

A live feed on the YouTube channel of Gandhi's party showed police officials taking him into a vehicle and driving away. His sibling and lawmaker Vadra was also detained but taken to a different police station, as per Indian media.

Rahul and Priyanka are siblings, born into one of India's best known political families descending from the nation's first prime minister Image: Vipin/AP Photo/picture alliance

Both were released sometime after 8:00 p.m local time (1430 GMT).

Gandhi and his fellow demonstrators have been demanding meetings with the Election Commission of India, Indian President Droupadi Murmu and a resignation from CEC Kumar.

They claim that Kumar is an agent of the Modi government and has been helping the Bharatiya Janata Party by rigging elections in their favor. These are significant and unprecedented accusations against the ECI — long regarded as one of the India's most trusted independent institutions.

"I am thankful to every INDIA alliance MP standing firm in defense of our democracy - in Parliament, outside on the streets, and today near Jantar Mantar. They can stop a march. They can refuse a meeting. But they cannot stop the will of our people," Gandhi said on a post on X. "Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, Gyanesh Kumar and the entire system will be brought to justice," he wrote.

Modi's party and the election body reject the allegations.

World.title: Security in the Black Sea region: is Bulgaria the weak link in Europe's defense against threats from Russia?
World.content:
Two ships have sunk off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania after drone attacks in recent days. Bulgaria has held back on pointing the finger at Russia. What does that mean for security in the Black Sea and the region?

Although security in the Baltic Sea and the threat of Russian provocation there are the subject of regular public debate, security in the Black Sea is a subject that sometimes gets less attention in the context of Russia's war in Ukraine even though the Black Sea is to a degree an active frontline in the war.

There are multiple reasons why the Black Sea's security is such a complex issue, but two incidents in recent days have highlighted just how precarious the situation there is.

On October 6, drones struck two cargo ships, the Alfa Watan and the Able, in the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.

The Alfa Watan sank, and its crew has not been recovered. Bulgaria conducted a search and rescue operation, which was called off on Wednesday morning.

The crew of the Able, which was damaged, was rescued by a passing Bulgarian ship. Two crew members were taken to the military hospital in Varna.

Crew members from a ship damaged in a drone attack disembark from a Bulgarian border police vessel on Tuesday Image: Petko Momchilov/REUTERS

The day before, another cargo ship, the Royad Mammadov, was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania, killing two crew members.

Multiple recent attacks on ships

These are not isolated incidents. In the past few months, there have been multiple attacks on cargo ships carrying grain from Ukraine.

As a result, doubt is increasingly being cast on the belief that the western part of the Black Sea — the area off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania — is relatively safe.

"Тhe Black Sea front is clearly expanding, and we should no longer look only to the Baltic Sea as a potential avenue for escalation and aggressive actions," said Ruslan Trad, global security expert and non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab.

PM downplays drone attacks

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev downplayed the attack on the ships, remarking that ships are constantly being sunk in the Black Sea and that Tuesday's drone attacks were "probably not the most serious incident."

Bulgaria's government called Tuesday's attack on the two vessels an "absolutely unacceptable violation of international law" but refrained from calling on Russia to end its war against Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on the other hand, was unequivocal. He said that the Ukrainian military had assured Bulgaria that it was not responsible for the attack and pointed the finger squarely at Russia .

After a meeting of the National Security Council on Wednesday, a declaration was issued, which once again did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.

Radev stated that the cargo and the direction of travel of the ships "logically speaking" provide grounds for a hypothesis pointing to Russia but stressed that there is no concrete evidence. He also contradicted Zelenskyy, saying no such conversation had taken place.

Earlier he said that "if the war is not brought to an end in due time, it will continue to expand."

Similarly, Bulgaria's Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said that "we need to support all possible diplomatic efforts to bring this war to an end."

Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev said that there is no concrete evidence that Russia was behind the attack Image: Spasiyana Sergieva/REUTERS

The refusal to state clearly that it is Russian aggression that is putting the region at risk is not new for the Radev administration.

Is Bulgaria a 'weak link' in European defense?

For Rumena Filipova, chairperson of the Institute of Global Analytics, this is an example of how Bulgaria seems to be a weak link in Europe's defense against malicious influence from Russia and China.

"This weakness stems from the lack of a serious institutional response to hybrid attacks of any kind, the absence of appropriate measures and a general tendency to downplay incidents," she told DW.

"The perpetrator is not named explicitly, even though our partners in the European Union and NATO have already issued numerous warnings about what aggressive steps Russia could take against Europe," she said.

According to Filipova, the Bulgarian government's narrative about peace without actually specifying the conditions or consequences for Ukrainian and European security is a demonstration of its leniency toward Moscow and raises the question of Sofia's geopolitical orientation.

No smoking gun

One of the surviving members of the Able's crew has said that he believes it was a Russian strike because the ship was carrying Ukrainian grain.

The cargo vessel Able (pictured here in Istanbul, Turkey, on an unknown date), which was carrying Ukrainian grain, was damaged when hit by a drone on October 6 Image: Tony Hogwood/REUTERS

Trad, the global security expert, says that the crew member's testimony is an eyewitness hypothesis, not hard proof.

"The logic of motive, however, points toward Russia, as it is the state systematically threatening navigation to Ukrainian ports," he told DW, adding, "Until more concrete data is revealed the most accurate phrasing is 'probable but unproven Russian responsibility' without excluding other possibilities."

Trad also pointed out that Bulgarian institutions lack experience in attributing maritime drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone (EEZ). "When the system is uncertain, the safest institutional reaction is to say nothing until certainty is achieved," he said. "That is caution, but it is also a political choice."

Economic consequences

A direct military response or the triggering of NATO's Article 5, which guarantees collective defense in the event of an attack on any member state, should not be expected.

A marine drone, which Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta said was destroyed by F-16 fighter jets in August Image: Radu Miruta via Facebook/Handout/REUTERS

Bulgaria's EEZ in the Black Sea is not Bulgarian sovereign territory and, as such, the strikes on the ships in this zone do not constitute a direct attack on Bulgaria — or on Romania in the case of the Royad Mammadov.

Nevertheless, Trad thinks these three incidents shatter the illusion that the western part of the Black Sea is a safe zone because of the distance between it and the frontlines in Ukraine.

"This will increase pressure for tighter maritime monitoring, anti‑mining capabilities, coordination between coastal guard services and intelligence‑sharing among allies," he said.

"The real effect will be a hardening of the shipping regime: stricter routing recommendations, higher insurance premiums and more difficulty hiring crews. Economic repercussions for local businesses can also be anticipated — imagine the impact on fishermen if they have to stay in ports constantly due to fear of further attacks. That is the intended effect of such strikes," he added.

Rumena Filipova believes that although Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey strengthened their Mine Countermeasures Black Sea Task Group at this year's NATO summit in Ankara, this is not enough.

She says there are far more substantial gaps in naval defense capabilities: "Modernization of Bulgaria's naval forces must be improved, much greater coordination — especially with Romania — is required. Yet, for more than a decade, Bulgarian authorities have downplayed or ignored the idea of developing joint naval defense forces and coordination, and that trend continues today," she said.

Turkey's leverage and China's role

Another question is how Turkey will react to recent developments. All three ships were owned by Turkish firms and some of the crew members were Turkish nationals. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the security of navigation in the Black Sea.

Another cargo ship, the Royad Mammadov, was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania on October 5. Pictured here: Firefighters and rescue workers wait to help the survivors Image: Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout/REUTERS

Trad notes that Ankara has several levers of influence in the Black Sea: control of the Straits under the Montreux Convention, the largest fleet in the Black Sea and its role as a mediator between Moscow and Kyiv.

"A realistic scenario is intensified diplomacy, coordination with Bucharest and Sofia, and pressure for safe navigation, probably within the existing trilateral anti‑mining cooperation. If it turns out that Turkish citizens were killed in a deliberate attack, Ankara's stance could become markedly tougher," he said.

Filipova thinks that Black Sea security is already being perceived as a core issue — not only for the region but for NATO as a whole.

In her view, there's not enough coordination between the countries in the region, which means that any response to threats does not come from a united front — something she feels has to change urgently.

Filipova says that China's influence in the region and how it's connected with Russia is another factor.

"We see not only the concrete military threat from Russia but also a subtler threat from China, which is less publicly discussed. But Beijing is trying to acquire strategic assets in ports, thereby gaining influence over both trade and critical infrastructure," she said. "Given that China and Russia cooperate closely, this constitutes a double threat for the Black Sea region."

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: French police arrest 5 suspects over Renoir museum theft
World.content:
Thieves broke into the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera last month and made off with two paintings. The heist follows a string of high-profile robberies from European museums.

French police have arrested at least five suspects in connection with the theft of two Renoir paintings from a museum in southern France last month, local media reported.

Two burglars cut through a fence and smashed a window to enter the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on September 8. They then used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, according to the local mayor.

The thieves initially took four Renoir artworks, valued together at around €9 million ($10.5 million), but dropped two in the museum's garden as they fled from police who had been alerted by the alarm system.

The daily Nice Martin newspaper, which first broke the news of the arrests, said six people were taken into custody, including the two suspected burglars.

Prosecutors in Marseille, who are leading the investigation, declined to comment.

The Renoir Museum is housed in the last home of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir Image: Johanna Hoelzl/picture alliance

What happened to the artworks?

The two paintings stolen from the museum were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

Nice Martin reported that the whereabouts of the artworks was not immediately known.

Founded in 1960, the Renoir Museum is located in the former home and studio of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir on the Cote d'Azur. The property houses 12 of his artworks and is surrounded by gardens and olive trees.

The heist in Cagnes-sur-Mer was the latest in a series of museum robberies, including the daylight theft of the French crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year.

Four suspects have been arrested over that case, but the jewels they are accused of taking, with a value of around $100 million, have not been recovered.

World.title: How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited the UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands
World.content:
Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now, the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.

Home to fewer than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines.

However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in the North Falkland Basin is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago.

Argentina has laid claim to the islands, which it calls Las Malvinas, for two centuries. In 1982, the dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a war between the UK and Argentina, though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands.

A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory.

The Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface. Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project was stopped within two weeks.

The oil project is being run by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028.

Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Rally around the flag?

Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim."

He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina.

"When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said.

Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falkand Islands' Legislative Assembly Image: Legislative Assembly of the Falkland Islands

Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism."

Howerver, he thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure."

Potentially transformative for the Falklands

Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned.

The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years.

That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP, which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful.

"It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible."

However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz.

Argentina's President Javier Milei says he is taking legal action against the Sea Lion oilfield project Image: Argentina's Presidency Press Office/AFP

Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were Milei's legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains.

"When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer.

However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years.

"They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us."

More economic pressure from Argentina

Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare."

Many international suppliers and shipping companies already refuse to supply the Falklands for fear of angering Argentina. Now, Milei's government has initiated sanctions against 60 people involved in the Sea Lion project.

The project could transform the Falklands' small economy Image: Ashley Cooper/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

In a televised address last month, the Argentine president also vowed to sanction the companies involved in the project. Such a move could cast doubt on the project, which previously collapsed in 2014 and 2020, due to financing troubles, oil-price weakness and delays caused by sanctions.

Navitas this week confirmed that two contractors had pulled out of the project due to sanctions concerns, and that it was replacing them. There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with US President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."

Bragger played this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer said it would be "very shocking" if the US came down on the side of Argentina.

While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.

"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

World.title: Nobel Prize in literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson
World.content:
Carson won for her "bold and inventive oeuvre." The decorated poet and essayist is known for her reverence for Latin and Greek classics.

The Swedish Academy awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature to Anne Carson on Thursday, praising her "bold and inventive oeuvre."

Her work has "in playful dialogue with the classical tradition...created new forms for contemporary literature," said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy.

The 76-year-old writer is a longtime professor of classics, creative writing, and comparative literature at prestigious institutions like McGill and Princeton universities. She is only the 19th woman of 123 laureates to win the award.

What is Anne Carson known for?

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson moved with her family among several small towns in Canada during her youth. She has credited a beloved Latin teacher for sparking her interest in language and classics.

Her first book of criticism, 1986’s Eros the Bittersweet, was published to great acclaim and has had significant influence on other classicists, poets, and even film and television. Carson has also published her own poetry such as the 2001 collection The Beauty of the Husband as well as highly regard translation of ancient Greek poets such as Sappho and Sophocles.

Carson is also heavily influenced by the King James Bible and more modern writers including Emily Dickinson and Virginia Woolf. She has received numerous awards such as the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur fellowship, and the PEN/Nabokov Award.

Deeply private, Carson often declines to speak about her personal life in interviews and discourages autobiographical interpretations of her work. However, she did revealed in 2024 that she has Parkinson's disease.

Who else has received a Nobel Prize so far?

What happens next?

The winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature receives prize money of 12 million Swedish kronor, equivalent to about $1.2 million. The winner also receives a medal and a diploma at an official ceremony in December, and is expected to deliver a speech known as a Nobel lecture.

On Friday, the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced, followed by the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel on Monday.
