World.title: Warsaw records EU’s highest employment rate
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data. The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013. Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%. The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030. At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%). After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU. In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%). And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%). Poland's unemployment rate of 2.6% in January is the lowest ever recorded in the country by @EU_Eurostat and was the joint-lowest that month among all EU member states For more, read our full report here: https://t.co/eP5A9JT4eg pic.twitter.com/A9oHu2zLZ6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%. The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation. At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts. World.title: Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, finds UN study
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Ukrainian refugees boosted the size of Poland’s economy by 2.4% last year, the equivalent of 94 billion zloty (€21.5 billion), according to a new report by the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and accounting firm Deloitte. The refugees’ level of employment has now also surpassed that of Polish citizens, but their growing presence in the labour market has had no negative impact on employment or wages for other workers, finds the study. “Refugees from Ukraine in Poland have entered a new phase characterised by deeper economic integration, increasing labour market participation, and a gradual transition from emergency support mechanisms towards long-term integration into public institutions,” wrote the UNHCR and Deloitte. 📉Facts matter. Refugees from Ukraine contributed 2.4% of Poland’s GDP in 2025, says new analysis by UNHCR and Deloitte. This is what happens when people forced to flee are given the opportunity to rebuild their lives with dignity. The full report: https://t.co/egUp8jjCwc pic.twitter.com/CSNONqdKGU — UNHCR Polska (@UNHCRPoland) October 1, 2026 The findings come in the latest edition of an annual report analysing the economic impact of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom were living in Poland in 2025. Modelling carried out by Deloitte showed that their presence is having an increasingly positive effect: in 2025, Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4%, compared to 2.3% in 2024, 2.0% in 2022 and 1.5% in 2022. Deloitte forecasts that the figure will rise to 2.8% by 2035 as Ukrainians integrate further. The company’s latest figures for 2023 and 2024 differ from those published in last year’s report, with Deloitte saying that it now uses a modelling strategy that is “similar to” but “improved” from before. The report also notes that the figure for 2025 likely understates the economic impact of Ukrainians who arrived in Poland as refugees, given that many – especially the most economically integrated – have shifted from refugee status to other forms of residency, meaning they do not count towards Deloitte’s data. The employment rate among Ukrainian refugees in Poland rose from 61% in 2023 to 76% in 2025. The latter figure was slightly higher than the rate among Polish citizens. However, the report notes that Ukrainian refugees are far more likely to be employed on a more precarious basis than native workers: only 42% have standard employment contracts, compared to 80% among Polish citizens. Ukrainian refugees also much more often work in positions they are overqualified for, while their median wage is only around 85% of the figure among all workers in Poland. Meanwhile, the report finds that, “contrary to concerns that a large increase in labour supply would negatively affect Polish workers, there is no evidence of deterioration in employment outcomes or wages”. In fact, employment among Polish citizens has continued to rise. The number of foreign workers in Poland rose 7.2% last year to reach 1.14 million. Immigrants now make up almost 7% of all workers. While Ukrainians remain by far the largest group, the fastest-growing nationalities last year were Colombians and Indians https://t.co/E0LNJXyyTx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 9, 2026 Through their high levels of employment, Ukrainian refugees also contribute to Poland’s public finances via taxes and social security contributions. The report estimates that general government revenues are 2.6% higher because of refugee-related economic activity. Meanwhile, although “the arrival of refugees from Ukraine represented a major stress test for the Polish healthcare system…healthcare expenditures on refugees remain substantially lower on a per-capita basis than expenditures on Polish residents”. At the same time, Poland’s understaffed hospitals have been boosted by the arrival of thousands of Ukrainian doctors, dentists, nurses and midwives. Ukrainians do have access to Polish social benefits, such as grants for children, but these account for only 10% of income in Ukrainian refugee households. The vast majority, 87%, is earned through work. Ukrainian immigrants pay more in taxes than they receive in benefits, a report by Poland's National Development Bank has concluded. The research also indicated that Ukrainians contribute between 0.5% and 2.4% to Poland's annual GDP growth https://t.co/KhXxLtif5W — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2025 The report notes that the status of Ukrainian refugees in Poland is becoming increasingly normalised, pointing to changes in Polish government policy introduced earlier this year that meant they no longer had special status. Meanwhile, surveys show a weakening of refugees’ intentions to eventually return to Ukraine. Research by the National Bank of Poland (NBP) found that the proportion who plan to settle permanently in Poland rose from 21% to 25% between 2024 and 2025. However, UNHRC’s report also highlights the negative shift in attitudes towards Ukrainian refugees in recent months, with a July poll showing for the first time that a majority of Poles are opposed to accepting refugees from Ukraine. Poland will examine whether Paramount Skydance can take control of TVN, one of the country’s leading broadcasters, following its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns TVN. The review is being conducted under a law that requires state approval for ownership changes of companies designated by the government as strategic and protected from takeovers deemed to threaten the national interest. TVN was added to the list in 2024, following reports of its possible sale. Minister Aktywów Państwowych zajmie się przejęciem TVN przez grupę Paramount Skydance#PAPinformacjehttps://t.co/FxxDnozx9i — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) October 6, 2026 Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, one of the largest mergers in the global media market, brings together major US media assets including Paramount’s CBS and MTV and Warner’s HBO, CNN and Discovery Channel. After the deal was completed on Tuesday, Poland’s state assets ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that, because the acquisition would give Paramount Skydance indirect control of TVN, the new owner must notify the ministry of the takeover. The ministry then has 90 days to “conduct an administrative investigation into this matter to verify the impact of the transaction on security or public order in Poland”. The ministry can either approve the change of ownership or block the new owner from controlling TVN. In the latter case, the state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, may order the sale of TVN’s shares. “I assure you that it will be an entirely substantive and objective administrative procedure, carried out in fulfilment of a statutory obligation, and nothing more,” Balczun told broadcaster Kanał Zero on Tuesday. The procedure is necessary because the Polish government added TVN and another large private broadcaster, Polsat, to its list of strategic companies in December 2024, bringing them under state protection against takeovers considered aggressive or contrary to the national interest. That move came amid reports that Warner Bros. Discovery was considering selling TVN and that a businessman linked to Hungary’s then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, an ally of Poland’s conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, was seeking to buy it. 🎙️Minister @wbalczun w @OficjalneZero o przeprowadzeniu postępowania ws. przejęcia TVN przez grupę Paramount Skydance: bardziej bym skupił się na organie, czyli ministrze aktywów państwowych. To jest odpersonalizowana procedura administracyjna, która wynika z ustawy o kontroli… pic.twitter.com/jp3J9zC0jh — Ministerstwo Aktywów Państwowych 🇵🇱 (@MAPGOVPL) October 7, 2026 Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at the time the move was intended to protect the broadcaster from hostile foreign takeovers and prevent foreign interference in Poland’s media and elections. TVN, which was originally founded in 1995, has been in American hands since 2015, when it was bought by US broadcaster Scripps, which was in turn acquired by Discovery in 2018. The station, which is known for taking a liberal position on many issues, has long been a target for Polish conservatives. In 2021, the then-PiS government passed a law that would have forced Warner Bros. Discovery to sell its majority stake. However, that was vetoed by then-President Andrzej Duda. Poland is adding the country’s two largest private TV stations, Polsat and TVN, to its list of “strategic companies” under special protection. That allows the government to block the sale of the firms to owners from “hostile states”, says PM @donaldtusk https://t.co/TwK9IFRPrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2024 Some in Poland have expressed fear that Paramount could push TVN in a more conservative direction, as it has been accused of doing with other media outlets it has acquired, notably US broadcaster CBS. Paramount’s owner, David Ellison, is a Trump ally, as are PiS and Poland’s current president, Karol Nawrocki. On Sunday, the Journalists’ Association, a Polish organisation representing journalists, called on TVN’s management to establish an editorial independence council similar to those being created at CNN and CBS under the settlement deal that paved the way for the merger in the US. Media reports claim that President Trump tried to persuade Poland's defence minister to leave the government and form a coalition with the right-wing opposition. We outline what is known so far and how the government, including PM @donaldtusk, has reacted https://t.co/m04H8VgoSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 5, 2026 In July, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) also raised concerns about the potential impact of the merger on TVN’s editorial independence, citing the new ownership structure and the risk of political interference. The NGO called for guarantees protecting the channel as a condition of approval for the takeover from the European Commission. The EU executive, however, approved the deal in July without imposing such conditions, following an antitrust review. The commission’s approval covered the entire European Union, meaning that national competition authorities have no grounds to challenge the deal, Tomasz Chróstny, head of Poland’s consumer protection authority UOKiK, told news service Wirtualna Polska before the transaction was completed. World.title: Poland launches new combat uniforms, including first designed for female soldiers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has launched new combat uniforms for its army. It is the first time that the designs have been updated in 33 years, and also the first time that they include a version specially created for women, who now make up around 16% of soldiers. “A soldier’s safety and comfort during service are paramount,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, announcing the new uniforms, which have been undergoing testing by various branches of the military, “[They are] adapted to the needs of women and men serving in the Polish army, because both deserve not only respect and gratitude, but also the creation of conditions that will encourage service as much as possible,” he added. The new tactical uniform features new camouflage patterns that are intended to better reflect the colours and shadows found in natural environments, “allowing the soldier to remain invisible for as long as possible”. According to the armed forces, testing shows it provides 30% better camouflage effectiveness. The defence ministry says that the outfits, which will be produced completely in Poland, are created from “lighter, more flexible and durable materials” than before. The women’s version features a more “closely fitted shape” with a “choice of tops and bottoms to suit women’s figures”, allowing “greater freedom of movement”. Wreszcie mamy mundur dedykowany dla kobiet – żołnierzy! Dzisiaj w polskiej armii 16% żołnierzy to kobiety, a Wojskach Obrony Terytorialnej to ponad 20%. Nie pozwolę nikomu obrażać i zbijać kapitału politycznego na tym, że próbuje się dyskredytować kobiety w mundurach.… pic.twitter.com/GzJOhkwgTO — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) October 5, 2026 “For the first time in the history of the Polish military, female soldiers will no longer have to choose the size that fits them from men’s uniforms,” said deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak. She noted that women now make up 16% of soldiers in the army, and as much as 20% of those serving in the Territorial Defence Force (WOT), a volunteer reserve formation. Kosiniak-Kamysz says that the new uniforms, which cost around 1,000 zloty (€228) each, will be rolled out gradually, with 7,500 delivered this year. The defence ministry recently signed an agreement with logistics giant InPost to use its parcel lockers to deliver uniforms to soldiers. Poland has dramatically increased the size of its armed forces in recent years. NATO figures show that the number of Polish military personnel has risen from 101,600 in 2016 to an estimated 263,600 this year. That means Poland now has the alliance’s largest armed forces in continental Europe, ahead of France (202,000), Italy (191,600) and Germany (183,200). In NATO as a whole, only the United States (1.3 million) and Turkey (395,800) have more military personnel. Meanwhile, both the number and proportion of women serving in the armed forces have increased dramatically. In 2015, there were only 4,000 professional female soldiers in Poland, a number that has now risen to almost 37,000. Poland has NATO’s third-largest military and the alliance’s largest in Europe, new figures show. For more, see our full report here: https://t.co/QBBVQ9cqzS pic.twitter.com/TA34KQrJ4k — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2024 “Women soldiers contribute significant value to the functioning of the armed forces,” said General Wiesław Kukuła, chief of the general staff of the Polish armed forces, earlier this year. “They successfully perform not only support tasks, but increasingly often stand alongside male soldiers in strictly combat roles,” he added. “They pilot aircraft and helicopters, serve on ships, operate missile systems, and serve in special units.” “Their service is guided by the overarching principle that it is not gender, but physical attributes, competence and determination that define a soldier ready to succeed.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Sweden to deploy Patriot air defence systems to Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Sweden has announced that it will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine. The decision follows a number of other recent moves to strengthen defence ties between Stockholm and Warsaw, with Poland’s defence minister today hailing Sweden as an “excellent, proven ally”. Sweden is deploying the Patriot air defence system to Poland to strengthen the protection of @NATO’s eastern flank. The Swedish forces will protect the logistics hub in south-eastern Poland that plays a key role in providing military and civilian support to Ukraine 🇺🇦. pic.twitter.com/EjGFYFLGnN — Försvarsmakten (@Forsvarsmakten) October 6, 2026 The Patriot deployment was announced on Tuesday by Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, days after Sweden had also revealed that its Gripen fighter aircraft would patrol Polish airspace from October. “The task for both the Gripen operation and Patriot [system] is to protect NATO’s logistics hub in Poland at the airport [in Rzeszów],” said Kristersson at a press conference alongside foreign minister Maria Malmer and defence minister Pål Jonson “[We will] thus ensure that important equipment comes to Ukraine from all the countries that support Ukraine in its defence against Russia,” he added. “This all strengthens NATO, strengthens Europe and strengthens Sweden.” Jonson added that “repeated violations of allied airspace and Russian attempts to influence support for Ukraine show the importance of protecting the logistics hub in Poland”. Malmer, meanwhile, made clear that the deployment was intended not only to protect supply lines to Ukraine, but “is also part of our contribution to NATO’s deterrence and defence”. Sweden will deploy its Patriots to Rzeszów in December and plans for them to remain there until the middle of next year. It will take over the mission from the Netherlands, which has had two of its Patriot batteries in Poland since last December. Colonel Sofia Westermark, the commander of Sweden’s air defence regiment, told broadcaster SVT that the deployment would be “the most complex operation that Sweden has undertaken as a NATO ally”. The country joined the alliance in 2024. Sweden will deploy Gripen aircraft to Poland to strengthen NATO’s eastern flank. Poland is a close ally and a vital hub for support to Ukraine. Swedish security is built together with our allies in NATO, and by taking responsibility together. (1/3) pic.twitter.com/4WaSp2UqYD — Pål Jonson (@PlJonson) September 30, 2026 Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, thanked both Sweden and the Netherlands for their role in defending Polish airspace and NATO’s eastern flank. “The continuity of this mission is an expression of allied solidarity and shared responsibility for the region’s security in the face of the threat from Russia. Together we are stronger,” he wrote on social media. His deputy minister, Paweł Zalewski, told broadcaster TVN that Patriot systems “are currently the only ones effective against ballistic missiles”, making them vital for protecting Rzeszów. He noted that around 90% of international aid for Ukraine goes through the hub. Poland has also been taking delivery of its own Patriot systems from the United States. The first were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport in 2023. Last year, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries. Dziękuję rządowi Szwecji za podjęcie decyzji o wysłaniu do Polski systemów Patriot. Szwedzi przejmą ochronę hubu logistycznego NATO w Rzeszowie. Dziękuję także Holandii 🇳🇱 za dotychczasowe wsparcie Polski i wschodniej flanki NATO. Ciągłość tej misji to wyraz sojuszniczej… — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 6, 2026 Earlier this year, Poland’s airspace was violated by a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, which landed in a field. On one night last year, around 20 Russian drones crossed the country’s eastern borders, and last month a Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad. Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. The growing threat from Russia has pushed Poland to forge closer military ties with other countries around the Baltic Sea, and above all with Sweden. In 2024, the two countries signed a strategic partnership to enhance cooperation on defence and economic development. Since then, they have held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic; Poland has ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab; and Sweden bought €274 million worth of Piorun man-portable air-defence systems from Polish firm Mesko. World.title: Prague 7 Turns Streets Into Outdoor Art With Designs by Local Children
World.content:
Prague 7 has transformed several streets around local schools with large-scale colorful paintings created with the help of local schoolchildren.

The new artwork can be seen on Rajská, Plynární, Jablonského and Antonínská streets, as well as part of Bubenská Street. The municipality placed the designs mainly near schools and along busy pedestrian routes.



On Antonínská Street, students from grades five through eight at Strossmayerovo Square Elementary School helped create the artwork. They produced the original drawings, which artist Jakub Karlík then combined into the final design.

Several other educational institutions are located close to the painted streets, including Bratrská Elementary School, the Holešovice Business Academy, the Higher Vocational School of Fashion Design and the Secondary Industrial School of Fashion Design.

The new designs have received mostly positive reactions from local residents. Comments on Prague 7’s Facebook page described the streets as more cheerful and said the artwork had made the area more interesting.

There has also been criticism, particularly over the cost and the practical impact of painting the asphalt. Some residents questioned whether the project was necessary and raised concerns about the roughness of the surface, pedestrian movement and whether the paint could become slippery.

Prague 7 said anti-slip paint was used, similar to materials applied to cycle paths and sports surfaces.

The project cost 755,000 CZK, covering the designs, preparation, materials and application. According to Prague 7 spokesperson Martin Vokuš, each of the two phases took around 20 days.

The municipality awarded the contract directly to Karlík. Before selecting his proposal for the Antonínská and Bubenská sections, Prague 7 compared three offers and chose his as the most advantageous.

World.title: Beer Consumption in Czech Republic Falls to Lowest Level on Record
World.content:
Czech beer consumption fell to its lowest level on record in 2025, with the average resident drinking 121 liters during the year, according to data from the Czech Association of Breweries and Malt Houses (ČSPS).

Total domestic consumption reached 14.86 million hectoliters, down 3.2% from 2024. The figure is the lowest recorded since nationwide beer consumption statistics began.

Overall beer production in the Czech Republic also declined last year. Breweries produced 19.96 million hectoliters of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer, 4.3% less than in 2024.



The decline affected nearly every category, with non-alcoholic beer the main exception. Production of non-alcoholic and flavored non-alcoholic beer increased by 4% to 1.68 million hectoliters.

Demand for non-alcoholic beer has been rising steadily for more than a decade. Between 2019 and 2024 alone, production increased by around 50%.

Pubs lose ground as more Czechs drink at home

The shift in drinking habits is particularly visible in restaurants and pubs. Draft beer accounted for 28% of beer sold on the Czech market in 2025, down one percentage point from the previous year.

The longer-term decline is more significant. Draft beer represented 35% of sales in 2019 and 51% in 2008.

The ČSPS said the figures reflect changes in consumer behavior, including greater interest in moderation and healthier lifestyles. When Czechs do go out for beer, they are increasingly looking for quality and variety rather than simply drinking larger quantities.

Czech beer exports also decline

Exports followed the domestic market downward. Czech breweries exported 5.48 million hectoliters of beer in 2025, an 8.2% decrease compared with the previous year.

European Union countries accounted for around 90% of Czech beer exports, with Germany and Slovakia among the largest buyers.

Imports also declined, falling by 18.3% year on year. Foreign beer accounted for only 2.5% of total beer consumption in the Czech Republic, down 0.5 percentage points from 2024.

World.title: Nearly Half of Czechs Spend More Than 30% of Their Income on Housing
World.content:
Nearly half of people in the Czech Republic spend more than 30% of their net income on housing, while around one in 10 spends more than half.

Housing is generally considered financially burdensome when rent, utilities and other related costs exceed 30–40% of household income. The EU average is around 24%.



The findings come from a survey by Česká spořitelna and Evropa v datech, conducted with Ipsos among 1,000 respondents in February.

Housing affordability remains particularly difficult for young Czechs. Among people aged 18 to 29, 58% live with their parents at least part of the time, while 29% live with friends or a partner.

The survey found that 60% of people under 30 who are dissatisfied with their housing situation have postponed a major life decision because of it. For around one-third, this has happened repeatedly. Starting a family is among the decisions affected by housing conditions.

Homeowners were considerably more likely to be very satisfied than renters, with 41% of owners describing themselves as very satisfied compared with 18% of renters.

Czechia still has the least affordable housing in the EU

The Czech Republic improved by six places in this year’s housing conditions ranking, reaching 17th among the 27 EU member states. The improvement was linked to increased investment in residential construction, fewer households facing excessive housing costs or difficulties paying for heating, and relatively favorable rental conditions.

Buying a home, however, remains more difficult than elsewhere in the EU.

An average-sized Czech apartment costs 13.3 average annual gross salaries, compared with 13.6 a year earlier. The figure has improved only slightly, while other countries have made faster progress. In Hungary, the ratio fell from 13.6 to 11.9 annual salaries, while Slovakia improved from 13.2 to 11.7 and Slovenia from 13.4 to 11.4.

Ireland has the most affordable housing by this measure, with an average home costing 6.2 annual salaries, followed by Belgium and Finland.

An average apartment in Czechia costs roughly the equivalent of 29 years of average rent. In city centers, the figure is close to 31 years, compared with less than 13 years in Ireland.

High housing costs are changing household decisions

Housing expenses are also forcing some households to reduce other spending. Last year, 40% cut their budgets because of housing costs. Nearly one-quarter reduced spending on holidays, hobbies and entertainment, while 16% cut spending on essentials such as food, clothing and personal-care products.

Around 38% of Czechs see living with parents as an economic necessity caused by high property prices. Another 26% consider it a reasonable temporary solution, while 9.4% see multigenerational living as a viable long-term model.

At the same time, 46% of young people expect to inherit property from their families.

World.title: Famous Dancing House Photo Spot in Prague Is Set for a Major Makeover
World.content:
Jiráskovo Square in Prague is set for a major redesign that will change one of the city’s best-known photo spots near the Dancing House.

The project, estimated to cost around CZK 35 million, will replace part of the damaged lawn with paving, restore a historic fountain and move the monument to writer Alois Jirásek.



The Prague 2 district plans to carry out the transformation over the next two years. The redesign is based on a 2022 study prepared by archiF studio.

The square’s lawn has long been a problem. Its location directly opposite the Dancing House makes it a popular stopping point for tourists, many of whom step onto the grass to take photographs with the distinctive building in the background.

One of the most common poses involves visitors appearing to support the Dancing House with their foot or kick it. The repeated foot traffic has left the grass heavily damaged, despite attempts to restore it.

Under the new plans, part of the lawn will be replaced with a paved surface. This will create a more durable area for visitors to take photographs while reducing pressure on the remaining greenery.

Historic fountain to return to operation

The redesign will also restore the Cubist fountain created by architect Vlastislav Hofman. The area around the fountain will be repaved, while the fountain itself will be returned to its original appearance and function.

Water is expected to flow through the fountain again after decades.

Architect Soňa Formanová, one of the project’s authors, said the team was able to locate Hofman’s original documentation, including plans covering the fountain and the approaches to the nearby bridge.

The project will also introduce a raised edge around the lawn that can be used for seating. New flowerbeds and trees are planned for the northern part of the square, while existing shrubs considered unsuitable for the area will be removed.

The monument to Alois Jirásek, the Czech writer after whom the square is named, will be relocated to the center of the small park.

World.title: Queer Arts Festival PINKBUS Returns With New Performances and International Guests
World.content:
The PINKBUS Festival will return to Prague on November 3-14 with several days of theatre, dance, drag, music, visual art and performance.

This year’s edition, titled Forward March!, will focus on the need to keep moving forward amid an uncertain social and political climate.

Organised by the PINKBUS queer arts platform, the festival aims to create a space for artists and audiences to meet, experiment and share experiences. The programme combines established artists with new projects and will also mark the beginning of a new season for the platform.



One of the highlights of this year’s festival will be the premiere of two original works developed through the PINKBUS open call First Ride.

Richard Eliáš, an Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague (AVU) student, will present the interdisciplinary drag fantasy I Guess It’s Kind of My Fault, or What?. The second project, by the performative art collective Izbová teplota & Alejandra, is Štúrovci Went to Devín and Had Some Fun, offering a new and unconventional take on the group of Slovak national revival figures known as the Štúrovci.

The festival will also feature international guests. French artists Nicolas Poggi and Giselle Hauscarriaga will present SUDOR (Sweat), a Czech premiere performed with a local cast. The post-performative work explores physical exhaustion, sweat and the limits of the body.

Another premiere, Lipsync Her Name… Because It’s Precious, is being created in collaboration with the Italian festival RAINBOW.IT and Slovak organisation DRAMA QUEER. The performance focuses on three figures from European LGBTQIA+ history: Lucy Salani, Romina Cecconi and Ota Tasinata.

Directed by Tomáš “Grófka” Procházka, the production combines three monodramatic sketches exploring identity and the determination to remain true to oneself. The cast includes Italian actor Antonello Foddis and his drag alter ego La Trave Nell’Okkio, as well as Czech performer Venice, also known as Martin Talaga.

The programme will also include the PINKPANEL discussion series. This year’s edition, titled (The Tinsmith’s) Hammer Against Queerness, will examine the potential impact of current cultural policy on LGBTQIA+ artistic production and discuss possible forms of resistance.

The festival will conclude with a special BEST OF edition of the PINKBUS variety show, featuring Venice, Just Karen, La Cuntessa, Tonic Garbáge, Helena Araujo and other performers, alongside special guests.

World.title: Roger Waters Brings New Pink Floyd Show to Prague in June 2027
World.content:
Roger Waters will bring a new Pink Floyd concert production to Prague next year, with LEGACY – A Pink Floyd Show scheduled for June 8, 2027, at O2 universum.

The new production has been created under Waters’ direction and will feature a ten-piece band led by his son, Harry Waters. The Prague show will focus on music from what is widely regarded as Pink Floyd’s most influential period, spanning 1971 to 1979.



The setlist will draw from four of the band’s best-known albums: The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

The music will be accompanied by a new visual production featuring high-resolution LED screens and imagery inspired by Pink Floyd’s original artwork and stage concepts.

Harry Waters will serve as the show’s musical director, performing on Hammond B3 organ and piano while also contributing vocals. He has a long history with the band’s music and spent more than 15 years performing alongside his father on major tours, including The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.

His connection to Pink Floyd goes back even further. As a child, Harry’s voice appeared on “Goodbye Blue Sky” from The Wall. He also saw the original The Wall concert production at a young age.

The band includes drummer Graham Broad, guitarist Edo Scordo, bassist and backing vocalist Dahniel Knight, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Ryan Saranich, keyboardist Matt Riddle, lead vocalist Clifton David Broadbridge and backing vocalists Eva Avila and Genevieve Little.

Roger Waters co-founded Pink Floyd in 1965 and became the band’s principal lyricist and conceptual leader following Syd Barrett’s departure. He played a central role in the creation of albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

Ticket prices start at 1,600 CZK

Live Nation Club and O2 presale starts October 8, 2026, at 10:00 AM

Tickets on sale via Ticketmaster and Ticketportal starting October 9, 2026, at 10:00 AM

World.title: GALLERY: Vltava Philharmonic Reveals Its Interiors for the First Time
World.content:
Prague’s planned Vltava Philharmonic has offered the first detailed look inside the building, releasing visualizations of its main foyer and the spaces serving its three principal concert halls.

The interior design will combine wood, glass and stone, with flowing shapes inspired by the Vltava River and the building’s distinctive sloping roof. The plans also emphasize open public spaces designed to connect the concert halls with the rest of the building.



The main foyer will be dominated by a large glass wall extending across several floors. Its curved geometry is intended to echo the movement of the Vltava and will separate the open foyer from other areas of the building.

Light-colored solid wood panels will cover the ceilings, following the contours of the roof above. Stone elements will be used in areas connecting the public foyer with the foyer of the main concert hall, including spaces designed for both seating and standing around bar counters.

´

The project has become significantly more expensive

The cost of the Vltava Philharmonic has increased sharply since the project was first estimated.

In 2021, the projected construction cost was CZK 6.1 billion. After the Danish architecture studio Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) won the international competition in 2022, the estimate rose to CZK 9.4 billion.

A more detailed architectural study completed in 2024 put the figure at CZK 11.65 billion. The latest estimate is CZK 11.98 billion for the building itself.

Once improvements to the surrounding area are included, the overall project is expected to cost almost CZK 17 billion.

Construction could begin in 2028

The city expects to obtain the permit in the first quarter of 2027. A general contractor would then be selected, with construction currently scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2028.

Trial operations are planned to begin in 2033.

The Vltava Philharmonic will occupy three underground and six above-ground floors. In addition to five concert halls, the complex will include facilities for the Czech Philharmonic and the Prague Symphony Orchestra (FOK), a music department operated by the Municipal Library of Prague, a creative hub, a restaurant and publicly accessible terraces.

The building is being designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, whose proposal was selected in the international architectural competition in 2022.

World.title: Up to 80 Startups to Pitch Investors at Prague’s Engaged Investments Conference
World.content:
The international Engaged Investments conference, taking place on October 21 and 22, 2026, is significantly expanding its scope this year.

The event, which brings hundreds of startup investors from all over Europe to Prague, is now fully opening its doors to tech founders and the broader innovation ecosystem.



Alongside the main program, the two-day event will feature two specialized industry tracks focusing on fintech and defense, pitches from up to 80 startups, and an extended accompanying program.

Real defense instead of geopolitical theories

The defense track is being organized in collaboration with the Invest in Bravery initiative, which is deeply involved in the Ukrainian ecosystem, alongside the European EUDIS Matchmaking program for defense and Cassini Matchmaking for space technologies.

A special guest will be Senior Lieutenant Mykyta Puz, Defense Industry Liaison Officer of the Azov Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine. He previously worked in business and AI product management before volunteering for the front lines in 2024.

He will shed light on what a modern army truly and urgently needs from the defense industry. Alongside him, speakers will include Erin Hallock, Managing Partner of the NATO Innovation Fund, a representative of the renowned Ukrainian fund Brave1, and others.

Fintech that solves business, not theory

The UnBundled Fintech track, which will run throughout the second day of the conference, is being prepared by The FinTechers in collaboration with Mastercard. The goal is to connect the traditional banking sector with technology companies and investors. The program will focus on stablecoins and tokenization, operational resilience of banks, liability for fraudulent payments, and the deployment of artificial intelligence in financial services.

In addition to new technologies, it will address what European companies need to grow into global players without relying on American capital and infrastructure.

Speakers will include Michal Vodrážka, Director of the Payment Systems Regulation Division at the Czech National Bank. In a debate with Jiří Raška, Chief Technology Officer of Partners Banka, he’ll raise the question of who takes the hit when a payment ends up in a fraudster’s hands. It’s a timely topic, with mandatory payee verification coming in 2027.

The block dedicated to stablecoins and new financial infrastructure will be opened by Dorothea Ysenburg, Vice President of Global Partnerships for Digital Assets and Blockchain at Mastercard. Maryna Muntian from J.P. Morgan will also present, discussing why Central European banks and investors still lack mutual trust when looking at the same deals.

A place where startups find real investors

Closing investments is one of the core components of the conference, which last year attracted investors from more than 20 countries. Up to 80 selected startups, ranging from early-stage to Series A, will have the opportunity to pitch their companies in three minutes to investors actively investing in their respective segments. This year will introduce new dedicated pitching blocks for startups in the fields of financial technology, defense, and space.

On October 22, the best fintech projects from the two-day “Coding the Future of Finance” hackathon—organized on October 19 and 20 by The FinTechers together with Deloitte, AWS, and other partners—will also be presented to investors.

World.title: Budapest’s Castle District votes on Airbnb ban: majority back a complete shutdown
World.content:
A majority of residents who took part in a local vote in Budapest’s District 1 support completely banning short-term rentals such as Airbnb, although the result does not automatically introduce a ban.

Majority back a complete ban

A total of 4,503 residents took part in an online consultation on the future of short-term accommodation in District 1, according to Mayor László Böröcz.

Of those who voted, 58.6% supported a complete ban on short-term property rentals, while 41.4% said a full ban was unnecessary.

Among those opposing a complete ban, 18% supported allowing short-term rentals subject to local conditions, while 23.4% wanted them to continue without restrictions. According to budavar.hu, the consultation was open to the district’s 21,450 eligible permanent residents, giving it a 21% participation rate.

The highest level of support for a ban was recorded in the Buda Castle area, where 66% of participants backed a complete prohibition.

No automatic Airbnb ban yet

The result does not mean that short-term rentals will immediately be banned in District 1. The local government will use residents’ views alongside an impact assessment to prepare a regulatory proposal. The concept will be published for public consultation before a formal regulation is drafted.

According to the municipality’s plans, the draft regulation could reach the relevant committees and the district council in November. Mayor Böröcz said the aim was to ensure that Buda Castle remains a liveable and peaceful home for local residents in the long term, while making local rules transparent and enforceable.

Have you heard? New EU housing rules could pave the way for tighter Airbnb restrictions in Budapest

Why is the district considering restrictions?

The consultation comes as a nationwide moratorium on registering new accommodation establishments is due to expire at the end of this year under the current legal framework. District 1 wants to establish its position before the moratorium ends, as the number of new applications for short-term accommodation could increase sharply afterwards.

The municipality stressed that short-term rentals affect more than property owners and tourism. They can also have an impact on residents’ everyday lives and the peace of apartment buildings. The issue is particularly significant in and around Buda Castle, which is both a residential area and one of Budapest’s major tourist destinations.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Other Budapest districts are also tightening rules

District 1 is not the only part of Budapest considering restrictions on short-term accommodation. District 6 (Terézváros) was the first Budapest district to introduce a complete ban on Airbnb-style short-term rentals following a local referendum.

In District 8 (Józsefváros), the municipal council approved a regulatory concept for short-term accommodation in June, with a decision on the detailed rules expected this month.

Meanwhile, District 13 has also been reviewing its rules. Public consultation on its draft regulation ended on 2 October, although the results have not yet been announced.

The District 13 municipality estimates that around 1,100–1,200 flats currently operate as short-term private accommodation there. It has said it wants to avoid a situation in which restrictions introduced elsewhere in central Budapest lead to a significant increase in the number of short-term rentals in the district.

World.title: Narendra Modi marks 25 years in government: From Gujarat to India’s global rise
World.content:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi marked 25 consecutive years as a head of government on 7 October 2026, a milestone spanning his tenure as Chief Minister of Gujarat and his leadership of India since 2014. The anniversary offers an opportunity to examine his political career, India’s economic development, its growing international role and the expanding relationship between India and Hungary.

Narendra Modi began his journey as a head of government on 7 October 2001, when he took office as Chief Minister of Gujarat, one of India’s most economically important states. Almost thirteen years later, he became Prime Minister of India following the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) victory in the 2014 general election.

Modi subsequently secured second and third terms as Prime Minister following the elections in 2019 and 2024, making him one of the country’s longest-serving national leaders.

The 25-year anniversary was marked by the Indian government, while several world leaders sent messages of congratulations recognising the milestone.

Over this period, India has experienced considerable economic and technological change, alongside an increasingly prominent position in international diplomacy.

From Gujarat to New Delhi: A quarter-century in government

Modi assumed office in Gujarat at a challenging time. The state was recovering from a devastating earthquake earlier in 2001, and reconstruction, infrastructure development and economic recovery were among the government’s immediate priorities.

During his tenure, Gujarat pursued industrial development, investment promotion and improvements to transport and energy infrastructure.

The Vibrant Gujarat investment summit, launched in 2003, became an important platform for attracting domestic and international businesses to the state.

In 2014, Modi moved from state to national politics after the BJP won a parliamentary majority in India’s general election. He was sworn in as Prime Minister on 26 May that year.

His government’s priorities have subsequently included industrial development, digitalisation, infrastructure investment, financial inclusion and expanding India’s international economic partnerships.

India’s economic development and digital transformation

India has strengthened its position among the world’s largest economies over the past decade, supported by domestic consumption, investment and the expansion of its services and technology sectors.

One of the Modi government’s flagship economic initiatives is Make in India, launched in September 2014 to encourage manufacturing, attract foreign investment and strengthen the country’s participation in global supply chains.

Another major programme, Digital India, introduced in 2015, focuses on expanding digital infrastructure, improving access to online public services and encouraging technology adoption throughout the country.

India‘s Unified Payments Interface (UPI), a digital payment system launched in 2016, has become an important part of everyday financial transactions, allowing users to transfer money directly between bank accounts through mobile applications.

Infrastructure development has also remained a major government priority. Investments in motorways, railways, airports, ports and logistics networks are intended to improve connectivity and support economic activity across the country.

Meanwhile, India’s pharmaceutical, information technology, telecommunications and automotive industries continue to play significant roles in its economy.

The government’s longer-term development strategy is centred on Viksit Bharat 2047, an initiative aimed at transforming India into a developed country by 2047, the centenary of its independence.

India’s expanding role in international affairs

India’s international profile has grown considerably during Modi’s premiership.

India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Soruce: depositphotos

The country has strengthened its engagement with major economic and political partners, including the European Union, the United States, Japan and countries across the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia.

India also maintains important relationships with Russia and participates in multilateral organisations such as the G20, BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

In 2023, New Delhi hosted the G20 Leaders’ Summit under India’s presidency, bringing together representatives of the world’s leading economies.

The summit addressed issues including global economic development, sustainable growth, financial cooperation and the interests of developing economies.

India’s approach to international relations continues to emphasise strategic autonomy, allowing New Delhi to pursue partnerships with different countries while maintaining its own foreign policy priorities.

As the world’s most populous country and a major emerging economy, India is expected to remain an important participant in discussions concerning international trade, technology, energy security and global governance.

EU–India free trade agreement: A major milestone in economic relations

One of the most significant recent developments in India’s international economic relations came on 27 January 2026, when the European Union and India concluded negotiations on a landmark Free Trade Agreement (FTA).

The agreement followed nearly two decades of negotiations and represents a major step towards closer economic cooperation between two of the world’s largest markets.

Together, the EU and India account for approximately two billion people, creating considerable opportunities for businesses, investors and exporters.

The agreement is designed to reduce tariffs, remove trade barriers and improve market access for companies operating in both economies.

According to the European Commission, the deal will eliminate or reduce tariffs on more than 96% of EU goods exports to India. It is also expected to support investment, strengthen supply chains and encourage further commercial cooperation.

The potential benefits extend to several sectors, including automotive manufacturing, machinery, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and other industrial products.

For Hungary, the agreement could create additional opportunities for exporters and manufacturers seeking access to the expanding Indian market.

Hungarian companies operating in automotive components, industrial machinery, pharmaceuticals and advanced technologies could benefit from improved trading conditions once the agreement takes effect.

The EU–India agreement is not yet in force. Following the conclusion of negotiations in January, the European Commission submitted proposals for its signature and conclusion to the Council of the European Union in September 2026. The necessary approval procedures must be completed before the agreement can be implemented.

Nevertheless, the conclusion of negotiations already represents an important development in relations between India and Europe, with potential long-term implications for Hungary’s trade and investment ties.

Hungary and India: Strengthening bilateral relations

India’s growing economic significance has also created new opportunities for cooperation with Hungary.

The two countries maintain longstanding diplomatic relations, with cooperation spanning trade, investment, education, science and culture.

According to figures published by the Embassy of India in Budapest, bilateral trade reached approximately USD 2.4 billion in 2025, compared with around USD 1.3 billion in 2024.

Indian investment in Hungary amounts to approximately USD 3.3 billion, underlining the importance of bilateral business relations.

Indian companies have established operations in Hungary across several sectors, while Hungarian businesses are also exploring opportunities in the Indian market.

Machinery, electrical equipment, pharmaceuticals, chemicals and automotive products feature among the major categories of goods traded between the two countries.

Diplomatic engagement remains an important part of this relationship. As we wrote in September, India and Hungary strengthen ties as foreign ministers meet in NY.

His Excellency Anshuman Gaur, the current Ambassador of India to Hungary, assumed his post in Budapest in 2025. The growing importance of EU–India economic relations has also featured in diplomatic and business discussions in Budapest. In February 2026, the Embassy of India organised a business seminar entitled New Economic Horizon: The India–EU FTA and the Union Budget 2026 – Opportunities for Hungary. The event brought together representatives of the Hungarian and Indian business communities, policymakers and other stakeholders to discuss the implications of the free trade agreement. Ambassador Gaur addressed the significance of the agreement and the opportunities it could create for Hungarian and Indian enterprises.

Beyond economic relations, educational and cultural exchanges continue to contribute to closer ties between the two countries.

Indian students attend Hungarian universities, including through international scholarship programmes, while cultural cooperation encompasses literature, music, academic research and other fields.

Looking ahead: India’s development ambitions

Narendra Modi’s 25 years as a head of government coincide with a period of substantial change in India’s economy, infrastructure and international engagement.

From his early years as Chief Minister of Gujarat to his third term as India’s Prime Minister, his political career has been closely associated with programmes aimed at modernising the country and expanding its economic opportunities.

The Indian government’s Viksit Bharat 2047 initiative provides a longer-term framework for its development ambitions, focusing on economic growth, technological progress, infrastructure and social development.

At the international level, India’s partnerships with the European Union and individual European countries are likely to remain important components of its economic strategy.

For Hungary, the conclusion of negotiations on the EU–India Free Trade Agreement, together with growing bilateral commerce and investment, provides a basis for further cooperation in the years ahead.
