World.title: Hungarian child abuse scandal: Government says there may have been far more victims than previously known
World.content:
A government investigation into the Bicske children’s home has found that far more children may have been abused by its former director than those who came forward or took part in the criminal proceedings, Child Rights and Child Protection State Secretary Szilvia Gyurkó said on Thursday.

Children did ask for help, investigation finds

Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Szilvia Gyurkó presented the findings of a government investigation into the past 20 years of the Kossuth Zsuzsa Children’s Home in Bicske, a case that became nationally notorious after a presidential pardon triggered a huge scandal.

Gyurkó urged the media to report responsibly on the abuse uncovered at the institution, warning against sensationalising the cases or downplaying the responsibility of those who committed or concealed crimes. She also stressed the need to respect the dignity of survivors and current and former staff.

The investigation examined the period between 2015 and 2025, while researchers also looked at earlier events where relevant. They reviewed more than 7,000 pages of documents and interviewed former and current employees.

Szilvia Gyurkó (right), and Léna Szilvási, Professional Director of SOS Children’s Villages, at the “Without Taboos” conference on the state of child protection in Hungary on 7 October 2026. Photo: MTI

Some records were lost when responsibility for the institution changed in 2013. The investigation has not ruled out the possibility that some documents may have disappeared deliberately.

According to Gyurkó, previous investigations failed to provide a comprehensive picture of what had happened at the home. The new investigation therefore also examined how institutional interests had repeatedly been placed above the needs and interests of children.

Warning signs had emerged years earlier

The investigation found that there had been warning signs concerning the former director, János Vásárhelyi, well before his crimes became the subject of a criminal investigation.

Gyurkó said Vásárhelyi may have been removed from a previous position in the 1990s because suspicions of sexual abuse had already emerged. Just three years after he was appointed to lead the Bicske institution, a report was also made suggesting that he had crossed boundaries with children there.

The state secretary stressed that it was not true that the children had failed to report problems or ask for help.

In 2011, several children reportedly disclosed sexual abuse to staff. A police investigation followed but was eventually closed after the children withdrew their statements. The current investigation says there may have been coercion or bribery behind those withdrawals.

Further inspections were carried out between 2013 and 2016, but they did not identify serious problems at the institution.

Gyurkó said the available evidence suggests that the number of victims may have been significantly higher than the number of people who came forward publicly or participated in the criminal proceedings.

2016 became a turning point

According to the investigation, 2016 could have marked a decisive turning point. A former resident died by suicide, after which a former resident filed a complaint. Further victims subsequently came forward.

Vásárhelyi was eventually convicted of sexual offences against children. He had run the institution since 1990 and was later found guilty of sexually abusing several underage boys over a number of years.

The case also implicated his deputy, Endre Kónya. He was convicted after attempting to persuade one of the abused children to withdraw testimony against Vásárhelyi.

The deputy director was sentenced to three years and four months in prison, but received a presidential pardon from then-President Katalin Novák in April 2023, shortly before Pope Francis’ visit to Hungary.

The pardon became the centre of a political scandal in early 2024. Novák resigned as president, while former Justice Minister Judit Varga withdrew from public life after having countersigned the pardon. The scandal also led to the emergence of now-Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

Péter Magyar at the press conference. Photo: MTI

Government sets up HUF 1 billion compensation fund

Gyurkó announced that the government would establish a HUF 1 billion (EUR 2.7 million) Child Protection Compensation Fund for victims.

Those who spent at least one day in a child protection institution after Hungary’s 1997 child protection law came into force will be eligible to apply. The scheme is intended to provide more than financial compensation, with legal, psychological and housing assistance also available.

An advisory board will monitor the operation of the fund. Gyurkó said the aim was to ensure that survivors do not remain without support and encouraged those affected by abuse to seek help.

Péter Magyar: Responsibility must be established

Prime Minister Péter Magyar thanked the experts involved in the investigation and, in particular, the young people who had the courage to speak about what happened to them. He said their actions had helped protect other children and argued that the case demonstrated the “moral bankruptcy” of the previous political system.

Magyar also questioned how the director could have operated for decades without those around him, including officials within the relevant ministries, becoming aware of what was happening.

He called for those responsible to be identified and said a large number of files relating to the Bicske case had disappeared, including some after the change of government. Although their contents are unknown, their number is known, he said.

Magyar placed personal responsibility for what happened on former Interior Minister Sándor Pintér, former State Secretary for Social Affairs Attila Fülöp and, ultimately, former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

Bicske case reignites debate over Hungary’s child protection system

The investigation comes just weeks after the government published a report on the state of child protection in Hungary.

That report warned that the system was close to collapse.

It found that around 130,000 children — roughly 8% of all children living in Hungary — are considered at risk because of abuse, neglect, substance use or problems linked to poverty.

Around 23,000 young people are currently being raised in state care, while institutions are struggling with overcrowding, staff shortages and deteriorating infrastructure.

When the report was presented in September, Magyar announced HUF 9.5 billion (EUR 26 million) in immediate funding to address the most urgent problems facing the child protection system.

World.title: Revolut users in Hungary wake up to unexpected refunds as card payments are cancelled
World.content:
Revolut has reportedly cancelled a large number of recent card transactions in Hungary, returning the money to customers, but the refunded amounts may not be theirs to spend.

Revolut users receive unexpected notifications

Several Revolut users in Hungary woke up on Thursday morning to find that some of their recent card purchases had been cancelled and the money they had paid had been returned to their accounts.

Many of those affected received notifications between around 7 and 8 AM, according to reports shared by users in the Hungarian-language Revolut Community Facebook group and reported by Hungarian financial news site RevB.

The affected payments appear to include a wide range of everyday purchases, from smaller transactions to larger shopping bills. Users have reported cancellations involving retailers including Penny, Rossmann, Lidl and dm, as well as transactions at National Tobacco Shops.

Both Visa and Mastercard transactions have reportedly been affected, with Maestro cards also mentioned among users’ reports. So far, the reports concern domestic Hungarian transactions.

Money returned after earlier purchases

The unusual notifications initially caused some users to worry that someone had attempted to use their cards.

One user, for example, reported receiving a notification about a failed KFC payment worth HUF 1,890, despite saying they had not been to KFC for two weeks and still had their physical card.

However, the transaction was not a new attempted payment. Other users pointed out that the notification related to an earlier purchase being cancelled, meaning the money was being returned rather than a new charge being made.

The incident seems to be a system error rather than evidence that customers’ cards have been compromised.

Don’t spend the unexpected refund

Customers who have received money back from cancelled transactions should not assume that the refunds are permanent.

The cancelled payments are expected to be charged again once the underlying issue is fixed. In other words, the money currently showing in an affected customer’s Revolut account may simply be temporarily available because of the error.

RevB reported that Revolut’s status page showed its systems as operating normally, while customers of other banks had not reported a similar issue. The exact cause of the problem has not yet been confirmed.

Revolut is expected to correct the issue and reprocess the affected payments. The company has been contacted for information about the incident, and further details are expected if it responds.

World.title: Finally: Budapest-Belgrade railway could welcome passengers this autumn!
World.content:
Hungary’s long-awaited Budapest-Belgrade railway is moving closer to completion, with domestic passenger services potentially launching in the second half of October and international trains following in December.

Key safety tests completed

The Hungarian section of the Budapest-Belgrade railway has passed two important tests ahead of its planned opening to passenger traffic. According to Dávid Vitézy, Hungary’s transport and investment minister, both the full-load test and the inspection of the European Train Control System (ETCS) train control system were completed successfully.

Vitézy said the results are particularly important because the proper operation of ETCS is a fundamental condition for launching passenger services on the newly built railway line. The official documentation needed to close the testing process is expected by mid-October.

If everything proceeds according to plan, domestic passenger services could begin in the second half of October.

Final track work still underway

The railway is not quite ready for full-speed operation yet. The contractor still has to carry out the final warranty track alignment work, which is expected to take almost two months.

The work involves precisely adjusting the tracks and points at stations as well as sections of open railway line. This is a standard final stage before a new railway is put into service, particularly when trains are expected to travel at speeds of up to 160 km/h.

If you missed it: Budapest-Belgrade railway runs at 160 km/h in final test before passenger launch

During construction and full-load testing, the crushed-stone track bed can become further compacted, meaning that the position of the rails and points needs to be adjusted again. Maintaining the correct track geometry is especially important for safe high-speed operation.

The work has been scheduled so that the track alignment on the Ferencváros–Kunszentmiklós-Tass suburban section can be completed by the end of October. This would allow domestic passenger trains to start operating while the remaining work continues with fewer restrictions.

Photo: MTI/Péter Lakatos

International Budapest-Belgrade trains could follow in December

If the first weeks of domestic passenger services run smoothly, the next major step could come in December. Vitézy said that the authorities could then move towards fully using the line’s 160 km/h design speed and launching international passenger services between Budapest and Belgrade.

However, both dates are conditional. Vitézy stressed that passengers will only be allowed onto the railway once all necessary safety requirements have been met.

The Budapest-Belgrade railway project has been one of Hungary’s most closely watched and controversial infrastructure investments. The Hungarian section has undergone extensive testing and technical checks before passenger services can begin.

World.title: Hungary’s clocks will change earlier than last year – here is when
World.content:
Hungary will switch back to winter time one day earlier this year than it did in 2025. The clocks will go back from 3 AM to 2 AM on Sunday, 25 October, meaning people will gain an extra hour of sleep.

The European Union’s plans to abolish the twice-yearly clock change have been debated for years, but no final decision has been made. For now, the current system remains in place.

When do the clocks change in Hungary?

The clocks are changed twice a year across the EU. On the last Sunday of March, clocks move forward by one hour for summer time, while on the last Sunday of October, they move back by one hour to winter time.

In 2026, the change to winter time will take place overnight from Saturday, 24 October to Sunday, 25 October. At 3 AM, clocks will be turned back to 2 AM.

This means that the same hour will occur twice during the night, and people will effectively have an extra hour available for sleeping. Last year, the change took place one day later, overnight from 25 to 26 October 2025.

The most recent clock change took place on 29 March 2026, when clocks moved forward from 2 AM to 3 AM.

Have you read this? Budapest addiction counsellor accused of selling drugs to patients as one dies after taking substances

Earlier sunsets are coming

The switch to winter time means an extra hour of daylight in the morning compared with summer time, but darkness will arrive earlier in the afternoon and evening.

Winter time is generally considered the standard time, with summer time introduced by moving the clocks forward by one hour in March. Although many people prefer having more daylight in the evening, experts generally consider winter time to be more closely aligned with the body’s natural rhythm, according to 24.hu.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Clock changes can affect the body

Moving the clocks by just one hour may seem minor, but the change can temporarily disrupt the body’s biological clock.

The circadian rhythm helps regulate several bodily functions, including sleep and wakefulness, digestion, body temperature and mood. It is closely linked to light and darkness, meaning a sudden change in the timing of daylight can affect the body’s usual rhythm.

The effects vary from person to person. Some people may experience tiredness, sleepiness or headaches, while others may need several days to adjust to the new schedule.

Will the EU abolish the clock change?

The abolition of seasonal clock changes has been debated at EU level for years. However, there is currently no final EU decision to end the system, meaning Hungary will continue to change its clocks twice a year for the time being.

So, if you are living in or visiting Hungary, remember: on Sunday, 25 October, the clocks will go back one hour, from 3 AM to 2 AM.

World.title: Pneumonic plague fears grip Russia after lab worker dies, quarantine measures imposed
World.content:
Local authorities in Russia’s Siberian region of Irkutsk have imposed quarantine measures on people and several hospital departments amid reports of a possible “plague” outbreak.

Russia’s consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology.” The employee died from her illness, according to numerous media reports and official statements, while authorities placed those who had contact with her under medical observation.

Rospotrebnadzor later said the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region was “calm.” The developments, however, have raised concerns and public health fears on social media.

Here is what is known about the reported outbreak, according to Anadolu Agency.

Reported outbreak

On Friday, Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said that he convened an extraordinary meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission following reports of a suspected “highly dangerous infectious disease” in a local resident.

Kobzev said Rospotrebnadzor organized and was implementing a comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures, adding that the watchdog and regional government were closely monitoring the situation.

“I would like to inform you that all identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, none of the contacts show any signs of illness, and laboratory test results have come back negative,” Kobzev said.

Maxim Modin, mayor of Irkutsk’s Shelekhovsky district, said the same day that several departments of the district hospital in Shelekhov suspended patient discharges and admissions.

Alexey Tsydenov, head of the neighboring Russian Republic of Buryatia, said the woman who died in Irkutsk “possibly from the plague” had not visited his region. Tsydenov said there were no “plague” outbreaks in Buryatia, including in areas bordering Mongolia.

Two days later, Rospotrebnadzor said no emergencies had been reported while working with pathogenic microorganisms at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute. It said the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov was “stable.”

The watchdog added that no cases of infectious disease had been reported among employees of the institute over the previous 10 days. Rospotrebnadzor said Monday that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was “calm.”

Media attention intensified after local outlet People of Baikal on Friday reported that the institute employee, identified as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, allegedly broke a test tube containing “pneumonic plague.”

The outlet reported that she became ill after allegedly breaking the test tube late last month and was hospitalized in Shelekhov, where she died Friday evening.

High-level reactions

Several high-level officials have commented on the situation, urging people to rely on official assessments from relevant authorities. “Rospotrebnadzor is the lead agency with competence in this area,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a news conference in Moscow on Monday.

“It is precisely Rospotrebnadzor’s official statements that should be heeded, rather than listening to various rumors or speculations,” Peskov said. He added that the watchdog employs top-tier professionals in the field and again urged people to “heed their official statements.”

US President Donald Trump said Monday that Washington was closely monitoring the reported case of “pneumonic plague” in Russia and pledged assistance. “Years ago you could treat pneumonia easier, and the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger,” Trump told reporters at the White House before departing for a campaign rally in Nebraska.

“But we’ll help them. We’ll help them,” he added.

Responding to Trump’s comments, Peskov said it is “always good when mutual assistance is offered.”

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday that it was closely monitoring reports of a “suspected case of pneumonic plague” in Russia that resulted in one death. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russia the same day to provide full transparency and share detailed information about the incident with the international community.

The World Health Organization told Russian state news agency Tass that it was maintaining contact with local health authorities over the incident. The WHO said that, based on “available unofficial information,” it assessed the public health risk in the region as low.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

What is plague?

While the exact cause of the reported illness remains unclear, official statements have raised questions about plague. Plague is an infectious illness caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, which spreads through small wild mammals and their fleas, according to the WHO.

The WHO said bubonic plague is the most common form, while pneumonic and septicemic forms are invariably fatal unless treated early. According to the WHO, pneumonic plague is the most virulent form, with an incubation period potentially as short as 24 hours.

Plague was historically responsible for the “Black Death,” a pandemic in Europe in the 14th century that resulted in more than 50 million deaths, according to the WHO.

World.title: Hungarian transport minister announces Budapest’s long-delayed Student City project restart
World.content:
Hungary’s Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy has announced the restart of Budapest’s long-delayed Student City (Diákváros) project, which aims to create new student accommodation and affordable housing in the capital.

Vitézy said the decision was made at a meeting of the re-established Budapest Public Development Council, with EU funding set to contribute to the project. The development has been stalled for years due to the former government’s plans to build a Chinese Fudan University campus on the same site.

Student City project to be revived after years of delay

Budapest has long struggled with a shortage of university accommodation, while the city’s housing crisis has made finding affordable housing particularly difficult for students. According to Vitézy, the Student City project could help address both problems while making higher education more accessible.

The minister said final plans supported by the capital and the affected districts had already been prepared before the project was put on hold.

“The goal is to give the brownfield site in Ferencváros new, valuable functions: we will create new student accommodation places with affordable housing in a liveable urban environment that is easy to reach,” Vitézy said.

He added that the next step would be to further develop the existing plans, with more details to be discussed by the Budapest Public Development Council.

Fudan plans put the project on hold

The Student City project was originally intended to provide a major expansion of student accommodation in the capital. However, the previous Fidesz government put the development on hold as plans emerged for a campus of China’s Fudan University on the site.

The proposed Fudan campus became a major political issue in Budapest, with the project facing strong opposition from the city leadership.

Former Budapest mayoral candidate and former Fidesz group leader Alexandra Szentkirályi announced in autumn 2024 that the Student City would nevertheless be built, presenting the project as a response to the capital’s housing crisis.

The original Snøhetta plan for the project. Photo: Karácsony Gergely

Earlier plans envisaged around 12,000 places at the Student City.

Mayor Gergely Karácsony had also repeatedly called for the project to be built. In 2021, he even warned that Budapest could refuse to host the 2023 World Athletics Championships if the government did not proceed with the Student City.

Budapest ultimately hosted the championships, but the Student City project did not materialise.

If you missed it: Good news for homebuyers and students: vast student city and residential district could rise on Budapest’s derelict waterfront

Site is now back in state ownership

Under the previous government, the state expropriated the land needed for the development. The Ferencváros local council had been set to receive HUF 3.5 billion in compensation for the property.

Vitézy said the site has now returned to state ownership, meaning the conditions are in place for the long-awaited project to move forward. He also said funding would be provided from EU resources brought back to Hungary.

The government now plans to revise and develop the existing plans before moving ahead with the project, which could eventually provide thousands of students with more affordable accommodation in Budapest.

World.title: Bosnia Charges Catholic Cleric with Glorifying War Criminal
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

The Bosnian state court on Thursday confirmed an indictment alleging that Father Petar Barbaric, a Catholic priest, gave a speech glorifying Slobodan Praljak after the unveiling of a monument to the deceased war criminal at a cemetery in the city of Capljina in November 2025.

“The speech was broadcast by various electronic media outlets and internet portals, garnering a large number of views, as well as reactions from the public and citizens,” the state prosecutor’s office said in a statement.

The indictment charges Barbaric with glorifying an individual who had been convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, under a final verdict, of crimes against humanity and war crimes, thereby committing the criminal offence of “provoking ethnic, racial and religious hatred, conflicts and intolerance”.

The investigation was opened in November last year after a photograph began circulating of the unveiling in Capljina of the monument to Praljak, wartime commander of the Main Headquarters of the Croatian Defence Council, the Bosnian Croat wartime military force.

The monument features Praljak’s likeness carved into stone, with the inscription: “Praljak, Croatian General,” his place and year of birth – “Capljina, 1945” – and the year and place of his death: “The Hague, 2017.”

In November 2017, the Hague Tribunal convicted Praljak, along with five other high-ranking officials of the unrecognised Croat-led wartime statelet of Herzeg-Bosnia, sentencing him to 20 years in prison for crimes against Bosniaks. During the reading of the verdict, Praljak took poison and died the same day.

Under amendments to the Bosnian Criminal Code imposed in July 2021 by the High Representative, the international overseer of the continuing implemetation of the Dayton Peace Agreement, denying genocide and other war crimes was outlawed.

It also became a punishable offense to bestow honours or awards, or erect monuments or any other form of memorial, to a person convicted under a final verdict of genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes.

When news of the installation of a monument to Praljak first emerged, Emir Hajdarevic, president of the Mostar Association of Camp Inmates, said it showed that some still see war criminals as heroes.

“This is yet another crime against the victims of Herzegovina committed in Capljina, which is known for the crimes at Gabela and Silos [wartime detention camps in the Herzegovina area],” Hajdarevic said.

World.title: Albanian Criminal Procedure Bill Slammed as Bid to ‘Neuter’ Anti-Graft Body
World.content:
Prosecutors in Albania were taken aback last week when the government unexpectedly unveiled a bill running to 106 articles and revising roughly a fifth of the country’s Code of Criminal Procedure.

The bill proposes scrapping pretrial detention in criminal cases carrying a maximum sentence of five years in prison, introducing new requirements for prosecutors in the conduct of investigations, and strengthening rules governing investigative secrecy. It would further prohibit the public disclosure of the fact that a person is under investigation.

In 2016, Albania introduced sweeping reforms to its justice system that established the Special Prosecution Office Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK. This body has since brought a string of cases against senior officials from the ruling Socialist Party and its main rival, the Democrats.

World.title: Bosnia’s 2026 Elections: Fewer Votes, Familiar Winners
World.content:
The biggest, if not the only, real novelty in Bosnia’s October 4 election was that the first preliminary results were announced on election night, before all the polling stations had even closed.

For a country with such a complex administrative system as Bosnia and Herzegovina, this came as a major surprise.

It was welcomed by most politicians, media and ordinary people alike, who formerly had to wait days or weeks before the Central Election Commission, CEC, announced the preliminary results in all the key races.

However, for many Bosnians, the excitement generated by this technical novelty was quickly replaced with disdain on hearing the actual results.

As soon as the CEC officials started listing them, they revealed the continued domination of Bosnia’s main Serb and Croat ethnic parties, as well as a major comeback by their Bosniak counterpart.

World.title: Justina Shiroka Pula, Another Woman at Kosovo’s Helm
World.content:
Justina Shiroka Pula was having a peaceful evening on Tuesday, taking with “guests from Sarajevo” when she hung up a phone call from a TV studio running a prime-time political debate.

She was not aware that she was the pick for Kosovo’s top state position at a dramatic moment, less than two hours before the deadline to elect a President expired.

“We will hear [about this] a bit later,” she said, switching off.

Minutes later, in another call, she sounded like she was coming to terms with her new situation.

World.title: Moldova Speeds Up Construction of Trump-Named Power Line
World.content:
Moldova’s government on Wednesday approved a draft law declaring the construction of a high-voltage power line linking Moldova with Romania a national public utility, allowing acquisition of land and other procedures required for the project to be accelerated.

The 400-kilovolt line will be about 190 kilometres long, with around 70 kilometres on Moldovan territory and 120 in Romania, according to government officials. It is expected to strengthen Moldova’s integration with Romania and the wider European electricity market.

Construction of the new power line is backed by a $130 million investment from the US and is expected to be completed in 2032.

The US embassy in Chisinau meanwhile announced on Monday that the planned line will be named the “Trump Liberty Line”, making it the latest infrastructure project to bear the name of the US President.

Moldovan authorities have stressed that the project will reduce vulnerability to energy pressure from Russia. “This is a very important project for Moldova’s energy security … and we are grateful to the American side for its support,” Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said during Wednesday’s government meeting.

Moldova, one of Europe’s poorest countries and an EU candidate, relies heavily currently on electricity imports from Romania and Ukraine.

But Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have repeatedly disrupted regional electricity supplies in recent years, exposing Moldova’s vulnerability to instability and underscoring the need for stronger and more reliable connections, particularly with Romania.

There has been no significant critical reaction in either Moldova or Romania to the planned name of the new power line connecting the two countries. The announcement has attracted little public controversy, with attention focused instead on the project’s potential to strengthen Moldova’s energy security.

Moldova meanwhile joins a number of other countries where local infrastructure projects have been associated with Trump’s name, as governments seek to highlight ties with the US administration.

In Eastern Europe, other examples include a planned Donald Trump Romanian-American Friendship Park in Bucharest, Romania, which is expected to be inaugurated early next year, and a proposed US military base in Poland that was previously promoted under the name “Fort Trump”.

World.title: Mayor of Turkey’s Third-Largest City Joins Ruling Party
World.content:
Izmir Metropolitan Mayor Cemil Tugay on Wednesday joined President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, giving it the mayoralty of Turkey’s third-largest city, which it has never won in an election.

Tugay was elected mayor as a candidate of the opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, in 2024. He received his AKP badge at the party’s parliamentary group meeting.

“I welcome Izmir Metropolitan Mayor Cemil Tugay, who joined us, the AKP family, today,” President Erdogan announced. “I want to emphasise that we will support him with all our means in his efforts to serve Izmir, the pearl of the Aegean, and our fellow citizens in Izmir.”

Tugay said: “I love Izmir very much,” adding: “Very good things await Izmir” and calling Erdogan’s “the greatest leader”.

Izmir, a major economic hub on Turkey’s Aegean coast, is home to some 4.5 million people and has been a stronghold of the opposition for decades.

Tugay’s move follows a wider realignment within Turkey’s opposition. Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavas left the CHP on September 23 following months of turmoil that split the party between the leadership, now restored to Kemal Kilicdaroglu, and the New Party, Turkey’s new main opposition party, established by the former CHP leader, Ozgur Ozel.

Yavas has remained an independent, however.

In the 2024 local elections, Tugay, running for the CHP, won 49 per cent of the vote, almost 12 per cent ahead of Erdogan’s AKP candidate, who received 37 per cent.

The balance of power on the metropolitan council remains heavily in favour of the opposition. The New Party holds 93 seats, compared with 38 for the AKP, 33 for the CHP, 12 independents and seven for AKP-allied Nationalist Party members.

New Party leader Ozel mocked Erdogan’s seeming victory in parliament on Wednesday. “You have never won Izmir at the ballot box, and you never will,” he said, addressing President Erdogan.

World.title: Kosovo Avoids New Deadlock With Last-Minute Presidential Election
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Newly elected President Justina Shiroka Pula takes oath in Kosovo Parliament, October 7, 2026. Photo: BIRN/Shqipron Xhema

After a roller-coaster of proposals for the vacant post of Kosovo’s President, MPs pulled off a last-minute save just before midnight on Tuesday, avoiding a constitutional deadline that would have triggered parliament’s dissolution and the fourth parliamentary election in less than two years.

Justina Shiroka Pula, a 73-year-old economist, former minister and MP and current head of the Academy of Sciences and Arts of Kosovo, was announced as the new President with 81 votes in favour and two votes not valid.

“I pledge to dedicate all my strength to safeguarding the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Kosovo,” Shiroka-Pula declared.

She is the third woman President of Kosovo.

She has directed the Academy of Sciences and Arts of Kosovo since December 2025. From 2008 to 2011, she was Minister of Energy and Mining in a government led by Hashim Thaçi. She was part of the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK’s, parliamentary group from 2011 to 2014.

Shiroka Pula was nominated by Prime Minister Albin Kurti at a press conference just before midnight, after earlier candidates did not get the backing of the opposition PDK.

The issue of electing the President had become tangled up with demands for law changes to curb the powers of the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which sparked anger after it convicted four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders of war crimes last month.

PDK leader Bedri Hamza said in a press conference after the election that “we do not want to hinder justice, we want to establish justice. The President is the people’s representative, I believe she will do her job with honour and high responsibility.”

The PDK and the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo, AAK, had called for draft amendments to the law governing the Chambers to be passed on a second reading before they would agree with the government on electing a President.

Kurti had claimed that electing a President was the priority – until he proposed voting through the law amendments prior to electing the President as a solution.

The law change was then adopted in an extraordinary session close to midnight on Tuesday just before the election of the President. It crucially limits the jail sentences the court can impose to 15 years.

On September 16, the court sentenced former Kosovo President Thaci and three other former KLA chiefs, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi, to 25, 25, 18 and 13 years in prison respectively for war crimes.

The sentences caused outrage in Kosovo, where many considered the verdict went against the just war against the Serbian regime in the 1990s. Protests became violent on Monday as protesters clashed with the police.

The adoption of the law by the parliament and the election of the President were welcomed with fireworks and patriotic music by protesters outside parliament in Pristina.

However, the election of the President could be subject to constitutional interpretation as, while the session started on October 6, which was the last day to elect a President, the results were not announced until 13 minutes after midnight.

World.title: One Resignation Doesn’t Prove Justice Operates Fairly in Turkey
World.content:
The crisis covers 131 investment funds with 455,758 investors, estimated to hold $18 billion to over $20 billion in assets. Those figures show the scale of the affair. Yet the political debate has quickly narrowed from the crisis itself to the symbolism of one resignation.

In pro-government media commentary, Kaya’s move is evidence that the ruling AKP is willing to hold its own people accountable – while Turkey’s secular opposition protected politicians facing corruption allegations. The argument works only because it compares gestures instead of procedures.

Kaya gave up a party post. Meanwhile, Istanbul’s opposition Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu has been in pre-trial detention since March 2025.

Prosecutors accuse him of leading a criminal organisation involved in corruption. He denies the allegations and claims political persecution while the government insists the judiciary acts independently.

Imamoglu is no longer a member of the opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP. After investigations against CHP-run municipalities widened, a court annulled the party’s 2023 congress, restored its former leader, Kemal Kilicdaroglu, as police enforced the transfer of the party headquarters. Imamoglu later joined an offshoot, the Yeni Parti (New Party).

So one person can answer a political demand by resigning, while the other has to answer to a vast criminal case from prison.

Turkey increasingly resembles a system of legal duality. Formally, there is one criminal procedure. In reality, burdens and degrees of coercion differ, depending on the political direction of a case.

The same question appears inside the funds scandal. Regulators first identified manipulation risks in late 2025, but the system continued growing until the following September.

By late 2025, the problem was already visible to the state. Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek publicly acknowledged manipulation through “certain funds” and regulatory gaps in November, while the SPK says it had observed economically inexplicable price movements in low-float shares and later introduced new valuation and fund rules through July and August 2026.

Ramazan Basak, a former deputy head of Turkey’s Financial Crimes Investigation Board, says he warned state bodies in 2025 about suspicious money flows connected to Tera, a financial services and investment banking group. He later filed a criminal complaint and was himself detained twice following complaints by Tera’s chairman, Emre Tezmen. Tezmen has rejected the core allegations, describing the turmoil as an organised speculative attack and a temporary liquidity problem. He later also denied allegations that fund money had been used to inflate Tera group shares.

Within days, however, falling prices and mass redemption requests turned that liquidity problem into a crisis. Tera itself disclosed defaults on redemption payments, before the SPK shut affected funds to trading and ordered their liquidation on September 17.

Ramazan Basak, a former deputy head of Turkey’s Financial Crimes Investigation Board, says he warned state bodies in 2025 about suspicious money flows connected to Tera, a financial services and investment banking group. He later filed a criminal complaint and was himself detained twice following complaints by Tera’s chairman, Emre Tezmen.

The former chairman of the capital markets regulator, the SPK, Ibrahim Omer Gonul, was questioned as a suspect on September 30, as the wider probe expanded.

Investigations now are under way. The question is why this level of intervention came only after the system had grown so large, and whether scrutiny can reach the political and bureaucratic networks that were supposed to supervise it.

Owners and regulators overlap

World.title: Hvar in Conde Nast Top 10 Islands for 8th Consecutive Year
World.content:
October 8, 2026 – More strengthening of the American love for Croatia’s premier island, as Hvar once more in top 10 islands in Europe in Conde Nast Traveler Readers Choice Awards.

These are good times for the relationship between Hvar Town and the sought-after American tourism market, with a marked shift in approach resulting in a boom in American tourism arrivals in recent years. According to official statistics, American tourists were the biggest number of arrivals and overnight stays in the town last year, and those numbers show no sign of slowing, with overnight stays from the USA in September up an impressive 17.83% year on year.

The success has been down to a number of key factors, including better promotion to the USA market, the introduction of the first direct flight from New York to Split this April, meaning one can get from New York to Hvar (with the aid of a good speedboat) in under 10 hours. So successful has the flight connection been that plans are being discussion to prolong the flight season as well as frequency of flights for 2027.

An additional factor has been the positive media coverage that the town has been attracting since moving away from its party focus in search of more upmarket tourism focused on families and couples, as well as adventure tourism. Arguably the most influential travel publication for American travellers is Conde Nast Traveler, which every year holds the prestigious Conde Nast Traveler Readers’ Choice Awards, a publication which known Hvar very well.

Often named one of the 10 most beautiful islands in the world, that claim has its roots in a Conde Nast award in the late 1990s (you can see a list of the islands on the map on the Jelsa waterfront), and the American publication’s readers’ love for Hvar has been pretty constant ever since. Indeed, this year’s 9th place as the best island in Europe is the 8th consecutive year that Hvar has featured in the sought-after top ten list, including 2019 and 2021, when Hvar was voted the best island in Europe.

Breakfast at Sirena Resort

American interest has been mirrored by a raising of standards in the hotel sector, which is also attracting plenty of international column inches. The latest addition is the superb Sirena Resort from Suncani Hvar Hotels, 1.4 km north of the town, set in an idyllic bay without neighbours, and offering access to the vibe of Hvar Town, as well as the laidback calm of the nature of Hvar, the island. Within weeks of opening, Sirena Resort was featured in the New York Times as one of the top 5 new hotels in Europe for an autumn getaway.

The main season may be over, but there is still plenty of life in the town, with this weekend hosting the Spartan World Championship, with around 3,000 competitors expected. All the signs are there for a bumper 2027 for Americans visiting one of Europe’s most perfect spots.

World.title: Dubrovnik Airport Could Surpass 3.2 Million Passengers
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – Dubrovnik Airport might surpass the figure of 3.2 million passengers, with passenger numbers climbing even during the month of September this year.

Dubrovnik Airport continued its passenger traffic growth throughout September this year as well. According to data from the airport itself, Dubrovnik Airport handled 474,212 passengers in September, which is almost 31 thousand more passengers than in the same month last year. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that for comparison, in September 2025 a total of 443,444 passengers passed through Dubrovnik Airport.

Compared to September 2025, the number of passengers increased by 6.9 percent, while the number of operations also rose. Dubrovnik recorded 3,718 operations in September this year, compared to 3,564 operations in the same month last year, which represents growth of approximately 4.3 percent. Growth is also recorded in the first nine months of this year. From the beginning of January to the end of September 2026, Dubrovnik handled a total of 2,820,860 passengers. In the same period last year 2,692,873 passengers were recorded, meaning that Dubrovnik handled almost 128 thousand more passengers in the first nine months of this year, or 4.8 percent more.

Last year, the airport handled a total of 3,090,245 passengers, which means that by the end of September 2026 more than 91 percent of last year’s total traffic had already been achieved, and the airport still has three months ahead of it. While significantly lower traffic is expected in November and December, October should bring strong numbers. Consequently, it would be no surprise if Dubrovnik Airport already matches last year’s figures by the end of October.

World.title: Radioactive Strontium in Gospić Jumps by a Staggering 961%
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – Radioactive strontium found in the soil in the Gospić area has jumped by an extremely concerning 961 percent, but what is being done about it?

In the surface layer of soil at the measuring point in Gospić last year, an almost 11 times higher concentration of radioactive strontium-90 per square metre was recorded than in 2023, according to the regular annual reports of the Zagreb Institute for Medical Research and Occupational Health (IMI), published on the Ministry of the Interior’s website. Slobodan Mufic reports for Index that the published activity per square metre rose from 24.5 to 260 becquerels, or by as much as 961 percent. The concentration of strontium-90 (Sr-90) per kilogram of material at the Gospić measuring point also rose drastically: from 0.605 becquerels per kilogram in 2023 to 4.08 becquerels in 2025, or almost seven times.

has radioactive contamination occurred?

It should be emphasised immediately that there is no evidence pointing to a connection between strontium-90 and the illegal waste at the former PPK Velebit in Bilajska Street in Gospić, nor does this change in itself mean that radioactive contamination has occurred or that the health of residents is endangered. The measuring point in Gospić is located about 7.6 kilometres southwest of PPK Velebit and so far there is no evidence that would confirm a link between the two locations.

Strontium-90 is a radioactive form of the chemical element of the same name, a silvery-white metal. This means that its atomic nucleus decays over time and in doing so releases radiation that can damage living cells. Strontium-90 does not exist originally in nature, but is created by the fission of atomic nuclei, for example in nuclear reactors and during nuclear weapons explosions. “All Sr-90 in the environment on Croatian territory is a consequence of the Chernobyl disaster back in 1986. Sr-90 has a half-life of 28.8 years. After the half-life has elapsed, the activity and quantity of the radionuclide fall to half of the initial amount, so it is not surprising that Sr-90 is still present in Croatia – there is still approximately 38% of the quantity that was initially deposited.

This radionuclide is anthropogenic; it is created by the fission of uranium-235. Sr-90 entered the environment from the atmosphere, via the radioactive cloud, and accumulated in the surface layer. Therefore it is not surprising that it is most present there, because it spreads into deeper layers by the slow process of diffusion,” states the response of IMI’s Radiation Protection Department.

Gospić is the only area to record an increase since 2023…

The origin of strontium-90 has been explained, but there is no adequate answer as to why its concentration on the surface has enormously increased only in Gospić over the last three years. Among the five measuring locations we compared, Gospić had the lowest surface value of strontium-90 in 2023, and two years later the highest. While between 2023 and 2025 that value fell in Zadar, Osijek, Buzet/Pula and Opuzen, in Zagreb it rose by approximately 92 percent, and in Gospić by 961 percent. Becquerel per kilogram (Bq/kg) indicates how much radioactivity is concentrated in a kilogram of soil, while becquerel per square metre (Bq/m²) indicates how much total radioactivity of Sr-90 exists under one square metre of surface. Since Bq/kg can fluctuate considerably if the sample one year is a little lighter, denser or richer in organic matter, Bq/m² is to some extent a better indicator.

If there is no new input or soil erosion, the total Sr-90 expressed in Bq/m² should mostly gradually decrease due to radioactive decay, and not increase as in the Gospić case. It should also be added that in the deeper layers of the earth, below the surface five centimetres, the opposite occurred: the concentration of Sr-90 is strongly declining.

The Radiation Protection Department offered this answer to the question about the professional interpretation of the increase in Sr-90 concentration: “In Gospić soil Sr-90 is continuously monitored, with a break in the period 2014–2022. It was reintroduced into the environmental radioactivity monitoring programme in the Republic of Croatia in 2023 and continues to be monitored. The measured values varied and no year-on-year upward trend was observed. For example, in 2003 440 Bq/m² was measured, in 2004 280 Bq/m², in 2005 180 Bq/m², and in 2007 270 Bq/m². In order to establish whether the increase in the period 2023–2025 represents the beginning of an upward trend, more time needs to pass.” The last measured and published value of 260 Bq/m² is not in itself a historical maximum in Gospić, but such a sudden jump from 24.5 to 260 in only two years is shocking. An additional problem is that IMI did not carry out measurements in Gospić from 2007 to 2023.

Although IMI wrote in its 2024 report that only in Gospić “is the activity concentration of Sr-90 is several times higher than last year’s”, there’s no data that because of this obvious anomaly, which was repeated in 2025, a new control measurement was proposed or requested.

nobody requested or paid for additional monitoring

“Sampling within the framework of environmental radioactivity monitoring is carried out in agreement with the client of the work, in this case the Ministry of the Interior. IMI cannot itself define where and how often sampling will take place. We have not received a request from the client for additional or extraordinary sampling in Gospić.

Every year, sampling for the following year is agreed with the Ministry of the Interior. We may propose the mentioned, but the Ministry of the Interior will decide. That is open for now. It should be emphasised that it is possible to carry out detailed research outside the regular monitoring; we have often done that so far. Someone has to order and pay for it,” the Radiation Protection Department replied to the question whether it would recommend to the Ministry of the Interior more sampling points, more frequent sampling, analysis of water, vegetation, food or sediment. An interpretation of this sensitive issue was sought from a renowned Croatian scientific institution, without revealing what it was about. A radioactivity expert, who requested not to be named, answered the question whether a multiple increase in the concentration of strontium-90 on the soil is possible without a new source of contamination: “NO. That would be a perpetual motion machine.”

When we explained to him what it was actually about, he said that the only reasonable explanation could be deficient sampling, or inadequate laboratory analysis: “Measuring low activities is very delicate and it can happen that laboratories have different instrumentation, so measurements near the detection limits can deviate significantly. This is especially the case with measuring Sr-90, which is quite complicated. The analysis takes about three weeks.”

no answers have come from institutions about potential health risks…

From the existing data, it is not possible to draw a concrete and reliable conclusion about the impact of the strontium-90 concentration on people in Gospić. The surface increase refers to activity per square metre of soil, and not to the radiation dose received by citizens. To assess the health risk it is necessary to determine what dose residents receive due to radiation from the environment and the possible intake of radioactive substances through food, water and inhalation of particles. The soil finding alone is not sufficient either for the claim that there is a danger to health or for the claim that it is completely ruled out.

Interestingly, the Radiation Protection Department did not want to comment on the possible danger to human health: “The assessment of the threat from a particular radionuclide, which includes the ways of its propagation through the environment and the food chain, is not part of our contract in monitoring environmental radioactivity. That topic is quite complex and requires an interdisciplinary approach that would consider all relevant aspects.”

There was no concrete answer from the Croatian Institute of Public Health to Index’s inquiry. Unofficially we received the message: “We do not deal with that.” And the Ministry of the Interior’s Civil Protection Directorate completely ignored several inquiries on this topic; that is, even after two weeks no answer arrived. The key question in this story is not the concentration of strontium-90 itself and its possible impact on human health, but the inertia and disinterest of the competent institutions in reacting and additionally checking findings that clearly deviate from trends and expectations. Just as in the case of the illegal waste at Bilajska 50.

World.title: For 75% of Croatians, a Dignified Salary Starts From 2,000 Euros
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – For 75% of Croatians, a dignified salary starts from 2,000 euros, but the reality of what salaries are actually paid out in Croatia is starkly different.

The topic of the average wage in Croatia is a frequent topic, and we talk about the minimum wage most often when another increase is announced. The real question for many, however, is just how much should a Croatian wage be to enable workers a fully dignified life? What some would be one in which, after paying rent, utilities and food, there remains room for socialising, going to the cinema, an annual holiday or putting some savings away for a rainy day. A life in which an unexpected expense does not mean that we have to spend the rest of the month counting every single euro.

Alma Career Croatia, the international company known for the MojPosao/MyJob brand, addressed precisely this question in a new survey in which more than 500 people participated. Poslovni reports that just two years ago participants said that a dignified wage should not be less than 1,500 euros. Given the constant increases in the cost of living, we checked where they set that boundary today.

Is 1,500 euros enough for a month, but not for a peaceful life? The minimum wage in Croatia currently amounts to 1,050 euros gross, or around 800 euros net, depending on the worker’s tax circumstances. But the legal minimum and the amount that survey participants consider sufficient for a dignified life are clearly quite distant, because none of them chose a wage lower than 1,000 euros. The next range did not receive many more votes either. Only 3% of participants believe that it is possible to live with dignity on a wage between 1,000 and 1,500 euros.

A somewhat larger number, approximately every fifth person (22%), chooses the range from 1,500 to 2,000 euros. For them 1,500 euros is the lower limit which, with inflation and rising living costs, still leaves the possibility of a life above merely covering obligations. Everything below that, they believe, means living ‘from month to month’. Everything below 2,000 euros is not enough for the vast majority.

The largest number of participants, 50% of them, place a dignified wage in the range from 2,000 to 2,500 euros. However, they note that even that amount does not tell the whole story. A lot depends on whether we have solved our housing situation or whether every month we have to set aside money from the same wage for rent or a loan. For every fourth person (25%) the boundary is even higher. A dignified life in Croatia, they emphasise, requires a monthly wage of at least 2,500 euros.

Compared with the survey from 2024, the change is visible. Then the largest number of participants, 47% of them, chose the range from 1,500 to 2,000 euros, while a third selected amounts from 2,000 to 2,500 euros. Today precisely that higher range gathers half of the answers.

World.title: Another Successful Croatian Tourist Season: Last-Minute Becomes the Rule
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – Another very successful Croatian tourist season is now behind us, with last-minute bookings seemingly becoming the new rule.

Croatia now has yet another very successful tourist season behind it, as assessed by Damir Krešić, director of the Institute for Tourism on HTV’s central news programme. Poslovni reports that he emphasised that the result is particularly important given the complex geopolitical and economic circumstances. “Although this tourist season may not have been a big leap forward compared to last year’s, given the extremely complex geopolitical and economic conditions in which it took place, I think we really should be satisfied,” he said.

As one of the most important trends he singled out the growing share of last-minute reservations, the so-called last-minute booking. “That is something we will have to get used to in the future. It is no longer an exception; it is becoming the rule in tourism, he said. Krešić also pointed out that the price increase this year was significantly milder than last year. Tourists, he added, are becoming more rational and are managing their money more carefully. In addition to safety, which has been one of the important factors in choosing a tourist destination since the pandemic, climatic conditions are also becoming increasingly important.

climate change is playing an increasingly important role

Climate change and increasingly pronounced temperature extremes during the hot summer are increasingly influencing tourist behaviour, but for now, there are no concrete indicators that tourist demand is being significantly redirected from the Mediterranean towards northern Europe because of high temperatures, Krešić assessed. It is, however, absolutely happening. According to him, due to ever-higher temperatures, some tourists may avoid travelling during the boiling months of July and August and shift them to more pleasant parts of the year. “Perhaps those trips during July and August are less attractive, where demand spills over into May and June, or into September and October, that is, into the pre-season and post-season period,” Krešić said.

croatia’s seasonality curse

He also pointed out that Croatia still has a pronounced seasonality of tourism, but, as he said, it is not only a Croatian problem, but a characteristic of tourism in all Mediterranean countries. As one of the ways to reduce seasonality he singled out the development of new and high-quality tourist facilities in the pre-season and post-season that are not necessarily linked to sun and sea. Sun and sea will remain our main tourist resource for many years to come, he said, but added that the offer needs to be supplemented with facilities that can attract guests outside the main season as well.

He also considers it important to open new, especially distant markets. Some guests from overseas markets, he says, may not prefer coming to Croatia at the peak of the season, but precisely in the pre-season and post-season. Krešić believes that Croatia should also target different sociodemographic groups of tourists more. Currently among the most important guests are families with small children, who have limited travel options due to school obligations. “There are business tourists, there are pensioners, there is a whole series of other sociodemographic groups, Krešić said, emphasising that attracting precisely such guests could contribute to reducing seasonality. Tourist development, in addition to revenues and benefits, also brings certain social, spatial and environmental costs, Damir Krešić warned. Among them he singled out the lower inclination of young people towards education in destinations with a high intensity of tourism.

education in tourism

Krešić said that the inclination towards education among people living in such destinations is a little lower than the Croatian average. “That is one of the social costs of tourist development that we rarely take into account when looking at what the benefits and what, in a way, the costs of that tourist development are, he said. According to him, when assessing the effects of tourism one should not look only at the revenues it generates, but one should also subtract the costs of tourist development from them.

“In order for us to correctly balance the development of tourism, we must not look only at foreign, or as we used to call them, foreign-currency revenues from tourism and total revenues from tourism, but from those revenues we need to subtract the costs, he emphasised. Among the more important costs he singled out the impact of tourism on the environment and space, but also the social consequences. “One of those social costs is actually the reduction in the inclination of young people towards education, Krešić said, Of course they are less inclined towards education because through rentierism, in a way, they can much more easily secure some kind of comfortable existence for themselves.

World.title: Why Tech-Forward Americans are Claiming Their Domovnica for Asset Protection
World.content:
October the 7th, 2026 – Tech-forward Americans with Croatian ancestry are claiming their Domovnica and EU passports not only to skip border lines and connect with their roots, but for better asset protection.

The USA is, as we know well, a massive melting pot. There are countless Americans who are entitled to a passport from another country from which their parents or grandparents emigrated. Naturally, the standard narrative surrounding dual citizenship has been romantic. US citizens are known for their love of tracking down their ancestral roots across Europe and the world. When those roots go back to somewhere like Croatia, the traditional reason for seeking closer ties has been to do with seeking a slower pace of life, buying a Mediterranean retirement villa, or harbouring a sentimental reconnection with the homeland of their ancestors.

A shift is occurring across the diaspora community, with a brand new (and decidedly modern) class of applicant is emerging, one driven not by nostalgia, but by geopolitical diversification, systemic asset isolation, and digital estate planning.

For tech-forward Americans such as software engineers, blockchain founders, digital asset managers, and remote technology executives, obtaining a Croatian Domovnica (Citizenship Certificate) and subsequent European Union passport is increasingly viewed as a sophisticated legal instrument. In an era where wealth is increasingly decentralized, digital, and global, holding an EU passport unlocks legal frameworks that allow Americans to shield their digital estates from the public, slow, and expensive mechanics of the UD probate system. Here is how modern asset protection, European civil law, and digital wealth intersect, and why tech-centric US citizens are utilising their Croatian heritage to secure their digital legacies.

digital asset vulnerability in american estate law

To understand precisely why a European Union passport is becoming a coveted asset protection tool, one must first look at the inherent flaws in how United States estate law handles digital wealth. Whether an individual owns a portfolio of cryptocurrency, decentralised finance (DeFi) liquidity tokens, valuable domain registries, intellectual property (IP) for a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platform, or monied digital media channels, the U.S. legal system treats these assets through a highly fragmented, state-by-state framework.

When a US citizen passes away, their estate generally enters probate. This court-supervised process identifies, validates, and distributes a deceased person’s assets. For traditional assets like real estate or local bank accounts, probate is tedious. For digital assets, it can be catastrophic for an array of reasons.

The first reason is known as the transparency paradox. American probate court proceedings are a matter of public record. For high-net-worth tech entrepreneurs or privacy-focused individuals, this means their entire digital asset portfolio, corporate structures, and valuations can become viewable by literally anyone, exposing heirs to security and privacy risks.

Then comes the dreaded custodian bureaucracy, a process where US-based digital custodians, domain registrars, and cloud services (from AWS to major financial exchanges) routinely freeze accounts instantly upon notification of a user’s death. Resolving these problematic freezes requires specific state-level court orders, a process that can take months or years, stalling active tech businesses or locking volatile crypto assets during erratic market swings.

Then come jurisdictional clashes where digital nomads or remote founders live across multiple states or hold international digital infrastructure. In these tricky cases, multiple state courts are free to claim jurisdiction, leading to astronomically high legal fees and an endless administrative gridlock that puts even Croatia’s love of red tape to shame.

an eu passport as a succession backdoor via “brussels IV”

This is where the legal architecture of the European Union changes the landscape completely. For an American who claims their Croatian citizenship by descent, they don’t just become a citizen of Croatia, they become a citizen of the European Union. This status grants them access to one of the most powerful cross-border estate planning tools available in the modern world, and that’s the EU Succession Regulation (known as Brussels IV).

Introduced to harmonise estate laws across the bloc, Brussels IV dictates that the law applicable to the succession of a person’s entire estate shall be the law of the country in which they have their “habitual residence” at the time of death. However, the regulation contains a critical provision: an EU can explicitly choose the law of their nationality to govern their global estate instead. For a bi-cultural Croatian-American who strategically aligns their digital operations, remote work, or residency within the EU, this framework provides an unparalleled level of flexibility that looks like this:

Traditional American route: public probate court – state-by-state gridlock – totally frozen digital assets



The EU passport route: Brussels IV opt-in – completely unified civil law – private, notarised transfer

By utilising an EU passport, an American tech entrepreneur can opt out of extremely fragmented US state probate systems for their EU and international digital holdings. Instead of relying on a local US judge who may not understand smart contracts or domain portfolios, estates such as these can be streamlined under a unified European Union civil law framework, executed very privately and discreetly through a notary system rather than a public courtroom with all eyes on it from who knows where.

strategic asset isolation through eu corporate structures

Securing Croatian is the foundational step that allows Americans to easily establish digital asset-holding companies within the European Union’s famed single market. While non-EU citizens can still technically open companies in the EU, they face severe administrative hurdles, complex compliance checks, and restricted access to local banking rails. A dual American-Croatian citizen, however, can establish a corporate entity (such as a Croatian d.o.o. or an Estonian OÜ via EU open market rules) as an EU citizen with no issues This capability unlocks three distinct operational advantages for digital wealth preservation.

The first and perhaps the most important to most is continuous operational liquidity. This means that if an entrepreneur’s digital assets, code repositories, or SaaS platforms are all held by an EU corporate entity owned by an EU citizen, the operational side of the asset doesn’t grind to a halt upon their passing. European Union corporate structures allow for the seamless, pre-programmed transition of directorial power. While the American side of an individual’s estate may be frozen instantly and for a long period of time in probate, the EU entity continues to operate freely, trade, and generate revenue uninterrupted.

The second is no less important, and that is a private, notarised estate settlement. Rather unlike the highly public theatre of American probate courts, many EU jurisdictions settle estates through civil law notaries. This process is entirely confidential, quick and highly contractual. For individuals prioritising so-called “stealth wealth,” holding Croatian and therefore EU citizenship allows for the unhindered transfer of corporate shares holding millions in digital property to occur entirely out of the public eye.

The third significant reason is hedging against troublesome American regulatory volatility. The current regulatory environment for digital assets and decentralised technologies across the pond in the United States remains very unpredictable. By establishing an elite legal foothold in the EU as an EU citizen, tech-forward Americans create an immediate, fully lawful alternative for their intellectual property and digital capital. If American regulatory overreach threatens a digital project or crypto fund, the infrastructure can be legally anchored to their EU identity without dirtying any waters.

domain registries, ip and code continuity

That might all sound like senseless words to those not involved with tech, but for software developers and digital creators, their wealth is often bound up in intellectual property. That can be GitHub repositories, private code bases, proprietary algorithms, and high-value domain portfolios. These assets are highly liquid but very legally fragile. If a tech founder passes away as a sole US citizen, the transfer of digital IP to their children can and regularly does become a legal nightmare. American tech platforms are globally notorious for their strict, unyielding terms of service regarding account transferability after death. That isn’t the case in the EU.

By holding dual citizenship, an individual can split their legal personality. They can vest the ownership of international domain registries and code copyrights into an EU-based structure tied to their EU identity. If the US legal system locks down local assets, the European Union side remains open and active, ensuring that the code keeps on running, the domains don’t expire, and the digital inheritance remains fully secure.

taking the “two passport” lifestyle trend beyond the basic

The concept of a second passport has been popularised but focuses entirely on travel freedom and tax optimisation. However, for the diaspora community with legitimate claims to Croatian citizenship by descent, the motivation is shifting toward structural permanence. Applying for a Domovnica through an expert team like Croatian By Descent is no longer seen solely as an administrative task to get a shorter line at EU airports. Instead, it’s treated as a foundational piece of a modern, international estate plan. The process of gathering historical records, verifying lineage, obtaining apostilles, and submitting an application package to a Croatian consulate is an investment in legal infrastructure. It provides a permanent, multi-generational safety valve that allows tech-forward families to operate across two distinct legal systems.

As the global economy becomes increasingly virtualised, the laws governing wealth preservation must evolve. The tech-forward diaspora has recognised that relying on a single passport and a single legal jurisdiction is a single point of failure for an asset portfolio built on code, crypto, and digital IP. Reclaiming Croatian citizenship by descent bridges the past and the future. It allows digital entrepreneurs to take the ancestral heritage of their parents or grandparents and convert it into a sophisticated, 21st-century shield for their digital wealth. By unlocking the unique cross-border legal benefits of the EU, these citizens ensure that their totally sovereign legacy (and their wealth) remains protected for generations to come.

how croatian by descent can help

Croatian by Descent is operated by members of the Croatian diaspora themselves. Instead of lawyers with no skin in the game looking at you with dollar signs flashing before their eyes, the experts who run this service know exactly what it means to seek and hold Croatian citizenship. Croatia’s roots are deep and often painful, and those seeking a passport have a multitude of reasons for doing so. Few understand this better than those who have gone through the process for themselves. Croatia is infamous for its love of paperwork and bureaucracy, and while this has improved markedly over the last decade or so, it will take a few generations before it all finally goes to the history books. Traversing the legal pathways entirely alone is not only daunting but often ends up hitting brick wall after brick wall. Croatian by Descent takes the wheel and helps you through the admin in order to sector your little blue passport, a concrete connection to your family history, and tech-forward security permanently.

World.title: Osijek-London Flights to Continue in 2027
World.content:
October the 7th, 2026 – Osijek-London flights will continue in 2027 despite the decline in overall passenger numbers from Osijek Airport.

Osijek Airport recorded a noticeable drop in passenger numbers during the month of September compared to the same month last year. As SIB.net reports, total of 3,026 passengers passed through Croatia’s easternmost airport last month, while back in September 2025 there were 5,449. According to information published on the Croatian Aviation website, this is 2,423 fewer passengers, or a drop of 44.5 percent year-on-year.

The result was also affected by the absence of regular traffic on the Osijek–London route. The Irish low-cost carrier Ryanair operated the seasonal route twice a week during September last year, while this year the route operated for a significantly shorter period. Total figures for the first nine months also show a decline. From January to the end of September, 28,605 passengers passed through Osijek Airport, which is 23.4 percent fewer than in the same period of 2025.

osijek airport winds down for the rest of 2026

Osijek Airport now faces a change in the schedule during the winter months. Traffic is ending on three more seasonal PSO routes – Trade Air to Zadar and Croatia Airlines routes to Dubrovnik and Split. Additional attention is drawn by the fact that, according to currently available information, tickets for domestic PSO routes from Osijek are not being sold for the period from January 2027. For now, this means that there is no available ticket sales for that part of the schedule, while any decisions on the continuation or changes to the routes will be known later. PSO routes are an important part of Osijek’s transport connectivity with other Croatian destinations, and decisions on their schedule and continuation fall under the competence of the Ministry of the Sea, Transport and Infrastructure.

ryanair confirms osijek-london flights for 2027

Low-cost and wildly popular airline Ryanair has confirmed flights between Osijek and London in 2027 as well. Unfortunately, as was the case during this season, they will operate only during three months – from the beginning of June to the end of August. This is quite unlike the situation elsewhere across the country, particularly in Zagreb which connects directly to London Stansted on a daily basis year-round. The first flight will operate from Osijek on the 2nd of June, a Wednesday, at the rather unfavourable time of 23:25, while the second flight of the week will be on Saturdays at the better time of 11:10.

From London to Osijek, the aircraft will depart on Wednesdays at 19:35 and on Saturdays early in the morning at 07:20. Unfortunately, this is the only route of this carrier to Osijek. The price varies, but the minimum is 55 euros one way, which is considerably more expensive than it is from Zagreb.

osijek airport is nearing reconstruction completion

Works on the reconstruction of Osijek Airport itself are nearing completion, so the new flight season will be welcomed by a completely renovated passenger terminal. This is a valuable investment and, it can only be hoped, an announcement of some new flights from the easternmost Croatian airport that is almost forgotten in comparison to others across the country. For that, many parameters need to align, and it doesn’t depend only on the airport but also on local self-government units and the related ministry.
