World.title: South Korea test-fires its first homegrown hypersonic weapon: presidency
World.content:
South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic weapon on Thursday, the presidential office said, days after Pyongyang announced the AI-assisted launch of an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung “observed the first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV) — currently under research and development using domestic technology,” the presidential Blue House said in a statement.

Hypersonic glide vehicles are sent into the upper atmosphere via rocket boosters or on ballistic missiles, then glide towards their target at five times the speed of sound or greater.

Hailing a “key strategic asset capable of changing the course of the battlefield,” the South Korean statement said that the missiles’ “unpredictable flight trajectories and overwhelming speed enable them to strike key strategic targets.”

The test was aimed at verifying “the performance of ultra-high-temperature heat-resistant materials — a core technology for glide vehicles — as well as guidance and control capabilities and the ability to fly irregularly at low altitudes under hypersonic flight conditions,” it added.

Analysts say North Korea, which is technically at war with the South, has stepped up testing of its own hypersonic weapons with technological support from Russia.

In response, “South Korea has also been devoting considerable effort to developing the technology — and can be said to have achieved a successful test this time,” said Hong Sung-pyo, senior researcher at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for Military Affairs.

Moscow has used hypersonic missiles in combat since around 2024, according to analysts.

Pyongyang has said its Saturday launch involved the use of AI, claiming there was “no way to avoid” the missile that was “capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude.”

It also said that the missile’s “wave-like trajectory mode” left South Korea and Japan unable to track it effectively.

Both Seoul and Washington have said the missile could be “sufficiently detected and intercepted using the defensive assets possessed by the two allies.”

South Korea said that the hypersonic glide vehicle tested Thursday “descended to a low altitude after separation, freely altered its trajectory both vertically and horizontally, and ... accurately struck its designated target.”

The weapon offered “a new deterrence capability capable of striking key targets within the Korean Peninsula’s operational environment,” the Blue House said.

World.title: BOJ raises economic assessment for Tohoku and Shikoku as tech demand remains strong
World.content:
The Bank of Japan revised up its economic assessment for two of the country’s nine regions in a quarterly report released Thursday while leaving it unchanged for the rest.

The central bank compiled the report at the day’s meeting of managers of its regional branches, which was held at its headquarters in Tokyo. Demand related to artificial intelligence remained strong, including for semiconductor manufacturing equipment and electronic components. When it comes to production, the BOJ raised its economic assessment for seven of the nine regions, excluding Hokkaido and the Tokai region.

In the report, the BOJ said the economy in all nine regions has been “picking up moderately,” “recovering moderately,” or “on a moderate recovery trend” while noting that “some weakness has been seen in part.”

The central bank revised upward its economic assessment for the Tohoku region from the assessment that the economy “has been picking up” to the view that the economy “has been recovering moderately.” It also raised its economic view for Shikoku from an assessment that the economy “has been picking up moderately” to the view that the economy “has been picking up.”

In interviews with companies, an electrical equipment maker in Osaka said that AI-related demand has been increasing faster than expected and that robust demand is likely to continue for about the next three years.

Many branch chiefs reported that private consumption has generally remained resilient, supported by improvements in real income. A department store operator in Shizuoka Prefecture said that sales of high-priced goods, such as luxury watches and jewelry, remained strong. Against the backdrop of rising stock prices, there were also reports that sales to wealthy consumers showed no signs of weakening.

Meanwhile, a retailer in Nagoya said that bad weather, including typhoons and heavy rain, weighed on consumption.

Kenji Fujita, manager of the central bank’s branch in Osaka, said at a news conference that small and midsize companies have made relatively smooth progress in passing on higher costs in business-to-business transactions, but that the process is still only halfway along and uneven among businesses closer to consumers.

Regarding the impact of the BOJ’s interest rate hikes to date, an official at the central bank’s Research and Statistics Department said only some companies had indicated that they would put off capital investment, while many said they would make necessary investments, including in labor-saving measures.

World.title: Germany arrests member of Qilin hacker group who was extradited from Japan
World.content:
A Russian national believed to be a key member of the notorious Qilin international hacker group was arrested by German authorities after being extradited from Japan, Japanese police said Thursday.

According to the National Police Agency, German authorities had obtained an arrest warrant for the 28-year-old Russian citizen on suspicion of extortion for allegedly attacking German companies and demanding cryptocurrency payments.

After learning that he planned to visit Japan as a tourist in May, the agency’s cyber special investigation department identified his whereabouts through a joint investigation involving the Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto police departments.

He was detained at a hotel in Osaka that month and handed over to German authorities this month following a decision by the Tokyo High Court under the extradition law.

Qilin has launched ransomware attacks worldwide since October 2022, affecting about 4,000 companies. It demands ransom payments to restore encrypted data and threatens to release stolen data if victims refuse to pay.

Since April 2023, it has hit 53 companies, hospitals and schools in Japan. The group claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Asahi Group Holdings in 2025.

Qilin operates through numerous affiliates that carry out cyber intrusions and extortion attempts using ransomware provided by core members responsible for malware development and system management.

“It was significant that we identified and arrested a (Qilin) member through international cooperation,” a senior NPA official said.

World.title: Nihon Hidankyo hears calls to pass cause to second generation
World.content:
Nihon Hidankyo, a Japanese atomic bomb survivor organization, heard calls Thursday for children of atomic bomb survivors to carry on its movement as it weighs whether to remain active or disband.

About 80 hibakusha survivors of the 1945 atomic bombings and other representatives of constituent groups from across Japan attended the meeting in Tokyo.

They reported their views on the future of the organization, formally known as the Japan Confederation of A- and H-Bomb Sufferers Organizations.

A group from Hiroshima, where the nuclear attack took place on Aug. 6, 1945, said Nihon Hidankyo received the 2024 Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of its efforts to spread awareness of the realities of the atomic bombings, and argued that “disbanding would have a major impact.” It said that the organization should remain active, centered on second-generation hibakusha.

A group from Nagasaki, which was attacked with an atomic bomb on Aug. 9, 1945, said it was still discussing the issue but that some viewed disbanding as “out of the question.”

A group from Kanagawa Prefecture, meanwhile, said disbanding would be realistic once hibakusha are no longer active, while arguing that the movement itself should be passed on.

Some other groups said they were still weighing their options.

The organization’s committee representing second-generation hibakusha also presented its views. The members said second-generation hibakusha are also “victims of the atomic bombings,” having grown up witnessing their parents’ suffering and living with anxieties of their own.

“We want to keep Nihon Hidankyo going together with our supporters and carry on its movement,” they said.

Nihon Hidankyo will decide its final policy at its regular general meeting in June next year.

World.title: Trump reportedly asked Xi to meet with Takaichi
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump asked Chinese President Xi Jinping at their summit last month to hold a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Hong Kong’s South China Morning Post reported Thursday.

Xi was not receptive to the proposal, according to the paper.

During the last U.S.-China summit in Washington, Trump expressed concern that China’s restrictions on rare earth exports to Japan were also affecting U.S. industries, adding that this situation indirectly violates the U.S.-China trade truce.

Xi responded that China-Japan relations should be separate from China-U.S. relations. He also claimed that the risk of a resurgence of Japanese militarism is growing.

The newspaper also reported that the Japanese government has requested a bilateral summit with China on the occasion of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next month.

However, China suggested that, instead of Xi, Premier Li Qiang, the second-ranking official in the Chinese Communist Party, would meet with Takaichi. Japan responded cautiously to this offer, according to the report.

World.title: Canadian writer Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
World.content:
Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson ⁠won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the award-giving body said on Thursday.

“She was very taken by ‌surprise. We ‌didn’t have so much time to speak, and all she had time ​to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind,” said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy.

Canadian ‌poet and essayist Carson’s work often blends verse, prose, ​dialogue and translation in a genre-defying mix. Born in Toronto, she has also held Icelandic citizenship since 2022.

World.title: Climate needs same urgency as defense spending, COP31 chief says
World.content:
Action to curb emissions and bolster resilience to the impacts of extreme weather needs similar urgency to international efforts to lift defense investments, according to the head of next month’s annual global climate change conference.

“The same responsibility, same determination, we expect each and every country to show in climate action,” Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister and president-designate of the COP31 summit, told reporters Thursday in Fiji at preparatory talks ahead of the November event. “What does it mean to spend 5% for defense if you don’t have a country to live on? What does it mean to defend it?”

North Atlantic Treaty Organization nations last year committed to spend at least 3.5% of national economic output on core defense programs, and as much as a further 1.5% on related areas by 2035. In contrast, the European Union has warned “there is no scope” for new climate finance commitments at COP31, according to a draft document.

The flow of finance to fund work to lower emissions or for climate adaptation projects is faltering as nations cut overall aid budgets, and following the withdrawal of the U.S. from efforts focused on global warming. Spending on the issue by Germany, Europe’s biggest economy, fell last year and the nation missed a pledge on climate financing.

Nations “must deliver on existing finance commitments,” and continue to advance a goal of delivering $1.3 trillion a year to developing countries by 2035, Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, said at the Fiji event.

“This is what COP31 can and must do, help convert promises into more real-world results,” Stiell said. “That depends on many factors, including scaling up, speeding up, and broadening access to affordable climate finance.”

The Pre-COP talks in Fiji have won some new pledges, including for the Pacific Resilience Facility, a mechanism established last year to direct financing for climate and disaster projects to vulnerable nations in the region. Fiji’s government offered $10 million and will press nations at the COP talks to “get climate finance into the hands of the people who really need it,” said Lynda Tabuya, the country’s minister for information, environment and climate change.

The U.K. pledged $13 million to the Pacific facility, the Netherlands offered $1.12 million and Denmark and Ireland both doubled previous commitments, according to a statement. Australia, which previously pledged 100 million Australian dollars ($70 million) to the resilience fund, made separate proposals this week totaling about AU$10 million for renewable energy projects in the Pacific and to protect infrastructure in the region.

However, the Pacific fund, which aims to build disaster preparedness without furthering the debt for participating countries, is yet to meet an initial target to win commitments of $500 million by the end of the year, and to hit a longer-term target for $1.5 billion.

With limited prospects for major new climate financing, organizers of the COP31 talks are focusing on work to improve access for developing countries — including in the Pacific, Caribbean and Indian Ocean — to already existing funding, and will seek new support from development banks and other countries.

“The countries that need the finance the most get it the least,” Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who will serve as COP31 president of negotiations, said in Fiji. “That has got to change.”

Bowen and Kurum on Tuesday led a delegation of dignitaries, including the heads of the Asian Development Bank and Green Climate Fund, to visit climate change-threatened Tuvalu in the western Pacific Ocean.

World.title: Samsung and TSMC fail to excite investors used to torrid AI growth
World.content:
Samsung Electronics earned a nearly ninefold rise in quarterly operating profit, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.’s sales jumped 51%, reflecting the spoils of relentless spending on AI infrastructure.

Yet investor reaction to a day of record-setting results was muted, weighed down by worries about the staying power of an investment boom propped up by rising debt levels. Samsung’s stock price shed 2.4% Thursday in Seoul. In Tokyo, shares of both companies’ suppliers including Tokyo Electron, Advantest and Ibiden declined.

Investors are questioning how long AI spending can last, especially as companies’ big capex plans come under pressure because of rising borrowing costs around the world.

World.title: CK Asset opts to rebuild 3 blocks at starter homes project after steelwork scandal
World.content:
Three of the six residential buildings at CK Asset’s “starter homes” project in Hong Kong will be demolished and rebuilt in what the developer called the most “time-saving” solution, two years after a scandal over substandard steel reinforcement work halted construction.

The Buildings Department confirmed on Thursday that it had approved demolition plans for three blocks at the Anderson Road development in Kwun Tong, while remedial work was under way at the other three.

Earlier investigations found significant discrepancies between steel reinforcement installed in parts of the six towers and the approved plans, including fewer reinforcing bars than required. Ten people were also arrested in connection with the project on suspicion of bribery and other offences.

World.title: Hong Kong police arrest students as alleged key figures in HK$2.16 million scam ring
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested two tertiary students suspected of being key members of a fraud and money-laundering syndicate behind fake job s, dating scams and bogus concert ticket sales.

The force said on Thursday that officers had arrested 10 people in an earlier operation targeting the syndicate, which allegedly swindled victims – mainly students – out of more than HK$2.1 million (US$267,578).

The suspects, five men and five women aged between 13 and 68, were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud and money laundering, according to Superintendent Leung Chi-hang of the regional anti-deception unit in New Territories South.

Leung said two of those arrested, a man and a woman studying at different tertiary institutions, were a couple and suspected core members of the syndicate.

World.title: Development chief dismisses fears Northern Metropolis supply will hit office sector
World.content:
Hong Kong’s development chief has dismissed concerns that commercial floor space in the Northern Metropolis megaproject will further depress the city’s struggling office market, stressing that incoming supply is primarily for the innovation and technology (I&T) sector.

Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho told the Legislative Council on Thursday that the 1 million square metres (10.8 million square feet) of economic floor space to be provided in the megaproject next to the Shenzhen border over the next five years was unrelated to traditional office supply.

She was responding to a question from real estate and construction sector lawmaker Augustine Wong Ho-ming, who voiced concern during a debate on the city’s first five-year plan and annual policy address that the additional commercial floor space could aggravate already high office vacancy rates in non-prime locations.

World.title: National security police arrest 2 over alleged seditious social media posts
World.content:
Hong Kong national security police have arrested two people, including an insurance broker, on suspicion of publishing seditious posts on social media.

A police spokesman said on Thursday that officers from the National Security Department had arrested a man and a woman, both aged 38, on Tuesday on suspicion of doing an act with a seditious intention under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance.

“The two arrested people, including a male licensed insurance broker, were suspected of operating pages on various social media platforms and publishing seditious posts that incite hatred against the constitutional order of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region,” the spokesman said.

A source said the pair were suspected of managing social media pages for YellowInsurance, a platform accused of posting content supporting the 2019 anti-government protests and arrested protesters, as well as smearing the central and Hong Kong governments.

World.title: Hong Kong child abuse case prompts calls to watch for signs of psychological harm
World.content:
Psychological abuse can be hard to detect, Hong Kong welfare experts have warned, urging social workers and teachers to look for subtle changes in children’s behaviour amid outrage over a viral video showing a girl carrying heavy bags of beer as her stepfather called her “useless”.

Welfare groups said on Thursday that emotional and verbal abuse were among the most common yet least recognised forms of child abuse. Signs often emerged through changes such as social withdrawal and anxiety, they said, but the harm could be as serious as physical injury.

They urged professionals working with children to consult the Social Welfare Department even when suspected cases fell short of the serious harm threshold for mandatory reporting.

Their calls came after police on Wednesday arrested a man and a woman on suspicion of ill-treatment of a child. The previous evening, their 10-year-old daughter had been filmed carrying two heavy bags of beer at Fu Tai Estate in Tuen Mun, with her backpack torn and gaping open.

World.title: Hong Kong IPO boom at risk as cornerstone backers get cold feet, sources say
World.content:
Exuberance among cornerstone investors in Hong Kong’s booming initial public offering (IPO) market seems to be fading, forcing some issuers that had hoped to list this month to postpone their offerings.

With more than 60 per cent of new listings in the third quarter now trading below their issue prices, cornerstone investors – who typically receive guaranteed allocations in exchange for holding shares for six months – are reconsidering whether to subscribe to coming deals, according to people familiar with the matter.

At least one IPO originally planned for October had to be delayed until next month at the earliest after some institutional investors pulled out of verbal agreements to be cornerstone backers, they said.

World.title: Police recover HK$30 million in gold swapped for fabric softener in hotel theft
World.content:
Hong Kong police have recovered about HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) worth of stolen gold and arrested two men in connection with an elaborate hotel-room swap in which 30kg of gold granules were replaced with eight bottles of fabric softener.

The force said it received a report early on Wednesday from a mainland Chinese man who said about 30kg of gold granules, valued at around HK$30 million, were suspected to have been stolen from his luggage in a Kwun Tong hotel.

The gold had been replaced with eight similarly weighted bottles of fabric softener and a friend travelling with him in the same room had disappeared.

Police traced the suspects using the city’s surveillance camera network.

World.title: Abby Choi’s ex-father-in-law ‘cunning old fox’ who clung to her wealth, court told
World.content:
The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has described her daughter’s former father-in-law as a “cunning old fox” who clung to her family’s fortune, dismissing his lawyer’s claim that he paid HK$30 million towards an upscale flat at the centre of a bitter dispute between the two families.

Cheung Yin-fa told the High Court on Thursday that her daughter had given Kwong Kau a monthly allowance of HK$20,000 (US$2,548) and paid more than HK$200,000 towards his medical expenses when he was seriously ill.

She appeared emotional when defence counsel suggested that Kwong, a former police sergeant, could afford a Rolls-Royce and a seven-seater car because he had made money from business activities in mainland China since retiring from the force.

“This is definitely impossible ... He couldn’t even afford his meals; how could he spend HK$6 million to HK$7 million on a Rolls-Royce?” Cheung said on the fourth day of her testimony.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.title: China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.content:
DeepZang, China’s first Tibetan-language large language model, is being upgraded to better adapt to Tibetan dialects, enable real-time translation between Tibetan and Mandarin Chinese, and support offline use.

At a Monday seminar in Hohhot, capital of northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, the model’s developer unveiled a series of upgrades scheduled between October and December. The seminar featured representatives from companies, research institutions, and universities.

DeepZang, developed by local technology company Choknor, was launched in March in Lhasa, capital of the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. Its app supports AI-powered conversations, translation, and speech transcription in Tibetan, Mandarin Chinese, and English.

At the model’s launch, organizations including the Xizang branches of China Mobile and the People’s Insurance Company of China, as well as Sichuan Minzu Publishing House, signed agreements with Choknor to promote its adoption.

According to Choknor, DeepZang has attracted nearly 400,000 users across Xizang, the northwestern Qinghai and Gansu provinces, and southwestern Sichuan province, where most of China’s Tibetan speakers reside.

The company has said the model has cut the time needed for some Tibetan-Chinese translation tasks involving two or three people from 40 minutes to just over 10 minutes for one person. It also reported that the model has been used in such varied settings as helping non-Tibetan-speaking doctors communicate with local patients, generating Tibetan-language contracts for yak sales, and assisting grassroots officials in drafting Tibetan work reports.

The model has been trained on nearly 70 million pairs of standardized Tibetan and Chinese texts, along with more than 30,500 hours of Tibetan speech covering its three major dialect groups — Ü-Tsang, Kham, and Amdo. The team collected the data from libraries, medical institutions, and monasteries, among other settings.

At Monday’s seminar, Choknor unveiled plans to develop offline language packages for Tibetan, Chinese, and English, allowing the app to function with limited or no internet access. The company also plans to pilot 50 simultaneous interpretation devices among at least 300 participants in Lhasa this December.

Tenzin Norbu, Choknor’s founder, said the company aims to bring DeepZang into “pastoral tents, tourist service counters, and grassroots hospitals,” enabling Tibetan speakers to “enjoy the benefits of artificial intelligence on an equal footing.”

Choknor said on Sunday that beyond fostering exchanges and integration among ethnic groups, DeepZang could help ensure the accuracy of Tibetan-language information and contribute to social stability and long-term security.

Founded in 2016, Choknor specializes in Tibetan-Chinese bilingual speech technology, scanning and translation tools, and optical character recognition. Its products include smart computer mice, scanning and translation pens, and an AI-powered Tibetan subtitling system.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.title: The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.content:
With hundreds of concerts scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, some fans found the cheapest way to upgrade a seat was to rent a better camera phone.

For about 100 to 200 yuan ($15 to $30) a day, concertgoers can rent flagship smartphones with powerful telephoto cameras that pull distant performers into clearer view, a useful option when high demand leaves fans seated far from the stage and professional cameras and long lenses are often barred from venues.

On Chinese rental platform Renrenzu and Xianyu, a secondhand marketplace owned by Chinese tech giant Alibaba, some flagship phones are listed as “concert essentials.”

One Renrenzu ad touted a “200-megapixel telephoto, crystal clear — even the nosebleed seats feel VIP,” while the platform has also offered concert ticket reimbursements through prize draws.

The phones on offer are among the latest flagships from Chinese smartphone makers such as vivo and OPPO, with high-resolution telephoto cameras, image stabilization, and, in some cases, detachable lens kits that extend their reach.

A vivo X300 Ultra bundled with a telephoto lens, for example, rents for about 215 yuan for one day, while a two-day rental brings the average daily cost down to about 125 yuan. Other popular models include OPPO’s Find X10 Pro Max, which packs three 200-megapixel rear cameras and is advertised as supporting up to “20x lossless zoom” with its official telephoto kit.

Such high-end models typically sell for about 5,000 to 8,000 yuan, while official telephoto lens kits can add another 1,000 to 2,000 yuan, making a short rental far cheaper for fans who only want the extra reach for one concert.

Online, concertgoers are comparing phones and lens attachments, posting photos from the stands, and swapping tips on which setups work best from distant seats.

Liu Hang, who attended Taiwan singer Steve Chou’s concert at Beijing Workers’ Stadium, told Time Finance that he brought a Ruiying Z10 camera module and telephoto attachment made by Chinese tech giant Huawei into the venue. “I had a 580-yuan ticket, but with the ‘Huawei cannon,’ it felt like a 1,680-yuan seat,” he said.

Another social media user, who said he had attended nearly 100 concerts, compared several phones and camera setups for live shows. He said such phones were easy to carry, worked well for close-up shots, and had a dedicated stage mode that automatically adjusted exposure, though adding a telephoto attachment made it tiring to hold through an entire concert.

Renrenzu said orders for concert-related equipment jumped 388% year on year over the summer, far outpacing a 67% rise in short-term rentals overall. A total of 257 concerts were scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, according to Alibaba’s entertainment data platform Lighthouse.

Chen Shenyu, a manager at consulting firm China Insights Consultancy, told Time Finance that smartphone photography was becoming less about simply recording daily life and more about performing well in specific situations. Concerts are especially challenging because fans may be seated far from the stage, lighting changes constantly, and they are often shooting handheld photos and video.

That also makes concerts a natural showcase for smartphone makers, Chen said. If consumers increasingly reach for telephoto cameras at sporting events, on trips, and during family activities, demand for the same high-end imaging features could extend well beyond concerts.

(Header image: Posts show concertgoers using flagship camera phones with telephoto attachments to capture performers from the stands. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.title: The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.content:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Your book explores how Transsion grew from the informal global phone market that emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when African and Arab traders began traveling to southern China to buy cheap knock-off — or shanzhai — handsets. What is the company’s connection to that era?

Lu Miao: Shanzhai phones were extremely common in the early 2000s. The Huaqiangbei electronics market in Shenzhen was a major hub, while Chungking Mansions in Hong Kong was an important gateway for knock-off phones going overseas.

The main buyers were small traders from Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Some scholars call them “suitcase entrepreneurs” because they would arrive with a few suitcases, buy phones, take them home, and distribute them to smaller towns.

By the time Transsion was founded in 2006, shanzhai phones had already swept through many African countries. On the one hand, they met the basic communication needs of many low-income users; on the other, they damaged the reputation of Chinese phones, which African consumers came to associate with cheapness and poor quality.

When I went to Ghana in 2019, I found that many of Transsion’s national distributors had started out-selling secondhand and shanzhai phones bought from traders in Chungking Mansions. After partnering with Transsion, they gradually became formal agents for a multinational company.

These local African distributors linked the shanzhai era to the Transsion era. The personal connections and distribution networks they had built up played a major role in helping Transsion establish itself.

There is also continuity in design. Features such as dual-SIM support and large batteries originated in the shanzhai phone ecosystem and were later adapted for African markets. Dual SIMs, for example, help users avoid costly cross-network calls in countries with patchy network coverage.

But Transsion also represented a break from that era. First, the phone business became more formalized and institutionalized. These distributors set up trading companies of their own, and their relationships with Transsion became governed by more formal contracts.

Second, Transsion did not want to make quick money and leave, as sellers had done in the shanzhai era; it wanted to build a brand and stay for the long term. That is why it invested heavily in its after-sales service network.

Shanzhai wasn’t simply about one manufacturer producing copycat phones. It was an ecosystem: factories, supply chains, designers, distributors ... Transsion grew out of that ecosystem, but also moved beyond the shanzhai model of the time.

Sixth Tone: Looking at the bigger picture, how has Africa’s digital communications sector evolved over time, and how has that affected Chinese companies like Transsion?

Lu: Take Ghana as an example. The country’s telecommunications companies were originally state-owned. But in the 1980s and 1990s, the country had to turn to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for loans to deal with ongoing economic and debt crises. One condition of these loans was structural adjustment, which meant privatizing the telecom sector.

After the reforms, one common outcome was a widening urban-rural gap. Commercial operators were reluctant to serve low-margin rural areas, where costs were high and consumer spending was low, so infrastructure such as base stations remained concentrated in cities.

The needs of rural and low-income communities were overlooked during the reforms, and after the state retreated, it did not step back in to meet those needs. That meant many people could only afford cheap Chinese shanzhai phones.

Transsion stepped into this market, offering affordable feature — or “dumb” — phones that were tailored to African users’ needs. It optimized its models for areas with sparse base-station coverage, making them better at picking up weak signals than many other phones. Electricity supply could also be unreliable in rural areas, so the long battery life of both shanzhai and Transsion phones was another important advantage.

Zhang Lin: Against this backdrop, you argue that we should understand global technology flows in terms of “technology translation” rather than “technology transfer.” What does this framework help us understand about how technology moves between countries?

Lu: I don’t really like the concept of “technology transfer” because it frames the process as one-way: advanced Western societies export technology to less-developed non-Western societies in order to help them develop. But the endpoint of development in this model is always Western modernity.

It also assumes that technology is neutral and fixed, as if transferring technology alone will solve social problems and generate economic growth. Yet many aid projects failed precisely because they transferred equipment without transferring the knowledge, skills, and institutional environment around it.

That is why I used the concept of “technology translation.” When a technology enters a new context, it is often reinterpreted, adjusted, and transformed. Examining the context and process of how technology is translated allows us to see how knowledge moves, and the politics embedded in the process.

Transsion did not simply take phones made in China and move them unchanged to Africa; its products were continually redesigned through their encounter with local markets. Chinese engineers and product managers, Ghanaian promoters, distributors, and repair workers all became “translators” in this process.

For example, Transsion’s dual- and multi-SIM functions were not simply extra hardware features; they responded to high communications costs, uneven network coverage, and users’ need to switch between operators. Cameras optimized for darker skin tones respond to the fact that imaging technologies have historically treated white skin as the default.

These features were not simply invented by an individual designer. They emerged through interactions among the company, users, distribution channels, and repair networks.

Zhang: You describe Transsion’s business strategy as “deep plowing” and contrast it with Silicon Valley’s “blitzscaling” model. How are they different?

Lu: “Blitzscaling” was a widely celebrated model in Silicon Valley from the mid-2010s onward. Popularized by (American internet entrepreneur) Reid Hoffman, it relies on large amounts of capital to expand rapidly, prioritizing speed over efficiency.

The idea is to capture the market first and then achieve winner-takes-all dominance. Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb are typical examples, as are Chinese companies such as ride-hailing firm Didi.

At its core, blitzscaling involves a deliberately inefficient use of capital. Companies sustain themselves through venture capital, and much of that money is wasted. It is a game only a small number of players can afford. Most fail; the few that survive can end up monopolizing the market.

“Deep plowing” is more commonly seen in the Global South. It is slower and depends much more on local knowledge and relationship networks. The term originally comes from agriculture, referring to a labor-intensive mode of production that requires long-term investment and continual care.

In business and technology, I use it to describe a market-driven, labor-intensive approach in which a company continuously interacts with local markets and adjusts its products and business strategies in response to feedback.

In many cases, this model is adopted out of necessity. Transsion chose to work deeply in rural markets overlooked by Western capital largely because it lacked large pools of capital and core technologies. It often had to create room for itself by understanding markets in much finer detail.

(Header image: An entrance to the Circle Market in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Courtesy of Lu Miao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.title: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.content:
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.

China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.

Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.

Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.

China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.

Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.

According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.

“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.

South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.

Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.

China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.title: When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.content:
SHANGHAI — “Great-grandma, your head seems to be a little loose,” Yu Mingrui jokes as he examines an ancestral portrait depicting nine members of a family across three generations.

The 28-year-old Shanghai restorer was commissioned to repair the Qing dynasty (1644–1911) portrait by a descendant of the family in Ningbo, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, which had been passed down through generations. Yu filmed the process and posted it on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

Amid the portrait’s cracks and damage, Yu found clean, deliberate cuts around one woman’s painted head, suggesting the section was once removed and replaced.

Yu commented that the painter might have added the faces after painting the bodies. But viewers offered their own explanations. Some hypothesized the painter had covered up a mistake and repainted the face. Others suggested that descendants of a male ancestor’s concubine had altered the portrait to replace his wife’s image.

The answer may never be known. But the mystery drew widespread attention online, with videos about the painting receiving more than 100 million views and likes across Chinese social media platforms.

On Chinese social media, independent restorers like Yu are demonstrating how damaged paintings, old books, and family records are taken apart, repaired, and preserved.

“A lot of people told me that they simply didn’t know that something damaged could actually be restored before watching my videos,” Yu told Sixth Tone.

The objects brought to independent restorers include ancestral portraits, genealogies, old books, and calligraphy passed down through families and kept in homes rather than institutions.

Often made from paper or silk, these objects are vulnerable to moisture, insects, light, and age. Even when damaged, they can retain names, images, and other details about the families that preserved them.

For restorers like Yu, the videos can also connect that work with owners who might otherwise have left such objects damaged at home. Those commissions provide restorers with work and, in some cases, allow families to recover information from records that had become too fragile or damaged to read.

Face value

When the Qing-era ancestral portrait arrived at Yu’s studio, its ink had faded, its paper had become brittle, and its edges were torn. A patchwork of old advertising flyers held it together, promoting everything from cakes to real estate.

At 3.4 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, the portrait barely fits into the worktable at the center of Yu’s roughly 40-square-meter studio in Shanghai’s rural Songjiang District.

Yu turned the makeshift repairs into another joke for his viewers. Families in China traditionally honor deceased relatives with food and other offerings. The flyers, Yu joked, had given the painted ancestors a modern assortment of their own.

“Whatever the ancestors are missing, they can just take it from behind the painting,” he said.

Repairing the portrait, however, was a more exacting process. Yu said the restoration is divided into four broad stages: washing away dust and stains, removing the backing paper and remnants of earlier repairs, patching tears and holes with paper matching the original, and retouching missing colors and lines.

Each stage depends on the painting’s condition. Even washing it requires the restorer to decide whether to use hot or cold water, whether mold and stains require chemical treatment, and how much the paper can withstand. Chemicals can remove stains quickly, but excessive treatment can damage the paper or alter the painting itself.

“The real difficulty lies in the uncertainty,” Yu said. “A restorer’s experience gives you certainty at the beginning, serving as a safety net to deal with the uncertainty that appears in the process.”

The portrait took around three months to restore. Before treatment, Yu said, face-detection software picked up only three of the nine painted faces. Afterward, when he photographed the restored portrait, the software marked all nine faces on screen. Yu charges around 10,000 yuan ($1,493) for a painting of this size and complexity.

Yu began posting restoration videos while studying Chinese antique restoration in college. After graduating in 2021, he opened his own studio. His videos often begin with an unusual detail, a question about an object’s history, or a joke designed to catch attention.

“History isn’t only made up of famous paintings or nationally protected cultural relics,” he said. “It is also made up of these seemingly insignificant objects. As I restore them, I’m also helping to pass that culture on.”

Genealogies, ancestral portraits, and other family documents offer a view of the past that differs from official histories and local gazetteers, Zhang Yi, a historian at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, told Sixth Tone. Genealogies, for example, can record more than 1,000 people, while larger volumes can include tens of thousands, sometimes with birth and death dates.

“These materials greatly enrich our understanding of the lives and personal histories of ordinary people in Chinese history,” Zhang said.

The videos have also helped Yu turn restoration into a livelihood. His online following attracts commercial sponsorships, which now account for roughly half his income, he said. Many clients bring him just one family object in need of repair, but together, those individual commissions have allowed him to build his own customer base.

Paper trail

Beijing restorer Lian Chengchun also works mainly for private owners, from collectors to families preserving books passed down through generations.

Her videos offer them a first lesson in how to handle and preserve those objects at home, and can prompt people to take a second look at old records before the stories they carry disappear.

“I see little distinction between collections held by organizations and individuals,” Lian said. “Whether a book is restored by a public institution, an independent restorer or a private collector, the goal is the same: to preserve it for future generations.”

Books kept in private hands can arrive in almost any condition. Some have been patched with tape, glue, calendars, or whatever paper was available, repairs that may hold them together temporarily but can cause further and sometimes irreversible damage.

“Others were stored in plastic bags, where trapped moisture can encourage mold and decay,” said Lian, 38, who’s spent 18 years restoring old books by hand.

Before starting such work, Lian studies a book’s age and history, along with its paper, printing style, and other materials, which can vary across periods.

“Only then can I decide how best to repair it,” she said.

Cai Yadong came across Lian’s videos just when members of his clan in Jiaozhu Village, in southern China’s Guangdong province, needed help repairing a badly damaged genealogy.

In 2023, two elderly clan members handed Cai a 111-page genealogy dating to 1920. The wider Huazhou Cai clan today numbers about 20,000 descendants across roughly 110 villages, but Jiaozhu’s own records had almost completely disappeared, leaving residents unsure how their branch fit into the family or even who its founding ancestor was.

“When I first saw it, it was barely recognizable,” Cai, secretary of the Huazhou Cai clan association, said. “The pages were mixed together. Some had been burned, and years of damage had left the book extremely fragile.”

After contacting Lian, Cai flew to Beijing to deliver it himself rather than risk shipping it. “It was simply too valuable to risk any accidents,” he said.

Restoring the genealogy took Lian nearly a year and a half. Because of the genealogy’s age and poor condition, the restoration required careful, piece-by-piece work, Lian said.

“We try to repair it in a way that preserves its original appearance, while retaining as much of the surviving text as possible,” she said.

Lian compared numerous samples before selecting restoration paper that matched the original pages in color and texture. She repaired torn fragments and holes one by one, reinforcing sections where the original characters remained legible.

“Saving each character felt like picking up the brush where the Cai ancestors had left off,” Lian said. “Each page I uncovered felt like a dialogue with people from hundreds of years ago.”

When the work was completed, the volume showed that more than 30 pages were devoted to Jiaozhu, detailing family members and major events.

One entry showed how Jiaozhu’s branch fit into the wider Huazhou Cai clan and identified its founding ancestor as Cai Wende. The restored volume also helped three other villages establish their own connections to the clan.

“If our generation does not do this, the family memory may be gone after another one or two generations,” Cai said. “Once it is lost, it will be very difficult to recover.”

Just weeks before the genealogy surfaced, Jiaozhu had held a ceremony to renovate an ancestral tomb. Villagers knew it as the tomb of their founding ancestor but no longer knew his identity. Once the book was restored, they added Cai Wende’s name to the tomb’s inscription.

Cai described the timing as uncanny. “Whenever we talk about it, we all get goosebumps,” he said.

World.title: Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.content:
Beijing Wildlife Park has turned its fight against a surge of invasive caterpillars into a public contest, offering up to 10 park tickets to visitors who collect the heaviest haul each day. From Sept. 28 to 30, participants caught an estimated 120,000 larvae weighing a combined 18.5 kilograms.

The safari-style zoo on the capital’s southern outskirts announced the event with a call for “warriors” to battle a leaf-eating pest it dubbed the “forest food monster.” Initially scheduled for two days, the contest was extended through Oct. 7 after drawing strong interest and now runs throughout the weeklong National Day holiday.

Participants first register and receive a brief lesson on identifying the pest before staff hand out disposable gloves, food containers, and chopsticks. They search the park for larvae and submit their catches by 2:50 p.m., when staff weigh them and determine the day’s rankings. The captured caterpillars are destroyed rather than fed to the park’s animals.

Prizes are awarded each day based on the total weight collected. The first-place entry receives 10 park tickets, with five for second place and two for third. Everyone who participates receives a commemorative pin, while those finishing fourth through 10th also receive a themed headband.

Competition was stiff from the opening day. A visitor surnamed Liang collected about 4,000 caterpillars weighing 596.3 grams, filling six containers but finishing second. The winning entry came from a five-person team that brought in 1,069.5 grams, while third place went to a catch weighing 391.4 grams.

“The winners were a team of five and caught nearly twice as many as I did,” Liang, a pianist who has visited the park for a decade, told Beijing Daily. “I couldn’t keep up.”

Liang said there was no particular trick to catching the caterpillars, though she found more in less crowded parts of the park and in the shade beneath taller trees. “I brought my own plastic bottles and tweezers, which I found more convenient,” she said.

The winner on the second day, Zhang Hanfang, 18, collected 1.3 kilograms with a six-person team. A taxidermist who runs a studio specializing in insect, reptile, and bird specimens, he made the two-hour drive from neighboring Hebei province with a friend’s family the day after seeing the park’s announcement. The group shares an interest in natural science.

“There’s no secret,” Zhang told Sixth Tone. “Just keep your eyes on the trees and keep at it. It was intense and thrilling. The contest also satisfied our October itch to go bug hunting.”

A video about the contest posted on the lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, known in English as RedNote, received more than 31,000 likes and 1,400 comments. One commenter described the initiative as “crowdsourced debugging,” while a related hashtag on Weibo attracted nearly 3 million views.

In recent weeks, residents across Beijing have reported seeing fall webworm caterpillars — the larvae of an invasive moth native to North America — on sidewalks, balconies, and even people’s shoulders.

The city is experiencing the peak larval period of the pest’s third generation this year, with mature larvae descending from trees in search of sheltered places to pupate and survive the winter.

Yang Zhongqi, chief scientist at the Chinese Academy of Forestry, said the species is a major invasive pest that threatens more than 300 plant species, including forest and fruit trees, flowers, and crops.

“During severe infestations, the caterpillars can strip a tree of every leaf, damaging urban greenery and hindering the tree’s growth,” Yang said. “But they do not kill the tree.”

Beijing had released nearly 700 million parasitic wasps this year before beginning the release of another 400 million on Sept. 28. Harmless to people and pets, the wasps lay their eggs inside fall webworm pupae, preventing adult moths from emerging.

Yang Sihan, head of monitoring and forecasting at the Beijing Gardening and Greening Resources Protection Center, attributed this year’s surge to a cyclical pattern of severe outbreaks, warmer winters, and frequent summer rain that disrupted spraying.

At sites monitored over five consecutive years, the survival rate of overwintering pupae rose from 65.3% in 2023 to 84.2% this year, Yang Sihan said. Heavy rain also left fewer clear days for spraying and washed away pesticides after they were applied. A single female moth can lay 300 to 600 eggs and sometimes as many as 2,000.

World.title: Rodrigo Duterte fit for trial, says ICC
World.content:
DUTERTE. Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court as the court hears arguments regarding Duterte's health and ability to stand trial, while he faces murder charges related to his war on drugs, in The Hague, Netherlands, on September 16 2026.

'[The chamber] is satisfied that the Accused is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings and is therefore fit to stand trial,' says the International Criminal Court Trial Chamber III

MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court has cleared an obstacle in Rodrigo Duterte’s upcoming November trial as the ICC Trial Chamber III found that the former Philippine president is fit for trial.

“For these reasons, the chamber is satisfied that the Expert Panel’s Reports are sufficiently conclusive to make a determination on the Accused’s ability to participate in the trial proceedings and to effectively exercise his procedural and fair trial rights,” the ICC Trial Chamber III said on Thursday, October 8.

“[The chamber] is satisfied that the Accused is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings and is therefore fit to stand trial,” it added.

Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity before the ICC due to the alleged killings of the Davao Death Squad and his war on drugs, which killed nearly 30,000 people according to several human rights groups.

In March 2025, the former president became the first Asian head of state to be arrested by the ICC over the same case. His trial is set to begin on November 30, following the ICC’s decision to confirm all the charges against him and the junking of his appeal on jurisdictional grounds.

Just last January, the ICC pre-trial chamber that handled the confirmation of charges found that the former president was able to stand trial. – Rappler.com

World.title: Genre-defying Canadian poet Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
World.content:
NOBEL LAUREATE. Copies of books by Anne Carson, winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize for Literature, are displayed at Waterstones bookshop in London, Britain, on October 8, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) 'Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's desire for new meaning,' the Swedish Academy says

STOCKHOLM, Sweden – Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Swedish Academy said on Thursday, October 8.

“She was very taken by surprise,” said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy, which awards the prize worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).

“We didn’t have so much time to speak, and all she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind.”

Carson’s work often blends verse, prose, dialogue, and translation in a genre-defying mix. Born in Toronto, the 76-year-old has also held Icelandic citizenship since 2022 and has spent considerable time on the Arctic island in recent years.

She is widely known for her translations of classical Greek literature, which heavily influence her work that ranges from opera libretti to literary criticism and verse novels such as Autobiography of Red from 1998.

“Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” the Academy said.

“She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work. Her translations from Classical Greek may be regarded as independent works in their own right.”

Her style is exemplified in Norma Jeane Baker of Troy from 2019, a performance piece, which mixes the stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides’ play Helen and Marilyn Monroe.

The Academy also praised her ability to explore “the possibilities of writing, a process by which the literary sketch has become of particular value to her.”

“Bearing witness to this is Float (2016), a work consisting of 22 chapbooks on different subjects, capable of being read in any order,” it said.

Life without Proust

Often heralded as her greatest work, Autobiography of Red demonstrates Carson’s ability to “actualize the classical literary tradition,” the Academy said. In the book, she re-examines age-old questions such as “What happens when you love someone who will ultimately destroy you?”

Tapping into more modern inspirations, Carson reflected on the character of Albertine, one of the narrator Marcel’s love interests in Marcel Proust’s In Search of Lost Time, in her own book The Albertine Workout.

Carson had spent seven years reading Proust’s masterpiece and said in an interview with Canada’s CBC Radio One in 2016 that she suffered withdrawal symptoms after finishing the book, leading her to write The Albertine Workout as a way to prolong the experience.

“You think life goes on after Proust, but it seems so gray,” she said.

Carson started taking boxing lessons when she was already in her 70s because of a Parkinson’s disease diagnosis. The sport is recommended as a therapy because it helps pay attention to hand-eye coordination and the sequencing of actions.

She reflected on the disease’s impact on her handwriting in an interview at the Louisiana Literary Festival in Denmark in 2024: “I scrub out whole paragraphs in shame…the shame of bad handwriting.”

Carson, who has taught classics at universities in Canada and the United States, has said that she considers herself a visual artist as much as a literary one.

“I think of making a poem as making an object. I have always thought of them more as drawings than as texts, but drawings that are also physically enterable through the fact of language,” she said in the CBC interview.

Carson had been among favorites this year

Carson had been among the favorites to win this year’s prize, according to bookmakers Ladbrokes, and takes a place beside luminaries such as Alexander Solzhenitsyn, Alice Munro and Ernest Hemingway as a recipient of the award, which often divides opinion among book lovers.

The Academy has been lambasted for ignoring some of the literary titans of the last 120 years such as Leo Tolstoy, Virginia Woolf and Jorge Luis Borges, criticized for snubbing US authors — though it gave the prize to singer-songwriter Bob Dylan in 2016 — and accused of being too obscure in its choices.

Defenders say the Academy has made popular picks, such as Colombia’s Gabriel Garcia Marquez in 1982 and Doris Lessing in 2007, and argue that part of its task is to highlight lesser-known literary traditions.

Last year’s prize was won by Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai.

Established in the will of Swedish dynamite inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in literature, science and peace have been awarded since 1901.

Literature was the fourth of this year’s Nobels to be announced this week, following medicine, physics and chemistry. The peace prize winner will be announced in Oslo on Friday, October 9. – Rappler.com

World.title: Mark Villar switches camps. Minutes later, family’s troubled firms make their move.
World.content:
It’s been a busy afternoon for the Villars, as Mark crosses to the Senate majority, Camille stays, and three of the family's suspended firms move to finally release their long-overdue financial statements

A Villar switches political camps, and seemingly on cue, parts of the family’s battered business empire stir to life.

On Thursday, October 8 – amid an extended lunch break in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, and with the Senate about to go on a month-long legislative recess – there was apparently just enough time for Senator Mark Villar to switch to the majority and promptly snag the powerful public works committee chairmanship and a seat in the Commission on Appointments. His sister, Senator Camille Villar, stayed put in the minority, leaving the family a foot in both camps.

Minutes later came the corporate disclosures. Between 2:12 pm and 3:09 pm, three companies under the Villar family’s corporate umbrella announced moves that could bring them closer to resuming trading on the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE), following months of suspension and controversy.

Talk about timing.

In separate, successive PSE disclosures, Vista Land & Lifescapes (VLL), Vistamalls (STR), and VistaREIT (VREIT) announced that their boards had approved the release of their long-overdue audited financial statements for 2025.

Coming just minutes after news of Villar’s flip in the Senate broke, the filings were enough to set tongues wagging in stock market analyst circles, with speculation about the family’s political maneuvering and whether its suspended companies might finally be inching toward a return to stock market trading.

But the three companies are only part of a bigger mess nagging at the Villars. In all, six of the family’s listed companies have been pushed out of stock market trading after repeatedly missing financial reporting deadlines. First came their overdue 2025 annual reports, then their Q1 2026 financial statements, followed by their Q2 reports. For months, investors have been left holding shares they cannot sell.

Thursday’s announcements are also far from enough to get the stocks trading again. The three companies have merely authorized the release of their 2025 audited statements, which have yet to be published on the exchange. There’s no word on their overdue quarterly reports either.

And that’s just three of the six. AllHome (HOME), AllDay Marts (ALLDY), and, most notably, Villar Land Holdings (VLC) made no similar announcements.

Trillion-peso controversy

The last of these is particularly conspicuous. Villar Land Holdings is at the center of the family’s biggest financial controversy, after initially reporting a staggering P1.3 trillion in assets for 2024, driven by an unbelievable revaluation of its properties in Villar City.

Its subsequently audited statements showed assets of only P35.7 billion, a fraction of the earlier figure.

Since then, it has been one controversy after another for the Villar family. Among their mounting troubles:

Francis Lim, the man tasked with keeping watch over the country’s corporations, has made clear that even the most powerful families are not untouchable.

“If you deserve to be sued, we will sue you,” the SEC chairman said in July, referring to the case against the Villars. The SEC’s criminal complaint remains under preliminary investigation at the Department of Justice.

Time will tell whether Mark Villar’s moves will be enough to build back the fallen family’s political and financial capital. – Rappler.com

World.title: In just 4 years, Marcos tops 2 predecessors in foreign travel budget, number of trips
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has already made 47 foreign trips, surpassing president Benigno Aquino III and Rodrigo Duterte’s number of trips.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will see the skies once again on a working visit to Singapore from October 7 to 11.

He may yet be the country’s most traveled president in more than a decade.

His itinerary to the Lion City includes a meeting with Prime Minister and finance chief Lawrence Wong, the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference, a visit to the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute, and watching the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix.

This is now his sixth visit to Singapore, his second to the country in 2026. This is also his third time off to the race tracks watching the Formula 1 Grand Prix.

In just his first four years in office, this brings his total international trips to 47, eclipsing his two immediate predecessors, former presidents Benigno Aquino III and Rodrigo Duterte.

Both former presidents were known to have an aversion to foreign travel, especially long-distance trips.

International Trips of the Last Three Presidents A comparison of the total number of foreign trips taken by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (as of October 2026), former President Rodrigo Duterte, and former President Benigno S. Aquino III during their respective terms.

Marcos, who was 64 when he became President, has already surpassed Duterte in international travel budget and is poised to exceed the two past presidents in terms of spending.

Duterte, who was in his early to mid-70s during his presidency, had been vocal about hating traveling overseas. His foreign travel was also limited by COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, with some multilateral meetings shifting online.

Aquino, who was in his early 50s, also hated long trips because he couldn’t stand being without cigarettes for hours.

The journeyman

Presidential foreign trips help strengthen a country’s foreign relations. These trips may also include discussions on the country’s defense, economy, and investments.

The President's International Travels Foreign presidential travels across state visits, working summits, and official engagements. Click any pin or flight chip below to inspect the reason for each trip. Year: All 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 Auto-Fly Tour Reset Zoom Loading map… Current travel being shown Travel #1 of 47 Manila (MNL) ➔ Indonesia September 4–6, 2022 • State Visit Trade talks, Defense talks, meeting Filipino communities

Marcos made his first overseas trip in his third month in office. He had seven in his first six months.

The President had the most in 2023 and 2024 at 12 each. In 2025, he slowed down to eight despite receiving the biggest allocation so far. For 2026, Marcos has had eight.

The President has been vocal in his commitment to promoting the country as an investment destination to other nations.

But University of the Philippines Diliman Department of Political Science Professor Jean S. Encinas-Franco said the increase may also be a part of Marcos’ plan to rehabilitate his family’s name.

She added that it may also be a way to diversify foreign allies amid rising tensions in the West Philippine Sea.

“The Marcos administration has decided to engage more with the international community to show that the Philippine government has support from other countries. And also to show that Marcos is trying to diversify the country's allies,” said Franco.

She also said that the trips will help make the country more visible on the global stage.

“The perception that the Philippines is out there in the world, has many allies, will always show up, or that we are always advocating for our causes or the global agenda,” said Encinas-Franco.

“It's also important that they get to talk to their potential partners. The government gets to introduce private sector companies who are sometimes part of this delegation," she added.

The President takes on different types of presidential trips. These vary depending on the level of formality and ceremony. (READ: Presidential trips: What you need to know)

State visits are the highest form of diplomatic visits, with grand ceremonies and meals that honor the relations of the two countries. Official visits, on the other hand, have less grandeur, and a state lunch or dinner is optional. They usually have a smaller delegation.

Lastly, working visits are trips meant for meeting with other government officials to tackle issues that concern bilateral relations.

Expenses in state and official visits are usually covered by the host country. Meanwhile, the Office of the President (OP) pays for expenses during working visits.

Rappler: Presidential Visits Data

Frequency of Presidential Visits by Type A breakdown of the foreign travels by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. categorized by the official diplomatic classification of each trip. By Type By Country Total Foreign Visits 47 100% of travels Hover or tap any segment or card to view details Official Classification Frequency & Share Source: Official Gazette, Presidential Communications Office

So far, 27 of Marcos' visits are official working visits for international summits and conferences. He also has had 12 state visits and seven official visits during his presidency.

Marcos had an “unofficial trip” to Singapore from September 30 to October 2, 2022. During the trip, he attended business meetings and talked about investments in the country. On the same trip, he was also spotted watching the Formula One (F1) Singapore Grand Prix.

Former executive secretary Lucas Bersamin clarified that the trip was “semi-official.”

Singapore appears to be among the President’s favorites, with six visits. This ties with the United States as his most frequent destination; two were official visits while the rest were working visits.
