He visited Washington DC three times to meet with the US president and attend meetings, and once in San Francisco for the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting. He has also been to New York twice, where their family lived for some time during their exile and where he met First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos.

Marcos also visited Indonesia four times, and Japan and Malaysia three times each. These five countries alone account for 46.9% of the President's reported trips.

Encinas-Franco said that most of the time, the US hosts the larger summits and United Nations general assemblies, which contribute to the recurring trips by the administration.

Allocated budget

Since his administration’s first year crafting the budget, the OP’s foreign travel expenses have dwarfed their local counterparts.

Travel Budget of the Office of the President A multi-year breakdown of foreign and local travel allocations for the Office of the President from 2023 to 2027. Hover over values to see variance between the proposed and enacted budget. GAA Foreign GAA Local | NEP Foreign NEP Local *Values in Philippine Pesos (PHP)

In 2025, Marcos received his biggest travel allocation so far at P1.7 billion — P1.6 billion was allotted for foreign trips. In the same year, his office benefited from a P720-million increase in the proposed P913.96 billion National Expenditure Program.

The President’s 2026 travel budget also received an additional P6 million.

Encinas-Franco explained that the additional funding granted may be due to the President’s increased international appearances.

Marcos has already surpassed Duterte in terms of foreign travel budget allocations, based on the General Appropriations Act (GAA) from 2023 to 2026. The President received P3.74 billion from 2023 to 2026, compared to Duterte’s P2.55-billion total allocations for the same period.

Meanwhile, Aquino’s appropriations for his international trips were included in the office’s contingent funds.

Actual expenses

Foreign travel expenses comprise the total cost incurred by an individual or office when traveling to other countries for official business meetings, work assignments, and government duties.

Each government agency must fund its own travel expenses from its allocated budget, according to Executive Order No. 77 and Memorandum Circular No. 50. Spending should be cost-effective and not excessive, and foreign travel must meet the agency’s needs and benefit the country.

While there is no official limit for the presidential delegation, the two guidelines require the person’s presence to be critical to the trip’s outcome.

For presidential trips, a cap of two officials per agency is set. Private individuals, spouses or children of officials, and consultants are not covered by government expenses.

During these trips, agencies must allocate funds for pre-departure expenses, daily subsistence allowance, accommodations (room sharing is mandated if possible), and clothing for their delegates.

These agencies declare their actual spending within a period in the financial statements submitted to the Commission on Audit (COA), which is included in the commission’s Annual Audit Report.

Based on these statements, Marcos is on pace to eclipse the two previous presidents in terms of spending.

President Total Expenditures declared in Financial Statements to COA Aquino P771,636,166.64 Duterte P1,654,321,928.07 Marcos Jr. (2022-2024) P1,461,250,701.76

In 2022, the President exceeded the P201-million budget allotted for foreign trips, spending P396 million. Duterte, who crafted that year’s budget, made no foreign trips in his last six months in office.

However, the president can realign expenses. Article VI, Section 25 of the Constitution states that the president may transfer leftover funds within his or her own office from one line item to another.

COA has already flagged the Marcos administration for over P14.4 million in unsettled funds for foreign travel from 2022 to 2024, covering hotel accommodations and airfare for various agencies.

In 2025, Malacañang said that the office has recovered 55% of the unsettled funds from concerned government agencies. - Rappler.com

World.title: Senate ratifies Philippines-France visiting forces agreement
World.content:
Members of the Senate minority bloc led by Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano and Senators Pia Cayetano and Robin Padilla, air their respective reactions to the State of the Nation Address delivered by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., during the plenary session on July 28, 2026.

This is the Philippines' first Status of Visiting Forces Agreement with a European nation

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Thursday, October 8, concurred in the ratification of the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA) between Philippines and France.

With 17 affirmative votes, senators approved proposed Senate Resolution No. 650, concurring in the ratification of the SOVFA, between the two countries.

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and French Minister for the Armed Forces and Veterans Catherine Vautrin signed the SOVFA in March. The agreement provides a legal framework for the presence and activities of the Philippine and French armed forces in each other’s territories.

“This is a historic moment because this treaty ratification of our visiting forces with France is the first for a European nation,” said Senate Majority Floor Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri

Newly designated French Ambassador to the Philippines Donatienne Hissard personally received the resolution at the Senate.

The SOVFA is a “reciprocal bilateral defense agreement that establishes the legal framework governing the presence and cooperative activities of the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the French Armed Forces, including their respective Civilian Components, in each other’s territories, and facilitates joint defense, training, humanitarian, and other mutually agreed activities.”

With the agreement’s ratification, France joins the growing list of countries with visiting forces agreements with the Philippines.

The Philippines has a long-standing Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA) with its treaty ally, the United States. In 2012, a SOVFA with Australia, which has since become a strategic partner of the Philippines.

The expansion of the Philippines’ defense ties has been a conscious push of the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration, especially in the face of a growingly belligerent China in the South China Sea. At the same time, however, Marcos has said he wants a “reset” of bilateral relations with Beijing, following years of tensions both at sea and in the diplomatic space. – Rappler.com

World.title: Jackie Chan Highlights Kazakhstan’s Film Potential After ‘Armour of God IV: Ultimatum’ Shoot
World.content:
ASTANA – Filming of the international action film “Armour of God IV: Ultimatum,” starring legendary actor Jackie Chan, has concluded in Kazakhstan, showcasing the country’s potential as a destination for major international film productions.

The project, Salem Entertainment’s first international production, was filmed in Almaty and the Almaty and Mangystau Regions, with support from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Culture and Information and China Film Group Corporation.

Speaking at a press conference on Oct. 6, Chan said the idea was first discussed during a meeting with Kazakhstan’s Vice President Erlan Karin in China in 2017 or 2018, when Karin served as State Counselor, Kazinform reported.

“I was surprised that the team had already started working on the script and selected a director,” Chan said, noting that the project moved from an initial proposal to production much faster than he had expected.

He also praised the shoot’s organization and government support.

Kazakh actor and producer Rustem Omarov said Chan sustained a shoulder injury and later fractured a rib during filming. Despite doctors advising him to rest, Chan returned to the set within days.

Filming will continue in Shanghai, with the film scheduled for international release in 2027.

The project is expected to promote Kazakhstan’s tourism and cultural potential and help attract further international film productions to the country.

World.title: Tokayev Calls for Stronger Regional Cooperation at Central Asia-Azerbaijan Summit
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for stronger economic integration, transport connectivity, water cooperation and artificial intelligence partnerships among Central Asian states and Azerbaijan at the eighth Consultative Meeting of Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan in Avaza on Oct. 8.

Held in the year marking 35 years of independence of the Central Asian states and Azerbaijan, the meeting focused on expanding regional cooperation and strengthening stability amid growing geopolitical tensions, Akorda reported.

Trade and connectivity

Tokayev proposed increasing intraregional trade from approximately $13 billion to at least $20 billion and called on governments to develop a joint action plan to achieve this target.

He also highlighted the potential of border trade and logistics hubs, as well as industrial cooperation centers, to create regional value chains.

Tokayev stressed Kazakhstan’s efforts to strengthen transport connectivity, noting the nearing completion of the Moyynty-Kyzylzhar and Darbaza-Maktaaral railway lines and the planned opening of the Bakhty-Ayagoz route next year.

He underscored the growing importance of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or the Middle Corridor, and said World Bank estimates indicate that cargo traffic across the Caspian Sea could increase almost fourfold by 2040 if planned infrastructure projects are implemented.

Tokayev also proposed discussing the possible integration of the Middle Corridor with the TRIPP transport initiative at the expert level.

Water and AI cooperation

Water security was identified as another key priority. Tokayev called for new approaches to managing transboundary water resources and proposed advancing a Framework Convention of Central Asia on Water Use.

He also reiterated Kazakhstan’s initiative to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations.

In the technology sector, Tokayev proposed creating a Central Asian Partnership Program on Artificial Intelligence to facilitate cooperation among universities, research centers and technology companies.

He also suggested developing a Declaration on the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence by Central Asian States and Azerbaijan.

Security and humanitarian ties

Tokayev stressed the importance of coordinated efforts against terrorism, drug trafficking, human trafficking, organized crime and other transnational threats, including the misuse of digital technologies by criminals and terrorists.

He also called for stronger cultural and humanitarian ties through youth exchanges, academic cooperation and a common information space.

Among the proposals were a regional television channel based on Kazakhstan’s Silk Way TV, a 2027 Youth Forum on Volunteering, and a common calendar of major cultural, scientific, sporting and tourism events.

Focus on implementation

Tokayev urged greater attention to implementing regional initiatives, noting that more than 200 initiatives have been put forward since 2018, while only a small proportion have been implemented.

He proposed that foreign ministries inventory existing initiatives and assess their relevance and prospects.

A Joint Statement was adopted following the eighth Consultative Meeting of Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Government Securities Added to J.P. Morgan Watchlist for Potential GBI-EM Inclusion
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s government securities have been placed on J.P. Morgan’s Index Watch – Positive list for potential inclusion in the Government Bond Index – Emerging Markets (GBI-EM), marking further progress in integrating the country’s government securities market into international capital markets.

Market accessibility under review

The status was assigned as part of J.P. Morgan’s 2026 index classification review. Over the next 12 months, the Finance Ministry said it will assess international investors’ access to Kazakhstan’s government securities market, the ministry reported on Oct. 8.

The review will include investors’ access through international clearing and settlement infrastructure, as well as the liquidity of bonds meeting the index’s eligibility criteria.

The move reflects joint efforts by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Finance and National Bank to develop the government securities market, strengthen market infrastructure and improve international investors’ access to Kazakh financial instruments.

Potential to broaden investor base

Placement on the positive watchlist marks a new stage in assessing Kazakhstan’s potential inclusion in the GBI-EM.

If Kazakhstan’s government securities are ultimately included in the index, the move could broaden the country’s foreign investor base, support greater market liquidity and help reduce borrowing costs.

The GBI-EM is a widely followed benchmark for local-currency government bonds issued by emerging-market economies.

World.title: Kazakhstan, UK Reaffirm Commitment to Expanding Strategic Partnership
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev received UK Minister of State for Trade Lord Anas Sarwar on Oct. 7 to discuss strengthening bilateral trade and investment ties and expanding cooperation in energy, transport, digitalization and artificial intelligence.

Strong trade and investment ties

Tokayev highlighted the importance Kazakhstan attaches to developing relations with the United Kingdom, noting constructive political dialogue and growing contacts between the two countries, Akorda reported.

“Kazakhstan and the United Kingdom are connected by constructive political dialogue and active contacts at various levels. I am confident that we have significant potential to expand cooperation,” Tokayev said.

The UK remains one of Kazakhstan’s key trade and investment partners. Bilateral trade increased by 83% in 2025 to more than $1.6 billion, while more than 500 British companies currently operate in Kazakhstan.

President Tokayev also underscored the importance of developing human capital alongside trade and investment, calling on Kazakhstan’s younger generation to broaden their international outlook and strengthen foreign-language skills, notably English.

Tokayev conveyed his warm wishes to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and invited him to visit Kazakhstan.

Lord Sarwar welcomed the continued development of the strategic partnership and thanked President Tokayev for supporting British business projects and efforts to maintain a favorable investment climate.

“We closely follow Kazakhstan’s dynamic development and highly value the closeness of our approaches to key topics on the international agenda. We are united by our commitment to open and trusted partnership, innovation, mutual confidence and free trade,” Lord Sarwar said.

Cooperation in emerging and priority sectors

Tokayev and Sarwar also discussed prospects for expanding cooperation in energy, transport and logistics, digitalization and artificial intelligence, while also highlighting the importance of strengthening humanitarian ties, academic exchanges and joint education initiatives.

The discussions continued during a separate meeting between Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin and Lord Sarwar, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

Zhumangarin described the UK as an important and reliable strategic partner, noting that the British delegation’s visit provides fresh momentum for bilateral relations and creates opportunities to translate existing agreements into concrete projects.

Lord Sarwar reaffirmed the UK’s readiness to deepen cooperation with Kazakhstan, and both officials expressed commitment to open, constructive dialogue and to advancing priority areas of partnership.

World.title: Kazakh FM Takes Part in CIS and Regional Meetings in Turkmenbashi
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi took part in a regular meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and a meeting of the Foreign Ministers of the Central Asian states and Azerbaijan in Turkmenbashi on Oct. 7.

CIS ministers prepare for upcoming summit

The CIS foreign ministers discussed pressing topics on the international agenda and prospects for multilateral cooperation within the commonwealth.

Tileuberdi outlined Kazakhstan’s approaches to cooperation within the organization and put forward several proposals aimed at strengthening the CIS’s potential, the ministry’s press service reported.

A key focus of the meeting was preparations for the upcoming CIS Summit, which will bring together the leaders of the Commonwealth’s member states in Turkmenistan on Oct. 9.

The ministers approved statements by the heads of state marking the 35th anniversary of the CIS and addressing the preservation of historical memory.

They also endorsed draft documents to strengthen cooperation in security, economic, cultural and humanitarian affairs, as well as transport, science, space and information and communication technologies.

The meeting concluded with the participants reaffirming their commitment to implementing the agreements reached and enhancing the effectiveness of multilateral cooperation mechanisms.

Central Asia and Azerbaijan discuss regional cooperation

Tileuberdi also participated in the meeting of the Foreign Ministers of the Central Asian States and Azerbaijan, where the participants discussed regional cooperation within the framework of the consultative meetings and current regional and international topics.

Tileuberdi highlighted the progress achieved since the first consultative meeting of the Central Asian Heads of State in 2018, noting that political dialogue had contributed to stronger mutual trust and closer ties between the Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan.

“Thanks to the political will of our Heads of State, relations between our brotherly nations have reached a qualitatively new level. The consultative meetings have provided significant momentum for deepening cooperation across trade, industrial cooperation, energy, transport, logistics and digital technologies,” Tileuberdi said.

Following the meeting, the ministers agreed on the draft agenda and outcome documents to be signed at the eighth consultative meeting, scheduled for Oct. 8 in Turkmenbashi.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is also in Turkmenistan for a working visit on Oct. 8-9 at the invitation of President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

World.title: Central Asia Has UK, US Investors’ Attention But Understanding Still Lags Behind Interest
World.content:
Kazakhstan remains the region’s economic anchor and its largest recipient of foreign capital. At the same time, Montfort Eurasia’s Investor Perception Report 2026 for the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (U.S.) suggests that Central Asia and the Caucasus are moving beyond a traditional foreign direct investment story toward a broader capital markets story.

Yet the report identifies a growing gap: investor appetite is advancing faster than investor understanding.

“Investors’ self-assessed knowledge of the region has plateaued,” the report notes, with average scores of 6.63 out of 10 among UK respondents and 6.79 among those in the U.S. At the same time, the proportion of investors expressing strong or moderate interest remains elevated at 67.1% in the UK and 65.5% in the U.S.

This is the central message of the 2026 survey: Central Asia has moved into a more serious phase of international investor attention, but it now needs to convert visibility into informed, committed capital.

From discovery to deliberation

Montfort Eurasia’s report covers 273 respondents — 137 in the UK and 136 in the U.S. The research used a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative questions with open-ended responses. The results were then benchmarked against the 2024 and 2025 surveys to identify changes in investor priorities, risk perceptions and strategic outlooks.

The year-on-year comparison is revealing. Investor knowledge has increased significantly from the roughly 4.9 level recorded in 2024, but the sharp improvement seen in 2025 has not continued. Instead, the region appears to have reached a higher baseline of familiarity.

The same pattern is visible in overall interest. The report describes the current stage not as one of discovery, but of “deliberation”. In other words, investors already familiar with the region are increasingly evaluating Central Asia and asking harder questions about political risk, market access, regulation, investment security and the quality of available information.

That is a meaningful change in audience. Two years ago, much of the international discussion around Central Asia still focused on whether global investors would notice the region at all. Today, the more relevant question is whether governments and businesses can provide enough reliable information for investors to move from interest to due diligence and eventually to transactions.

The report itself captures that transition. Financial analysis has overtaken international media as the leading source of information about the region, cited by 68.6% of UK respondents and 56.6% of U.S. respondents. That suggests that the market is becoming less dependent on headlines and more dependent on numbers.

Kazakhstan remains the anchor

For Kazakhstan, the report reinforces a familiar position while adding an important new dimension. The country remains by far the largest economy and the leading recipient of foreign capital in Central Asia. According to the report, Kazakhstan attracted around $440 billion in total FDI between 2005 and 2025 and continues to account for close to 70% of all FDI entering Central Asia. Real GDP growth accelerated to 6.5% in 2025, compared with 4.8% in 2024, with strong contributions from industry, transport, construction and trade. Construction expanded by 15.9%, while transport grew by 20.4%.

The report also points to Kazakhstan’s large infrastructure pipeline. The National Infrastructure Plan envisages more than 200 projects with a combined value of around $81 billion through 2029. The government is targeting economic growth to $450 billion and an additional $150 billion in FDI over the same period.

These figures help explain why Kazakhstan continues to occupy a different position from its regional peers.

Among UK respondents, Kazakhstan was identified as the most business-friendly Central Asian market, selected by 10.9% of investors, compared with 2.9% among U.S. respondents. For UK investors, ease of market entry and existing trade links were each cited by 60%, followed by a stable environment at 46.7% and corporate governance at 33.3%.

The distinction between the UK and U.S. views is important. Kazakhstan’s position is stronger among UK respondents, while its standing among U.S. investors has weakened compared with last year. The report notes that Kazakhstan fell from 8.5% to 2.9% among American investors, suggesting that broader geopolitical narratives may be affecting perceptions of the country despite its economic weight.

This is a perception issue rather than an economic one, and those two things increasingly need to be considered separately. Kazakhstan’s fundamentals remain substantial, but investors do not assess fundamentals in isolation. The country is part of a region exposed to the Russia-Ukraine war, tensions around energy infrastructure, changing global supply chains and intensifying competition over critical minerals.

That explains why investment security and political stability remain at the top of the investor agenda. Investment security was a concern for 72.3% of UK respondents and 64.7% of U.S. respondents, while political stability was cited by 56.2% and 52.9%, respectively. For Kazakhstan, the implication is straightforward: scale alone is no longer enough.

The capital markets story is becoming more important

One of the report’s most significant developments is the growing importance of capital markets. Kazakhstan has long relied heavily on FDI, particularly in oil, mining and infrastructure. But the emergence of a broader regional capital markets ecosystem is changing how Western investors view the region.

Vladimir Mikhailovsky, Partner, Capital Markets at Sidley Austin LLP, points to increased Kazakh bond activity in 2026, including debut transactions. He expects diversification to remain a key market feature.

“The popularity of “dim sum” or offshore RMB offerings is likely to continue to grow, as Kazakh issuers seek to diversify their investor base and capitalize on the favorable interest rate environment, ” he said.

This matters because capital-market access can signal financial maturity. A country that can attract investors not only into physical assets but also into bonds, equities and other financial instruments is gradually becoming integrated into a more sophisticated international capital ecosystem.

The regional picture is also changing quickly. In May 2026, Uzbekistan’s National Investment Fund completed the country’s first international equity listing, with the offering more than four times oversubscribed. Sovereign credit ratings across the region were upgraded, while critical minerals moved higher on the strategic agenda of both the U.S. and the European Union (EU).

For Central Asia, that is a notable transition: the story is no longer exclusively about attracting greenfield investment into resource projects. It is increasingly about building investable financial instruments and institutions around the region’s economic expansion.

Critical minerals are changing the conversation

The renewed international focus on Central Asia is also inseparable from the global race to secure critical minerals and diversify supply chains.

Kazakhstan remains particularly well positioned because of its role in uranium and its broader mining potential. The report describes the country as the world’s leading uranium supplier, accounting for 40% of global output in 2025. Mining exploration spending reached a decade high of $127 million in 2025, with almost half directed toward copper projects. Uzbekistan, meanwhile, is emerging as another important mining center, with newly announced deposits of tungsten, lithium and germanium as well as 14 rare-earth sites.

This is where economics and geopolitics increasingly intersect. The report points to the November 2025 C5+1 White House Summit, which generated more than $130 billion in commercial commitments, as well as the EU’s commitment of up to 12 billion euros through Global Gateway. Both developments are presented as evidence that Western governments are no longer viewing Central Asia purely through the lens of traditional development or trade policy.

The region is becoming strategically relevant to discussions about energy security, supply-chain resilience and access to critical raw materials. For Kazakhstan, that creates an opportunity but also raises expectations. Resource wealth can attract capital, but investors increasingly want to know how resources are governed, processed and integrated into longer-term value chains.

Uzbekistan is becoming harder to ignore

While Kazakhstan remains the region’s economic anchor, Uzbekistan is becoming increasingly important to the investor story. The country’s first international equity listing by the National Investment Fund was one of the report’s defining transactions. The offering was more than four times oversubscribed, demonstrating that international investor appetite is not limited to Kazakhstan’s established market position.

The report also highlights the planned launch of the Tashkent International Financial Center, alongside Uzbekistan’s growing mining potential and efforts to deepen its financial infrastructure. But perhaps more importantly, Uzbekistan offers a different investment proposition: a large population, a rapidly transforming economy and the possibility of expanding the region’s consumer and industrial base.

Executive Chairman of East-West Group and Founder and Board Member of the Europe-Uzbekistan Association for Economic Cooperation Oybek Shaykhov argues that international investors still face an information deficit.

“Transparent, consistent and credible communication is not simply a reputational tool; it is a fundamental pillar of investor confidence,” he said.

That observation applies to the wider region, particularly to countries trying to attract investors beyond the traditional circle of state-backed or resource-focused projects.

The geopolitical premium and discount

For Central Asia, the external environment has become more favorable and more complicated at the same time. Associate Director at the Eurasia Center of the Atlantic Council Andrew D’Anieri notes that Central Asia’s growth outlook for 2026-27 looks relatively strong compared with regions more directly exposed to the fallout from the Iran war and higher energy prices. He also points to Russia-related instability and growing water pressures as tests of the region’s resilience.

That combination is likely to define the next stage of the region’s investment story. Central Asia is gaining strategic importance precisely because the international system is becoming less predictable. Supply chains are being redesigned, competition for critical minerals is intensifying, and governments are looking for alternative transport and energy routes.

But the same geopolitical environment also raises the risk premium. The Montfort survey shows that investors are willing to engage with the region despite these uncertainties. The harder question is whether that interest can translate into long-term commitments.

This is where Kazakhstan’s next phase of economic development becomes particularly important. Maintaining high growth is one objective. Converting growth into deeper capital markets, greater financial diversification and more international investor participation is another.

The report suggests that the opportunity is there. Interest among Western investors is dramatically higher than it was two years ago, even if the extraordinary surge of 2024–25 has now stabilized. The challenge is that investors are becoming more sophisticated just as the region competes for larger, more strategic pools of capital.

World.title: Caspian Summit: Can Cooperation Keep Pace With Falling Waters?
World.content:
ASTANA — Leaders of the five Caspian states are set to meet Oct. 9 in Turkmenistan’s Avaza National Tourist Zone for a summit focused on the sea’s mounting environmental challenges, as declining water levels increasingly intersect with transport, infrastructure and regional economic interests.

The Caspian Environmental Summit comes amid efforts to turn years of scientific warnings and regional dialogue into coordinated policies. Experts say its significance will depend not only on the issues leaders raise, but on whether the meeting strengthens mechanisms for monitoring, adaptation and cooperation among Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Russia and Turkmenistan.

The summit is part of a broader series of high-level events in Avaza on Oct. 7-9, including meetings of Caspian states’ environmental ministers, the heads of state of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Council of Heads of State.

Falling waters raise the political stakes

The scale of the Caspian’s decline is already visible along Kazakhstan’s coast.

In a comment for this story, Zamira Zholdaskyzy, a chief expert at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies (KazISS), said observations by Kazhydromet, Kazakhstan’s national hydrometeorological service, show the sea level fell by 1.76 meters between 2005 and 2022, while its water surface contracted by more than 26,000 square kilometers. Approximately half of the lost area was in Kazakhstan’s part of the Northern Caspian, where the shoreline retreated by more than 25 kilometers in some areas.

“The central issues on the shared environmental agenda of the Caspian states are changes in the sea level, biodiversity conservation, the quality of the marine environment and the condition of coastal areas. These issues are closely interconnected, as changes in the water balance affect the coastline and natural habitats, as well as the operation of ports, water intakes and other infrastructure. Of particular importance is the conservation of the Caspian seal, sturgeon and wetlands that support the sea’s biodiversity,” Zholdaskyzy told The Astana Times.

Scientists attribute the decline to a combination of factors. Zholdaskyzy said research cited by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the World Bank points to increased evaporation amid rising air and water temperatures as the leading contributor in recent decades, alongside changes in precipitation and river flows.

The Volga accounts for approximately 80% of river inflow into the Caspian, while irrigation, industrial use and municipal water consumption across the wider basin also affect the amount reaching the sea.

The uncertainty surrounding the relative contribution of these factors makes shared monitoring particularly important.

“Climate trends cannot be changed through the efforts of one region alone. At the same time, the Caspian states can achieve tangible results in water use and scientific cooperation. This includes joint monitoring, improving water-use efficiency, particularly in agriculture, coordinating water releases during spawning periods and conducting joint risk assessments,” said Zholdaskyzy.

Kazakhstan has also sought to elevate the issue politically. At the Regional Ecological Summit in Astana on April 22, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan had initiated an interstate program aimed at preventing further degradation of the Caspian and established a dedicated research institute to strengthen regional scientific cooperation.

The following day, a high-level dialogue under the Tehran Convention, the legally binding environmental agreement among all five littoral states, focused specifically on sea-level fluctuations. The Caspian Sea Level Fluctuation Action Plan for 2026-2036 was introduced during the meeting, with participants discussing financing, scientific cooperation and implementation.

From environmental problem to strategic risk

The decision to bring the issue to the level of heads of state reflects how far its implications now extend beyond environmental policy, according to Kamila Amurtayeva, an expert consultant at the Center for Institutional Analysis and Reforms at the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development (KIPD).

“Declining sea levels affect ecosystems, fisheries, coastal infrastructure and economic activity simultaneously. These impacts have already been documented in materials published by the Tehran Convention Secretariat. Addressing them therefore requires decisions that extend beyond the remit of environmental agencies,” Amurtayeva told The Astana Times.

She said the Avaza meeting also builds on broader diplomatic efforts, including Turkmenistan’s Caspian Environmental Initiative, proposed in 2023 as an international platform for cooperation on protecting the Caspian environment and the 2026-2036 action plan addressing sea-level fluctuations.

“The Caspian’s political significance is growing because environmental sustainability is becoming a prerequisite for implementing national economic and strategic plans. Declining sea levels constitute a shared risk that has been raised repeatedly, but their consequences and countries’ capacities to adapt differ. Reconciling these interests requires the involvement of national leaders,” she said.

Those interests are particularly visible in transport. According to data published by the Kazakh government in September, freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, increased 5.6-fold over the past five years, from 800,000 tons to 4.5 million tons. Kazakhstan plans to expand the combined capacity of its seaports from 21.8 million tons to 30 million tons by 2030, while dredging, berth reconstruction and fleet expansion are underway.

The expansion increases the importance of navigational conditions and coastal adaptation for Kazakhstan’s transport plans.

“States are investing in connectivity, but the returns on those investments depend on navigational conditions. In my view, environmental discussions will therefore also involve the costs of adapting ports, the resilience of freight operations and the coordination of infrastructure decisions,” said Amurtayeva, noting that the challenge concerns both the TITR and the North-South corridor.

Energy adds another dimension. According to Amurtayeva, environmental safety in hydrocarbon production and transportation, accident prevention and marine protection could form part of the broader discussion, although she said an environmental summit should not be expected to produce agreement on major energy projects.

“Its strategic value may lie in agreeing on rules that allow transport and energy development to proceed while taking shared environmental constraints into account,” she said.

Existing institutions face an implementation test

The Tehran Convention provides an existing framework for regional environmental cooperation, with protocols covering biodiversity, land-based pollution, oil-spill response and transboundary environmental impact assessment. A further protocol on monitoring, assessment and information exchange remains under negotiation, putting the focus on strengthening existing mechanisms for coordinated action.

“The practical question is therefore how to equip existing frameworks with adequate resources, authority and sustained data exchange. (…) Promising steps could include a joint monitoring program, harmonised measurement and forecasting methods, regular joint research expeditions, and coordination of adaptation measures across government agencies. Data comparability is particularly important,” said Amurtayeva.

“Without it, countries may struggle to agree even on a baseline assessment of risks, let alone funding priorities,” she added.

Amurtayeva also pointed to the Blueing the Caspian Sea project as an example of existing cooperation. She said the four-year, $11.7 million project, launched in April and funded by the Global Environment Facility with participation from the United Nations Environment Program and the World Bank, supports Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan in areas including pollution monitoring and biodiversity conservation.

“It should be understood specifically as a project supporting three countries; comprehensive coordination among all five Caspian states remains a separate task,” said Amurtayeva.

Kazakhstan is also developing its own scientific capacity to support regional cooperation.

“The Kazakh Scientific Research Institute of the Caspian Sea conducts observations of the marine environment, while its participation in the association of scientific organizations of the Caspian states expands opportunities for exchanging knowledge and research findings,” said Zholdaskyzy.

What would make Avaza consequential?

When asked what concrete outcomes could indicate progress after the Avaza summit, Amurtayeva highlighted a common plan with clear deadlines, designated agencies and identified financing, alongside arrangements for data exchange, joint research and coastal infrastructure adaptation.

“The summit’s substantive significance will become clear from the extent to which the leaders’ agreements shape subsequent joint action. (…) I would therefore pay particular attention to the follow-up after Avaza: who will coordinate implementation, when the countries will review progress, and whether the results will be made publicly available,” she said.

Another indicator would be whether shared environmental assessments begin to influence economic decisions, including port development, infrastructure location and coastal protection.

“For the Caspian, it is particularly important that economic planning draw on shared scientific assessments of changes in the marine environment,” she said.

“A realistic measure of success will be the five states’ ability to assess risks jointly, coordinate measures and finance adaptation. Any promises to restore sea levels rapidly would require separate scientific substantiation,” Amurtayeva said.

World.title: Religious Leaders Explore Faith’s Role in Tackling Global Challenges
World.content:
ASTANA – Religious leaders and international experts gathered in Astana on Oct. 7 to discuss how faith communities can contribute to addressing pressing challenges, with artificial intelligence, climate change and the rights of children with incurable diseases among the key issues on the agenda.

The discussions took place at the 24th Meeting of the Secretariat of the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions, which brought together representatives of Islam, Christianity, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, Shinto and the Baha’i Faith, as well as government officials, international organizations and experts from 20 countries.

Participants considered two draft international documents: the Code of Ethics for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Religious Sphere and the Role of Religions in Combating Climate Change. The meeting also presented the Charter on the Rights of Children with Incurable Diseases as a separate agenda item.

Vice President of Kazakhstan and Head of the Secretariat of the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions Erlan Karin said the documents reflect the need to strengthen the practical role of spiritual diplomacy amid growing global instability.

“Armed conflicts and humanitarian crises have weakened respect for international law. Radical ideas and hate speech are growing. This is also happening online. Climate and technology risks are deepening existing social inequalities, and the crisis of trust is becoming a systemic challenge,” Karin said.

“In this situation, spiritual diplomacy can play a special role. It does not replace political talks, but complements them and keeps communication channels open where diplomatic dialogue is difficult. It helps rebuild trust and reminds us of the value of every human life,” he added.

Karin noted that the Astana Peace Declaration, adopted at the eighth congress, provides a common framework for advancing peace, security and efforts to counter extremism.

“One of the first results of implementing the Astana Peace Declaration is the launch of the International Online Center for Spiritual Knowledge. It brings together the congress materials, expert research and studies, as well as educational resources about world religions and cultures,” he said.

Climate change as a moral responsibility

Speaking about the document on the role of religions in combating climate change, Karin described climate change as not only an environmental or economic issue but also a moral challenge.

“The document enshrines universal principles of environmental responsibility and encourages religious communities to promote education, solidarity and support for the most vulnerable groups and regions,” he said.

Karin noted that the document is aligned with Kazakhstan’s international initiatives on environmental and water security, including President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations.

“Human beings and nature are part of one whole. That is why the initiative seeks to foster an environmental culture, change daily habits and affirm personal responsibility for preserving nature,” Karin said.

Fatih Mehmet Karaca, deputy president of the Presidency of Religious Affairs of Türkiye, emphasized the concept of stewardship and humanity’s responsibility toward nature.

“Waste is not merely an individual economic behavior. We see food and energy waste, a culture of fast consumption, and single-use products. Fighting waste means respecting nature’s rights. The values Islam calls us to are clear: gratitude, contentment, moderation, sharing and responsibility,” Karaca said.

Karaca also highlighted the issue of climate justice, noting that vulnerable communities often bear a disproportionate share of climate change consequences.

“It is not enough to see this as a matter of protecting nature. It is also a matter of justice and of the right of future generations to clean air, clean water and safe food,” he said.

Ethics of AI

The proposed code on AI seeks to establish ethical principles for the use of emerging technologies in religious contexts, including protecting spiritual heritage and preventing the distortion of religious texts.

Karin said Kazakhstan views AI as an important tool for development but highlighted that technological progress must be accompanied by greater ethical responsibility.

“Our country considers AI a powerful tool for progress. At the same time, technological development cannot outpace our moral responsibility. The broader the capabilities of algorithms, the greater the human responsibility,” he said.

Karin noted that AI could help preserve spiritual heritage and expand access to religious knowledge, while also creating new risks.

“It is really important to counter the distortion of religious texts and the creation of digital fakes on behalf of spiritual leaders. We have to avoid algorithmic discrimination and manipulation of people’s convictions,” he said.

Director of the United Nations Alliance of Civilizations, Nihal Saad, said AI presents both opportunities and challenges for societies. Its responsible use requires keeping human dignity and ethical considerations at the center.

“Used wisely, AI could help transform education, improve health care, strengthen food security and support sustainable development. The challenge is ensuring that it advances in ways that uphold human dignity and ethics. We have to ensure that ethics are built into the design of AI systems rather than added as an afterthought,” Saad said.

She noted that although the two draft documents address different issues, they share an emphasis on responsibility, dialogue, cooperation and common values.

A call for unity

Jo Bailey Wells, deputy secretary general of the Anglican Communion and bishop for Episcopal Ministry in the Anglican Communion, said the three issues on the agenda, climate change, AI and the rights of children with incurable diseases, are not traditionally viewed as specifically religious matters. However, they are closely connected to values shared across faiths.

“Each expresses the values we have been talking about for many years. For example, human dignity, protecting family life, raising the role of women, combating radicalism, reducing poverty, valuing integrity in public life, countering corruption and defending human rights. They are all reflected here. We have come a long way with these shared declarations,” Wells said.

She highlighted that the challenges cannot be addressed by individual governments, professions or religious communities alone.

“The opportunity is to walk together and not just talk together. To put our convictions into action as we serve causes beyond our individual interests,” Wells said.

“The crises described cannot be resolved by the specialists and technicians, whether in climate and the environment, in artificial and superhuman intelligence, or in medicine and palliative care. Nor can they be resolved by any single group, government, or nation. They require a level of cooperation that transcends our differences,” she added.

Karin outlined several priorities for the congress, including promoting the agreed documents and initiatives, establishing mechanisms for expert support and consolidating the results of discussions.

The upcoming 25th anniversary session of the Secretariat in 2027 and the ninth Congress in 2028 are expected to serve as important milestones in the organization’s development.

“We need to enter a new stage in the development of the congress with concrete results and a clear understanding of the steps required to address future challenges,” Karin said.

World.title: UN Human Rights Council adopts resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories
World.content:
UNHRC resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories

On 7 October, the UN Human Rights Council adopted a resolution in Geneva concerning Georgia‘s occupied regions.

According to Georgia’s Foreign Ministry, the resolution, entitled “Cooperation with Georgia”, addresses the human rights situation in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia).

The UN Human Rights Council calls for unhindered access to the occupied territories for the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as international and regional human rights mechanisms.

The resolution also condemns Russia’s actions aimed at annexing Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, and reaffirms support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

It expresses concern over discrimination and human rights violations against ethnic Georgians in the Russian-occupied regions.

The document also highlights the importance of the Geneva International Discussions, established under the ceasefire agreement of 12 August 2008.

The resolution, submitted by Georgia, was adopted by consensus, as it was last year.

World.title: ‘No right to enter classroom’: Teacher beats pupil at Armenian school
World.content:
Teacher beats pupil at school in Armenia

A video showing a teacher beating a second-grade pupil at a school in the Armenian village of Vardadzor has shocked people across Armenia. A relative of the girl told journalists that she was so frightened by the incident that she had refused to return to school.

The girl’s parents appealed to the Gegharkunik regional administration, demanding that the teacher be dismissed. However, they were told that this would only be possible if complaints were filed by at least seven parents.

Social media users responding to the video called on the Interior Ministry to investigate the incident and launch criminal proceedings.

The Education Ministry said it had contacted the Interior Ministry, the Education Inspectorate and the National Centre for Educational and Psychological Support to ensure a thorough investigation.

“Relevant legal procedures will begin shortly to strip this teacher of the right to teach,” the ministry said.

Armenia’s Human Rights Defender, Anahit Manasyan, described the violence against the schoolgirl as “unacceptable and deeply concerning”.

The Investigative Committee opened a criminal case over allegations of “inflicting severe physical pain or serious mental suffering on a minor”.

By the time of publication, reports had emerged that the teacher had been detained.

What happened

A relative of the second-grade pupil told Shamshyan.com that the class teacher had first beaten the girl in the classroom. The violence continued in the corridor after the pupil left the classroom. The girl returned home with swollen eyes and marks from the blows on her neck and arms.

“There had been slaps before, but never beatings like this – with hands and a pointer,” the relative said.

The girl has not attended school since the incident. According to family members, she later encountered the teacher by chance in the street and ran home in terror.

The girl’s mother said she did not want the teacher to face criminal prosecution but insisted that she be dismissed.

Armenian media reported that the incident was discussed at the school the following day.

“The teacher admits her guilt. She submitted a written statement acknowledging what she had done and asked not to be punished. As a result, I issued her a written reprimand,” school headteacher Gevorg Nersesyan said.

He also said such incidents were unacceptable and expressed surprise that a teacher with 30 years of experience could have treated a second-grade pupil in this way.

‘Schools must be a safe environment for children’

Armenia’s Human Rights Defender, Anahit Manasyan, stressed that schools must provide a safe environment for children.

“Any form of violence against a child or any other form of inappropriate treatment is fundamentally incompatible with respect for the child’s dignity, safety and rights,” she said.

According to Manasyan, children must be protected not only through responses to individual incidents, but also through effective measures to prevent and address potential cases of violence.

Manasyan also questioned the effectiveness of mechanisms designed to protect pupils in schools, particularly the work of pupil protection groups.

“The effectiveness of these mechanisms should be assessed primarily on the basis of how they work in practice,” she said.

Pupil protection groups were established in all schools on 1 September 2026 by order of the Minister of Education, Science, Culture and Sport. They were specifically set up to prevent violence, bullying and other high-risk situations. Following the incident at the school in Vardadzor, the pupil protection group held a meeting. However, according to the girl’s relatives, no steps were taken to help her return to school.

The Office of the Human Rights Defender said it had launched an investigation into the incident.

Not the first case of violence since start of school year

Two weeks ago, a maths teacher at a school in the village of Berdavan in Armenia’s Tavush region slapped a 13-year-old boy across the face. He also pushed the pupil, forcibly made him sit at his desk and hit him on the head with a notebook, striking the child’s eye with its edge.

According to the boy’s mother, the teacher’s wife, who is the school’s deputy headteacher, also treated him harshly. She slapped him across the face, pushed him into her office and made him stand in the corner.

Although the boy continues to attend school, his mother told journalists that he had been left psychologically distressed by the incident.

The teacher has also been charged with “inflicting severe physical pain or serious mental suffering on a minor”. He has been released on an undertaking not to leave the country and suspended from his duties.

Social media reactions

“A written reprimand is not enough. A teacher like this should be barred from working in education.”

“If people like this were prosecuted, teachers would think twice before raising a hand against someone else’s child.”

“Someone who displays such aggressive and unacceptable behaviour simply has no right to call themselves a teacher. What can such a person teach children – respect, kindness or compassion for others?“

“If a similar incident had happened in Germany, for example, the teacher could have faced up to five years in prison. Moreover, if the headteacher had seen the footage – had seen a child being beaten – but failed to take appropriate action, questions would also arise about his professional responsibility.“

“If the teacher behaves so brazenly in front of a camera, it is frightening to imagine what she might have done in a classroom without cameras. She should be dismissed, made to apologise to the child and permanently banned from teaching.”

“The situation is much the same in almost every school. In some, there is physical violence; in others, psychological pressure; and in some, children are simply ignored. At parents’ request, cameras should be installed not only in school corridors but also in classrooms.”

“When such incidents become public, headteachers condemn the teacher’s actions and express utter surprise that someone with more than 30 years of teaching experience could behave this way. But before things reach that point, when we ask for cameras to be installed, those same headteachers come up with a thousand excuses to prevent it.”

“They just don’t want teachers to be embarrassed or parents to see how often a teacher talks on the phone during lessons.“

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘Everything is in place for Prime Minister Kobakhidze’s resignation’
World.content:
Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili predicts that Georgia’s Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze could resign soon. The analyst focuses on Kobakhidze’s remarks at a government meeting on 7 October, where he spoke about projects completed and currently under way during his time as prime minister.

Also on 7 October, Kobakhidze appointed Economy Minister Mariam Kvrivishvili as deputy prime minister. Khukhashvili sees this as a possible signal of upcoming changes in the government. He believes Kvrivishvili could eventually replace Kobakhidze.

On 7 October, the government held its first meeting in a month. Irakli Kobakhidze spoke about projects completed and currently under way in various sectors during his time as prime minister. Kobakhidze spent more than half an hour reviewing the government’s record.

Gia Khukhashvili: “Everything is in place for his [Kobakhidze’s] resignation. In fact, he has been powerless for a long time. No minister in the executive branch feels accountable to him. A purely technical government has been formed.

I would not rule out the possibility that [his lengthy speech at today’s government meeting] means exactly that. I can support this with the fact that Mariam Kvrivishvili has been promoted to deputy prime minister. That also happened today, and it is another sign that the end of his premiership is near.

It is possible that during the transition period, Mariam Kvrivishvili could become acting prime minister to ensure continuity until a new prime minister takes office. However, I would not rule out the possibility that Kvrivishvili herself could become the new prime minister.”

“Anything is possible — these are games at the royal court, after all. I do not see either Kobakhidze or [former prime minister] Garibashvili as real actors in the political process. There have been periods when they were given more room to manoeuvre, but they are not real players.

Anything is possible. The main and most important decisions, the fundamental ones, are made elsewhere. Someone else decides whom to hang and whom to pardon, and we all know his first and last name [Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of Georgian Dream — JAMnews].

And this is just some petty squabbling among small-time people.”

Gia Khukhashvili on possible resignation of Kobakhidze

World.title: EU prepares to expand without Georgia: what ‘candidate status on paper’ means
World.content:
The European Union is preparing for a new round of enlargement and drawing up concrete roadmaps for four leading candidates — Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.

Georgia is no longer part of this process. The European Commission does not mention it at all in its main communication. An accompanying 149-page document explicitly says that Georgia’s EU accession process has effectively been put on hold.

Against this backdrop, the political conflict between Tbilisi and Brussels has become increasingly clear. So has their different understanding of European integration itself. The European Commission says democratic reforms and alignment with EU foreign policy form part of the conditions for membership. Leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party, meanwhile, have increasingly openly portrayed some of Brussels’ demands as pressure that harms the country’s interests.

“A candidate only on paper”

On 6 October, the European Commission published a communication titled “Communication on Pre-Enlargement Policy Reviews – Preparing for a Wider Union” (“Pre-Enlargement Policy Review — Preparing for a Wider Union”).

The document outlines how the EU itself should prepare for future enlargement. One of the main areas involves gradually integrating candidate countries before they achieve full membership.

At the same time, the European Commission is considering stronger safeguards in case a new member violates the EU’s fundamental principles after joining. In the most serious cases, such a mechanism could even suspend the member state’s voting rights in the Council of the EU.

The European Commission will prepare roadmaps for four countries — Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.

The main 25-page communication does not even mention Georgia.

On 6 October 2026 in Brussels, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos described Georgia’s position in response to a question from a Georgian journalist:

*“As you know, Georgia is a candidate country only on paper. I regret that. I would like Georgia, with the huge support of the Georgian people, to be at the same level as Moldova and Ukraine today.

How we continue working with the country will depend to a large extent on how the member states assess its future. But much of what is happening in the country [in Georgia] will appear in the enlargement reports at the end of October. You can imagine which direction things will take.”*

The working document accompanying the communication does mention Georgia among the enlargement countries, but it adds an important caveat:

“Georgia’s accession process has been de facto halted in line with the conclusions of the European Council.”

This is an important point: the EU has not revoked Georgia’s candidate status, and it did not take any new decision to do so on 6 October.

However, despite retaining its formal status, Georgia does not rank among the candidates for which the European Commission is now planning the next stage of accession.

A common starting point, different trajectories

Georgia applied to join the European Union in March 2022, at the same time as Ukraine and Moldova.

It received candidate status in December 2023, subject to fulfilling nine steps set out by the European Commission.

The three countries then took sharply different paths.

The EU opened accession negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova in 2024. In Georgia’s case, however, EU documents state that steps taken by the authorities since 2024 have harmed the country’s European path and effectively halted the accession process.

[On 28 November 2024, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the government would not put the opening of EU accession talks on the agenda until the end of 2028 and would reject all EU budget grants — JAMnews]

The new 2026 package makes the difference even clearer: Moldova and Ukraine now rank among the four leading candidates, while Georgia does not.

“Moldova listens to Brussels, while we don’t”

Statements by Georgian Dream show that relations between Tbilisi and Brussels have become increasingly confrontational.

Georgian authorities respond to criticism from the EU not only by defending their policies, but also by openly rejecting and criticising Brussels’ demands themselves.

Government representatives also frame compliance with some EU demands as a question of protecting Georgia’s national interests.

Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili contrasted Marta Kos’s statement about Moldova’s progress with economic indicators. He said Georgia’s economic growth was higher.

Papuashvili linked this difference to Georgia’s approach to Brussels’ recommendations:

“[Moldova] deserves more and more praise, but our experience tells us that the more Brussels praises you, the more its decisions and imposed directives harm you.”

Papuashvili also compared poverty rates in the two countries and linked the differences to their respective approaches to Brussels’ policies.

*“What is the difference? Moldova listens to Brussels, while we don’t. […] The conclusion is clear: those who listen to Brussels suffer; those who do not listen to Brussels but listen to their own people come out ahead economically. The only thing Moldova is really ahead of us in is Brussels’ beautiful words.

We certainly do not need such beautiful words if those words only mean that we suffer from policies imposed by Brussels,”* Papuashvili said.

Parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirchkhalia gave a similar response.

He said the Georgian authorities were ready to carry out the reforms needed for European integration, but that Georgia had “red lines” and national interests that it could not sacrifice to join the EU.

He compared compliance with Brussels’ political demands to “blind obedience” and said Georgia wanted EU membership “not at any cost”.

“If Brussels now considers a country’s ‘progress’ to depend on how blindly it follows specific political demands, then this is no longer merit-based European integration, but an assessment of blind obedience. […] So when we are told that Georgia is ‘lagging behind’ Ukraine and Moldova, our answer is simple: Georgia chooses dignity and peace!” Kirchkhalia said.

What the European Commission says

The European Commission’s 2026 document sets out very different criteria. Alongside economic development, the central issues in the accession process include the rule of law, democratic standards and alignment with the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP).

According to the document, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and North Macedonia fully align with the CFSP, while Moldova and Ukraine demonstrate a high level of alignment. Georgia and Serbia need to make significant progress in this area, while Georgia and Turkey have low levels of alignment.

The European Commission sees this as an indication of a candidate country’s strategic choice and says these issues must be resolved before accession.

The document also gives Russia a separate focus. According to the European Commission, enlargement directly counters Russian influence because the accession process requires countries such as Georgia and Serbia to fully align with EU foreign policy and legislation. This includes sanctions, energy, trade, foreign investment and visa policy.

The document also states:

“At present, the Georgian authorities are not actively pursuing EU and NATO membership, while Ukraine is making changes to achieve full compatibility with NATO.”

This ranks among the strongest formulations in the new document because the assessment concerns not just the implementation of a specific reform, but the authorities’ overall political course.

The opposition on Moldova’s example

Salome Samadashvili, one of the leaders of the opposition Lelo — Strong Georgia alliance, contrasts Moldova’s example with Georgian Dream’s narrative about a so-called “second front”.

She says Moldova did not open a “second front” against Russia. Instead, the EU is helping Moldova strengthen its security and defence capabilities in response to threats from Russia.

Samadashvili also links Moldova’s European progress to its efforts to tackle oligarchic influence, arguing that Georgia has gone in the opposite direction.

“Unfortunately, Georgia has gone in the opposite direction: an oligarch has taken complete control of the government, destroyed all state institutions, and as a result, our EU accession agenda has been cancelled,” Samadashvili says.

Ban on opposition parties

The political context of Georgia’s relations with the EU is also visible in the European Parliament’s current agenda.

On 7 October, the European Parliament is due to hold a debate officially titled “Attempts by the ruling Georgian Dream party to ban opposition parties in Georgia”. A vote on the corresponding resolution will take place on 8 October.

This is a separate procedure from the European Commission’s enlargement package, and it would be incorrect to directly link the two.

However, the two processes also illustrate the different political contexts between Georgia and the other leading candidates. The EU is working on the next stages of integration with four countries, while the European Parliament is discussing the possible banning of opposition parties in Georgia.

The next important assessment of Georgia will come at the end of October, when the European Commission publishes its enlargement reports.

EU enlargement without Georgia

World.title: Ex-German intelligence chief arrested as investigators probe links to Azerbaijani intelligence
World.content:
German intelligence passed information to Azerbaijan

Former German foreign intelligence chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of obtaining information constituting state secrets, attempted treason and acting on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.

Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office has not specified which foreign country is involved. However, according to Der Spiegel, investigators are examining Hanning’s possible links to an Azerbaijani intelligence officer and whether he prepared analytical materials for the officer using classified information.

Hanning has also served for many years on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum.

Hanning, 80, who headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was detained on 6 October. His former chief of staff, Manfred D., was also arrested as part of the same investigation.

According to the Federal Prosecutor’s Office, Hanning is under strong suspicion of espionage involving treason, obtaining information constituting state secrets, attempted treason and acting as an agent for a foreign intelligence service. Manfred D. is suspected of attempted treason and aiding and abetting espionage.

The investigation is ongoing, and the allegations have yet to be considered by a court on their merits. No final judicial decision has been made in Hanning’s case.

Around 2,000 BND documents

According to investigators, several years after leaving the BND, Hanning reached an agreement with his former employee to provide him with classified information.

The Federal Prosecutor’s Office believes that around spring 2010, Hanning and Manfred D. struck an agreement under which D. would regularly provide his former boss with important information obtained from the BND in exchange for payment.

Manfred D. worked with Hanning at the BND before following him to Germany’s Federal Ministry of the Interior. In 2012, he returned to the BND, where he held a senior position in the offices of subsequent heads of the intelligence service until March 2026. In this role, he had access to classified information.

According to preliminary findings by investigators, between 2010 and 2022, Manfred D. provided Hanning with around 2,000 documents. A significant proportion contained classified information and were intended exclusively for internal use within the BND.

Some of the materials contained information intended for the BND leadership, as well as for regular meetings of intelligence service representatives at the German Federal Chancellery. According to an investigation by WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, the documents included material on Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military, as well as information obtained from Germany’s partner intelligence services.

Prosecutors say Hanning intended to use the information for commercial purposes as part of his private consultancy work.

How did Azerbaijan connection emerge?

The Federal Prosecutor’s Office does not mention Azerbaijan or any other country in its official statement.

According to the official account, Hanning once used classified information obtained from Manfred D. to prepare an analysis for “an employee of a foreign intelligence service”. Investigators have so far been unable to establish whether the analysis was actually passed to its intended recipient.

The possible Azerbaijan connection emerged in reports by German media citing sources familiar with the investigation.

According to Der Spiegel, investigators are examining Hanning’s possible links to an Azerbaijani intelligence officer. The magazine also reports that the analysis Hanning prepared using classified BND information was intended for this individual. The same information has also been reported by WELT, t-online and other German media.

Hanning sits on board of German-Azerbaijani Forum

Another factor drawing attention to the possible Azerbaijan connection is Hanning’s longstanding public ties with the country.

He has for many years served on the board of the Deutsch-Aserbaidschanisches Forum (German-Azerbaijani Forum).

In an announcement about the election of the forum’s new leadership in August 2025, Hanning was again listed as a board member. The same list also included Elmar Mammadov, a representative of Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR in Germany.

The forum describes itself as an independent platform promoting political, economic, academic and cultural ties between Germany and Azerbaijan. LobbyControl, a German organisation that monitors lobbying in Germany, has previously described the forum as one of the lobbying organisations with close ties to the Azerbaijani authorities.

Hanning has served on the forum’s board for many years. As early as 2017, Tagesspiegel reported that the former BND chief was a member of the organisation’s board. It said that even then, the forum’s structures included former ministers, MPs and senior government officials.

Previous ‘Azerbaijan case’ in Germany

The current espionage investigation is not the first major scandal in Germany involving Azerbaijan.

In recent years, German authorities have investigated a number of criminal cases involving the alleged bribery of politicians in Azerbaijan’s interests.

In July 2025, a Munich court gave former CSU MP Eduard Lintner a nine-month suspended prison sentence for his role in transferring funds originating from Azerbaijan in an effort to influence decisions by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE). The court explicitly described this as vote-buying.

In January 2026, former CDU MP Axel Fischer was given a 14-month suspended prison sentence. According to the court, while serving in PACE, Fischer received tens of thousands of euros from Azerbaijan and, in return, made positive statements about the country and passed on confidential documents.

Legally, these cases are unrelated to the current investigation into Hanning. The Lintner and Fischer cases concerned political corruption and lobbying on behalf of the Azerbaijani government’s interests. The Hanning case concerns state secrets and suspected activity on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.

Classified documents discovered during unrelated investigation

Suspicions of espionage involving Hanning emerged under unusual circumstances.

In September 2025, German law enforcement officers searched Hanning’s home and offices as part of a separate criminal investigation into the kidnapping of the children of businesswoman Christina Block. Hanning also denied the allegations in that case.

During the searches, investigators reportedly discovered classified BND material. The documents were subsequently handed over to federal authorities, and in May 2026 a covert investigation into Hanning and Manfred D. was launched.

The findings of the investigation could have serious implications for Germany’s intelligence service. BND chief Martin Jäger said an internal review was also under way and that the initial suspicions had been further substantiated. German lawmakers responsible for overseeing the intelligence services have called for a comprehensive investigation into what happened.

If reports of Hanning’s links to Azerbaijani intelligence are confirmed, the case would go beyond previous scandals involving Azerbaijani lobbying in Germany: this time, the issue is not political influence but the possible transfer of classified German intelligence to a foreign intelligence service.

World.title: Real risks or empty threats? Reaction to Medvedev’s statement about ‘Ukrainisation’ of Armenia
World.content:
Medvedev on the “Ukrainisation” of Armenia

“Armenia turning into a new Ukraine represents another sign of Russia’s geopolitical anxiety and the deepening crisis in Armenian-Russian relations,” political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan said in response to Dmitry Medvedev’s sensational statement.

“Armenia’s current leadership decided that changing the country’s course would serve its interests. I am sure that this will not lead to anything good either. The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” said Russia’s deputy Security Council chairman.

By a change in course, he meant Armenia’s drive towards European integration. Yerevan has not officially responded to his remarks.

Only parliament speaker Ruben Rubinyan told journalists: “Armenia cannot be anything else. Armenia is Armenia, and it will always be Armenia.”

Political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan believes that Russia “is irritated and unbalanced because the situation in the war is not just bad, but very bad”. At the same time, the analyst says Armenia should take the statement from Moscow seriously and try to assess how real the threat is:

“We should not treat this threat as either an absolutely inevitable scenario or empty bravado. It involves real risks stemming from Armenia’s energy and economic vulnerabilities. It also contains elements of psychological pressure.”

Comment

Political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan says Russia fears losing its influence in the South Caucasus:

“Against the backdrop of setbacks on the Ukrainian front, Moscow’s resources remain limited, while its influence across the post-Soviet space has weakened. But the most unwelcome development for Russia is that all of this now shows a clear trend towards further deterioration.”

In his view, Russia can still wage a war of attrition in Ukraine, but casualties, economic sanctions and international isolation are creating significant tensions inside the country.

The analyst says that under these conditions, Russia sees the departure of any ally as a “stab in the back”. This leads to an unbalanced response, as Medvedev’s statement demonstrates:

“The aim of the threat is to instil fear in Armenian society and stop the process of rapprochement with the West, which stems from our security and development interests.”

Mehrabyan believes the threats from Moscow carry some real risks:

“The possibility of a direct military invasion is currently close to zero for one simple reason. No matter how many threats Medvedev spews, Russia has no way to invade a country with which it has no border. But Russia has powerful hybrid tools, and it can and does use them.”

Among the existing risks, the political analyst highlights Armenia’s economic and energy dependence on Russia.

He points to the Upper Lars checkpoint, the only land route linking Armenia with Russia. Whenever the route closes, it creates problems for Armenian exporters and importers. Mehrabyan also notes that Armenia receives gas from Russia, as well as fuel for its nuclear power plant:

“Cutting off gas supplies or suspending deliveries under the pretext of repairs, or closing the border on sanitary grounds, could trigger internal upheaval in Armenia and force the country to operate under a state of emergency.”

According to Mehrabyan, Yerevan has so far managed the potential risks without shocks or conflicts, but he is not confident that it will continue to do so.

He stresses that the current situation also creates potential security risks. In particular, he suggests that “Baku could sell its pressure on Armenia to Moscow”, and that Russia would have no objection to such a deal.
