The political analyst says Russia is behaving like a wounded beast. He urges the Armenian authorities to summon the Russian ambassador to the Foreign Ministry and hand him a formal protest note instead of making public demarches.

At the same time, he says Armenia needs to emphasise once again that its closer ties with the European Union and the United States serve Armenia’s interests and do not target Russia.

Mehrabyan identifies energy and economic diversification among Yerevan’s priorities. He says Armenia urgently needs to secure gas supplies from Iran, which could cover 85% of the country’s needs. He also expects the authorities to:

continue army reforms and work to strengthen the country’s borders;

deepen military and technical cooperation with various countries, including France, India and Greece;

ensure domestic stability and resilience;

strengthen strategic communications and combat disinformation.

Ruben Mehrabyan believes Armenia needs to prepare for modern warfare, including hybrid attacks:

“Armenia must not give Azerbaijan or Russia any reason to be tempted to commit aggression against us.”

Medvedev on the “Ukrainisation” of Armenia

World.title: Giorgi Davitadze case: how it drew attention to what is happening in Georgia’s prisons
World.content:
36-year-old prisoner Giorgi Davitadze says that about 10 prison staff at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi, Georgia, sexually assaulted him.

Authorities have not yet investigated Davitadze’s case. The Penitentiary Service, however, calls his allegations “a complete lie” and has released silent video footage as evidence. Davitadze’s family says the footage is incomplete and that authorities have not released the actual footage showing the alleged abuse.

Georgia’s Public Defender says the video provided to the office does not show the abuse Davitadze described.

Davitadze’s case has unfolded in a particularly sensitive context for Georgia. The allegations concern sexual abuse inside the very system that Georgian Dream made one of the main targets of its promised reforms when it came to power.

What Giorgi Davitadze says

The public learned about the alleged sexual abuse of Giorgi Davitadze on 2 October, during a hearing at the Court of Appeals.

Davitadze told the court that on 21 December 2025, about 10 prison staff sexually assaulted him and subjected him to degrading treatment in a de-escalation room, a special facility for temporarily isolating prisoners experiencing severe emotional or psychological distress.

“They took me down to the de-escalation room and raped me — with a finger, with a hand. […] Ten people, the guards, raped me. You can see everything on the camera,” Davitadze told the court.

He said he later attempted suicide.

Davitadze demanded that the authorities punish the prison staff he named, threatening to go on hunger strike if they failed to do so.

Davitadze’s allegations sparked widespread attention in the media and society.

The severity of the allegations drew particular attention, as did Davitadze’s claim that surveillance cameras should have captured the incident he described.

Davitadze’s family demanded the full release of the footage, while civil society organisations said the prisoner’s allegations required an effective and comprehensive investigation. The Penitentiary Service, in turn, categorically denied the allegations of sexual abuse.

It later emerged that government agencies had known about the alleged abuse since December 2025.

The Public Defender’s Office was also aware of the case. On 26 December, Davitadze’s lawyer told the office that his client had suffered ill-treatment.

That same day, a representative of the Public Defender’s Office went to the Rustavi prison and spoke with Davitadze. He repeated his account, saying prison staff had subjected him to abuse, including sexual abuse.

The Public Defender’s Office passed the information to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which opened an investigation. The office also demanded that video footage from the period identified by Davitadze be preserved in the archive.

More than nine months have passed since then. The investigation remains incomplete, and Davitadze is still being held in the same prison whose staff he accuses of abuse.

What the video released by the Penitentiary Service shows

On 2 October, the Penitentiary Service released footage that, according to the agency, shows Davitadze being taken to the de-escalation room on 21 December 2025 and the events that followed.

The video has no sound.

The footage shows Davitadze and about 10 prison staff members. One of them wears disposable medical gloves.

The staff search Davitadze, including with a metal detector. Several people hold the prisoner’s arms behind his back. The staff then forcibly search Davitadze after pinning him down on a bed.

The Penitentiary Service says prison staff must search prisoners when moving them to a de-escalation room. According to its account, Davitadze refused to undergo the search and insulted the staff, so they carried out the search by force.

The service calls the allegations of sexual abuse “a complete lie” and says “there was not only no sexual violence against Davitadze, there was no violence of any kind.”

The Penitentiary Service says it had not previously released the footage because the case remains under investigation. The agency also says it has continuously archived video footage related to Davitadze since 3 March 2026.

Family says the released video is incomplete

Davitadze’s family says the video released by the Penitentiary Service is incomplete.

His mother, Irma Davitadze, says she saw five video files covering about 20 minutes in total and believes the footage had been edited.

On 3 October, family members and Davitadze’s supporters held a protest outside the prison. They demanded the release of the full footage, an impartial investigation and the resignation of prison director Shota Trapaidze.

Another demand from the family is to transfer Davitadze to another prison, away from the staff members he accuses of abuse.

The prisoner’s father, Avtandil Davitadze, says:

“[These staff members] come to his cell, shout something, say something that insults his dignity, provoke him, and then what should never happen begins.”

However, Justice Minister Paata Salia says transferring a prisoner to another facility requires the authorities to follow certain procedures and meet specific conditions. The minister says officials are considering the request and will transfer Davitadze if he meets those conditions.

What the ombudsman says

The Public Defender’s position has become one of the most contentious aspects of the case.

According to an official statement from the Public Defender’s Office, its representatives requested and reviewed the relevant video footage but found no details showing the severe abuse Davitadze described.

However, the office stresses that authorities must investigate the allegations regardless and verify the prisoner’s complaint by collecting and comparing all available evidence.

The Public Defender also calls on the Prosecutor’s Office to make the findings of the investigation public as soon as possible.

On 5 October, Public Defender Levan Ioseliani repeated on TV Pirveli that the footage released so far does not show sexual abuse itself. When asked whether inserting a finger into a prisoner’s body could form part of a search procedure, Ioseliani initially said he needed to check the relevant regulation:

Journalist: [Davitadze says] he felt a finger penetrate his body. Is that part of the search procedure?

Public Defender: We need to see what the regulation says — whether it allows such a thorough search. However, the regulation does require searches, including with a detector and scanner.

When the presenter asked whether he therefore ruled out the possibility of something that does not appear in the footage, Ioseliani replied: “The Prosecutor’s Office must investigate what we cannot see.”

Questions that remain unanswered

Public organisations say the footage and explanations released by the Penitentiary Service cannot provide an adequate response to such a serious allegation. More than ten organisations have called for an effective and comprehensive investigation. They include the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), the Social Justice Center, Transparency International — Georgia, the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED), the Institute for Development of Freedom of Information (IDFI), the Civil Society Foundation, Safari and others.

In their statement, they raise eight main questions:

Why did authorities need to move Davitadze to the de-escalation room?

What exactly did he do before the authorities took this step?

Was the measure necessary and proportionate?

Why were about ten staff members in the room?

Who were they and what did each of them do?

Does the published video show the full sequence of events without interruption?

Does the original video still exist, and can an independent expert examine it?

Do recordings from other cameras exist?

“The video released by the Penitentiary Service cannot replace an independent and effective investigation,” the organisations say.

Why the video has no sound

Another question concerns the fact that the released footage has no sound.

On 5 October, journalists asked Justice Minister Paata Salia whether the original recording had sound. The minister did not answer. When they asked whether cameras installed in de-escalation rooms can record sound at all, Salia said he could not comment. Later, speaking on Imedi TV, the minister said Georgian law does not provide for audio recording.

Salia also could not explain why authorities moved Davitadze to the de-escalation room on 21 December 2025 and referred journalists to the Penitentiary Service for an answer.

The minister says authorities are investigating Giorgi Davitadze’s original allegation and that they need to complete the investigation before giving a final answer.

“If anyone attempts to destabilise or disrupt the operation of penitentiary institutions, whether from inside or outside, the authorities will respond strictly, as provided by law,” Salia said.

He also mentioned that some public statements may contain signs of a criminal offence, but he did not name any specific individuals or give examples.

Prisons — one of the most painful issues in modern Georgia

The issue of violence in Georgian prisons goes beyond human rights.

It holds a special place in the country’s recent political history. In 2012, conditions in the penitentiary system became one of the key factors behind the change of government.

On 18 September 2012, less than two weeks before the parliamentary elections, Georgian television channels broadcast footage recorded at Prison No. 8 in Tbilisi.

The footage showed guards beating, humiliating and sexually abusing prisoners. The broadcasts triggered mass protests in Tbilisi and other cities.

The footage exposed a problem that human rights groups had already raised. A 2013 Human Rights Watch report said the images highlighted a longstanding problem of torture and ill-treatment of prisoners.

The government at the time acknowledged the systemic nature of violence in prisons. The ministers responsible for prisons and internal affairs resigned, and authorities arrested several penitentiary staff members. Within days, the prison system became one of the central issues of the election campaign.

In the parliamentary elections on 1 October 2012, Mikheil Saakashvili’s United National Movement lost power, and Bidzina Ivanishvili’s Georgian Dream coalition took control of the government.

One of the new government’s main political promises was to reform the penitentiary system that had developed under the previous government and protect prisoners’ rights.

But data from recent years and reports by human rights organisations show that violence and ill-treatment by security, law enforcement and penitentiary authorities remain serious concerns. The problem extends beyond prisons to police stations, the detention process and protests.

In June 2026, Georgian human rights organisations said in a joint statement that, in their assessment, torture and ill-treatment in Georgia had become a “systemic and widespread practice”. Amnesty International describes a similar situation.

At the same time, the penitentiary system continues to grow in scale. According to official statistics, Georgia’s penitentiary system received a total of 22,767 convicted people in 2025 — 25.5% more than the previous year. This marks the highest figure since the authorities began keeping the relevant statistics.

In 2024, Georgia ranked second among 46 Council of Europe countries in terms of the number of prisoners per 100,000 people.

What is happening in Georgia’s prisons

After the allegations by Giorgi Davitadze became public, several incidents occurred at Rustavi Prison No. 6. According to the Public Defender, its representatives met three prisoners on 3 and 4 October who had protested against the treatment of Davitadze. They told the representatives why they were protesting and described their conditions in prison.

The Penitentiary Service denies that the authorities moved these prisoners to de-escalation rooms because they had expressed solidarity with Davitadze. According to the agency, the authorities moved them to protect the safety of the prisoners and prison staff.

For example, the service says that on 2 October one prisoner kicked the prison’s deputy director in the stomach. On 4 October, two other prisoners allegedly “physically insulted” staff members — that is, attacked them — while returning from a walk. The agency also released video footage showing these incidents.

Later that same evening, on 4 October, an incident also involved Davitadze himself. According to the Penitentiary Service, he called over a prison employee and, in front of him, swallowed “several small objects of unknown origin”. Staff offered to transfer Davitadze to Vivamedi Clinic, but he refused.

The following day, the Public Defender’s Office said its representative had met with Davitadze. According to the prisoner, he felt well and had refused the transfer to the clinic as part of his protest. Davitadze said he would not go to the clinic until the authorities returned the three prisoners who had protested in his support from the de-escalation rooms to their cells.

Amid these events, reports also emerged of possible violence against another prisoner. According to lawyer Anna Akopova, her client Lasha Chachanidze suffered a beating at the same Prison No. 6 after he shouted from his cell to express solidarity with Davitadze. The lawyer says authorities transferred Chachanidze and two other prisoners to Prison No. 3 in Batumi.

Akopova says the prisoner has multiple injuries on different parts of his body. According to her, about ten people took part in the alleged assault. The lawyer is demanding a medical examination and the preservation of the relevant video footage, which could establish Chachanidze’s condition when staff took him out of his cell and when they returned him.

The Penitentiary Service categorically denies the allegation and says nothing of the sort happened. The Public Defender’s Office said it had received information about the case and would visit the prisoner.

Saba Skhvitaridze, who authorities detained during pro-European protests, also wrote about the tense situation at Prison No. 6. According to a statement published on his Facebook page, authorities transferred some prisoners to other facilities, placed others in de-escalation rooms and several prisoners went on hunger strike. Skhvitaridze also reported that authorities beat a prisoner and that some prisoners injured themselves.

Giorgi Davitadze remains in the same prison, whose staff he accuses of sexual abuse.

The Prosecutor’s Office investigation, which it launched in December 2025 after the Public Defender’s Office filed a complaint, remains incomplete. The Public Defender’s Office says it continues to monitor the investigation and calls on the Prosecutor’s Office to make its findings public as soon as possible.

The Penitentiary Service denies all the allegations, including reports of a hunger strike among prisoners, and insists that “complete calm” prevails at Rustavi Prison No. 6.

The Giorgi Davitadze case

World.title: SJC: Extradition of prisoners from Georgia to Russia must be stopped immediately
World.content:
Following the killing of Dmitry Pushkaryov, who Georgia extradited to Russia, the Georgian Social Justice Center (SJC) said that Georgia should immediately halt the extradition of prisoners to Russia.

The organisation said resuming the practice of extraditing prisoners to Russia was incompatible with human rights.

After Georgia extradited Dmitry Pushkaryov, he was killed in an attack on Russian Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) officers. According to Russian authorities, Pushkaryov killed one officer and wounded three others while attempting to escape.

“The mere fact that Dmitry Pushkaryov was killed does not directly establish that Georgia violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights by extraditing him. However, his death raises even more serious questions about how thoroughly the Georgian authorities assessed the risks he faced in Russia, what guarantees they obtained from Russia, whether an independent mechanism existed to monitor compliance with those guarantees, and whether the Georgian side subsequently monitored the person’s situation,” the SJC said.

According to the organisation, the case law of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) indicates that information that emerges after a person’s transfer can also matter when assessing how well-founded the state’s initial risk assessment was.

The SJC believes that continuing extraditions to Russia — particularly without proper public justification, a rigorous individual risk assessment and effective independent monitoring mechanisms — could put Georgia in breach of its international human rights obligations.

The organisation calls on the Georgian government, the Ministry of Justice and the Prosecutor General’s Office to immediately suspend extraditions to Russia. The SJC believes the practice should remain suspended until the situation in Russia changes significantly and the international community reaches a consensus on the issue.

The Centre also calls on the Prosecutor General’s Office to publish statistical data on extradition requests received from Russia since 16 March 2022, the decisions made on those requests and the extraditions carried out.

The organisation is also demanding that the Ministry of Justice explain the legal grounds for changing the moratorium recorded before the European Court of Human Rights in the case of Sumbaev v. Georgia.

The ECtHR found Georgia’s 2021 extradition of Aslan Sumbaev, who faced serious criminal charges in Russia, lawful only after Russia provided official diplomatic assurances that it would prevent torture and ensure proper detention conditions.

“Please also specify what individual guarantees and subsequent monitoring mechanisms were applied in relation to the extraditions that have already taken place,” the Social Justice Center wrote.

World.title: Azerbaijan, World Bank discuss support for AI-based infrastructure
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. Azerbaijan and the World Bank have discussed possible support for the development of artificial intelligence (AI)-based infrastructure, the Azerbaijani Ministry of Digital Development and Transport reported.

The issue was discussed during a meeting between Deputy Minister of Digital Development and Transport Rashad Hasanov and World Bank Country Manager for Azerbaijan Sasha Bakes.

The meeting addressed opportunities for cooperation in priority areas identified under the Action Plan for 2026-2028 on accelerating digital development in Azerbaijan.

The sides also exchanged views on possible World Bank support for digital transformation, the development of AI-based infrastructure, data centers and the Government Cloud, as well as training cybersecurity specialists and personnel with digital skills.

Cooperation between Azerbaijan and the World Bank covers various areas alongside digital development, including infrastructure, energy, transport, agriculture, water management, employment and institutional reforms. Since Azerbaijan joined the World Bank, a total of around $4.9 billion in financing has been allocated for 53 projects.

One of the main areas of cooperation with the World Bank has been the implementation of projects aligned with Azerbaijan's development priorities and reform agenda. Projects carried out within the partnership have covered infrastructure development, expansion of energy and transport capabilities, improvement of water management, employment growth and strengthening institutional capacity.

At the same time, attention is being paid to Azerbaijan's growing role in the international development agenda. After attaining upper-middle-income country status, Azerbaijan has increased its support for international development initiatives as a donor.

The World Bank has expressed interest in continuing long-term cooperation with Azerbaijan and expanding the partnership into new areas.

Digital transformation and AI are currently being considered among the new areas of cooperation. In this context, discussions on possible support for data centers, the Government Cloud, cybersecurity and digital skills development are creating new opportunities to strengthen Azerbaijan's digital infrastructure.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Georgia agree on 2027–2028 parliamentary roadmap
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. Uzbekistan and Georgia agreed to develop a joint roadmap for parliamentary cooperation for 2027–2028 during a meeting in Tashkent.

This was reflected in the statement by the Senate of Oliy Majlis of Uzbekistan, following a meeting between Tanzila Narbayeva, chairwoman of the Senate of Uzbekistan’s Oliy Majlis, and Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili on the sidelines of the 153rd Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union.

The sides discussed further developing strategic partnership relations and strengthening interparliamentary cooperation between Uzbekistan and Georgia.

The establishment of bilateral strategic partnership relations during the Uzbek president’s state visit to Georgia in July opened new opportunities for cooperation between the two countries, according to the Uzbek side.

The officials emphasized the need to intensify contacts between relevant parliamentary committees and interparliamentary cooperation groups and involve them more actively in discussions on specific areas of bilateral cooperation.

"The joint roadmap for 2027–2028 is intended to support the consistent development of interparliamentary dialogue, identify concrete measures in priority areas of cooperation and support the Uzbekistan-Georgia strategic partnership at the parliamentary level," the Uzbek Senate said.

In addition, the sides exchanged views on prospects for expanding trade and economic ties, transport connectivity, investment and digitalization.

They highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation in education, tourism, culture and humanitarian affairs.

The meeting was held as part of the 153rd Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union, providing an opportunity for the two parliamentary leaders to discuss mechanisms for translating the countries’ strategic partnership into practical cooperation at the legislative level.

World.title: Azerbaijan's parliament calls European Parliament resolution biased
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. Azerbaijan’s parliament has rejected the allegations contained in the European Parliament’s October 8 resolution on human rights and freedoms in Azerbaijan, describing the document as a biased political action.

The Azerbaijani parliament made the remarks in its response to the European Parliament’s resolution.

The parliament said the European Parliament’s targeted political approach toward Azerbaijan had become more confrontational following the Second Karabakh War. It said resolutions adopted in recent years, along with calls for political pressure and sanctions against Azerbaijan, demonstrated that the organization had failed to accept what it described as the new geopolitical realities in the South Caucasus.

The response also criticized the European Parliament for seeking to determine the scope of authority of Azerbaijan’s state bodies, issue instructions to law enforcement and judicial institutions, and set political conditions for bilateral relations. According to the parliament, this raises questions about whether the European Parliament seeks to build relations with Azerbaijan based on equality, mutual respect and non-interference in internal affairs.

The parliament also referred to issues of corruption and illicit lobbying influence within the European Parliament, stressing the importance of the organization consistently applying its own standards.

The response further said that the European Parliament applies double standards in its approach to human rights. It noted that while resolutions are adopted concerning Azerbaijan, European countries themselves continue to face problems related to police violence, restrictions on freedom of peaceful assembly and accountability for human rights violations.

The parliament said the adoption of the resolution at a time when the Azerbaijan-Armenia peace agenda is advancing was also a matter of concern. It said unilateral initiatives and what it described as misguided assessments make it more difficult to build an environment of mutual trust and create additional obstacles to normalizing relations.

The response also highlighted what the parliament described as a contradiction between the European Parliament’s call to restore cooperation with the Azerbaijani parliament and its adoption of documents that create interparliamentary tensions. The parliament said restoring trust requires abandoning confrontational rhetoric and recognizing the equal nature of interparliamentary relations.

The Azerbaijani parliament said the country remains committed to protecting human rights and fundamental freedoms, ensuring the rule of law and implementing the principles of a state governed by law.

The response also said that, while making allegations against Azerbaijan, the European Parliament remained silent about the rights of Azerbaijani refugees and internally displaced persons who, according to the parliament, were subjected to ethnic cleansing and other serious human rights violations during Armenia’s occupation of Azerbaijani territory.

The Azerbaijani parliament called on the European Parliament to abandon what it described as confrontational rhetoric toward Azerbaijan and refrain from interfering in the country’s internal affairs.

The parliament stated that no force can divert Azerbaijan from its path of democratic development.

World.title: Azerbaijan re-elected to ITSO Advisory Committee (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. Azerbaijan has been re-elected to the Advisory Committee of the International Telecommunications Satellite Organization (ITSO) for the 2026–2028 term, according to the Azerbaijan Space Agency (Azercosmos).

The decision was made during the 42nd Meeting of the ITSO Assembly of Parties (AP-42) in Washington, D.C., held from September 30 to October 2, 2026.

Representatives of ITSO member states met at the Assembly to discuss the development of international satellite communications, service accessibility, regulatory issues and the organization’s future activities.

Azerbaijan also participated in the international symposium “Satellite Developments Shaping Connectivity – An ITSO Perspective,” held on September 29 ahead of the Assembly. The symposium included a “Voices of the Regions: National Perspectives” panel, where Azercosmos represented Region C.

The panel focused on national priorities in satellite communications, including service access and affordability, the resilience of communications services, radio-frequency spectrum management, regulatory challenges and international cooperation.

The discussion also covered practical and regulatory challenges faced by countries in Region C, including complex “landing rights” requirements in some countries for foreign satellite operators to provide services and their impact on market access. The need to strengthen the technical and institutional capacities of developing countries, expand knowledge and experience sharing, and improve international cooperation mechanisms was also highlighted.

Azercosmos said Azerbaijan’s re-election to the ITSO Advisory Committee for 2026–2028 will allow the country to continue contributing to the organization’s activities and discussions on international satellite communications.

Azercosmos said it will continue participating in international platforms to represent Azerbaijan’s interests in satellite communications, expand cooperation on global regulatory processes and contribute to the development of sustainable satellite connectivity.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan draft justice cooperation program
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan have drafted a cooperation program to further develop ties between their justice ministries and agreed to sign it at a later date.

According to the Azerbaijani Ministry of Justice, the issue was discussed during a meeting between Azerbaijani Justice Minister Farid Ahmadov and Kyrgyzstan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Justice Minister Almaz Aiylchiev during Ahmadov’s working visit to Türkiye.

The sides noted that relations between Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan are at a high level and that mutual visits by the countries’ heads of state have made an important contribution to the development of bilateral ties.

Ahmadov congratulated Aiylchiev on his appointment to the new position and wished him success in his work.

The sides noted that cooperation between the two countries’ justice ministries is based on a solid legal framework. They said that experience is being exchanged in the areas of notary services, the penitentiary system, probation, mediation and forensic examination.

The meeting also included an exchange of views on further developing existing cooperation, implementing new initiatives and strengthening interaction in the fields of law and justice within the framework of the Organization of Turkic States.

World.title: Breaking: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor wins court battle to have police search warrants quashed
World.content:
UK police have accepted warrants they use to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes earlier this year were unlawful, after the former prince won a court battle on Thursday.

The King's brother launched legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants executed in February, when he was arrested on his 66th birthday.

Police are investigating allegations of misconduct in public office, relating to his time as a UK trade commissioner between 2001 and 2011.

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his royal titles last year, has not been charged. He has always maintained his innocence.

In London on Thursday, local time, the High Court of England and Wales heard police took possession of documents and electronic devices during their raids of the former Duke of York's home on the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk, and his former long-time residence at Royal Lodge, near Windsor.

But police now accept information they gave to a judge when applying for the warrants at the Central Criminal Court — more commonly known as The Old Bailey — earlier this year was incorrect.

It remains unclear what will happen to the evidence police seized during their raids.

The police investigation into Mr Mountbatten-Windsor will continue despite Thursday's development.

World.title: South Korea recalls ambassador as row with Ukraine escalates
World.content:
South Korea will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the foreign ministry has said, as tensions between the two countries escalate over a prisoner of war return.

South Korea’s Foreign Ministry did not specify when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, would return.

It added the country would continue to negotiate with Kyiv and hoped the current issues between the two nations could be resolved.

The countries have been locked in a diplomatic dispute after Seoul accused Kyiv of breaching a confidentiality agreement over the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers.

South Korea wants apology over POW transfer by Ukraine Seoul accuses Ukraine of announcing the transfer of North Korean soldiers caught fighting for Russia to South Korea in breach of a non-disclosure agreement.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed the supposedly secret transfer during a UN speech last month.

South Korea accused the president of violating a non-disclosure agreement on their transfer, but Kyiv denied ever agreeing to such a deal.

The move to recall its ambassador came just days after South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for an apology over the incident and threatened to take further steps if Ukraine refused.

Earlier this week, Ukraine also accused South Korea of helping Russia ease its fuel crisis caused by drone strikes.

More than 30 per cent of Russia's fuel imports in August came from South Korea, Ukraine's top sanctions official Vladyslav Vlasiuk said on Tuesday.

Soldiers wanted to resettle in South Korea

Thousands of North Korean troops have been deployed to support Russia in its war against Ukraine. (Supplied: KCNA via Reuters)

The two prisoners of war returned to South Korea recently were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia in its war against Ukraine.

North Korea benefits from Russia alliance Almost two weeks ago, what is believed to be a North Korean missile was fired in an attack that killed a Ukrainian family. It could be part of a major escalation in North Korea's involvement in the war in Ukraine.

Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had asked to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home.

South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards North Korea as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

North Korea's state media has not commented on the soldiers' transfer.

But Pyongyang has previously reacted angrily to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them.

South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement with Ukraine was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives, but some experts say South Korea may be worried the disclosure could hurt their efforts to improve relations with North Korea.

South Korea has previously supported the Ukraine war effort, providing more than $640 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, the country promised $143 million in aid during a meeting with Mr Zelenskyy.

AP

World.title: Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
World.content:
Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize in literature.

The 76-year-old was honoured "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature," the Swedish Academy said.

"She was very taken by surprise. We didn't have so much time to speak, and all she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she's listening to the wind," said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy.

Toronto-born Carson draws on themes and stories from ancient Greek and Roman literature for works that often blend elements of poetry, essay and fiction.

Her books include Eros the Bittersweet, a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, verse novel Autobiography of Red, Men in the Off Hours, a collection of poetry and prose that won Canada’s Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001 and Norma Jeane Baker of Troy, which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.

A bust of Alfred Nobel at the Swedish Academy, where the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature was announced, in Stockholm. (Reuters: Tom Little)

Last year, Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai, whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humour, won the Nobel Prize in literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror.”

Three science awards were announced earlier this week.

The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.

The physics award recognised a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.

The chemistry prize recognised two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.

This week ends with Friday's peace prize.

The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.71 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organisation.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Russian attack on bus stop kills at least 33 in Ukraine, officials say
World.content:
A Russian strike on a bus stop in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 33 people, authorities say.

Another 18 people were wounded in the attack on Thursday, local time, on a street where two city buses were operating, police said.

Police said the buses were hit with a glide bomb.

Images posted to X by the Ukrainian parliament's commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, showed a burned-out shell of a bus. Another image showed several bodies strewn on the ground.

"Russia is systematically destroying Kramatorsk and terrorising civilians," Mr Lubinets said.

The Ukrainian parliament's commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, posted several images to social media calling for accountability. (Supplied: Dmytro Lubinets)

Several hours after the attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced negotiators will ​visit the United States for talks on Friday ​and ‌Saturday, urging ‌US President ⁠Donald Trump to step up pressure ‌on ​Russia.

"One ‌cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the ​Russians about ‌future economic projects, whilst ⁠on the ‌other hand ‌say that we find ourselves ‌in some sort of … ‌diplomatic ​stalemate," Mr Zelenskyy ⁠said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that Russia's war in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate and the United States will continue to try to facilitate a settlement to end the conflict.

"We'd love to see a negotiated settlement to this war that is permanent, enduring, and fair," Mr Rubio told reporters during a visit to Portugal.

Mr Zelenskyy also said there would be a response to the latest attack.

"This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must," he posted on X.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says search and rescue efforts are still underway after an apartment building was struck in Pryluky. (Supplied: Volodymyr Zelenskyy)

The strikes come just a day after five children were among 22 killed when a Russian missile struck a five-storey apartment block in Pryluky, in the northern Chernigiv region.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband visited the scene with Mr Zelenskyy on Thursday morning, local time.

Mr Miliband posted on social media, "My message was clear: we will stand with the people of Ukraine for as long as it takes".

Moscow's forces have stepped up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine's so-called "fortress belt", local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk region.

Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest of the region still under its control before it stops fighting, which Kyiv refuses to do.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband (left) and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speak to the media in the town of Pryluky. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

Civilian deaths increase

There has been mounting concern about the increase in civilian casualties in the conflict, as both sides step up long-range attacks beyond their borders.

Germany at risk of 'violent conflict' with Russia, intelligence chief warns The warning from a German intelligence chief comes as Russia carries out strikes across Ukraine and on a Turkish civilian boat in the Black Sea.

Since Russia first invaded in 2022, Ukraine has accused its forces of deliberately attacking and killing civilians.

The United Nations has verified more than 17,000 civilian deaths throughout the war, but says the real number is considerably higher.

Kramatorsk City Council called the bus stop attack "another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".

"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it added.

Ukraine hits Russian data centre

Drones hit a data centre owned by Russia's Yandex, the country's leading AI and technology company said on Thursday, in the first major attack on a Russian data hub since the start of the war with Ukraine.

The company, often dubbed "Russia's Google", said its core consumer services were not affected, but did not describe the extent of the damage.

Russia has conducted a strike campaign on Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.

Yandex said the attack on its Sasovo hub, one of its five large data centres, caused a fire and forced it to suspend operations at the site, which hosts tens of thousands of servers.

Reuters/AFP

World.title: Kids turning to chatbots to disclose online sexual victimisation
World.content:
More than one in three Australian children who are sexually victimised online either tell no-one or turn to an AI chatbot for help, according to data from Adelaide University.

The data has prompted Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett to warn law enforcement cannot be the only safety net for vulnerable young people.

In an interview marking her first year in the top job, Commissioner Barrett stopped short of directly endorsing an extension of the federal government's under-16 social media ban to AI chatbots, but stressed that "anything that helps to keep our kids safer is obviously something we support".

The study, an initiative between Adelaide University and the AFP-led Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation, has delivered sobering data on how generative tools are altering youth safety.

Strengthening social media ban The federal government has announced tougher laws that it says will hold big tech to account and keep kids safe online.

Amid a sharp increase in children as young as 12 being manipulated through AI-altered nude images and sadistic online exploitation, the study found 35 per cent of children sexually victimised online confided in an AI chatbot or did not tell anyone.

More than 15 per cent of young people report seeking personal or counselling advice from AI at least once a week.

Among victimised boys, two in five disclosed their experiences solely to an AI bot or kept quiet entirely.

Commissioner Barrett called the trend "heartbreaking" and warned that automated software cannot provide the human support or protection vulnerable youth require.

"Young people are turning to AI more and more for advice and for support and for guidance and that should be concerning to all of us, not just parents," she said.

Addressing the limits of police intervention when children reach out to AI instead of adults, Commissioner Barrett was realistic about the role of law enforcement.

“We're right at the end of the suite of tools here, and we're a pretty blunt object. Let's be honest, by the time we become involved, the options are reduced," she said.

When pressed on whether the federal government should extend its landmark social media ban for under-16s to conversational AI tools to protect young people, Commissioner Barrett cautioned that legislative bans were not a panacea.

Young people who often feel awkward talking to parents about issues are increasingly turning to AI. (ABC News)

"I won't speak specifically to what government should or shouldn't do," she said.

"I would just say generally that anything that helps to keep our kids safer is obviously something that we support."

Bans were "not the whole solution," she added, noting that while regulatory limits were effective for "starting conversations in households around dinner tables," they could not replace community vigilance.

How parents and communities can step up

Comissioner Barrett said parents, carers, family, educators and community leaders were best placed to notice when a child began to withdraw or alter their behaviour.

"It starts in the home, it starts with parents knowing what their kids are doing online, creating those safe opportunities for conversations,” she said.

“You remember when you're at that age, it is awkward talking to your parents about anything, but we need to create that trust in those safe spaces, because as we know, AI technology, it's not a human."

Online cult horrors exposed They are sadistic and manipulative, often targeting children through digital platforms. Now, as part of an ABC investigation, a teen tells how an online cult incited her into ritualistic acts.

While the use of artificial intelligence in the exploitation of young people was a major concern for the AFP, Commissioner Barrett was just as emphatic that AI had a place in policing.

To help identify potential exploitation earlier, the AFP is working with Monash University's AiLECS Lab on a welfare tool that triages reports of harm to the Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation and refers them to a human for assessment.

“It's quite forward leaning. This is something that we need to be doing more and more: partnering with academia, and with tech companies around how do we bring all of our knowledge, expertise and access together to come up with these solutions.”

The AFP released its first AI strategy last month, a "human-led" approach to matching the "scale and pace" of offending, particularly in child exploitation and youth radicalisation.

Extremist material and counterterrorism

On counterterrorism and the rise of violent extremism, Commissioner Barrett said the bulk of the AFP's terrorism caseload was still predominantly religiously motivated, but police were increasingly seeing more "mixed and unclear ideologies".

“Sometimes, particularly with our young people, what we see is perhaps they're not actually driven by a particular ideology, they are driven by a grievance,” she said.

“They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose.”

Comissioner Barrett said the rapidly evolving threat environment had validated her decision to establish national security investigation teams designed to target the "grey zone" of radicalisation, including hate crimes, misogyny, and online hostility that fell just below statutory thresholds for joint counterterrorism charges.

Misogyny named as red flag for violent extremism A new study finds that violent attitudes towards women are not just a social issue but a matter of national security.

The teams have charged 65 people since they were created at the end of last year and she expects those volumes to increase.

"We're going through doors and arresting and charging people very quickly after we receive the reports," Commissioner Barrett said.

Asked whether she believed the definition of terrorism needed to be changed to reflect the evolving security environment, Commissioner Barrett said violent extremist material laws were already working well as a key preventative measure.

"That legislation gives us the ability to go and conduct a search warrant, to seize the devices, to intervene early," she said, describing the possession of extremist material as frequently being the start of a continuum that can lead to violence.

Krissy Barrett says she supports any legislation that will help keep children safe. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Commissioner Barrett said it also provided police with more options "around how we deal with a young person who's come to our attention".

She said most young people in the extremism cases showed behavioural warning signs before they came to police attention, and called on parents and carers to watch out for these.

"I don't want to be arresting and charging young people. We want to be intervening earlier and we want to be getting them the assistance and the support that they need," Commissioner Barrett said.

In 2026, 23 juveniles and 24 adults have been charged for possessing violent extremist material.

The commissioner is working to strengthen ties with other nations and is scheduled to travel to Tokyo later this month.

World.title: NT government departments hit by massive network outage
World.content:
A massive network outage interrupted all government departments in the Northern Territory today, affecting services from hospitals to police.

The widespread, intermittent outage began about 3am and affected all government agencies, from education to housing, in both urban and remote areas.

Earlier today, NT Police said the outage was not affecting Triple Zero (000) calls. However, this afternoon, Assistant Commissioner Terry Zhang said three Triple Zero calls had been missed.

Terry Zhang says police were informed by Telstra of the three missed Triple Zero calls "very soon after". (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"Since the start of the outage … there have only been three phone calls that we couldn't answer in time that were referred to us very soon after that by Telstra," he said.

"We have conducted follow-ups with all three of those missed telephone calls, and there have been no issues identified.

"None of them were high risk or had any consequences; it was just routine police follow-ups."

NT Police advised there had been interruptions to the police non-emergency line throughout the day.

The NT government said the issue occurred inside a "core" IT gateway for NT government services.

The outage impacted police services across the NT. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said the Territory-wide IT outage had caused "significant disruption to all of our IT networks".

"We have mechanisms in place to continue with business as usual until we find the source, which will be subject to a serious inquiry," she said.

'Not a hack'

Department of Corporate and Digital Development deputy chief executive Greg Connors said a team of up to 40 people had been working all day to isolate the cause of the outage.

Mr Connors said workarounds had been implemented this afternoon and the systems were effectively back to normal.

He also said the team believed it had identified the root cause and expected to resolve it this evening.

Greg Connors says workarounds are now in place and the issue is expected to be resolved later today. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I can guarantee you this is not a cyber hack; this is something that is internal," he said.

"It's a bit like getting in your car one day, and it goes, even though there have been no signs it was going to break down prior.

"It is just one of those things that happens. We have found [the issue], which is great kudos to all my team that spent all day looking for it.

"We are confident once we have fixed it, it will be back to normal."

Mr Connors said the outage had a "widespread impact", including in hospitals, where staff had to initiate continuity plans.

"Clinicians in hospitals would have experienced delays, [they] would have experienced not being able to get to services, not being able to get to impacted systems," he said.

He said he could not rule out future outages, but said any that did occur would not be because of the same problem.

World.title: Serial underwear thief's missing map teased link to child who vanished
World.content:
An attempt to reopen an inquest into the disappearance of Mackay schoolgirl Marilyn Wallman failed in 1988 because evidence linked to a sex offender had disappeared.

Fourteen-year-old Marilyn disappeared soon after 7:42am on March 21, 1972, after cycling a kilometre down a dirt road to catch a school bus.

A fragment of her skull was found in October 1974 in bushland at McGregor Creek, about 40 kilometres from where she was last seen.

The current inquest has heard that a convicted repeat sex offender, Michael Anthony Frances, who died in Victoria in 2020, was in Mackay when she went missing.

Michael Anthony Frances, a convicted sex offender who died in Victoria in 2020, was in Mackay when Marilyn Wallman went missing. (Supplied: Department of Justice)

Counsel assisting Coroner David O'Connell, John Aberdeen, said Frances was first arrested in Mackay in 1974 after falling through the ceiling of a women's change room at Eimeo Beach.

"When he was apprehended at Eimeo riding his landlady's scooter, found on the scooter were also a woman's dress, halter top, brazier, panties and two false breasts," Mr Aberdeen said.

The inquest heard Frances dropped a notebook in the change room that referred to other sexual assaults, including one at the Mackay School of Arts where he wrote he had "got a young girl".

Police located a crime report that fit the scenario, and he was arrested after admitting his guilt.

"It seems Mr Frances kept a record of what he had been up to," Mr Aberdeen said.

A search of his house found diaries, notebooks and a mud map with references to Marilyn Wallman, along with 400 pieces of women's underwear he "snow dropped" from clotheslines.

Mr Aberdeen said Frances kept diaries from 1971, but a section surrounding the dates of Marilyn's disappearance had apparently been torn out.

Evidence existed until 1976

The diaries, notebooks and mud map were still in police evidence in 1976, as it was referenced in a statement from a new detective who was briefed on Marilyn's disappearance.

"Detective Mitchelson gave evidence that he located a mud map, drawing or sketch of an area in Eimeo which featured roads which matched the area of Wallmans Rd and Eimeo Road," Mr Aberdeen said.

"He noted that on that sketch was written the initials MW."

He said "not surprisingly", Frances's possible involvement in Marilyn Wallman's disappearance was seen as a distinct possibility, and he was questioned by homicide detectives.

Mr Aberdeen said Frances claimed entries in his books and diaries were in general not referable to any particular person.

Local Mackay newspaper The Daily Mercury two days after Marilyn went missing. (ABC News: Sourced State Library)

When questioned, Frances claimed he was home when Marilyn disappeared, waiting for a phone call about a new job in the railway.

Mr Aberdeen said the diaries and mud map no longer existed.

He said reports indicated they were stored in a locked "steel press" at Mackay police station but that the CIB and exhibit room had since changed.

" Quite simply, Your Honour, no one knows what happened to those documents after 1976. "

In 1987, Daphne Wallman told police underwear had disappeared from her bedroom drawer in the 12 months before Marilyn disappeared; however, she was never shown the underwear Frances was found with.

The inquest heard Frances had a record of violent sexual offending against young women, including abduction, sexual assault, assault with intent to rape and detaining by force.

Inquest rejected

Mr Aberdeen said police requested to reopen the inquest in 1988, but the coroner rejected this due to the missing evidence.

The coroner referred his decision to the under-secretary of the Department of Justice and later the Crown Law Office, as well as the Director of Public Prosecutions, who supported his view that there was insufficient evidence.

"It should be specifically mentioned that Coroner Bradshaw said had the map been available it would have provided the necessary evidence as it established a provable link between Marilyn and Mr Frances."

Car in sand dunes

Mr Aberdeen said Frances first came to police notice two days after Marilyn's disappearance when he was found in the sand hills north of Mackay Harbour by a search party.

Police believe a sedan similar to this was seen in the area when Marilyn disappeared. (Supplied: Queensland Police)

Searchers came across a Wolseley car and Frances, who said he was there digging sand for his landlady's garden.

Mr Aberdeen said that despite the encounter being logged in the police "running sheet", it was two years later, in 1974, that police checked anything to do with the vehicle despite having its complete registration number.

By this time, Frances had sold the car, which had been stripped and used in a kindergarten playground at Bluff in central Queensland and could not be forensically examined.

The inquest is expected to hear from more than 20 witnesses over the next two weeks.

World.title: Matildas coach backs Mary Fowler's absence from friendlies
World.content:
Coach Joe Montemurro has said the Matildas support Mary Fowler's decision to miss upcoming friendlies for personal circumstances and is adamant they have the creative players available to cover her.

Fowler, 23, withdrew this week from the squad to play world number three Germany on Saturday (AEDT) and Haiti on Wednesday.

"It's really important that we create an environment that is important for the player, and as the circumstances are private, I'm not going to elaborate," Montemurro said.

Fowler out of Matildas internationals Mary Fowler will be replaced by Leah Davidson for the upcoming friendlies, with the Matildas star withdrawing due to personal circumstances.

"But yes, absolutely, discussions were had with Mary, with the club (Manchester City), and with the relative people, and we believe that we've made the right decision and I think everyone's in support of the situation."

There has been speculation that Fowler has returned to Australia to support her partner, Nathan Cleary, which Football Australia has not confirmed.

The Penrith rugby league star required emergency surgery after suffering a career-threatening badly broken leg in the Panthers' NRL preliminary final loss in late September.

Players opting out of windows for personal reasons is not rare, especially given the intense schedules of club and international football.

"At the end of the day, we're all human. You can't always base your life around football," Australian goalkeeper Mackenzie Arnold said.

"I have never personally been in that experience, so I don't really know how to put it into words.

"But I would say if I had that situation that I felt the need to go home and I asked the coach for that and I had full trust in him that he was going to give me that permission — then of course, it's important.

"But I think the the bottom line is, at the end of the day we're all human, so if we need to make that decision, then that's what we need to go with."

The Matildas are without three of their best creative outlets — Fowler, Kyra Cooney-Cross and Katrina Gorry — for this window.

But Montemurro backed Australia's "very, very talented" midfield depth.

Montemurro name-dropped Vittsjo gun Dani Galic, Nottingham Forest midfielder Alana Murphy and uncapped Valerenga playmaker Hana Lowry.

"They're names I want you to remember, because I really do believe that they're going to be the next generation of midfielders," he said.

World.title: Police search warrants for former prince Andrew were unlawful, judge rules
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

A British judge has ruled in favour of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in a dispute over police searches of his homes earlier this year when they arrested the former prince on suspicion of misconduct due to his ties to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The decision is a significant victory for the former prince nine months after his arrest made global headlines, and it raises questions over the evidenced gathered and whether he may ever be charged.

The former prince, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. AP

The judge said on Thursday in London – about 12.30am on Friday AEST – that the Thames Valley Police had relied on the wrong law when seeking approval from the courts for the search warrants days before the raids in February.

The police are seeking to ensure they can keep the evidence they gathered on the day in order to support their investigation, arguing that they are still pursuing the case and want more witnesses to come forward.

World.title: Russian bomb kills 33 civilians in Ukraine, as Rubio warns of ‘dangerous’ stalemate
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Russian bomb kills 33 civilians in Ukraine, as Rubio warns of ‘dangerous’ stalemate Updated October 9, 2026 — 12:01am ,first published 10:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A Russian bomb attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people, with authorities describing it as a targeted strike on civilians in the key stronghold sought by Moscow. Another 18 people were wounded in one of the largest single attacks this year, which took place on a street where police said two city buses were operating at the time of the strike. President Volodymyr Zelensky described it as a bus stop. A bus burns following a Russian air strike in the city of Kramatorsk. Press service of the National Police of Ukraine Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. “For them (the Russians), a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app.



There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack. Russia denies targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets during its full-scale invasion that began in February 2022. Hours after the news of the bombing, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the conflict was at a “dangerous stalemate”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made the comments during a joint press conference with Portugal’s Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel on in Lisbon on Thursday. Mark Schiefelbein/POOL AP via AP “We’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war that is permanent, enduring, and fair,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Portugal. He added that the United States would continue to try to facilitate a settlement to end the conflict.



Moscow’s forces have stepped up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine’s “fortress belt”, local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk region. Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest of the region still under its control before it stops fighting, which Kyiv refuses to do. The pace of Moscow’s battlefield gains in the region has significantly slowed this year. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Russian drones attack Kyiv as Merz meets Zelensky Filashkin said he had ordered city authorities in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, another key fortress-belt city, to halt public transport, saying “we have no right to risk” citizens’ lives. Thursday’s attack came a day after dozens were killed in a massive Russian air attack across Ukraine, primarily targeting the country’s power grid.



Separately on Thursday, three people were killed and 14 wounded in morning drone strikes on the capital Kyiv, said Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Russian forces have unleashed frequent waves of attacks on Kyiv amid a shortage of Ukrainian air defences. World.title: Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in literature
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature prizes Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in literature Jill Lawless , Hillel Italie and Kostya Manenkov Updated October 8, 2026 — 11:01pm ,first published 10:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize in literature for playful, genre-blending works that fuse the classical and the modern. Toronto-born Carson, 76, draws on themes and stories from ancient Greek and Roman literature for works that often blend elements of poetry, essay and fiction. Canadian poet Anne Carson, pictured in 2015. Pontus Lundahl/TT News Agency via AP Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said the author was in Iceland “listening to the wind” when the academy reached her to notify her of the win. “She was very taken by surprise,” Carlberg said on Thursday.



Carson’s books include Eros the Bittersweet, a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, verse novel Autobiography of Red, Men in the Off Hours, a collection of poetry and prose that won Canada’s Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001 and Norma Jeane Baker of Troy, which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy. Permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, announces Canadian writer Anne Carson as the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. Christine Olsson/TT News Agency via AP She also has translated works of classical Greek literature that, the Swedish Academy said, “may be regarded as independent works in their own right”. They include If Not, Winter, based on poem fragments by Sappho, Sophocles’ tragic plays Electra and Antigone and Euripides’s Bakkhai. “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the literature committee. Olsson added that Carson’s juxtaposition of influences ranging from the ancient Greeks to John Keats, Virginia Woolf and Emily Brontë “leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and art forms”.



Anne Carson’s Red Doc>. Soeren Stache/DPA via AP Carson has taught classics at several North American universities and has lived in Iceland, where she and her husband, Robert Currie, were granted citizenship in 2022. She also has drawn on her own life for works such as Nox, which was published in 2010 and dealt with the decades-long absence and then death of her brother Michael. Olsson called it “a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother”. It also includes Carson’s translation of an elegy by the Roman poet Catullus for his own brother. Among her most recent work is, Wrong Norma, a 2024 wide-ranging collection of pieces from publications including The Paris Review and The New Yorker, accompanied by Carson’s hand-drawn illustrations. Also that year, Carson wrote in the London Review of Books about being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. She said, “a symptom particularly mortifying to me was that my handwriting disintegrated”.



“Hard to describe or explain the shame of bad handwriting,” she said. “Bad handwriting is ugly. Also it is inauthentic. In the sense it is not you.” The prize was announced by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm. The Associated Press’ efforts to reach Carson’s literary agent, Nicole Aragi, were not immediately successful. Last year, Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai, whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humour, won the Nobel Prize in literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror.” Related Article Review Short stories, dogs and Judith Lucy: 10 new books our critics recommend Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognised a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognised two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.



This week ends with Friday’s peace prize. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.72 million). AP What else is happening in the book world? Magda Szubanski’s memoir is full of tender truths
