World.title: ‘Absolutely reprehensible’: AFP chief reveals her top overseas target
World.content:
NationalCrime ‘Absolutely reprehensible’: AFP chief reveals her top overseas target Riley Walter October 8, 2026 — 9:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Australian Federal Police will expand its overseas operations into more countries to target offshore organised crime figures orchestrating violence in Australia, as it works to keep pace with evolving criminal methods being enhanced by artificial intelligence and emerging technology. AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett will this month travel to Japan to meet with law enforcement counterparts as part of efforts to strengthen diplomatic ties with the country – a key partnership for Australia in the Pacific and South-East Asia. Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett says Sayit Erhan Akca, the orchestrator of a hoax terror plot, is her top offshore target. James Brickwood In a wide-ranging interview marking a year since her appointment as the AFP’s first female commissioner, Barrett identified Sayit Erhan Akca, the alleged orchestrator of a hoax terror plot purportedly targeting Sydney’s Jewish community, as the agency’s number one overseas target. “He still remains a high-value target for me,” Barrett told this masthead.



The discovery of an explosives-laden caravan in Dural, on Sydney’s north-western fringe, last January sparked fears of a potential attack on the Jewish community amid increased antisemitic attacks across the city. Notes found in the caravan led authorities to believe that several locations in Sydney, including the Great Synagogue, would be targeted. Sayit Erhan Akca says he offered authorities the explosives in exchange for a reduced sentence and for his bail to be reinstated if he returned to Australia. Authorities believe Akca, who has been living in the Middle East and Asia since fleeing Australia on drug importation charges in mid-2023, orchestrated the plot in an attempt to leverage a return to the country. Akca previously told the ABC that he offered the cache of explosives to authorities in exchange for a reduced sentence and for his bail to be reinstated if he returned to Australia. “What he did in terms of taking advantage of a very fearful, vulnerable, wounded Jewish community at that time ... and using that and praying on that, I mean, that’s absolutely reprehensible,” Barrett said.



“So he is absolutely one of my targets.” Related Article Exclusive

Crime How Australia’s underworld is weaponising AI for drug imports Barrett said a major focus in the next 12 months was expanding the AFP’s global operations, including deploying more officers overseas to disrupt organised crime networks targeting Australia. “How do we intervene earlier? That is much cheaper for us. It’s much quicker for us, and it’s much safer for us as a country to do it that way,” she said. Targeting offshore criminal ringleaders orchestrating violent conflicts in Australia has become increasingly challenging for authorities, who are unable to apprehend high-value targets living in foreign jurisdictions beyond the reach of Australian law enforcement agencies.



One of Barrett’s top priorities in the year ahead is leveraging relationships with foreign partners to stymie the influence of organised crime figures operating in countries where extradition to Australia is unlikely, including that of exiled tobacco kingpin Kazem Hamad, who was this year sentenced to life imprisonment in his home country of Iraq. “We have capabilities that no other law enforcement agency has. We have reach, we have access that no other law enforcement agency has,” Barrett said. Barrett says the AFP will work to disrupt offshore criminal networks, like in the case of exiled tobacco kingpin Kazem Hamad, who was jailed in Iraq this year. Australian Federal Police “This is where I’ve really challenged the workforce today. We need to really lift in terms of how we are using those unique capabilities that we have.” Several of the AFP and NSW Police’s highest priority targets are believed to be living in the Middle East, South-East Asia and Europe, including members of Sydney’s Alameddine crime family, and rival group the Coconut Cartel.



As the AFP explores where its resources are best utilised, Barrett said Japan’s strategic positioning in South-East Asia and the Pacific offered an opportunity for Canberra and Tokyo to combine efforts to impact crime in the regions. Related Article Exclusive

Crime Swedish extremism network member jailed for abuse of Australian girl “That goes beyond operational law enforcement, talking regional stability and regional security and sovereignty,” Barrett said. The Pacific has emerged as a key focus for the AFP during the first year of Barrett’s tenure as the region is increasingly targeted by organised crime networks trafficking illicit drugs into Australia via vulnerable island nations. Barrett wanted the AFP to adopt an aggressive, front-foot approach to defending Australia and its future from domestic and global security threats, she said.



Another of Barrett’s key focuses is protecting children from exploitation, abuse and radicalisation, including by sadistic online networks increasingly targeting young Australians. “We’re just seeing a growing caseload of young victims and perpetrators in that tech-enabled crime space,” she said. Barrett raised concerns about research findings from the Australian Cybercrime Observatory, published in July, that found young victims of online sexual exploitation were more likely to seek help from artificial intelligence platforms than authorities. “Parents and caregivers need to know that this is happening and I urge them to have conversations with their children about coming forward to a trusted adult, including law enforcement, if they are being sexually exploited online, so the appropriate help and support can be provided,” she said. Combatting organised crime networks’ use of emerging technologies and artificial intelligence to streamline and upscale their drug trafficking operations is another challenge facing authorities, Barrett said.



“Tech-enabled crime used to be sort of constrained to a few crime types,” Barrett said. “Now everything we investigate, there is a tech aspect to it.” The AFP’s traditional operating method – which Barrett described as siloed – is no longer the best practice to investigate and disrupt organised crime, she said. Increasingly blurred lines between criminal groups now collaborating to orchestrate large-scale drug imports required the agency to restructure its approach to international organised crime. “We need to be more dynamic in how we do that,” Barrett said. “We need to continue to evolve.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Queensland Theatre keeps an eye on the box office with stars, beloved stories – and a TV tie-in
World.content:
NationalQueenslandEntertainment Queensland Theatre keeps an eye on the box office with stars, beloved stories – and a TV tie-in Nick Dent October 8, 2026 — 9:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In times of financial stress, it seems like everybody’s jumping into bed with everyone else. I’m speaking metaphorically about theatre companies, of course. Queensland Theatre has announced its 2027 season of eight mainstage plays, and five of them are co-productions – “co-pros” – with other Australian theatre organisations. Queensland Theatre’s 2027 Christmas would-be blockbuster is an adaptation of Little Women. Queensland Theatre It’s no secret the arts are in a perilous place, with major musicals cancelling their tours mid-run and companies making cuts to claw back eye-watering losses, so cost sharing via co-production is naturally an attractive option.



The downside is fewer shows and the relative lack of employment for casts and crews. But as Queensland Theatre artistic director Daniel Evans points out, his season offers big shows – only one of which has a cast smaller than seven. “I’m swinging big, and it feels like Queensland Theatre Company is now punching into a larger space and establishing ourselves, not just for Brisbane, but also for Queensland, and joining that national conversation,” he says. Queensland Theatre artistic director Daniel Evans. Georgia Haupt Evans’ second season also continues his policy of “event theatre” – familiar titles to draw audiences who may prefer to know what they are getting. He says he always imagines how potential audience members would react to hearing about the shows in their feeds.



“Would that be enough to pull you away from your scrolling to go, ‘I’m gonna put pants on, come out into the world, put my money down, and be part of that’?” In times past a season featuring a top Broadway musical, a beloved Shakespeare and an adaptation of a popular novel might be considered pretty commercial for a state theatre company. QT’s 2027 has all that and more: a murder mystery featuring a popular TV sleuth; a Homeric legend perfectly timed after The Odyssey’s box office triumph; and a hit rock’n’roll play clearly based on the making of Fleetwood Mac’s album Rumours. Queensland Theatre 2027 season breakdown An Iliad Feb-Mar



A Sydney Theatre Company co-production starring David Wenham, An Iliad sold out its run at the Wharf Theatres earlier this year and scored five-star reviews. “I thought it’d be big news that he’s coming to Brisbane, but a lot of people see him in the New Farm Coles,” Evans quips about Brisbane resident Wenham. “You’re watching an actor at the height of their powers. Imagine the Trojan War being told to you by this brilliant poet-cum-Aussie larrikin, who breaks the fourth wall and brings you on this incredible journey.” Brisbane local David Wenham unleashes his full power in An Iliad. Daniel Boud Romeo & Juliet Feb-Mar



The star-crossed lovers get re-imagined with song, movement and First Nations storytelling. “The Capulets and the Montagues are transposed into two warring tribes,” Evans says. “One is of the sky, one is of the earth, and their conflict comes around because of a broken song circle. “High schools are studying Shakespeare and recontextualised myths, and we’re hoping that this really pulls in some educational audiences.” Miss Fisher’s Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair Apr-May This co-pro with Sydney Theatre Company and Jones Theatrical Group is having its world premiere in Brisbane.



Amber McMahon is Phryne Fisher in the stage reboot of the TV series from the show’s original writer, Deb Cox, based on Kerry Greenwood’s novels. Miss Fisher’s Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair is a co-production of Queensland Theatre, Sydney Theatre Company and Jones Theatrical Group. “It’s sort of Knives Out on the ocean, meets Downton Abbey via The Great Gatsby and it’s very, very fun,” Evans says. Stereophonic May-Jun In 1976, a British-American band labours in the studio to match the smash success of their first album. If you ever thought the making of Fleetwood Mac’s Rumours would make a good fictional narrative, then this is it.



QT has teamed up with both Melbourne Theatre Company and Sydney’s Belvoir St Theatre for a play Evans says moves like “an Aaron Sorkin choreographed dance”. Geraldine Hakewill (left), and Alex Malone in Stereophonic, which plays in both Melbourne and Sydney before Brisbane. Daniel Boud “Everyone breaks up, makes up, they have complete nervous breakdowns, fall into addiction, and all the way through you hope against hope that they’re going to actually land the album.” Counting and Cracking May-Jun Queensland Theatre and Belvoir St Theatre have joined forces with Brisbane Powerhouse to remount this landmark Australian play, which travels to the West End and New York after playing at the Powerhouse.



“It’s massive: 21 people on stage, a sweeping saga that goes across many generations,” Evans says. “It moves between contemporary Sydney and past events in Sri Lanka, and so what you’re watching is a story of a family reconciling who they are with who they were.” Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street Jul-Aug With another Queensland Theatre-Opera Queensland co-production, Into the Woods, about to open at the Glasshouse, Evans is returning to Stephen Sondheim and what many regard as the composer’s dark masterpiece. Andy Conaghan plays the murderous hairstylist, and Naomi Price (Calamity Jane) is his partner in crime, Mrs Lovett. “Naomi was over the moon, it’s one of her dream roles. She is thrilled, as you can imagine, to be going from the wild west to a deliciously deviant baker.”



My Roman Empire Oct Related Article Performing arts Waitress is gone, Beetlejuice too. Where is the next Hamilton? The sole new Queensland work in the season is the winner of the Queensland Premier’s Drama Award from playwright Alberto di Troia. A queer Australian writer travels to his ancestral village in Italy to scatter his father’s ashes, only to find the family history he imagined is complicated. “It’s this funny, dark and sublime take on Eat, Pray, Love,” Evans says.



“Alberto’s playwriting voice is somewhere between Mike White from The White Lotus, it has that searing political bite, mixed with the poetry of Christos Tsiolkas.” Little Women Nov Louisa May Alcott’s novel of sisterhood and self-actualisation gets a new stage adaptation with Courtney Cavallaro (A Few Good Men) as Jo. “When I tell people that we’re doing it, women say, ‘I’m a Jo March, I wanted to cut my hair off because I was such a Jo.’ “I’m hoping that audiences embrace it so it becomes our seasonal Christmas classic. Something that grandmas can bring their granddaughters to.” Get alerts on significant breaking news as it happens.

Peter Riley of Penrith asked AI (C8): “‘What’s the best way to get published in Column 8? A cash bribe? Or holding Granny’s dog to ransom?’ AI replied: ‘Neither! The gatekeepers of The SMH’s legendary Column 8 are notoriously resistant to both financial corruption and canine hostage situations. The only currency they accept is wit, whimsy, and a sharp eye for the absurdities of daily life. Aside from the fact that dognapping, extortion and bribery are entirely illegal, Granny does not negotiate with terrorists. You are much better off trying the legal route’.”

“I can’t see what all the worry is about AI getting rid of humanity,” opines Peter Berman of Balgowlah. “When the inevitable software glitch happens, and it needs to be turned off and on again, we can just leave it off.”

“I’d gladly trade John Turnell’s bogong moths and Dave Pyett’s koel (C8) for our channel-billed cuckoo, which has a squawk likened to that of a prehistoric dinosaur or a pterodactyl,” says Peter Miniutti of Ashbury. “I’m not sure who has been around long enough to make that comparison unless AI is older than we think.”

“With the recent C8 emphasis on nature, I wish to add another discovery,” offers Warren Finnan of West Ryde. “While working in the backyard, I was whistling the theme song to the TV show, Bewitched, and a nearby koel answered back by warbling the same first four notes. Try it yourself. You might get Samantha back!”

“I loved the mention of ‘couth’ (C8) by Messrs Reid and Polgaze,” says Marilyn Irons of Narrabeen. “I can remember my father saying ‘That’s very couth of you’, and it’s stuck with me. Susie Dent in one of her books mentions a character as looking ‘shevelled’. Why some words stick and some fall out of favour is a fascinating subject.”

World.title: Cross River Rail staff left ‘abandoned’ despite reporting union threats
World.content:
NationalQueenslandConstruction Cross River Rail staff left ‘abandoned’ despite reporting union threats Matt Dennien October 8, 2026 — 8:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Management figures on Queensland’s largest passenger rail project have described being abandoned by their bosses after flagging threats received during a 2023 CFMEU-led blockade of work sites, in which interstate muscle and weapons were said to be present. One of the Cross River Rail contractor staff who gave evidence to the state inquiry in the union and construction sector on Thursday also told of a direction from higher-ups to not call police amid the days-long standoff sparked by a serious workplace injury. The Commission of Inquiry has spent this week probing the multibillion-dollar state taxpayer funded project – bringing a new inner-city rail line in-part tunnelled beneath the Brisbane River – largely focused on an infamous brawl during an earlier blockade. An aerial view of construction at the Northern Tunnel Portal of the Cross River Rail project at Normanby late last year. Cross River Rail Delivery Authority Middle-management figures within the CPB Contractors joint venture delivering the $9.83 billion project were among those called to give evidence on Thursday, and detailed their experience of the aftermath of a serious fall by a worker at the Boggo Road station site.



This incident on July 25, 2023, resulted in all work being halted across the project. CFMEU-led blockades of main site access points, including locking gates and telling workers arriving to go home, began from the morning of July 26. A direction later the following day was given to site-based managers to stop work until further consultation on July 27, the then electrical superintendent for the northern tunnel section, Shane Rasmussen, said. Peter Bennett, a senior electrical supervisor with CPB joint venture partner UGL at the time of the 2023 incident, giving evidence on Thursday. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry That night, Rasmussen told the inquiry he was confronted by a group of about 10 figures, including CFMEU organiser Matthew Vonhoff – who told him they knew how Rasmussen travelled to work and would “come and get me”. Others told of hearing similar threats. On July 28, Rasmussen and colleagues who gave evidence on Thursday described an “escalation” in the union blockade of the sites with about 35 people positioned at the front gate of the northern tunnel portal site, some of whom wore balaclavas, with vehicles blocking their entry.



Site office-based staff including Rasmussen and some of those colleagues who entered via a back gate were said to have had rocks thrown at their vehicles and the building. Once there, he said he called an Australian Workers’ Union delegate, Jayce Emmerton. Related Article Updated

Construction Contractors accused of failing to prevent CFMEU ‘army’ from attending brawl site Emmerton is said to have told Rasmussen, and other colleagues including senior electrical supervisor Peter Bennett, that he had been threatened and told to leave when he attempted to enter, by people carrying weapons including a machete, baseball bats, and at least one firearm. None of those appearing on Thursday said they saw a gun, but took Emmerton’s remarks seriously. Bennett said he had been told by a shaken Emmerton he knew some of the group to be “part of a bikie group”, later described as Comanchero members from Victoria and Gold Coast-based members of another organisation. Bennett said he then suggested they call police before Jamey Purvis, the project’s southern area manager filling-in for the northern area during that time, called more senior figures and ultimately made the call to evacuate the site.



Purvis, who also gave evidence on Thursday, said he had heard from multiple people that some of the men were “mercenaries” who had come from Victoria. He said he was told “not to call the police … a couple of days prior” by a human resources director named Chris Butler. Related Article Queensland government How the CFMEU tried to, and did, influence Qld’s biggest rail project Work did not resume on any Cross River Rail site until 31 July, after the culmination of the “safety reset” meetings with senior project figures and unions, in which more than a dozen CFMEU delegates were agreed to be installed. Rasmussen and Bennett were then directed to work from the project’s Milton office, with no explanation. Bennett wrote an email, tendered as part of his written statement, on August 1 outlining the incident in writing to Purvis, who escalated the matter to Butler. Neither ever returned to the northern site, and Rasmussen worked from home until his contract was ended in January last year. Both described seeking ongoing effects on their mental health and seeking psychiatric support.



Bennett said he was told informally that the removal of the pair and their colleague, Peter Cullen – who gave separate evidence of public statements made about him by the union which had led him to launch defamation action until CPB support ceased – was “one of the stipulations of the reset”. Bennett and Rasmussen were reluctant to make formal complaints without approval or direction from management, Bennett said. The pair, while working at Milton, did report the matter to Brisbane detectives and were told it was being investigated by outlaw motorcycle gang-focused “Taskforce Mayima”. The unit was “dealing with related matters”, the pair were told. They provided written material for a formal record but did not ask police to commence an investigation because they were “uncertain about the support available from our employers and the project”. “I’ve worked for CPB on some other projects, and I’ve worked for some quite large tier one infrastructure companies, and this is the first time I’ve ever seen something that was so, so inept of responsibility, and I still can’t believe it,” Bennett told the inquiry. “It’s disgusting.” Commissioner Stuart Wood, while noting relevant CPB figures would be given an “opportunity to be heard on any final findings”, said it seemed extraordinary that the trio were “abandoned” – a word which both Cullen and Bennett also used to describe the situation.



Wood closed the hearing by suggesting he would write an interim report this month, to make a decision on the inquiry’s proposed reintroduction of a building and construction code and regulator. A sixteenth block of public hearings by the now-$95 million inquiry will resume on October 27. The inquiry is due to report to government by December 2027. A British judge has ruled in favour of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in a dispute over police searches of his homes earlier this year when they arrested the former prince on suspicion of misconduct due to his ties to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The decision is a significant victory for the former prince nine months after his arrest made global headlines, and it raises questions over the evidenced gathered and whether he may ever be charged.

The former prince, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. AP

The judge said on Thursday in London – about 12.30am on Friday AEST – that the Thames Valley Police had relied on the wrong law when seeking approval from the courts for the search warrants days before the raids in February.

The police are seeking to ensure they can keep the evidence they gathered on the day in order to support their investigation, arguing that they are still pursuing the case and want more witnesses to come forward.

World.title: Russian bomb kills 33 civilians in Ukraine, as Rubio warns of ‘dangerous’ stalemate
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Russian bomb kills 33 civilians in Ukraine, as Rubio warns of ‘dangerous’ stalemate Updated October 9, 2026 — 12:01am ,first published 10:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A Russian bomb attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people, with authorities describing it as a targeted strike on civilians in the key stronghold sought by Moscow. Another 18 people were wounded in one of the largest single attacks this year, which took place on a street where police said two city buses were operating at the time of the strike. President Volodymyr Zelensky described it as a bus stop. A bus burns following a Russian air strike in the city of Kramatorsk. Press service of the National Police of Ukraine Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. “For them (the Russians), a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app.



There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack. Russia denies targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets during its full-scale invasion that began in February 2022. Hours after the news of the bombing, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the conflict was at a “dangerous stalemate”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made the comments during a joint press conference with Portugal’s Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel on in Lisbon on Thursday. Mark Schiefelbein/POOL AP via AP “We’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war that is permanent, enduring, and fair,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Portugal. He added that the United States would continue to try to facilitate a settlement to end the conflict.



Moscow’s forces have stepped up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine’s “fortress belt”, local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk region. Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest of the region still under its control before it stops fighting, which Kyiv refuses to do. The pace of Moscow’s battlefield gains in the region has significantly slowed this year. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Russian drones attack Kyiv as Merz meets Zelensky Filashkin said he had ordered city authorities in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, another key fortress-belt city, to halt public transport, saying “we have no right to risk” citizens’ lives. Thursday’s attack came a day after dozens were killed in a massive Russian air attack across Ukraine, primarily targeting the country’s power grid.



Separately on Thursday, three people were killed and 14 wounded in morning drone strikes on the capital Kyiv, said Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Russian forces have unleashed frequent waves of attacks on Kyiv amid a shortage of Ukrainian air defences. World.title: Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in literature
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature prizes Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in literature Jill Lawless , Hillel Italie and Kostya Manenkov Updated October 8, 2026 — 11:01pm ,first published 10:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize in literature for playful, genre-blending works that fuse the classical and the modern. Toronto-born Carson, 76, draws on themes and stories from ancient Greek and Roman literature for works that often blend elements of poetry, essay and fiction. Canadian poet Anne Carson, pictured in 2015. Pontus Lundahl/TT News Agency via AP Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said the author was in Iceland “listening to the wind” when the academy reached her to notify her of the win. “She was very taken by surprise,” Carlberg said on Thursday.



Carson’s books include Eros the Bittersweet, a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, verse novel Autobiography of Red, Men in the Off Hours, a collection of poetry and prose that won Canada’s Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001 and Norma Jeane Baker of Troy, which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy. Permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, announces Canadian writer Anne Carson as the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. Christine Olsson/TT News Agency via AP She also has translated works of classical Greek literature that, the Swedish Academy said, “may be regarded as independent works in their own right”. They include If Not, Winter, based on poem fragments by Sappho, Sophocles’ tragic plays Electra and Antigone and Euripides’s Bakkhai. “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the literature committee. Olsson added that Carson’s juxtaposition of influences ranging from the ancient Greeks to John Keats, Virginia Woolf and Emily Brontë “leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and art forms”.



Anne Carson’s Red Doc>. Soeren Stache/DPA via AP Carson has taught classics at several North American universities and has lived in Iceland, where she and her husband, Robert Currie, were granted citizenship in 2022. She also has drawn on her own life for works such as Nox, which was published in 2010 and dealt with the decades-long absence and then death of her brother Michael. Olsson called it “a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother”. It also includes Carson’s translation of an elegy by the Roman poet Catullus for his own brother. Among her most recent work is, Wrong Norma, a 2024 wide-ranging collection of pieces from publications including The Paris Review and The New Yorker, accompanied by Carson’s hand-drawn illustrations. Also that year, Carson wrote in the London Review of Books about being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. She said, “a symptom particularly mortifying to me was that my handwriting disintegrated”.



“Hard to describe or explain the shame of bad handwriting,” she said. “Bad handwriting is ugly. Also it is inauthentic. In the sense it is not you.” The prize was announced by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm. The Associated Press’ efforts to reach Carson’s literary agent, Nicole Aragi, were not immediately successful. Last year, Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai, whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humour, won the Nobel Prize in literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror.” Related Article Review Short stories, dogs and Judith Lucy: 10 new books our critics recommend Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognised a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognised two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.



This week ends with Friday’s peace prize. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.72 million). AP What else is happening in the book world? Magda Szubanski’s memoir is full of tender truths

World.title: ‘Absolutely reprehensible’: AFP chief reveals her top overseas target
World.content:
NationalCrime ‘Absolutely reprehensible’: AFP chief reveals her top overseas target Riley Walter October 8, 2026 — 9:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Australian Federal Police will expand its overseas operations into more countries to target offshore organised crime figures orchestrating violence in Australia, as it works to keep pace with evolving criminal methods being enhanced by artificial intelligence and emerging technology. AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett will this month travel to Japan to meet with law enforcement counterparts as part of efforts to strengthen diplomatic ties with the country – a key partnership for Australia in the Pacific and South-East Asia. Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett says Sayit Erhan Akca, the orchestrator of a hoax terror plot, is her top offshore target. James Brickwood In a wide-ranging interview marking a year since her appointment as the AFP’s first female commissioner, Barrett identified Sayit Erhan Akca, the alleged orchestrator of a hoax terror plot purportedly targeting Sydney’s Jewish community, as the agency’s number one overseas target. “He still remains a high-value target for me,” Barrett told this masthead.



The discovery of an explosives-laden caravan in Dural, on Sydney’s north-western fringe, last January sparked fears of a potential attack on the Jewish community amid increased antisemitic attacks across the city. Notes found in the caravan led authorities to believe that several locations in Sydney, including the Great Synagogue, would be targeted. Sayit Erhan Akca says he offered authorities the explosives in exchange for a reduced sentence and for his bail to be reinstated if he returned to Australia. Authorities believe Akca, who has been living in the Middle East and Asia since fleeing Australia on drug importation charges in mid-2023, orchestrated the plot in an attempt to leverage a return to the country. Akca previously told the ABC that he offered the cache of explosives to authorities in exchange for a reduced sentence and for his bail to be reinstated if he returned to Australia. “What he did in terms of taking advantage of a very fearful, vulnerable, wounded Jewish community at that time ... and using that and praying on that, I mean, that’s absolutely reprehensible,” Barrett said.



“So he is absolutely one of my targets.” Related Article Exclusive

Crime How Australia’s underworld is weaponising AI for drug imports Barrett said a major focus in the next 12 months was expanding the AFP’s global operations, including deploying more officers overseas to disrupt organised crime networks targeting Australia. “How do we intervene earlier? That is much cheaper for us. It’s much quicker for us, and it’s much safer for us as a country to do it that way,” she said. Targeting offshore criminal ringleaders orchestrating violent conflicts in Australia has become increasingly challenging for authorities, who are unable to apprehend high-value targets living in foreign jurisdictions beyond the reach of Australian law enforcement agencies.



One of Barrett’s top priorities in the year ahead is leveraging relationships with foreign partners to stymie the influence of organised crime figures operating in countries where extradition to Australia is unlikely, including that of exiled tobacco kingpin Kazem Hamad, who was this year sentenced to life imprisonment in his home country of Iraq. “We have capabilities that no other law enforcement agency has. We have reach, we have access that no other law enforcement agency has,” Barrett said. Barrett says the AFP will work to disrupt offshore criminal networks, like in the case of exiled tobacco kingpin Kazem Hamad, who was jailed in Iraq this year. Australian Federal Police “This is where I’ve really challenged the workforce today. We need to really lift in terms of how we are using those unique capabilities that we have.” Several of the AFP and NSW Police’s highest priority targets are believed to be living in the Middle East, South-East Asia and Europe, including members of Sydney’s Alameddine crime family, and rival group the Coconut Cartel.



As the AFP explores where its resources are best utilised, Barrett said Japan’s strategic positioning in South-East Asia and the Pacific offered an opportunity for Canberra and Tokyo to combine efforts to impact crime in the regions. Related Article Exclusive

Crime Swedish extremism network member jailed for abuse of Australian girl “That goes beyond operational law enforcement, talking regional stability and regional security and sovereignty,” Barrett said. The Pacific has emerged as a key focus for the AFP during the first year of Barrett’s tenure as the region is increasingly targeted by organised crime networks trafficking illicit drugs into Australia via vulnerable island nations. Barrett wanted the AFP to adopt an aggressive, front-foot approach to defending Australia and its future from domestic and global security threats, she said.



Another of Barrett’s key focuses is protecting children from exploitation, abuse and radicalisation, including by sadistic online networks increasingly targeting young Australians. “We’re just seeing a growing caseload of young victims and perpetrators in that tech-enabled crime space,” she said. Barrett raised concerns about research findings from the Australian Cybercrime Observatory, published in July, that found young victims of online sexual exploitation were more likely to seek help from artificial intelligence platforms than authorities. “Parents and caregivers need to know that this is happening and I urge them to have conversations with their children about coming forward to a trusted adult, including law enforcement, if they are being sexually exploited online, so the appropriate help and support can be provided,” she said. Combatting organised crime networks’ use of emerging technologies and artificial intelligence to streamline and upscale their drug trafficking operations is another challenge facing authorities, Barrett said.



“Tech-enabled crime used to be sort of constrained to a few crime types,” Barrett said. “Now everything we investigate, there is a tech aspect to it.” The AFP’s traditional operating method – which Barrett described as siloed – is no longer the best practice to investigate and disrupt organised crime, she said. Increasingly blurred lines between criminal groups now collaborating to orchestrate large-scale drug imports required the agency to restructure its approach to international organised crime. “We need to be more dynamic in how we do that,” Barrett said. “We need to continue to evolve.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Queensland Theatre keeps an eye on the box office with stars, beloved stories – and a TV tie-in
World.content:
NationalQueenslandEntertainment Queensland Theatre keeps an eye on the box office with stars, beloved stories – and a TV tie-in Nick Dent October 8, 2026 — 9:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In times of financial stress, it seems like everybody’s jumping into bed with everyone else. I’m speaking metaphorically about theatre companies, of course. Queensland Theatre has announced its 2027 season of eight mainstage plays, and five of them are co-productions – “co-pros” – with other Australian theatre organisations. Queensland Theatre’s 2027 Christmas would-be blockbuster is an adaptation of Little Women. Queensland Theatre It’s no secret the arts are in a perilous place, with major musicals cancelling their tours mid-run and companies making cuts to claw back eye-watering losses, so cost sharing via co-production is naturally an attractive option.



The downside is fewer shows and the relative lack of employment for casts and crews. But as Queensland Theatre artistic director Daniel Evans points out, his season offers big shows – only one of which has a cast smaller than seven. “I’m swinging big, and it feels like Queensland Theatre Company is now punching into a larger space and establishing ourselves, not just for Brisbane, but also for Queensland, and joining that national conversation,” he says. Queensland Theatre artistic director Daniel Evans. Georgia Haupt Evans’ second season also continues his policy of “event theatre” – familiar titles to draw audiences who may prefer to know what they are getting. He says he always imagines how potential audience members would react to hearing about the shows in their feeds.



“Would that be enough to pull you away from your scrolling to go, ‘I’m gonna put pants on, come out into the world, put my money down, and be part of that’?” In times past a season featuring a top Broadway musical, a beloved Shakespeare and an adaptation of a popular novel might be considered pretty commercial for a state theatre company. QT’s 2027 has all that and more: a murder mystery featuring a popular TV sleuth; a Homeric legend perfectly timed after The Odyssey’s box office triumph; and a hit rock’n’roll play clearly based on the making of Fleetwood Mac’s album Rumours. Queensland Theatre 2027 season breakdown An Iliad Feb-Mar



A Sydney Theatre Company co-production starring David Wenham, An Iliad sold out its run at the Wharf Theatres earlier this year and scored five-star reviews. “I thought it’d be big news that he’s coming to Brisbane, but a lot of people see him in the New Farm Coles,” Evans quips about Brisbane resident Wenham. “You’re watching an actor at the height of their powers. Imagine the Trojan War being told to you by this brilliant poet-cum-Aussie larrikin, who breaks the fourth wall and brings you on this incredible journey.” Brisbane local David Wenham unleashes his full power in An Iliad. Daniel Boud Romeo & Juliet Feb-Mar



The star-crossed lovers get re-imagined with song, movement and First Nations storytelling. “The Capulets and the Montagues are transposed into two warring tribes,” Evans says. “One is of the sky, one is of the earth, and their conflict comes around because of a broken song circle. “High schools are studying Shakespeare and recontextualised myths, and we’re hoping that this really pulls in some educational audiences.” Miss Fisher’s Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair Apr-May This co-pro with Sydney Theatre Company and Jones Theatrical Group is having its world premiere in Brisbane.



Amber McMahon is Phryne Fisher in the stage reboot of the TV series from the show’s original writer, Deb Cox, based on Kerry Greenwood’s novels. Miss Fisher’s Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair is a co-production of Queensland Theatre, Sydney Theatre Company and Jones Theatrical Group. “It’s sort of Knives Out on the ocean, meets Downton Abbey via The Great Gatsby and it’s very, very fun,” Evans says. Stereophonic May-Jun In 1976, a British-American band labours in the studio to match the smash success of their first album. If you ever thought the making of Fleetwood Mac’s Rumours would make a good fictional narrative, then this is it.



QT has teamed up with both Melbourne Theatre Company and Sydney’s Belvoir St Theatre for a play Evans says moves like “an Aaron Sorkin choreographed dance”. Geraldine Hakewill (left), and Alex Malone in Stereophonic, which plays in both Melbourne and Sydney before Brisbane. Daniel Boud “Everyone breaks up, makes up, they have complete nervous breakdowns, fall into addiction, and all the way through you hope against hope that they’re going to actually land the album.” Counting and Cracking May-Jun Queensland Theatre and Belvoir St Theatre have joined forces with Brisbane Powerhouse to remount this landmark Australian play, which travels to the West End and New York after playing at the Powerhouse.



“It’s massive: 21 people on stage, a sweeping saga that goes across many generations,” Evans says. “It moves between contemporary Sydney and past events in Sri Lanka, and so what you’re watching is a story of a family reconciling who they are with who they were.” Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street Jul-Aug With another Queensland Theatre-Opera Queensland co-production, Into the Woods, about to open at the Glasshouse, Evans is returning to Stephen Sondheim and what many regard as the composer’s dark masterpiece. Andy Conaghan plays the murderous hairstylist, and Naomi Price (Calamity Jane) is his partner in crime, Mrs Lovett. “Naomi was over the moon, it’s one of her dream roles. She is thrilled, as you can imagine, to be going from the wild west to a deliciously deviant baker.”



My Roman Empire Oct Related Article Performing arts Waitress is gone, Beetlejuice too. Where is the next Hamilton? The sole new Queensland work in the season is the winner of the Queensland Premier’s Drama Award from playwright Alberto di Troia. A queer Australian writer travels to his ancestral village in Italy to scatter his father’s ashes, only to find the family history he imagined is complicated. “It’s this funny, dark and sublime take on Eat, Pray, Love,” Evans says.



“Alberto’s playwriting voice is somewhere between Mike White from The White Lotus, it has that searing political bite, mixed with the poetry of Christos Tsiolkas.” Little Women Nov Louisa May Alcott’s novel of sisterhood and self-actualisation gets a new stage adaptation with Courtney Cavallaro (A Few Good Men) as Jo. “When I tell people that we’re doing it, women say, ‘I’m a Jo March, I wanted to cut my hair off because I was such a Jo.’ “I’m hoping that audiences embrace it so it becomes our seasonal Christmas classic. Something that grandmas can bring their granddaughters to.” Get alerts on significant breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Blackmailers put the bite on
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Peter Riley of Penrith asked AI (C8): “‘What’s the best way to get published in Column 8? A cash bribe? Or holding Granny’s dog to ransom?’ AI replied: ‘Neither! The gatekeepers of The SMH’s legendary Column 8 are notoriously resistant to both financial corruption and canine hostage situations. The only currency they accept is wit, whimsy, and a sharp eye for the absurdities of daily life. Aside from the fact that dognapping, extortion and bribery are entirely illegal, Granny does not negotiate with terrorists. You are much better off trying the legal route’.”

“I can’t see what all the worry is about AI getting rid of humanity,” opines Peter Berman of Balgowlah. “When the inevitable software glitch happens, and it needs to be turned off and on again, we can just leave it off.”

“I’d gladly trade John Turnell’s bogong moths and Dave Pyett’s koel (C8) for our channel-billed cuckoo, which has a squawk likened to that of a prehistoric dinosaur or a pterodactyl,” says Peter Miniutti of Ashbury. “I’m not sure who has been around long enough to make that comparison unless AI is older than we think.”

“With the recent C8 emphasis on nature, I wish to add another discovery,” offers Warren Finnan of West Ryde. “While working in the backyard, I was whistling the theme song to the TV show, Bewitched, and a nearby koel answered back by warbling the same first four notes. Try it yourself. You might get Samantha back!”

“I loved the mention of ‘couth’ (C8) by Messrs Reid and Polgaze,” says Marilyn Irons of Narrabeen. “I can remember my father saying ‘That’s very couth of you’, and it’s stuck with me. Susie Dent in one of her books mentions a character as looking ‘shevelled’. Why some words stick and some fall out of favour is a fascinating subject.”

World.title: Cross River Rail staff left ‘abandoned’ despite reporting union threats
World.content:
NationalQueenslandConstruction Cross River Rail staff left ‘abandoned’ despite reporting union threats Matt Dennien October 8, 2026 — 8:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Management figures on Queensland’s largest passenger rail project have described being abandoned by their bosses after flagging threats received during a 2023 CFMEU-led blockade of work sites, in which interstate muscle and weapons were said to be present. One of the Cross River Rail contractor staff who gave evidence to the state inquiry in the union and construction sector on Thursday also told of a direction from higher-ups to not call police amid the days-long standoff sparked by a serious workplace injury. The Commission of Inquiry has spent this week probing the multibillion-dollar state taxpayer funded project – bringing a new inner-city rail line in-part tunnelled beneath the Brisbane River – largely focused on an infamous brawl during an earlier blockade. An aerial view of construction at the Northern Tunnel Portal of the Cross River Rail project at Normanby late last year. Cross River Rail Delivery Authority Middle-management figures within the CPB Contractors joint venture delivering the $9.83 billion project were among those called to give evidence on Thursday, and detailed their experience of the aftermath of a serious fall by a worker at the Boggo Road station site.



This incident on July 25, 2023, resulted in all work being halted across the project. CFMEU-led blockades of main site access points, including locking gates and telling workers arriving to go home, began from the morning of July 26. A direction later the following day was given to site-based managers to stop work until further consultation on July 27, the then electrical superintendent for the northern tunnel section, Shane Rasmussen, said. Peter Bennett, a senior electrical supervisor with CPB joint venture partner UGL at the time of the 2023 incident, giving evidence on Thursday. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry That night, Rasmussen told the inquiry he was confronted by a group of about 10 figures, including CFMEU organiser Matthew Vonhoff – who told him they knew how Rasmussen travelled to work and would “come and get me”. Others told of hearing similar threats. On July 28, Rasmussen and colleagues who gave evidence on Thursday described an “escalation” in the union blockade of the sites with about 35 people positioned at the front gate of the northern tunnel portal site, some of whom wore balaclavas, with vehicles blocking their entry.



Site office-based staff including Rasmussen and some of those colleagues who entered via a back gate were said to have had rocks thrown at their vehicles and the building. Once there, he said he called an Australian Workers’ Union delegate, Jayce Emmerton. Related Article Updated

Construction Contractors accused of failing to prevent CFMEU ‘army’ from attending brawl site Emmerton is said to have told Rasmussen, and other colleagues including senior electrical supervisor Peter Bennett, that he had been threatened and told to leave when he attempted to enter, by people carrying weapons including a machete, baseball bats, and at least one firearm. None of those appearing on Thursday said they saw a gun, but took Emmerton’s remarks seriously. Bennett said he had been told by a shaken Emmerton he knew some of the group to be “part of a bikie group”, later described as Comanchero members from Victoria and Gold Coast-based members of another organisation. Bennett said he then suggested they call police before Jamey Purvis, the project’s southern area manager filling-in for the northern area during that time, called more senior figures and ultimately made the call to evacuate the site.



Purvis, who also gave evidence on Thursday, said he had heard from multiple people that some of the men were “mercenaries” who had come from Victoria. He said he was told “not to call the police … a couple of days prior” by a human resources director named Chris Butler. Related Article Queensland government How the CFMEU tried to, and did, influence Qld’s biggest rail project Work did not resume on any Cross River Rail site until 31 July, after the culmination of the “safety reset” meetings with senior project figures and unions, in which more than a dozen CFMEU delegates were agreed to be installed. Rasmussen and Bennett were then directed to work from the project’s Milton office, with no explanation. Bennett wrote an email, tendered as part of his written statement, on August 1 outlining the incident in writing to Purvis, who escalated the matter to Butler. Neither ever returned to the northern site, and Rasmussen worked from home until his contract was ended in January last year. Both described seeking ongoing effects on their mental health and seeking psychiatric support.



Bennett said he was told informally that the removal of the pair and their colleague, Peter Cullen – who gave separate evidence of public statements made about him by the union which had led him to launch defamation action until CPB support ceased – was “one of the stipulations of the reset”. Bennett and Rasmussen were reluctant to make formal complaints without approval or direction from management, Bennett said. The pair, while working at Milton, did report the matter to Brisbane detectives and were told it was being investigated by outlaw motorcycle gang-focused “Taskforce Mayima”. The unit was “dealing with related matters”, the pair were told. They provided written material for a formal record but did not ask police to commence an investigation because they were “uncertain about the support available from our employers and the project”. “I’ve worked for CPB on some other projects, and I’ve worked for some quite large tier one infrastructure companies, and this is the first time I’ve ever seen something that was so, so inept of responsibility, and I still can’t believe it,” Bennett told the inquiry. “It’s disgusting.” Commissioner Stuart Wood, while noting relevant CPB figures would be given an “opportunity to be heard on any final findings”, said it seemed extraordinary that the trio were “abandoned” – a word which both Cullen and Bennett also used to describe the situation.



Wood closed the hearing by suggesting he would write an interim report this month, to make a decision on the inquiry’s proposed reintroduction of a building and construction code and regulator. A sixteenth block of public hearings by the now-$95 million inquiry will resume on October 27. The inquiry is due to report to government by December 2027. World.title: RSA audit finds 'significant governance mistakes, failures', but no evidence of fraud
World.content:
A review has found no evidence of fraud or misappropriation by an RSA that used poppy trust funds to prop up its club.

However, the Royal New Zealand RSA's audit of the Papanui Returned Services Assocation's poppy trust did find "significant governance mistakes, failures, and breaches of duty by successive Papanui RSA Executives and Charitable Trust trustees," the RNZRSA said in statement.

Failures the audit identified included "a lack of separation between the association and its trust, inadequate management of conflicts of interest, insufficient documentation and oversight, and the use of trust funds to support the association's operations".

The review found Papanui RSA's welfare trust retained enough money to meet all approved support applications, and no evidence that any veterans who had applied for support and met criteria had been denied support, RNZRSA said.

It also found an outstanding loan owed to the trust by Papanui RSA was repaid after the RSA sold its property.

RNZRSA board chair Rhys Jones told RNZ most RSAs had a separate trust for money that's collected from poppy sales around Anzac Day.

"The money is put into a special trust that's designed to just purely be used for the welfare support of ex-service people in need."

Papanui RSA operated as a hospitality club, including a bar, and went through hard times, Jones said.

RNZRSA board chair Rhys Jones. RNZ

"They borrowed some money from the poppy trust to do some work on the building. When the club decided that they weren't going to continue having a club, they sold the building.

"They were considering dissolving, so someone volunteered to become the president of the club to resolve it, and he uncovered the fact that this loan had gone on but needed to be repaid."

That new president "put his hand up and said 'hey, something's happened here'" and RNZRSA sent in a forensic auditor to "see what the concern was", Jones said.

The review provided an important opportunity to strengthen the management of poppy funds across the RSA network, which should be held in a separate trust to the RSA accounts, he said.

The issue with Papanui RSA was that "the executives on the RSA were also the trustees of the trust, and so they were acting in a manner that it was just another bank account, rather than it being separated".

Jones said there needed to be a clear separation of responsibility.

"The review identified serious shortcomings that must be addressed, but it also found these arose from a lack of knowledge, experience and understanding, not from deliberate wrongdoing."

The wider lessons from the review would be used to strengthen the management of poppy funds nationally, he said.

"Local associations and their trusts are largely governed by volunteers who give their time because they care deeply about their communities. The RNZRSA is committed to giving those volunteers clearer guidance and practical support so they can carry out their responsibilities confidently and protect the public's trust in the RNZRSA and the poppy appeal."
