World.title: One dead after two-vehicle crash on Temuka-Orari Highway
World.content:
One person has died after a two-vehicle crash in Canterbury on Thursday afternoon.

Police said the crash happened on Temuka-Orari Highway, near the intersection with Opuha Street East, at about 3.30pm.

The person died at the scene, despite efforts to save them.

The road was blocked while the Serious Crash Unit examined the scene, but was expected to re-open shortly.

World.title: Parliamentary committee echoes calls for greater oversight of animal welfare system
World.content:
A parliamentary committee has partially endorsed concerns raised by tens of thousands of petitioners, recommending the government investigate improvements to animal welfare oversight.

Earlier this year, a petition with more than 31,500 signatures led by animal welfare organisation SAFE - along with 20 other groups, urged the government to establish an independent Commissioner for Animals, to improve welfare outcomes for farmed, companion and wild animals.

The primary production select committee reviewed the petition, which had been received by Green Party agriculture spokesperson Steve Abel in March.

In a report published by the committee, it said that if a commissioner's role was to be established, there would need to be consideration of a wide variety of possibilities for its structure, duties and functions.

Audio player for " Midday rural news for 8 October 2026 " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/country/1796007%2Fparliamentary-committee-echoes-calls-for-greater-oversight-of-animal-welfare-system

Midday rural news for 8 October 2026 Rural News Download MP3 4m

"The majority of us are not convinced at this time that a Commissioner for Animals, as put forward by the petitioner, is necessarily the best solution to address these concerns," it said.

"We consider that the concerns about system issues that have been raised with us through this petition need to be examined further and addressed.

"To this end, we recommend that the Government investigates how oversight of the animal welfare system could be improved."

It said this could include identifying ways that better provide for "formal and appropriately resourced" independent avenues within the system, to advocate for animals, raise awareness, and facilitate accountability to Parliament.

Petitioner and SAFE chief executive Debra Ashton welcomed the report, and said the system protecting farmed, companion and wild animals was "broken" and failing, due to limited enforcement and accountability.

"Independent oversight could build public trust, it could deliver significantly better outcomes for animals, and it could vastly improve our international reputation," she said.

"The concerns during the coalition government's term have highlighted risks within the current system.

"It's raised questions about industry influence and predetermined outcomes and decisions made by Associate Minister for Agriculture, Andrew Hoggard. And we don't see how that current system will address those concerns."

How could NZ improve its animal welfare system? Let us know: monique.steele@rnz.co.nz

SAFE last year claimed the minister had a conflict of interest, which the prime minister later rejected. But possible conflicts had seen the minister taken off work to finalise the dairy cattle animal welfare code, his office confirmed.

Ashton said she was concerned advice by the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee (NAWAC), regarding the use of farrowing crates in pig farming, had been allegedly undermined by the minister.

NAWAC featured veterinarians and industry leaders, including a senior leader from industry group Federated Farmers - which used to be led by Minister Hoggard, as president, before he became a politician.

Ashton said having an interest in improving animal productivity did not instil confidence that the welfare of animals was being prioritised.

SPCA backs watchdog calls

SPCA senior scientific officer Marie McAninch said New Zealand has watchdog commissioners who represent children and the environment, and can speak on their behalf, but not for the millions of animals.

"We've been calling for that independent oversight, accountability and transparency across the system, so that people can be confident that things are working as they should," she said.

One of six emaciated dogs rescued by Whangārei SPCA inspectors in one month, in 2014. SUPPLIED

A watchdog would be a trusted adviser, McAninch said, separate from existing ministries, and be able to identify any conflicts of interest in the system.

"We suggest that until that's sorted out, then animal welfare topics might continue to be quite contentious and hotly debated where they don't always need to be. And potentially, influenced by lobbying activity."

She was concerned that completing code of animal welfare reviews was prioritised for production animals, over companion animals, with codes for dogs, cats and rabbits all outdated.

NAWAC was "under pressure" with stretched resources, she said, and there could be other ways to increase their independence and function.

"Obviously we've submitted in support of the Commissioner for Animals, but that might not be the only solution," she said.

"One way of increasing independence could be to ringfence that or give them a certain amount of budget or resource."

McAninch said the SPCA received 15,000 public complaints last year, which its 60 funded inspectors responded to.

Decision-makers of 'complex' welfare matters

The Animal Welfare Act 1999 set out New Zealand's legal framework for the prevention of ill treatment of animals. Regulations and animal welfare codes sat within the Act, and the various sector codes set minimum and best practice standards, though they were unenforceable on their own.

NAWAC developed the codes, which were ultimately decided by the minister of agriculture, who is responsible for animal welfare.

Submitters responding to the parliamentary petition included the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) and SPCA, but NAWAC and Minister Andrew Hoggard rejected opportunities to submit on the petition.

NAWAC chairman, Dr Matthew Stone said submitting on the petition was not part of its statutory role.

"When structural considerations or proposals from stakeholders that would have significant political and regulatory dimensions in terms of restructuring or adding new componentry to the animal welfare regulatory system, we considered that a bit beyond our mandate and that's why we didn't participate in that process."

A horse photographed by the SPCA in poor condition. (file photo) Supplied / SPCA

Stone said system improvements could happen by considering system design, how parties worked together, and compliance and enforcement.

"They're complex matters," he said.

"We're striving for optimisation across regulatory systems, so it's hardly surprising that we all recognise the opportunities there are for the animal welfare system to be further optimised."

Hoggard said he did not think it was appropriate to direct NAWAC to take a position on the petition, while it worked steadily on the welfare codes, led by Matthew Stone.

"Getting these codes done well is good for animals, and it gives farmers clarity about what's expected of them. I don't see those two things as being in conflict," he said.

"All the feedback I've heard from people involved is [Matt Stone's] got a very good system in place, in terms of ensuring there's good processes through the meetings to work through and chunk these issues out."

Hoggard said system improvements were already underway within MPI.

"I think there's been some actual good improvements over this term," he said. "I know the previous term, there hadn't been a code passed for quite a while, up until the deer code.

"So we've managed in this term to get the deer code, dairy code. There's been the update for the poultry worked on, rodeo's progressed, sheep and beef's nearly done, pig code is nearly done."

MPI working on improvements

Last year, MPI's inspector-general of regulatory systems - who advised MPI boss Director-General Ray Smith - independently reviewed the animal welfare regulatory system, and found it was "fundamentally sound".

But it identified areas requiring improvement, including governance, stakeholder engagement and performance monitoring.

MPI acting director of animal health and welfare Trish Mead said MPI had started to implement a programme of improvements, following the review.

"MPI brings together the policy, science, and compliance expertise needed to lead the animal welfare system and deliver strong animal welfare outcomes," Mead said.

"MPI accepts the review's recommendations and is using them to further strengthen an already sound system."

Some work underway included a memorandum of understanding and operational agreement signed with SPCA, to provide a clear framework for the two agencies to work together, Mead said.

She said the first cohort of warranted Animal Welfare and NAIT inspectors with animal welfare emergency management training had graduated, which would increase confidence in the system and improve enforcement capability.

The ministry also established a stakeholder forum and approved new reviewers in its Research Testing and Teaching team.

World.title: Scrub fire near Queenstown fully contained, firefighters stand down
World.content:
The scrub fire near Queenstown has been fully contained, with firefighters demobilised on Thursday evening.

The fire has burned at Walter Peak since Tuesday, scorching about 1350 hectares of land.

Fire and Emergency District Commander Blair Kiely said the fireground was being handed back to landowners, after an assessment of conditions and expected weather.

"Some areas may continue to smoulder over the next few days and people may notice smoke," he said.

The exclusion zone for vessels near the Walter Peak shoreline has also been lifted.

A further aerial inspection of the fireground will be carried out on Monday.

World.title: Southland District Council seeks to revoke resource consent for slink skin factory
World.content:
The Southland District Council is fighting in the Environment Court to strip a slink skin factory of its resource consent, arguing repeated breaches have harmed the environment and neighbouring properties.

Da Cheng "Eddie" Zhi and his Tuturau business, NZAgri Development, have been the subject of court orders and legal action by both local and regional authorities over alleged illegal discharges.

Neighbours have complained about offensive smells and piles of carcasses at the factory.

Zhi, who is representing himself in court, has defended his operation.

Six charges brought by the regional council relate to discharges of blood, leachate and/or contaminants to land where they could enter water, and a seventh alleges failure to comply with abatement notices.

The district council has also laid charges and is seeking to revoke the business' resource consent.

At an Environment Court hearing in Invercargill on Thursday, district council lawyer Laura Bielby said this was a significant step.

"This is one of those rare situations that the provision was intended to capture, where significant non-compliance has been both repeated and ongoing and where over a year of formal enforcement action has failed to achieve compliance," she said.

"For district council the compliance issues at the property kicked off in September of last year when council became aware through complaints that thousands of carcasses were piled up at the property and had not been disposed in accordance with the land use consent."

Nearby resident Alyce Perkins told the court her family had struggled with strong odours from the site.

"Physically you're just smelling that all the time. It makes you gag, it gets in your nose and you feel like you're wearing it," she said.

"It affects the way we live in our home. On when days it's smelly you can't open the windows, you wouldn't hang the washing out."

When cross-examining Perkins, Zhi apologised for her experience but questioned whether she could be certain the smell came from his property.

"There is no mistake where the smell is coming from. It is coming from the thousands of carcasses that you have piled up in your yard," Perkins replied.

The Environment Court granted interim enforcement orders on 9 September preventing NZAgri Development from receiving or processing carcasses.

Zhi is separately challenging those orders, arguing his business is being unfairly restricted.

Zhi became emotional in court on Thursday, saying the interim enforcement orders had left his business struggling.

He told the court about workers losing their jobs, unpaid wages and customers who had already paid large sums of money.

"My heart is absolutely shattered. I have had enough. I have really had enough," he said.

World.title: Caucus: National takes aim at coalition partners in scramble for 'soft centre' voters
World.content:
Analysis - What's a right-leaning voter to do?

The past few weeks have seen debates about strategic voting, as polls have consistently placed National below 30 percent and a centre-left bloc, Opportunity permitting, more likely to form a government.

Voters wanting to give the existing coalition the best chance of remaining in power are wracking their brains on where to cast their ballot. Stick, twist or return?

In turn, that means National, New Zealand First and ACT strategists are trying to figure out, not just how to win the "soft centre", but how to steal from each other.

Audio player for " National’s panic and pivot as it tries to win back its fractured base " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics/1795692%2Fcaucus-national-takes-aim-at-coalition-partners-in-scramble-for-soft-centre-voters

National’s panic and pivot as it tries to win back its fractured base Caucus Download MP3 46m

As RNZ deputy political editor Craig McCulloch says in this week's Caucus episode, National wants to fish for voters who will add to the overall centre-right bloc, especially the undecideds (approximately 11 percent in the TVNZ-Verian poll and 6 percent in the RNZ-Reid Research poll) and those who are dallying with Opportunity.

They are the most useful and consequential votes to be won, but with Labour polling as badly as National, and New Zealand First and ACT both polling well by their own standards, the party in blue is in a bind. The soft centre will be hard to crack.

At 25.9 percent in the RNZ poll, National is nearing its humiliating 2020 result of 25.6 percent, just without the leadership changes and pandemic.

Does it behave like a leader of the pack, or does it grab the nearest life-raft and go after traditional National voters who have drifted - or strategically shifted - to its coalition partners?

For example, ACT is on 9 percent in both the TVNZ and RNZ polls. For a party that received 0.5 percent in 2017 and had its best-ever result of 8.6 percent in 2023, it's a strong number.

Eight weeks out from the last election, ACT was on 12 percent. National won back roughly 3 percent from ACT late in that campaign and has to wonder how it can do that again.

Can it also go after Team Winston?

Audio player for " Caucus for 8 October " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics/1795692%2Fcaucus-national-takes-aim-at-coalition-partners-in-scramble-for-soft-centre-voters

Caucus for 8 October Caucus Download MP3 46m

Its medicines policy, released this week, did just that, boldly stomping into ACT and New Zealand First territory, or as political editor Jo Moir says in the podcast: "National is, in an election campaign, trying to pull back the narrative."

National promised a further $604 million for new medicines, significantly increasing Pharmac's buying power. As the associate health minister responsible for Pharmac, ACT leader David Seymour has owned the coalition's funding increases for medicines.

National is trying to claim a greater share of the credit. More controversially, National tied its increased medicines budget to a cut in foreign aid, saying it was "bringing money back from overseas to fund more medicines and cancer screening".

That sort of nationalist jingoism is pure New Zealand First, except in this case, it messes with Winston Peters, because it's taking funds from his sacred foreign affairs budget. Moir says National is gambling on the idea there are "potential National Party voters who are increasingly feeling like things need to be concentrated more domestically then internationally and that, actually, you need to protect your own".

National's willing to gamble because, as McCulloch tells listeners, party figures he's spoken to confess to "a degree of panic and concern at the polls". While they claim their internal polls have National about 30 percent, McCulloch says they admit "this very negative 'no new taxes' strategy is not generating the huge boon or boost for National it is hoping for".

At best, it's weighing down Labour's vote. Labour Party figures fear it's having an effect, which is why it's pushed back this week, calling National liars on taxes and fiscals.

That aligns with what a National Party insider told me. They said the over-the-top claims about Labour's "nine new taxes" and the like had gone beyond clever negative campaigning, and made the party look panicked and weak.

Its key message should be, 'We've got this, the other lot don't'.

National seems to be changing tack. Moir points out that National has suddenly stopped talking about Labour's "nine new taxes" and Luxon hardly mentioned the tax attacks in the TVNZ Leaders' Debate this week.

"That is a fascinating turn around, isn't it?" Moir says. "If you think about the rhetoric and the robotic chanting of no new taxes... for Christopher Luxon to go into that and only mention it once, and not even in as a direct way as it has been, it's a hell of a pivot in terms of strategy."

The polls due out next week will show whether National's pivot bears fruit.

Follow and listen to Caucus with Jo Moir, Craig McCulloch and Tim Watkin on any podcast app.

World.title: NZ First surge extends coalition lead, latest Taxpayers' Union Curia poll shows
World.content:
A new poll shows the coalition has slightly extended its lead over the left bloc thanks to a surge in support for New Zealand First, while both the major parties remain languishing in the twenties.

The Taxpayers' Union Curia poll has National and Labour neck and neck: since its September results, National dropped to 28.5 percent (down 0.5 percentage points), while Labour rose to 28.2 percent (up 2.3).

The Greens dipped slightly to 13.3 percent (down 0.6) while New Zealand First rocketed to 12 percent (up 3.6).

ACT is on 9.2 percent (down 1.3), Opportunity reached 4.8 percent (up 0.3) and Te Pāti Māori has dropped to 1.4 percent (down 0.6).

On these numbers, National, New Zealand First and ACT have a path to power with 65 seats.

However, the left bloc of Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori would have 55 and be unable to form a coalition with Opportunity out of reach of Parliament.

The pollster - which also carries out National's internal party polling - noted due to the margin of error there is a 42 percent chance Opportunity is above the five percent threshold to enter Parliament.

In the preferred Prime Minister stakes, National's Christopher Luxon is unchanged on 21.2 percent, while Labour's Chris Hipkins has leapt 4.1 points to 21 percent.

New Zealand First's Winston Peters is up 3.2 points to 13.9 percent, ACT's David Seymour is down 1.8 points to 6 percent, and the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick is down 2.1 points to 4.9 percent.

World.title: Loafers Lodge fire trial: Survivor recounts rescue from burning building
World.content:
A elderly Loafers Lodge resident says he owes his life to firefighters who rescued him.

The claim comes on the fourth day of the manslaughter trial of four people involved in the operation and maintenance of the building.

Five people died, when a deliberately lit fire ripped through the multi-storey accommodation building in 2023.

John Tepania told the Wellington High Court he woke to the smell of smoke and, looking out the window, could see the shadows of a firetruck's ladder in the carpark on the northern side of the building

He said he tried to leave his top-storey room, but was beaten back by the heat and smoke so thick, he could only see about 10cm in front of him.

"I came out and I couldn't, I couldn't." Tepania said. "I tried three times all together.

"I knew where the steps were, but I thought the bottom might be burnt out. I went back to my room."

Tepania said he considered jumping from his fourth-floor window.

"I thought, 'What do I do? I haven't got much choice here', but then, bang, the door flew open and the fireman was standing at the door.

"If they hadn't come in, I would've been history. I would've been cooked.

"I owe my life to those firemen."

Hayden Moncrieff was that fireman.

He had attended two callouts to the lodge before the fire and had worked on the mezzanine floor of the rearward annex of the building.

On Wednesday, the jury heard that, while firefighters received reports of people trapped on "the mezzanine", the plans they had access to were from 2005.

Those plans pre-dated the addition of the forward mezzanine, where the five victims of the fire - Michael Wahrlich, Melvin Parun, Peter O'Sullivan, Kenneth Barnard and Liam Hockings - all lived.

On hearing reports of people trapped on the mezzanine, Moncrieff headed to the rear of the building, where he'd been before.

"I thought this was the mezzanine referred to on the radio as being the one where the people were trapped," he said. "I realised at this stage that there must be another mezzanine."

Moncrieff and another firefighter made their way up an external staircase to the rearward roof level, and helped four trapped residents into the basket of a ladder appliance working from the VTNZ carpark below.

After scanning the roof for others, he headed back down into the building to keep searching for people.

"The smoke was thick and had lowered to approximately chest height," Moncreiff said. "I found an elderly man... sitting in his room by the window, looking out."

He and another firefighter escorted the man - Tepania - from his room, and led him to the third floor, handing him over to another firefighter, who helped him from the building.

When Moncrieff resumed his search, he found conditions had grown even closer to "flashover", where any burnable material in an area spontaneously combusts.

"I could see that the smoke was starting to flicker," he said. "Sparks could be seen in it.

"This showed that the smoke was going to ignite. It would likely have been fatal for us to have been on the fire floor, when the flashover occurred."

Would up-dated floorplans have saved lives?

Assistant Commander Martin Wilby, who took over command of the scene from SSO Clark Townsley, said - on arriving at about 1am - he saw "jets of flames" from the roof of the building.

He surmised they must have come from sky-lights on a level not shown in the plans available to his fire crews.

Wilby told the jury he doubted the availability of accurate plans would have saved the lives of the five residents, who died in the fire.

"Due to the fire dynamics and the intensity of the fire, the data that we had, while it may not have been indicative of the changes in the buildings, I personally believe it would not have made a difference on the night," he said.

Under further examination from counsel for Greg Mein, Christopher Stevenson KC, Wilby conceded that, on his way to the fire, he had stopped to view the building's plans.

Realising they were not up to date, he requested Wellington City Council bring updated plans to the scene. Those plans arrived at about 2 am.

"We've already heard that time is of the essence and that a fire can double in 30 seconds," Stevenson said. "Save time, save lives, yes?

"The reason you stop is that you want more information about this building. Information is power isn't it?

"It's vital that you know the layout of the building."

Stevenson suggested to Wilby that, given the confusion created by calls from residents saying they were on a mezzanine level that did not correlate with the plans the initial response team had, it was reasonable to expect that correct plans would have assisted their response.

"It would've helped, yes," said Wilby.

Water weight threatens to collapse building.

Wilby described the scene as "chaotic", when he arrived shortly after 1am, and said he encouraged staff in the command unit to calm down.

He told the court he formally took over command of the scene from Clark Townsley at 1.09 am, and he quickly counted up the number of hose lines and appliances operational at the scene.

"I estimated the water was being put into the building at a rate of approximately 9000 litres per minute, but the rate of water exiting the building was far lower than that,

"The building contained within it approximately 250,000 litres

He said he was very concerned about the floors "pancaking", where they collapse one after another, due to the weight of water.

Wilby instructed crews to withdraw from the building and would later learn that, at a similar time, crews fighting the blaze on level three were also about to escape, as fire conditions approached unsurvivable levels.

"I knew that this decision may have altered the number of deceased, but I knew I had to do this to protect my staff," he said.

From the outside, he saw sign of extremely high temperatures, as well as the partial collapse of the mezzanine level near the eastern face of the building on Adelaide Road.

"I made the assessment that the collapse would have been insurvivable [sic]," Wilby said.

A short while later, he would meet two of the accused - McAllister and Murphy - and with their advice, a plan was formulated to retrieve a list of the building's occupant's from Murphy's office on the first floor.

On Wednesday, the court was told the court Townsley had also encountered McAllister and had taken keys to the building from him.

Locked rooms slow searches.

Station officer Joshua Leceve was initially tasked with searching for occupants on the third level, where the fire was situated.

His crew took over attacking the fire, as other teams withdrew, due to exhaustion and low oxygen levels.

"All I could see was a long hallway with lots of smoke. There was almost no visibility."

He made a decision not to break down locked doors along the north hall of level three to focus on pushing toward the fire source.

"The situation was deteriorating," Leceve said. "We were making good progress down the hallway on our hands and knees."

At one point, Leceve stood up to get his bearings.

"To my surprise, I felt the ceiling just above my head. When I touched the ceiling I felt heat through my glove and had to pull my hand away."

He told the court this and smoke emanating from the walls around him were clear signs the building was becoming structurally unsafe, and temperatures were nearing flashover.

He told his crew to withdraw and they left the fire floor, leaving their hose in their haste.

After a brief rest and replenishing his air supply, Leceve returned to the second level of the building, using a sledgehammer to smash his way past locked doors, but finding no-one.

Counsel for the prosecution Grant Burston asked Leceve if, had he known master keys to the building had been surrendered to firefighters, he would have used them in his search.

World.title: Kai Allen shines as Ford gets engine change for Bathurst
World.content:
Kai Allen has fired the first warning shot ahead of Sunday's Bathurst 1000 with the fastest time across today's two practice sessions.

In perfect conditions at Mount Panorama, Allen topped the time sheets in the first practice session of the weekend with a time of 2:05.5460, more than three-tenths better than the next fastest.

The blistering time for Allen, who drives a Ford for Grove Racing, comes after Supercars confirmed the engine in all Ford competitors would be changed for this weekend.

Bathurst 1000: How to watch, race start time and weather forecast Here is what you need to know about this weekend's Bathurst 1000, including when the race begins and how you can follow the action.

Barometric pressure testing before last year's Bathurst 1000, and again before this weekend, found the Ford engine lost power at high altitude.

A change to the engine, developed by Triple Eight Race Engineering, which is Ford's homologation team, has been approved by Supercars to level the playing field this weekend.

There will be no change to the Toyota or GM (Chevrolet) engines.

"As you're aware, Supercars have conducted Barometric engine testing over the last 12 months and recently completed a further test," a note to teams read.

"The results of this test have been provided to the Homologation Teams following which consultation has taken place.

"The testing has identified a power loss on the Ford at lower Barometric pressure and as such Supercars have approved a change of ESD developed by the Ford Homologation team to correct this for the Bathurst event only."

Six of the top 10 cars from Thursday's first session were Fords, with Chevrolets making up the other four spots, including PremiAir's Jayden Ojeda who was second fastest with a 2:05.8737.

The fastest Toyota belonged to reigning Supercars champion Chaz Mostert who was 17th fastest for the number 1 Walkinshaw TWG Racing.

While Allen shone, it was not all smooth sailing for Grove Racing with Matthew Payne, last year's Bathurst 1000 winner, being called in early after his team found power steering fluid on the garage floor.

Lochie Dalton, driving for the Chevrolet number 99 Erebus Motorsport, topped the co-drivers practice session later on Thursday with a 2:05.874.

Again, only Fords and Chevrolets were in the top 10. Again, Walkinshaw TWG Racing's number 1 was the fastest Toyota, with co-driver Fabian Coulthard at the wheel.

There will be two more practice sessions on Friday ahead of qualifying.

World.title: Dropped Aussie opener out of Sheffield Shield match with concussion
World.content:
Jake Weatherald's wretched run has continued, with the discarded Test opener forced out of the start of the domestic cricket season with concussion.

Weatherald was subbed out of South Australia's opening game against Victoria at Junction Oval on Thursday, before the start of day two.

He crashed into the picket fence while chasing the ball on Wednesday during Victoria's first innings.

Weatherald then faced only faced six balls at the end of day one before Victorian debutant Harry Hoekstra had him caught behind for a duck.

It is understood Weatherald had delayed symptoms, prompting the decision on Thursday morning to take him out of the game.

Matthew Gilkes took Weatherald's place in the SA line-up.

Weatherald was dropped from the Test team in August after their shock first-Test loss to Bangladesh in Darwin.

Hoekstra also top-scored with 45 at number nine as Victoria rallied to reach 244 in their first innings.

South Australia resumed at 1-4 and were 5-185 approaching tea.

Opener Henry Hunt made 71 before David Moody bowled him in a crucial breakthrough for the fourth wicket.

Jake Lehmann was 52 not out and Hoekstra had continued his fine debut with three wickets.

AAP

World.title: 'Live on forever': Brock inspires Bathurst 20 years on
World.content:
Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.

It is just that this year's Great Race feels a bit more special, with Australian motorsport marking 20 years since the nine-time Mount Panorama conqueror's tragic death.

A long-time protege of Brock, seven-time Bathurst 1000 winner Lowndes will line up for his 33rd bid at claiming the holy grail of Australian motorsport.

Bathurst 1000: How to watch, race start time and weather forecast Here is what you need to know about this weekend's Bathurst 1000, including when the race begins and how you can follow the action.

The 52-year-old will share the number 15 Team 18 wildcard with Super2 racer Bayley Hall after Triple Eight Racing Engineering ditched Chevrolet for Ford last year.

Lowndes has paired with rookies since former Triple Eight teammate Jamie Whincup's retirement in 2021, a move that helps the three-time Supercars champion pass on Brock's legacy.

"I'm somewhat gone full circle," Lowndes said today.

"Bayley, we did a track walk the other day, and I literally recalled everything that Peter taught me; from Turn 1, from Hell Corner, all the way around to Murray's Corner.

"For me, I'm hopefully passing on that legacy in some way … it is a milestone year. There's no doubt about that."

Peter Brock, pictured in 2004, won the Bathurst 1000 a record nine times. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Ask Lowndes what he remembers of Brock's counsel, and he will condense his knowledge of the track's 23 corners into a minute: advice like doing all your braking over Skyline or looking for the kink on the inside of the Elbow for your turn-in point.

"Peter was more than just a teammate," Lowndes said.

"His legacy will live on forever. He was bigger than the sport in some regards.

"He was just very much a person that could capture people's attention, hold their attention, but also inspire them for greatness.

"Those are the parts that I miss 20 years on."

Just weeks after Brock died in 2006, Lowndes roared to an emotional Bathurst 1000 win with an up-and-coming Jamie Whincup to pay tribute to his great mate.

Just weeks after Peter Brock's death, Craig Lowndes (left) and Jamie Whincup won the Bathurst 1000 in 2006. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Mark Horsburgh)

"History shows that the gap at the end of the day was 0.5, and that was Brock's number for a long time," Lowndes said.

Whincup added: "The minute's silence, I'll never forget that."

"You generally got someone on the hill yell out or whatnot, but that day, even the birds stopped chirping.

"It was my first (Bathurst) win for the team and a memory that I'll take to the grave."

Seven-time champion Whincup won't be on the grid for the first time since his 2002 debut, making way for Nick Percat to link up with title contender Broc Feeney, and allowing him to focus on his duties as Triple Eight team principal.

Feeney and Percat will be smarting after a horror outing at last month's The Bend 500, finishing 24th out of 26 cars at the Bathurst 1000 curtain-raiser.

The Triple Eight star has never won the 1,000km epic and is second in the standings behind last year's race winner and Grove Racing star Matt Payne.

World.title: NZ Rugby goes to court over PNG 'Chiefs' name
World.content:
Rugby union officials have launched New Zealand High Court proceedings to prevent the National Rugby League's (NRL) new Papua New Guinea-based franchise from using the "Chiefs" name in New Zealand.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) said the move was an effort to protect the brand of the Waikato-based Chiefs, who have played in the Super Rugby competition across Australasia since rugby union turned professional in 1996.

The NRL, which is Australia-based but has one team in the New Zealand city of Auckland, announced the expansion of the league to Papua New Guinea in 2024.

The island nation's Prime Minister James Marape unveiled the name "Chiefs" the following year.

James Marape (front, second from right) announced the PNG Chiefs' name in October 2025. (Supplied: NRL)

NZR said attempts to engage the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) over the issue had been unsuccessful and it was seeking an interim and final injunction against the use of the name before the Papua New Guinea team was officially launched later this month.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said in a statement today.

"We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand."

Action branded 'hypocritical'

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys said the complaint was hypocritical given the New South Wales rugby league team had used the "Blues" brand for more than half a century before the Auckland Blues Super Rugby franchise was launched 30 years ago.

"We will defend this vigorously," he said.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

Super Rugby Chiefs chief executive Simon Graafhuis told Pacific Beat that he was confident of a resolution, adding that he would prefer the NRL team to change its name.

"Peter V'landys is the head honcho [and] is pretty adamant he's not going to do that. IP law is pretty clear. I think we're on pretty solid ground. So it could be an interesting ride," he said.

"We're open to working with them [the NRL]. This is all about protecting our brand that's taken 30 years to generate value and that's what's important to us at this stage.

"This week we had a request from a funeral celebrant to see if our logo could be used on a headstone. It's just a reminder of what it actually means to our community and yeah, absolutely worth fighting for."

Mr Graafhuis said a drastically different colour scheme would not be enough to satisfy the club that the PNG team was not infringing on its name and trademark.

"I suppose it'll come down to the courts, won't it? The longer this goes on, the higher the costs, but also the bigger the damages. So, hopefully we're all keen to avoid that one," he said.

IP Australia, the government agency that administers rights to trademarks, has examined the PNG Chiefs' case and given it an initial acceptance, triggering an "opposition period".

Any party that opposes the application has two months to lodge an appeal.

Rugby league split from rugby union in the late 19th century in a dispute about amateurism.

PNG Chiefs face 'danger of brand confusion' over team name Australia's intellectual property agency tells PNG's rugby league franchise that its chosen name, the Chiefs, risks being confused with the name of a Super Rugby club.

While union is the more popular game globally, league rules the roost on Australia's eastern seaboard and has been making great strides in New Zealand.

Papua New Guinea is the only country in the world where rugby league is the most popular sport.

The new team has already signed a slew of top NRL players ahead of its first season in 2028, and will be backed by hundreds of millions of dollars in funding from the Australian government, which is looking to shore up its influence in the Pacific Islands.

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific," Mr Lancaster said.

"We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."

The ABC has contacted IP Australia and Mr Lancaster for comment.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Amateur players' chance to win $1m against pros returns to Australian Open
World.content:
The Australian Open's 1 Point Slam will again have some star power in January with Carlos Alcaraz, Coco Gauff, Naomi Osaka and Jannik Sinner among the players set to compete against pros and amateur qualifiers for a $1 million prize.

At the Australian Open launch today, organisers said qualifying events for the 1 Point Slam are underway at clubs across the country, and a further two days of qualifying will be held during opening week ahead of the first grand slam tournament of the year from January 17 to 31.

The 1 Point Slam final will see the pros competing against amateurs and wild cards for the prize at Rod Laver Arena on January 13.

Jordan Smith, a little-known local amateur player, beat Sinner and went on to make himself a millionaire after winning the 1 Point Slam last January.

Smith won on the third stroke of the final when Joanna Garland, the women's number 117 from Taiwan, sent a two-handed backhand wide.

Jordan Smith cashes in Jordan Smith comes from a tennis-mad family in Sydney and is now a millionaire thanks to a couple of days' work at the Australian Open.

All the matches lasted just one single point in a knockout bracket that included men and women, professionals and amateurs, plus celebrities such as Taiwanese pop star Jay Chou, who was knocked out without hitting a ball after an ace from Petar Jovic.

"At the heart of the creation of the 1 Point Slam is our desire to even more deeply connect the Australian Open to every tennis community in the country," Andrew Abdo, Tennis Australia's new chief executive, said.

More than 1.3 million fans attended the 2026 Australian Open, and organisers are planning to increase viewing capacity, seating and offer more shade across the Melbourne Park precinct next year.

AP

World.title: Wallabies resist urge to shift Suaalii from wing for Bledisloe Cup Test
World.content:
The Wallabies have kept Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the wing for Saturday night's Bledisloe Cup Test at Auckland's Eden Park, with Isaac Henry named in the centres.

Henry has been included at outside centre to partner Len Ikitau in the Wallabies' midfield against the All Blacks.

Ikitau, who has recovered from an ankle injury, moves from outside to inside centre in the wake of Hunter Paisami's suspension.

Wallabies upset Boks in Perth The Wallabies manage to overcome four late yellow cards to defeat world champions South Africa 42-38 in a pulsating Test in Perth.

Wallabies coach Les Kiss resisted the temptation to shift Suaalii from the wing back to the centres.

He has shown faith in 27-year-old Henry, who he coached at the Queensland Reds.

Kiss also handed Henry his Test debut two months ago, against Japan in Osaka.

Henry, who will be playing his fifth Test, is the only change to the Wallabies' starting XV following their stunning 42-38 win over world champions South Africa in Perth late last month.

The Wallabies made four changes on the reserves bench, opting for a 5-3 (forwards-back split).

Hooker Josh Nasser, prop Massimo De Lutiis, back-rower Nick Champion de Crespigny and fly half Declan Meredith earned call-ups.

De Lutiis and Champion de Crespigny are the respective replacements for Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper, who have returned to their European clubs.

Isaac Henry will wear the number 13 jersey against the All Blacks. (Getty Images: Paul Miller)

"Keeping consistency in the starting side gives us a solid foundation, while adding some freshness on the bench will provide energy late in the game," Kiss said in a statement.

The Wallabies have enjoyed a six-match unbeaten streak after beginning the Test season with defeats to Ireland and France in the Nations Championship.

Since Kiss took over from Joe Schmidt as coach, the Wallabies have recorded four wins and a draw.

But the All Blacks pose an almighty challenge, especially at Eden Park.

The Wallabies have lost 24 consecutive Tests against the All Blacks at the venue, with their most recent victory coming in 1986.

They did, however, beat Wales at Eden Park in the third-place play-off at the 2011 Rugby World Cup.

"There aren't many tougher challenges than playing New Zealand at Eden Park, but it's one we're excited by and know that we will need to be at our best in all aspects of our game," Kiss said.

Damian McKenzie will start at fly half for the All Blacks. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

Meanwhile, injury has forced the All Blacks to name Damian McKenzie at fly half as they look to maintain their stranglehold on the Bledisloe Cup.

McKenzie will start at 10 after Ruben Love (ankle) and Richie Mo'unga (calf) were ruled out.

Beauden Barrett will play fullback, with McKenzie having held down the role for all four Tests in the All Blacks' recent 3-1 series loss to the Springboks.

All three Barrett brothers will start against the Wallabies, with ex-captain Scott named at lock and Jordie slotting in the backline at inside centre.

The All Blacks have held the Bledisloe Cup since 2003.

Wallabies squad (1-15): Angus Bell, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Allan Alaalatoa, Jeremy Williams, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Rob Valetini, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson (C), Ryan Lonergan, Ben Donaldson, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Len Ikitau, Isaac Henry, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright

Replacements: Josh Nasser, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Lachlan Shaw, Nick Champion de Crespigny, Tate McDermott, Declan Meredith, Harry Potter

All Blacks squad (1-15): Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor (C), Fletcher Newell, Scott Barrett, Josh Lord, Tupou Vaa'i, Peter Lakai, Wallace Sititi, Cam Roigard, Damian McKenzie, Leroy Carter, Jordie Barrett, Quinn Tupaea, Will Jordan, Beauden Barrett

Replacements: Asafo Aumua, George Bower, Pasilio Tosi, Shannon Frizell, Anton Segner. Kyle Preston, Rieko Ioane, Josh Moorby

World.title: Roosters lose fifth NRL premiership player as Leniu joins Eels
World.content:
Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

Leniu finished his three-year stint at the Tricolours on a high after a stellar performance in the 19-18 win over Newcastle to secure the 2026 trophy.

The NSW Origin representative added the Roosters' premiership ring to the three he won with Penrith between 2021 and 2023.

Leniu was granted a release from the final year of his Roosters contract, which will give the club some salary cap reprieve.

Whyte primed to be even better following GF win Naufahu Whyte wouldn't have looked out of place should he have won the Clive Churchill Medal after the Roosters' grand final victory, and the Tricolours prop is adamant we have yet to see his best.

The hard-hitting forward's Eels contract is reportedly worth more than the $850,000 a year he was making with Easts, where he spent much of his time coming off the bench.

He is expected to play a more active role in blue and gold, leading the line for the Eels' forward pack.

The move will see the former Panther reunite with good friend Jarome Luai, but first the pair will both suit up for Toa Samoa at the Rugby League World Cup.

Earlier, the Roosters announced that the 26-year-old had been granted an immediate release from the final year of his contract, allowing him to join Parramatta.

From the premiership line-up, Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase are rugby-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans is joining Hull FC, while Daniel Tupou has retired this week after his 307-game career.

Connor Watson, who missed the title decider due to concussion, has signed for a season with St George Illawarra Dragons.

With his exit announced at the Roosters' awards night on Wednesday, Leniu said he would leave the club on a high.

"I'm proud to have worn the Roosters jersey, and I'll always have a lot of love and respect for the club, the boys and everyone who has supported me during my time here," Leniu said.

"Winning a premiership with this group and sharing that with the boys, our families and everyone at the club is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life."

AAP

World.title: Sally 'couldn't run to the mailbox'. Now she tackles ultramarathons
World.content:
Sally Beggs has been running for 10 hours.

Traversing tough terrain since 6am, it's now late afternoon, and the downhill course allows her to pick up speed.

"This race owes no-one anything," she tells herself.

"No dilly dallying; I'm not allowed to stop for photos. Stop for nothing. Just keep going as fast as you can."

Beggs is competing in the Grampians Peaks Trail 50-kilometre ultramarathon, and is on her way to cross the finish line in a personal best time of 10 hours and 24 minutes.

Sally Beggs says running has helped her make changes to her lifestyle. (ABC: Tony Hill)

Chasing a runner's high wasn't how Beggs imagined life would look in her 50s, but she, like more and more Australians, has made heading off the beaten track for hours on end her sport of choice.

Beggs says when her interest in running began, she "couldn't even run to the mailbox".

"My sister phoned me up and said, 'Sal, come and run a half marathon'. I actually had a cigarette in one hand and a drink in the other," she tells ABC iview's Back Roads.

Unfit and overwhelmed by small decisions, Beggs took to running laps of the paddocks on her family's wool farm in regional Victoria to help escape the "craziness of the world".

Now, she runs 50 kilometres on race day.

The GPT 100 is the main event and is 100 miles or about 160 kilometres long. (ABC iview: Back Roads)

An ultramarathon, or ultra, is any running race longer than a regular marathon's 42.2 kilometres. Trail runs use forest and hiking tracks rather than the road.

Ultra events and trail running are seeing more sell-out events, larger participant numbers and greater diversity in entrants, according to president of the Australian Ultra and Trail Running Association (AUTRA) John Claridge.

"While the sport has traditionally attracted runners in their 30s and 40s, we're seeing increasing numbers of younger adults looking for experiences beyond road running, alongside older runners who value the variety of terrain and the social nature of trail events," he says.

Loading...

There are events of varying lengths, from short introductory runs to the longest ultras, which exceed 300 kilometres and take days to complete.

Claridge says this means there's something for all runners.

"We're seeing increasing participation across different ages, abilities and backgrounds, which is helping to build a stronger and more inclusive community," he says.

Unlike many sports, trail and ultra running is said to be as much about the journey as the result.

"Every course is different, with changing terrain, weather and conditions, so success is often defined by completing a personal challenge rather than simply achieving a placing," Claridge says.

A sense of adventure

The Grampians Peaks Trail 100 Miler is right on Beggs's doorstep.

Grampians Peaks Trail 100 miler is not the faint-hearted. (ABC iview: Back Roads)

It's one of more than 100 organised ultra-marathon events held across the country annually and is recognised as one of 10 World Trail Major events, alongside races in Canada, the USA, Japan, Spain and South Africa.

Hosting races of varying distances, the event traverses Gariwerd/Grampians National Park from Mt Zero to Dunkeld, over tough terrain and often through tumultuous weather.

The main event, the 100 miler, features 7,700 metres of elevation and is completed over four days.

The 50-kilometre event is Beggs's race of choice, and it's the beauty of the outdoors that keeps her coming back for more.

Ultramarathons offer races across all kinds of terrain. (ABC New England: Matt Bedford)

"I just love being in nature. I love all the surprises that you get. You never know what you're going to see," she says.

Claridge says this strong connection with Australia's landscape draws people in.

"People are increasingly looking for experiences that combine physical activity with time outdoors and a sense of adventure," he says.

It's a sense of adventure that John Claridge says is increasing the sport's popularity. (Supplied: GPT 100)

Camaraderie alongside competition

Halls Gap police officer Greg Kew and his wife Nicole are self-proclaimed running addicts.

They serve as each other's support crew and travel the world to participate in ultra marathons.

"People go out for cake and coffee on a date. We go running," Greg Kew says.

In the 2025 Grampians Peaks Trail 100 miler, they ran for almost 44 hours through wild weather and bitter cold.

Greg and Nicole Kew met through the running community.

But on the trails, Greg Kew says people look out for each other and are mindful of the landscape.

The couple are active members of the ultra and trail-running community and volunteer at local events.

Claridge says members like the Kews help foster the sport's strong camaraderie between competitors.

"While people challenge themselves individually, the culture of the sport is notably supportive, and that sense of belonging is something many participants talk about," he says.

Women are finding new ways to move and connect outdoors A growing number of women say they want community, physical activity and time outdoors — just without the gasps for air that come with trying to chat mid-run.

Not to mention the health benefits of being active. For Beggs, this has helped her kick old habits.

"I've quit smoking. I used to drink a lot, and now I don't," she says.

"I feel like I'm setting a better example to my boys, and I just find that it just brings me such enormous pleasure. It's a way that I recharge."

Stream Back Roads free on ABC iview or watch Thursdays at 8pm on ABC TV.

Tech.title: GTA VI leaks continue with a lengthy (and very nude) gameplay video
Tech.content:
The GTA VI leaks keep coming — and the latest is almost as long as the game’s official “extended look” on Netflix. Only instead of showing off all the various gameplay details, this one is more of an “extended look” at Jason running around Vice City naked. As Kotaku reports, GTA leaker Cyberleek, who cashed out on a memecoin and seemingly disappeared earlier this year, is back with a new 25-minute video of GTA VI gameplay.

The video suggests players will be able to play through GTA VI with their characters completely unclothed. According to Kotaku, Jason is naked throughout almost the whole video, including while on a motorbike, “at a beach-side coffee store,” and while talking to other characters. Lucia is also mostly naked in a clip at the end of the video, where Cyberleek reportedly briefly shows her from behind.

Some of the leaked footage appears to include light story spoilers, with Kotaku noting that the video opens with a cutscene of Jason and Lucia leading into a dirt bike race for one of the game’s scripted missions. Cyberleek goes on to show some first-person driving footage from Jason, followed by a street race. Kotaku also says Cyberleek “seemingly conjures a tank out of the air” and, of course, uses the video to advertise a crypto coin.

Tech.title: Hands-on with Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 12 Pro and its wild new matte display
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon’s Fire tablets are notable for being dirt cheap. While they’re great for kids, they don’t offer a premium Android tablet experience. The company’s new $499 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is an attempt to build a device someone might actually want to use. It’s one of a few new Android tablets Amazon announced today, and it’s the one you need to know about.

Unlike the Fire Tablet lineup, the Alexa Tablet doesn’t run some hobbled version of Android stuck with Amazon’s app store with ads for Amazon services at every turn. It has full access to the Google Play app store. It’s powered by 8GB or 12GB of RAM with a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 8-core CPU. That’s more than enough for light gaming, powering Alexa, and running basic apps, but don’t expect Alien: Isolation to run super smoothly. The aluminum unibody feels great. It’s light at 550 grams (1.2 pounds), but not flimsy. It’s slightly lighter than the 13-inch iPad Air (617 grams) but heavier than the 11-inch (465 grams).

The screen is the truly exciting thing about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. The $549.99 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro has a 12.3-inch 3:2 display that can be configured with Corning’s Nanomatte tech, similar to Apple’s nano-texture, which reduces glare and gives the screen a more paper-like feel.

The difference between the Nanomatte display and the standard glossy one is dramatic. Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

It’s impossible to do it justice in photos or video. The Nanomatte coating doesn’t simply reduce glare; it almost completely eliminates it. Amazon held a briefing in a brightly sunlit room, and I thought the 12 Pro was a dummy unit when I first saw it. It looked like a cardboard placeholder image was placed inside. Then an Amazon rep started swiping around the screen.

There’s also a standard glossy option, and the difference is shocking. In the bright sunlight of the room, the glossy screen was basically a mirror and was easily washed out when viewed at an angle. The Nanomatte display, however, was clearly readable at any angle and barely reflected any ambient light. Only at extreme angles in the brightest patches of light did it become difficult to see.

The screen pairs particularly well with the immersive Kindle mode. Here, background activities are limited, notifications are silenced, and blue light is lowered to reduce eye strain. There are three different Kindle-specific display modes. Standard delivers the full vibrancy of the screen; Color offers a softer, more muted experience; and Ink is full grayscale. In Kindle mode, battery life is also extended from 16 hours to 20 hours.

Without having the two side-by-side, it’s hard to say how it compares to Apple’s matte display on the iPad Pro, but anecdotally it seems to retain slightly more contrast. Using a stylus with it is much more pleasant than on a glossy display, but I can’t say I noticed a difference between it and an iPad.

The Alexa Tablet Pro Pen and Pro Keyboard attach magnetically and seem serviceable enough. I wouldn’t want to type on its shallow, cramped keys all day, but they’re fine for knocking out a few emails. The keyboard case was a little clunky to get on and off, though. It’s actually two parts — the back cover and stand are separate from the keyboard base.

Alexa Everywhere

Go ahead, ask Alexa. I dare you. I double dare you. Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

The tablet shoves Alexa down your throat at every turn. In the bottom right-hand corner is an “Ask Alexa” bar that lets you quickly chat with the AI assistant. And in the top left-hand corner is what Amazon calls the Dynamic Tab. It offers up proactive suggestions from Alexa. That can be something as simple as picking up where you left off in a book or movie, or offering an itinerary for a three-day trip to New York. This is, of course, powered by Amazon’s deep well of information it gathers from your reading, viewing, and shopping habits.

Amazon keeps some of Alexa’s more invasive features off by default. On-Screen Intelligence, which can see what you’re doing and take actions based on what’s actually on your screen, is strictly opt-in. There are also robust controls for limiting what Alexa can hear and remember.

If you do opt in, though, Alexa becomes a pretty powerful shopping companion. I was able to open random photos from the internet and ask Alexa to find me something in them, like a coffee table or a mirror, and, even if it couldn’t track down the exact thing, it found something close. Then it would add it to my Amazon cart if I asked. How likely am I to ask Alexa to track down a bathroom fixture for me from a Pinterest photo and deliver it to my house in two days via Prime? Not very. I’m also unlikely to have it automatically add school holidays to my calendar from the Department of Education site, but it will if you ask it to.

Previous Next

















1 / 10 The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is the company’s first proper Android tablet. Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $499.99, but you’ll have to shell out at least $549.99 for the Nanomatte model. If you want to tack on the keyboard case and the Pro Pen, that will be an additional $149.99 and $89.99, respectively.

Amazon also announced two smaller models that lack the Nanomatte screen options. The Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $329.99, while the Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $229.99. Those come in more fun colorways, including rosette and matcha, in addition to the drab but functional graphite of the Tablet 12 Pro.

Tech.title: Amazon’s Alexa Tablets are coming for the iPad
Tech.content:
Amazon is launching a new lineup of tablets that bear almost no resemblance to any tablet Amazon has ever launched before. They’re not even called Fire, the name Amazon has used for its tablets for the last 15 years. They’re called Alexa Tablets, and they’re designed to do two things: bring Alexa Plus to the center of your whole computing life, and be straight-up excellent tablets.

The most important thing about these new tablets’ software? They run Android. Full, Google Play-supported, all-the-apps Android. There are plenty of preloaded Amazon apps, of course, and some built-in ways to quickly access Prime Video content or shop for basically anything anywhere at any time, but it’s finally offering a proper Android experience. Panos Panay, Amazon’s SVP in charge of all things hardware and Alexa, tells me that “Google Play was a necessity, end of story.”

But Panay picked Android as the second most important thing about the Alexa Tablet. The first, he says, is the hardware. The Alexa Tablet is two and a half years in the making, Panay says, and he directed the team to start completely fresh in their tablet design. “Start from zero, don’t use any components we’ve ever used,” he says he told them. “Just ask, what is it? What is a great piece of hardware and what is it supposed to do?”

The three flavors of Alexa Tablet. Image: Amazon

There are three devices in the Alexa Tablet lineup, all of which go on sale October 14th. The Tablet 8 has an 8.7-inch screen, starts at $229.99, and seems mostly designed for reading; the Tablet 11 has an 11-inch screen, starts at $329.99, and is more for watching stuff. They’re aimed squarely at the iPad Mini and base iPad, and seem nice enough. But the biggest device in the lineup, the one Panay really wants to tell me about, is the one he thinks really shows off what Amazon is doing here.

It’s called the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, and it starts at $499. It’s 6.5mm thick and weighs 550 grams — a little thicker and a little lighter than the latest 13-inch iPad Pro — and comes with either 8 or 16 gigs of RAM and either 128 or 256 gigs of storage. It runs a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor, a chip you might have found in a high-end phone a year or so ago. All these specs are… fine. Good enough to run an Android tablet, but nothing to write home about.

The feature that really matters, Panay says, is the screen. Panay has this concept of the “one thing,” a single feature on a product that absolutely cannot be compromised on, no matter what. Make tradeoffs where you need to, he tells his team, but not on the one thing. “And the one thing on this product was, let’s go make the perfect screen.”

That screen is a 12.5-inch, 2800 x 1840 display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz and 500 nits of brightness. Its 3:2 aspect ratio, Panay says, is perfect for running two Android apps side by side. And on the most expensive, $549 model Alexa Tablet, the screen comes with what Amazon calls a Nanomatte display. The company partnered with Corning to actually etch a unique texture into the glass itself that is meant to be richer, higher contrast, and less prone to glare than a typical display. The process sounds similar to Apple’s excellent nano-texture finishes, but Amazon seems to believe its method comes with even fewer tradeoffs in contrast and sharpness. I haven’t seen the device in person yet, but The Verge’s Terrence O’Brien has, and it sounds like it has a chance to be as good as advertised.

Add the attachments, squint a little, and it’s an iPad Pro.

The screen also adapts to what you’re doing on the tablet. If you launch the Kindle app, it turns off blue lights to make the reading experience warmer and more serene; if you start reading comics, it’ll render them extra glossy. Amazon understands well that tablets are primarily consumption devices — and the company is very happy to optimize for your time in Kindle and Prime Video.

The Alexa Tablet isn’t just for watching and reading, though. Amazon also made a keyboard case and a stylus, and Panay says he hopes people will use it as a secondary or even primary computer. He also hopes you’ll use it to do Alexa things. Amazon has been working on the LLM-powered version of its assistant for the last few years, and believes Alexa Plus can be more than just a smart home assistant. (Our testing suggests… otherwise.) You’ll be able to ask Alexa about anything you see on the screen, and the chatbot will try to offer recommendations, find information, and, of course, try to sell you anything it can find on Amazon.com. On these devices, Alexa Plus appears to be nearly as pervasive as Gemini or Siri on other tablets, and that’s precisely the point.

It has always made sense for Amazon to make tablets. But for so many years, the company that has seemed to be happy to simply make everything as cheap as possible in the hopes you’ll
